The appellant was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The foodgrains found in his possession were also ordered to be forfeited to the State. The appellant appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge, Santhal Parganas, Dumka and his revision in the High Court was summarily dismissed. The defence of the appellant was that he was an agriculturist and that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands he had taken on lease from various parties. He produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother were in possession of 80 90 bighas of land on which Paddy and other foodgrains found therein. The documentary evidence consisted of certain lease deeds executed byhim and his brothers in favour of the lessors. Oral evidence showed that he had stored foodgrains above the permitted quantities for a wholesale dealer, but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, he was regarded as a wholesale trader within the meaning of section 49 of the Registration Act. The learned Magistrate rejected the defence of appellant on the ground that the presumption under paragraph 3(2) could not be drawn. He held that the lease deeds were not registered and were not admissible in evidence under section 49. On appeal, the High court set aside the order of forfeiture. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the appellant had successfully proved that he is an agriculturist. Held, that the words "carrying on the business" in the context of the Act postulate a course of conduct and continuity of transactions. Therulingmaynof be applicable in certain circumstances as for example where even a single transaction can be demonstrated to be in the course of business. But in the present case, the presumption Under section 3(1) could ,not be drawn, because the presumption was not drawn, but it is easy to see that the evidence which was 'brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. The total circumstances in the case show that the accused was in fact carrying on agricultural ,operations. He executed a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. In his case, therefore, the presumed under para 3(3) could be drawn and not the presumption against him. The presumption under section 4 of the Essential Commodities Act was not based upon them.

The defendant was a monthly tenant in respect of the premises in suit. The plaintiff respondent claimed that he was a tenant from month to month under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, and that the tenancy was determined by a notice to quit. The trial judge held that the defendant was not a tenant on the ground that the rent was paid, and consequently the defendant ceased to be a tenant. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the District Judge and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the respondent had become a tenant by virtue of section 116 Of the Transfer o f Property Act and that by reason of the payment of rent on 8th March, 1925 he became a tenant under section 106 of the TP Act. Held, further, that the High court was not right in holding that the suit was one for ejectment of a lessee on the expiration of the period provided for in the lease. The High Court was clearly wrong in holding so because it held that by payment and acceptance of rent a new tenancy was created by payment, acceptance of rents from him in the year 1925, and after 1926 the defendant continued to be tenant from day to month. It was not open to the High ' Court to hold that on the facts of this case it would be quite proper to hold whether the respondent was a mere monthly tenant under the plaintiff in respect o the premises. The only question left open was whether payment to the Receiver amounted to payment to him himself.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. S.K. Industries, was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1961 by the Income Tax Officer, Delhi. The appellant filed an application before the Commissioner for permission to produce documents relating to assessment years 1964 65 onwards, and including year 1961 62 in proceedings for the said assessment years taking place under the 1961 Act. The Commissioner rejected the application on the ground that the disclosure of information respecting assessees had no relationship to the power of the court to summon a record from the income tax authorities after April 1, 1964, and authorised the Commissioner to furnish or cause to be furnished the sought for information. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected his application holding that the omission of Section 137 did not make any difference and that the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under Section 138(1)(b) had no relation to the powers of the Income tax Officer to furnish the sought information asked for on being satisfied that there were no circumstances justifying its refusal. The High Court, however, held that the failure of the legislature to provide that no document from the assessment record should be produced in a court on being summoned by it without the approval of the commissioner of Income Tax, was not an impediment left in the way of a civil suit to summon the production of documents filed by an assessee before the income Tax authorities after March 1,1964. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The omission of section 137 did make any distinction and that it was restricted to the cases where the information sought for therein was called for by any person other than a court of law on summons for their production being issued by the court and that there was no longer any impediment left with the authority to furnish such information. [560G] (2) The finality attached thereto is, thus, limited to the matters where the document from which the information etc. as contemplated by the Section is called for. [561F] (3) The effect of introduction of Section 138 (1)(a) of the 1961 act was that it entitled a person to make an application to the Commissioner in the prescribed form for any information relating to any assessee in respect of any assessment made either under the 1922 Act or under the1961 Act on or after April1, 1964.

The appellant was a minor and the respondent was married to Seinaba on April 7, 1944. The gift was made by Mammotty to his minor wife. On May 3, 1946, the father of the respondent gifted his properties including immovable property to Seinsaba on June 4, 1944 by a registered deed. Mammotsty died soon afterwards on February 25, 1947. After the death of Mammosty, the appellant and her mother filed a suit for partition of the properties in their possession. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the gift was not valid must be accepted on behalf of the appellant. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the appellant had made a gift to Sewinaba but to her mother, the first appellant and she accepted the gift on behalf Of her minor wife and that even a change in the mode of enjoyment was sufficient evidence of such an intention. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf the appellant that the High court erred in holding that neither express acceptance nor transfer of possession is necessary for the completion of a gift when the donor is himself the guardian or the de facto guardian or 'quasi guardian ' provided there is a real and bona fide intention on the part of the father to transfer the ownership of the subject matter of the gift to the donee. HELD: (1) The gift by a husband to his wife, being an infant, was completed ordinarily by the acceptance of the guardian of his property under the Muhammadan Law, that is to say, by handing over the deed to his mother in law and accepted by her on behalf. [560 G] (2) The intention to make the gift is clear and manifest because it was made at a deed which was registered and handed over by Mammanotty, to his father, was accepted by his mother on behalf, of the minor. There can be no question that there was a complete intention to divest ownership on the ground of the mother or of other near relative or even a stranger.

The respondent temple was a religious institution. The State Government issued a notification under section 100 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 19 of 1951, to provide for better administra tion and governance of Hindu Religious institutions and Endowments in the State of Madras. The petitioners applied for restraining the State from enforcing any of the provisions of the Act or its scheme. The Commissioner rejected the application on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 101(1) of the, Act. The High Court held that the audit fee was not less than one thousand rupees, and therefore, the demand for levy of contribution was Premature, and that audit fee demanded by the Commissioner was without jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Commissioner had not determined the amount payable by the respondent temple under section 76(2) of Madras Act 19, and since the petitioners had applied for calling upon the State to make a contribution, the question did not fall to be determined because rules prescribing the method for determining contribution were applicable to each temple separately and prescribing the mode for determining the fee for auditing the accounts of each religious endowment. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Act does not contemplate separate rules to be made in respect of each religion institution likely to obtain the benefit of services rendered by the State for which the contribution is to be levied. Under section 76 (2) the annual income of which as calculated for the purposes of section 76 for the fasli year immediately preceding the date of commencement of the levy of the contribution under sub section (1), is not less exceed one thousand Rupees, and it is sufficient to say that until such rule was made no contribution could be demanded. [924 E] 2. The question whether there is a reasonable relation between the expenditure incurred by the Government for providing services and the amounts intended to be collected from the religious institutions for whose benefit the services are to be rendered. Under the Act, audit fee is not to be prescribed by rules : the Commissioner has to determine the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of the accounts. That im.plies that the amount demanded was not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred for auditing purposes. But the percentage of income levied as audit fee must of necessity be based on an estimate, and the demand will not be struck down merely because it turns out that the amounts demanded are not exactly equivalent to cost actually incur for auditing accounts. [1024 E F] 3. The contention that under the Act the Government had to make under section 80 rules applicable to every religious institution, was rejected by this Court in H. The fact that the petitioners applied before the Commissioner for calling for a report from the Commissioner and the High Court did not decide whether the audit fees were in truth for meeting the expenses incurred on account of such services. [1124 E G] 4. The demand made of the appellants temple for the payment of a sum of Rs. It was not the case of the respondents that the respondent had applied under section 78(2). It was only the Commissioner who had to form an estimate of the reasonable costs which may have been incurred in rendering an effective Audit of the religious institution and to state it in terms of a percentage of the income. [1224 F] 5. The audit fee cannot be demanded merely because the amount sought to be recovered is not precisely what equivalent to that cost actually spent for auditing its accounts. It depends on the estimate, or the demand which may not be incurred. If the Commissioner does not determine the audit, he has to form a estimate of reasonable cost and the demands will not become struck down simply because it turned out that there was no reasonable relation to the expenditure actually incurred by him for auditing his accounts.

The appellant was a contemner under section 19(1) of the Act. He filed an application for initiating proceedings against him under section 17 of the . The High Court dismissed his petition and directed that the notice be issued to him to show cause why he should not be proceeded against for committing con temptation of the High Court. The appellant challenged the order of the Single Judge in a writ petition before this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right under section 20 of the , and that an appeal does lie to this court as a question of law from any order or decision of a bench of the Court. Held, that the present appeal filed by the alleged contemner against whom the proceeding has remained pending in the High court is not maintainable. The order of this Court in Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court,(1) was not an order initiating contempt proceedings. It could not be said that an application under section 18 of the ; ,of the Act does not lie to the Supreme Court as it did not decide any question. [515 G H] (a) The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the High Courts adjudicating upon any matter raised before them by the parties, affecting their right, the mere order issuing the notice does not decide anything against the alleged contemnor and cannot be appealed against as a matters of right tinder section 19. [615 A B] (b) The present appeal is, therefore, dismissed as being not maintainable under section 21 of the 'Act.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another in the Court of the Magistrate, First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) of the Act for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the . The trial court acquitted the accused. On appeal by the State, the High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted the appellant under section 5 (1A) of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction could be sustained under section 4(1A), because the amendment made in the year 1952 did not affect any other enactment in which the repealed enactment had been applied, incorporated or referred to; and that the amendment was not a textual amendment but a substantial one. Held, further, that section 6 (1 A), inserted in the Act of 1933 by the amending Act of 1949, did not apply to a case of a later amending Act inserting new provisions in an earlier Act which had been repealed by the repealing enactment and, therefore, the conviction under section 3(A) could be upheld. The amendment made by the Amending Act of 1948 was not merely a texture but a substantive one. It was only a procedural provision which did not have any application to a particular case. The amending Act was repealed by Act XLVIII of 1952, and it was in force when the offence was committed by the appellant. The amended section 6 A was not applicable to a situation of a subsequent amendment made after the commencement of the Amending act. The words "if any person establishes, maintains or works a telegraph within India" were comprehensive enough to take in a wireless transmittedter which had already been applied. The language used in the amending statute did not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. Therefore, it cannot be said that section 4 of the 1952 Act continued to be on the statute book even after the amending act was repealed.

The appellant, a son of Adwaita, was the managing Shebait of the debutter estate. The respondent 's husband Aghore Nath Roy, died in 1943 leaving behind his widow and two daughters, who were minors. On the 28th August, 1941, the deities represented by some of the Shebaits filed two applications under section 36(6) (a) (ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for the reopening of the two compromise decrees mentioned above and the passing of new instalment decrees to have the properties, which were in possession of the real decreeholder. The trial court dismissed both the applications holding that Oramba Sundari was a mere benamidar for her husband Achore Nath Ray, and that the Kobala executed by the Chakrabortys in favour on July 26, 1940, was a fictitious transaction. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the decreeholders were not entitled to have two compromise decree decrees reopened and on the passing o fresh instalment decrees, Oramb Sundari did not bona fide acquire any right which could be protected under clause (c). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order for restoration of possession made by both the courts below should stand. [163D] 2. In a proceeding under section 37 of the Act it is not open to the court to go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the decreeholder on record was himself a benamidar or for another person in respect of the decree, does not come within the purview of these provisions. If there is default in the payment of any one of the instalments, the properties are returned to the decree holder purchaser. [164E] 3. The subsequent conveyance of these properties in favour of Oramda Sundari, the appellant has been held by both of the courts to be a benamidars for another persons in respect o the decree. [165G H] 4. In the instant case, the sale itself was not annulled and in case of default in payment of instalments, OOrambaundari did no bona fide acquired any right, which could legally be protected by clause (b) of section 36 (2). [164H] 5. The decreeholders, therefore, must be deemed to have been the purchasers of these lands within the meaning of clause (d) of Section 36(2). In this case, O.Orambundari was not a benamirer for another purpose in respect Of the decree but it is only a benamist for another who in turn purchased the same either by himself or through Orambi Sundari. [166H] 6. The earlier conveyance of the properties in question in favour Aghoria Nath Roy was not cancelled and there was no proof of the order being reopened. [167B] 7. In view of clause(e) of sub section (2), the court can at all enter into the question as to who the decree holders obtained the decrees in reopening the decrees and launch a enquiry as regards whether the judgment debtor consequential relief under clause(c). [166G H; 167A] 8. The previous conveyance of O. Oramma Sundari on July 27, 1940 was not void but it was only a device for the purpose of avoiding the payment off the decretal dues. [176B] 9. In these circumstances, clause (e) cannot be attracted in favour o judgment debtors so far as this property is concerned and the possession of it must remain with the appellant.

The respondent entered into a contract for providing and fixing "S.H. Windows 'W ' Type" "T.H., Window 'W1 ' Type "T, H. W. W/C. W./C.W. /C.M. Wocky Road, Jaipur, and to promote sales of goods manufactured by it "voluntarily offered to fit the goods and had made no separate charge for that service. The respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, its tender for providing doors and windows in a specified building, undertook to fix the windows without demanding any charge for the service, and the Board was justified in holding that the contract was one of service in the execution of which some movable property passed to the respondent. The Deputy Commissioner Excise & Taxation in appeal held that from the acceptance of the tender, two contracts resulted : one for providing windows and other for "fixing" those doors and window leaves in a certain specified building and that the price of, the supplied but not the charge for service, was taxable. The High Court held that the agreement was one for work, in the executing of which certain movable property passing to the War Office under the head contract. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contracts were for work and labour and that they were divisible between two parts representing the sale of the window, , and the labour charges in fixing the same and thus partly liable to sales tax. HELD : (1) The terms of the contract and the circumstances that the respondent had agreed to and did supply "motor bus being one for sale of a chattel" were not decisive and the Court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the contracts as disclosed by the nature of the work, and in determining whether the contract is in substance one for works and labour or one for the sale. [419 E] (2) The test in each case is whether the object of the party sought to be taxed is that the chattel as chattel passes to the other party and the services rendered in connection with the installation are under a separate contract or are incidental to the execution thereof. If the windows were not properly "fixed" the contract would not be complete, and if the windows had become a part of the building construction it would not have matter that ultimately the property was to pass to the Umpire. [519 F] (3) The tests in each cases are whether the objects of the parties sought to tax are that the transfer of the property in, and delivery of the possession of, a chattels to the buyer. If it is a contract between "fix" certain articles made by a manufacturer the contract must be deemed one for Sale and not of service.

Criminal Appeal No. 370 of 1970 The appellant State was a partnership with the complainant and his brother Ram Avtar, who were also present along with Shanker Lal, and Raj Kumar Agarwalla, were arrested by the police on November 8, 1967. On November 16, 1967 Shanker Lal and Raj Kr. Agarwalla were arrested in connection with the offence under section 420 read with section 511 Indian Penal Code read with Section 120B Indian Penal code read with sections 120B I.P.C. The prosecution case is that on November 9, 1967 Shankar Lal and Ram Avtar were seen going to Ram Avtar and thereafter they were taken into custody by the Police. It appears that the police did not submit any charge sheet on the basis of the report which had been lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Aggarwalla respondent because it is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar was a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he was present along alongwith Shanker Lal when the latter brought washer plates in a taxi and demanded the price of the washer plate from Ram Avtar on November 16. 1967 Shankerlal and Raj Kumari Agarwalla respectively. The charge under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian PenalCode read with [section 120B] I. P.C., was framed against Raj Kumar, who was also present alongwith Shankerlal, when the former brought was her plates in taxi. The trial court acquitted the accused of all the charges framed against him. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that there is no infirmity in the judgment of the High Court as might induce us to interfere with the judgment and order of the Trial Court as may induce us, to interfere. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The report which was lodged by Shankar Lal in the same very nature, would hardly warrant an inference that Raj Kr Kumar respondent too was a person who had been present alongwith Shanker Lal. [280B] 2.2 The part of which is alleged to Raj Pal Agarwalla and demanded for the price washer improvements from Ram pal Avtar. That circumstance, as pointed out by the High court, would not warrant an conclusion that RajKumar respondent too did not commit any conspiracy or defraud Ram Avtar; and Rajkumar Agarwalla was a necessary party to the conspiracy to cheat RamAIL. [281C] 3.3 The part attributed toRaj Kumar is only that he had been seen going along with Shankar Lal when he brought washers in a vehicle and demanded price of his washer clothes from Ram Pal. That factor, as mentioned by the Trial court, will hardly warrant any inference thatRaj Kumar respondent alone was a signatory to any agreement to defraud RamAIL by Raj Kumar. [283E] 4.3 In the instant case, there is nothing on record to show that Raj kumar Agarwalla respondent was a witness to any criminal conspiracy to deceive Ram Avtar or to cheat him. The entire part which has been attributed to Ram Pal was that he did not make any mention of his name because it was the case that Rajbir Kumar had appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the FIR. [284E] 5.4 In the present case, the part which was attributed to Shankar Lal, when he came to the shop of Ram Avtar with washer marks in a motor vehicle and demanding the price thereof from RamAIL Avtar. Raj Kumar respondent also did not file any charge sheets on the ground that Raj Pal had been arrested by police. The whole part of the thing which is said to have been committed by Raj karam, cannot be an inference of guilt that Rajkumar was a stranger to any conspired to defraud the accused.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in village Kheda, Taluka and District. The appellants filed applications for restoration of their lands under Regulation 21 of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations, 1958. The application was dismissed by the Collector on July 18, 1961. Thereafter the appellants filed an application for restoration before the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal which was rejected on July 19, 1961, but the appellants did not appear either in person or through his agent and hence the applications were made in time under Regulation 20 of the Saurashtra Revenue Tribunal Regulation, 1958, and the restitution applications filed by them were dismissed. The appellant contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961 they were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence there was no delay in filing the application for restoring the appeal. Held: (i) Regulation 21 applies to the present case and the period of limitation prescribed by that Regulation is 30 days from the date of receipt of an order of rejection of the application or dismissal of the appeal, as also an application under section 20 of that Act. The words "decide it on merits" in Regulation 19(1) are wide enough to include within its scope and ambit an application made under regulation 20 shall be filed within 30 day from the receipt thereof. [144G H] (ii) The Tribunal committed an error of law in dismissing the applications of restoration made by the appellants in all the four appeals. The order of the Gujarat High Court dismissing the application of restoration was received by the appellant on April 10 and April 19, 1962. The Tribunal had no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it was obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits even though there was default on the part of the appellants to appear when the appeal or application was heard and declared ex parte. [145G H; 146A] (iii) The expression used is "decided ex parte" and we see no reason, either in the language or context of Regulation 20, why it should not include in its scope or ambit an Application for restoration filed under regulation 19(2). If the view that we have taken as to the interpretation of Regulation 21 is correct, it follows that Regulation 21 applied to the facts of this case and to the previous approval of the State Government, the President may make regulations for regulating the practice and procedure of the tribunal including the award of costs by the Tribunal, the sittings of the members either singly or in 143 benches constituted by the President or such member as is authorised by him from amongst the members of the Tribunal or the bench thereof, of any proceedings before it notwithstanding that in the course thereof there has been a change in the persons sitting as members of that Tribunal or bench. [146A B] (iv) The words used are "decided exparte" and they are not to include in their scope and meaning an application seeking restoration of an appeal decided 145 on merits under Regulation 19.

The appellant 's case in the plaint was that Telibandha was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy as early as 1857 by Dinanath Sao himself and later on in the year 1896 when a partition took place between his descendants who were up till that time living jointly, all the coshares not only re affirmed the dedication made by Dinnath Sao of this village but also dedicated the village Teli Diseases to the deities in this temple by accepting the award made by the Panchas. The Trial Court held that there was no absolute dedication of the village for the purpose of the temple by the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 and no trust was created thereby. On appeal, the High Court agreed with the Trial Court that the dedication of Teli terminable was made in favour of Shri Ramachandra Swamy temple or whether the village was given in full proprietorship to Ramsaran Lal with only a charge on it to meet the expenses of the family or that he made certain alienations of the property for the expenses. The High Court held, that there had been no absolute trust of the Village Telibari and that the plaintiff 's suit was not maintainable. On reference, the Trial Judge held that the gift by Din Nath Sao to Ramrani Lal with merely a charge over the property was made by him as the manager on behalf of the deities for this property. The appellant ' appeal to this Court by special leave was dismissed by this Court. In the appeal to the Supreme Court it was contended on behalf Of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that there could be no absolute gift of the land to Ramkrishan Lal absolutely with only an charge on the property and did not make an absolute dedication for the expenditure of the Temple. HELD: The document (the Panch Faishla Award) clearly shows an .absolute dedication of a village to Shri Ramchandra Swami temple, set aside the judgment and decree of the High ' Court. [419D] In view of its decision that absolute dedication by Dinkar Sao was made with only one charge on this property for expenses of tumemonials, it would not be right to take the indication of the words "from the profits and income" as out weighing or neutralising the several other provisions which point to an intention that Ramsar Raman Lal would not have absolute ownership of the house.

603 The two appellants before us are the President of Avadh The two parties were the President and Action Committee of the Avadh Bar Association. They were the Chairman, Action Committee and the Avadh bar association. There were three charges against the appellants. It was alleged that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a most parti san manner under the influence of Allahabad Bar quite unbecoming of the office which he held. The High Court dismissed the notices. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Chairman of the Action Committee, described as contemner No. 2 was actively associa ted with the passing of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Judge and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he is guilty of contempt as contemner Nos. 1 & 2 were guilty of contumacious conduct, and the High Court committed an error in discharging the notices, and that the appellants were liable to be punished under section Contempt of Courts Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The language used by them was unfortunate. It is a matter of regret that the members of the Bar did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. They did not commit contempt as contemners Nos.1 & 2 for the contumacious act were considered only "indiscreet" by it. [605B] 1.2 The language employed by them is unfortunate. The appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother, respondent No. 5 were entered into a partition of joint movable and immovable properties and the same was referred to three arbitrators; namely, three appellants Nos 6 and 7 herein. On or about November 28, 1977 the arbitrators declared that they had been entered into with regard to partition of the joint movable property and that the award was presented within time as the period during which judicial proceedings were pending. The arbitrators made an application before the Sub Judge for registration. The Sub Judge rejected the application holding that it was the Registrar and not the Sub Registrar who could determine the question of limitation for the purpose of registration of the award. On appeal, the High Court held that the order passed by the Sub judge directing the arbitrators to keep the award in the custody of the court was wrong and without jurisdiction. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order made by the court directing the arbitrator to keep his award in custody of his court was erroneous and without Jurisdiction. [696B] 2.2 The Sub Registrar pursuant to the order of the High court on 24th of June, 1985 found that the arbitrators had tried to obtain the custody from the custody o the court. It was therefore, not necessary to discuss in detail the ratio of A the decision of the Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in M. The appeal is allowed and the order dated 24th November, 1983 is restored. [796C] 3.3 In the facts and circumstances of this case, however, the parties are directed to pay and bear their own costs.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent gave notice to the defendant to vacate the premises on the ground of nonpayment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The defence of the appellant was that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises to the sub tenants and that the sub tenant had waived his right in regard to the prohibition against sub tenancy and the provision in section 13(1)(e) was for the protection of his rights which he was entitled to waive. The trial court held that the tenancy by the letter of June 7,1948, was a new tenancy and not a continuation of the old and that it was for a period of six years. On appeal the High Court reversed the finding of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that under section 15 of the Act the tenant had the power to sub letting the premises, but the right of the landlord to sue for ejectment on the grounds of subletting being a personal right for his benefit, the respondent could not evict the appellant under section 13 (1)(a) and (b). Held: (i) The right of a landlord to file an application for eviction on the basis of a notice issued by him under section 12(2) is a statutory right which flows directly from an infraction of a provision of the statute. It is not enacted solely for the benefit of one party and which he may waive. In the instant case there was no express contract between the parties to the agreement which recognised sub letting as follows : " The trustees under this Act had no power to mortgage the toll houses. The trustees were bound to take notice that the trustees under the Act had waived their right in respect of the prohibition regarding sub tenancy, and the provisions in section 15 were for the purpose of protection of private rights of the landlords and unless there is in the Act itself any provision to the contrary such rights as far as they are personal rights may be parted with or renounced by the landlord. The Courts are bound to follow the procedure prescribed under the law for enforcing a term of the agreement, which is not merely of waiver of statutory rights enacted for the purposes of protection against the revenue and to be enforced solely at the instance of the revenue officials, nor is the prohibition limited to cases for which a penalty is exigible In the absence of any express contract it was a waiver of the provisions introduced into the Statute for the enforcement of the agreements. [227 G] (ii) The rights of a tenant under section 14 are not merely personal rights but they are also personal rights and they are not mutually exclusive. It may be open to the landlord in such cases to take recourse to the procedure provided by law for recovery of possession of his premises. But it is not necessary that the tenants should be given notice before taking action against them under section 16(1) (a). The right to recover possession of any premises if the Court is satisfied (i)(ii) is an absolute right which can be enforced only when there is a provision in an agreement which is for the welfare of the public and unless it is made by the Legislature that disputes mentioned in the section of the act should be determined by an Expert nominated by the Board of Trade and it was not necessary to give notice before the action is taken. The right conferred on the tenant under Section 14 is a personal one and not merely waiver of such statutory rights as well as legal rights enacted under the statute for the relief of private right.

The respondent was appointed as a teacher in the appellant school. The appellant school was affiliated to the Board and the respondent was selected for appointment on the post of Assistant Teacher. The respondent was declared successful in the written examination held by the Board. The Board, after considering the recommendations of the Selection Committee, decided to conduct an examination for selection of candidates for appointment as Assistant Teachers. The Selection Committee took the decision that the examinees/parents/guardians were parties to the fabrication and the fabrication was done at their behest. The Divisional Board, however, rejected the claim of the respondent. The State Government issued a notification dated August 31, 1990 appointing the appellant as an Assistant Teacher in the school. In pursuance of the said notification, the Board decided to hold an examination by the Selection Committees. The selection Committee took into consideration the recommendations made by the Committee and held that the fabrication of moderators ' mark sheets was done after the scrutiny by the concerned officials in the office of the State Board at Bombay and before the moderators 'mark sheets were taken out to Pune to feed the computer. The Government, however did not agree with the recommendation of the Committee. The High Court, on appeal, held that since the Act, Regulations and the Resolutions empowered the Divisional Board and its Standing Committee to deal with use of unfair means at final examinations including fabrication of documents issued by the State Government as an integral part of the power of the Divisional Boards, it was not necessary to go into the question of quantum of punishment. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The conclusion reached by the Education Standing Committee that the fabric was done in the presence of either the examinee or their parents or guardians is amply borne out from the record. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. [515E] 2.1 In dealing with question as to whether the conclusion reached at by the Educational Standing Committee was justified in arriving at its conclusions against the respondent it is not necessary for us to go through the question whether the inference deduced by the School Standing Committee, that the fabricated moderators ' Mark sheets were done at the instance of either of the examinee nor the parent or guardian was based on the evidence on record. [615B] 2:2 The conclusion arrived at by this Court that theexaminees/ parents and guardians were parties in the examination hall is not a matter which can be gone into by the High Court under article 226 or Article 136 of the Constitution, but it depends on whether the order as passed in contravention of the statutory provisions of the law or in violation of the principles of natural justice, the court has no jurisdiction to quash the order merely on the ground that different view could possibly be taken on the basis of the evidence available on the record, if the order is passed in violation Of the principles Of natural justice. [715C] 3. The conclusion drawn by the Labour Standing Committee regarding the fabrication/ tampering of moderators' mark sheets is based on records. It has to be seen whether the conclusions 798 reached by it were based on evidence or was sufficient to support such conclusion reached. If the order passed in breach of the mandatory provisions of law or principles of Natural justice, it is the duty of the Examination Committee to take action against the erring examinees to maintain the educational standard. [815E F] 4. The question whether a conclusion reached on the facts and circumstances justified the examination Standing Committee or the Enquiry Officer is based upon the evidence adduced by the parties. If it is found to have used unfair means, it would be the duty and obligation of the examining body to take appropriate action against such erring examinee to maintain standard or proof of the charge. [915E H] 5.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court acquitted all the accused and convicted them under sections 120B and 5(1)(d) of that Act. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the conviction of the appellant in the case was based solely on such presumption and that it could not be said to be based solely upon such presumption. Held, further, that the intention of the Legislature was to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and that the offence as defined in section 21 of the Act did not come with. In the instant case there is no offer to give an d acceptance of a bribe by a public servant. The mere fact that the accused person was interested in giving or attempting to give any bribe for hushing up the case would not make him a public Servant for purposes of Chapter IX of the Code. The offence as described in section 5 does not come within the meaning of bribery is to place too narrow a construction on the sub clause. Under the Act as it stood before it was amended by Act XVII of 1955, every railway servant was deemed, to be a public servants for the purposes of that Chapter and under sub clause (4) it is made punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine or with both. The object of section 5 is to create an offence distinct from a one act of bribe and that before a charge under section 6 has been framed, there must be threat or inducement, or promise proceeding from the public servant or duress or extortion practised by him to obtain pecuniary advantage. It was not necessary for the purpose of this Act to create a new offence of bribery which may provide only when there is any offer to giving an d accepted bribe by the voluntary giver and that after a charge has been made, there should be threat, or inducement or promise proceedings from the person who knows to have been, or to be likely to be concerned in any proceeding or business transacted or about to be transacted by him or under any public servant to whom he knows to be interested in or related to the person so concerned. The intention of Parliament was to make a new section 5 and under section 409 of that Code there must also be threat of inducement, threat or promise or proceeding from a public officer or duress and extortion practised through his position as a publicservant. The purpose of section 6 is to provide by means in the Act an offence which may come into play only when it there is a offer to given an d Acceptance of a gratification by a person for himself or for any other person, any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, and that when a charge is under section 7, the fact that he has received a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position in as a Public servant would not be invalid by reason only that it is based solely On such presumption the Court shall presume unless the contrary is proved that the person is guilty of criminal offence in the discharge of his official duty and his conviction therefor shall not be valid by reason merely that it was based purely on such presumptions. The Court has to presume, unless the contra is proved, that he is guilty for criminal misconduct in the discharging of his duty. The word 'may' in section 6(1) is used in a wide sense and it is used as a verb or dictionary meaning. It is not necessary that the words "shall be deemed" should be given so as to enable the Court to presume that the public servants are guilty of civil misconduct in discharge of their duty.

The appellant Bank of Saurashtra (hereinafter referred to as 'the Bank') entered into a contract for the sale of certain goods and the surety agreed to pay the amount of Rs. 76,368 04 P. from the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor Harilal Parmanaddas Adatia and his surety original defendant 2 Chitranjan Rangnath Raja. The surety gave two securities on the specific understanding that the principal debtor had offered two securities one the pledge of goods and another personal guarantee of the surety. The security was to be supervised by the Bank, whether the surety knew of the existence of such security or not; and if the creditor loses, or without the consent of the sureties, parts with such security would be discharged to the extent of the value of the security. The principal debtor was the guarantor for the advance and, therefore, two securities were offered, namely, pledge of oil tins and another Personal guarantee of surety. On September 16, 1957, the surety executed two bonds in favour of the Bank Ext. 81, and one the pledged oil tIns but as the contract of guarantee entered into by the surety with the Bank was independent of the pledge, the sureties were discharged to that extent. The bond executed by the principal borrower in favour Of the Bank as also the bond executed between the principal creditor and the guarantor in favour thereof was independent and it was independent from the pledge. The High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the express understanding and with full knowledge of the bank that the Principal debtor was offering another security, namely pledge of the goods and that as in this case the entire security was lost, the bail bonds were discharged. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The Court of first instance, i.e. the Court of First instance, has to be shown that the creditor had taken more than one security from the principal employer at the time when the contract was entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the guarantor knew of such other security offered by the Principal Debtor, if the debtor knows of such another security offer or not, the principal is discharged to it. [83D] 2. The creditor having lost one security, the bond would not be discharged from the obligation undertaken under the letter of guarantee. [84G H] 3. The guarantor having lost two security, he was wholly discharged to his liability under the guarantee. The bail bonds executed by him at one sitting on September 16 1957, therefore could not be discharge even if it is found that a creditor had committed breach of any condition of the contract entered into between the surety and the principal Debtor which itself may be a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee and the creditor by its own negligence lost one of the securities. [85G] 4. The debtor having lost another security and, being discharged to this extent, the guarantor would not get any benefit from the liability undertaken under section 141. 31(a) of the Act even if he loses or without that consent of surety, the creditor would not discharge him even if the surety given personal guarantee on the good faith of other security is offered by it. The sureties were also discharged to their liability under guarantee. They had no option but to sign the bond and to sign it. In such a situation clause (a) would be attracted and an application for restitution will have to be made to the Court o first instance. [86E] 5. The court of first example, i e. the court of First illustration, has held that in view of combined operation of sections 138 and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, the debtor was liable to discharge the liability under section 140.

The appellant was a member of the family of Nawabag. The lands in suit were allotted to the share of the appellant, and his father, who died on August 28, 1922, was also a member thereof. On August 28,. 1922, Government excluded the " patelki inam" lands from the resumption proceedings relating to the jagir on the footing that they were separate from and independent of the jagir. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the properties in suit, which was dismissed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (1) the lands in question were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for 91 714 services to be rendered by the patel and the grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government; (2) the appellant had no right to resume " p Patelki inam " lands which were given as emoluments of his office to the working patel from the Rokade family burdened with service; and (3) the orders of Government dated August 28 1922, did not confer any new right nor did they deprive anybody of any subsisting rights in respect of the " Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900. Held: (i) that the lands were given by way Of remuneration or wages for 91 715 services to the p Pateldi inam ' lands, so long as a member performs the service or not; and the orders passed by Government dated September 28, 1961, did no confer any right nor do they deprive anyone of any existing right in respect thereof. The grant was made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag and not by the sovereign authority and neither the Inam Rules nor the provisions of the Patets and Patharis Law 1900 applied; (ii) that even if the lands had been shown as excluded from the jagir of Nawabg, it was open to Government to resume the lands under section K. 1, and (iii) that Government has no right either to resume or regrant the same to respondent No. 1. The order dated August 29, 1922 did not give any new rights nor did it deprive anybody or any subsisting right in regard of the ' patelka inam " land.

The appellant 's family was governed by the Hindu Law of inheritance and succession. The respondents ' father, who had settled down in Madras, filed a suit for partition of the properties of their family. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the rules of Hindu law were consistently acquiesced in and applied to their family and the other Cutchi Memons settled in Madras. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that as there was only one solitary decision of the Bombay High Court which limited the application of Hindu Law to matters of succession and inheritance, the general trend of judicial opinion in Bombay was that both the Khoias and the Cutchi memons had retained considerable portion of their personal law and that the rule of devolution of property by survivorship would apply to CutchiOMons governed matters of inheritance only. The High Court also held that the respondents ' suit for a partition of properties was not maintainable as they had settled up first in Madras and then in Bangalore sometime between 1928 and 1930, and that as they were governed by Hindu Law, they could prefer the Madras as against the Bombay view. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that as the Khojas and the Memons had settled their affairs, since they had been born lone before 1948, they held that they had never adopted as part of their customary law the Hindu law of be joint family property and that they were entitled to prefer the Bombay decision. HELD : (1) The rule of succession in matters of pro perty is applicable only in matters relating to succession and succession by the rules as to joint family properties, the right of a son therein by birth and the devolution thereof by survivorship. [723 E] (2) The rules of Hindus, such as, the Khudchi Memon, were accepted by them as customary law in matters Of pro perties, succession and descent only. [824 F] (3) The Bombay High Courts Act, 1953, was not applicable to Cutch Memons governed matter of succession or inheritance.

The appellants manufactured the fabrics of different types. The yarn was obtained at an intermediate stage in the mill of the appellants and subjected to the integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics, will be liable to payment of excise duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 of the Rules. The appellants contended that the retrospective effect given by section S I will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act ') and also that the retrospectivity given by Section S l of the Finance Act 1982, is not applicable. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the retrospectively retrospective effect gave retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force, that is to say, from February 28, 1944, it was only when the goods are manufactured or cured or if such excisable goods are used in the manufacture of another commodity, then it will be removal and when the excisable goods manufactured or produced in any place or premises appurtenant thereto, it will not be a case of removal for the purpose of payment of duty. In appeal to this Court by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that retrospective effect has given retrospective effect to the retrospective operation given by sub rule (1) of Rule 9 and rule 49 did not, in any manner, indicate that it is only when goods are removed from the factory premises it will become a case for removal and if such goods are consumed or utilised for the manufacture thereof, then they will be deemed to have been removed from such place or places as mentioned in sub rule(1)of Rule 9. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The definition of 'place of removal' is not required to be made and, in our view, cannot be made of the place where the goods were manufactured or manufactured but any premises appurtenant to such place, in that case, the Collector has to specify such premises for the purposes of collection of excise duties. [707B] 2. The specification is not necessary to be mentioned in the definition. It is only if a commodity is taken outside the factory it will have to specify the place of manufacture and also any premises adjacent thereto, in which case, it would be removal, but rule 9 does not, In any manner indicate that the specification that has to be make of the places of manufacture or production of the excisable product at an intermediary stage, is inapplicable. [807F] 3. The Explanation to rules 9 & 49 contemplates the collection of duty levied on the production of a commodity at an integrated process for weaving the said commodity by deeming such production or manufacture but any place appurtenant thereto. It does not indicate that there is no specification that it was merely when the raw material is produced, cured or manufactured, but any such premises appurtenant lo the factory is used for the manufacturing of another product in a continuous process. [907F G] 4. The Notification No. S.O. No. 965 dated February 28 1944, issued by the Central Government under section 3(1), provides that commodity obtained at intermediate stage and consumed or utilized for the production or manufactured or any premises ancillary thereto, which may be specified by the Collector in this behalf whether for consumption, export or manufacture of any other commodity in or outside such place. [1007F H] 5. The notification does not refer to the place wherein the goods have been manufactured or removed but only provides that excisable goods produced or manufactured in any factory shall be deemed liable to pay excise duty.

The petitioner filed a suit for injunction restraining the Hearing Authority appointed under section 68 of the Act from proceeding with the hearing and approving the scheme. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was not maintainable in a civil court for an injunction restraining it from proceeding further with the proceedings under that provision and that the plaintiff had no locus standi to file the suit. In appeal, the Additional District Judge held that the plaint did not disclose a cause of action and that it did not contain a cause o f action. The High Court dismissed the revision petition holding that since the jurisdiction of the civil courts in such matters was impliedly barred, the suit could be said to have been maintainable for the reliefs prayed for by the petitioner since the court had no power to issue an order of injunction restraining a Hearing Authority under section68 L) of the , Act from taking proceedings with regard to the merits of the scheme or the desirability of bringing such scheme. In revision petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The suit was maintainable in civil courts for an order restraining the hearing authority under section 69 C of the . [145E] 2.2 The jurisdiction of a civil courts is expressly barred. It is not open to a civil Court to issue any order of interim injunction restraining, the Hearing Authorities concerned can issue only in accordance with the scheme and the other provisions contained in Chapter IVA of the ille sate Act. [145F] 3.1 Section 68 D of the The Act empowers the State Government to publish the scheme either with or without modification. When the scheme is approved or modified under section 71 C of .the Act, such approved or modify scheme is required to be published in the official Gazette and on such publication it becomes final. [146B] 3:2 The procedure laid down for the preparation of the Scheme is contained in sections 68 C and 68 D. The jurisdiction Of the State Legislature is exclusive in character and it is not permissible to a Civil Court to entertain an application under section 66 D of .he Act. It cannot be said that the scheme had been duly published under section 70 C of ,the Act by an authority which had the power to publish it and that, therefore, the trial court was right in refusing to stay the further proceedings in the suit.[147G] 3 :3. The procedure for preparation of a scheme enabling the State Transport Undertaking to operate road transport services to the exclusion complete or partial of other persons is contained In sections 68 D and 68 C of The , the jurisdiction Of a civil Courts in such cases is exclusive, character and It is open to the civil court to issue a direction to the Hearing authority under Section 68D of the. Act to publish its scheme and also in such manner as the State Govt may direct. [147G H] 3 4.3 In view of the provisions contained under section 67 C of ) the Act, the jurisdiction conferred on the Civil Courts in matters of procedure laid therein is exclusive. The power of the State government (the Hearing Authority) to publish a scheme or to do so cannot be exercised by an aggrieved person before the HearingAuthority under section 65 D of , the Act and it can only issue in accordance therewith. [148G H; 148A] 3 5.4 In view Of the provisions of section 68 C, the civil Court is competent to issue such directions as it may deem fit to the State transport undertaking or any local authority or police authority within whose jurisdiction any part of the area or route proposed to be covered by the scheme lies, and it cannot issue an injunction against the Hearing authorities under section 64 D of. The Civil Judge was right while refusing to staying the further proceeding in the case. [149G H, 148A B] 3 6.5 In view o the provisions made in Chapter III A of the )

The appellant was charged under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. He pleaded that he had been falsely implicated in a case by his father and that he was falsely implicated. The Special Judge acquitted him on the ground that the appellant had obtained money from Russel Nathaniel and his wife expressed their reluctance to send Miss Eylene with him to the police station and therefore the appellant was guilty of grossly abusing his position as public servant within the meaning of section 5 (1)(d) of Prevention of corruption Act. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction of the accused under section 161, Indian Penal code or any other criminal statute is not excessive. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant had been rightly convicted by the Special Judge and the High Court erred in setting aside the order with regard to the payment of fine or imprisonment in default. [620 E] 2. The offence charged and that a prima facie case was made out against the appellant. [ 620 C] 3. The concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child is not an offence under section 6(1)(a) of Act, because it does not fall within the definition of "public servant" in section 5 of the Act. [721 E] 4. The mere fact that there was a gross abuse of his official position on the part or the appellant and in the circumstances of the case we are satisfied that the sentence imposed is not unreasonable. [ 723 C] 5. In the present case, it is manifest that the concealment of birth of a illegitimate child was not an act which could be said to be an offence within the ambit of section 6 (1) (a). The appellant grossly abused his position in as public servants within the scope of section 161 Indian Penal Act or any criminal statute and obtained for himself a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, and the charge under that section is established.

The appellant was a public servant and was charged with having accepted illegal gratification as a motive or reward for doing an official act and showing in the exercise of his official functions favour to Doraiswamy in seeing that a speedy and favourable settlement of the claim cases preferred by him against the Bengal Nagpur Railway, subsequently the Eastern Railway. Chatterjee in cross examination clearly showed that he had not applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the sanction accorded was not a valid one. The Special Judge rejected this contention and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for five years and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 in default to undergo further rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the sanction granted in this case was not valid one; (2) the Special Judge had erred in holding that exhibit 6 on the face of it disclosed a valid sanction; (3) the evidence of Mr. Bokil was inadmissible as being inadmissible and, therefore, the conviction was bad. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The sanction accorded by the appellant was not invalid one. When the sanction itself and the evidence thereof were placed before him apparently gave him the necessary material upon which he decided that it was necessary in the ends of justice to accord his sanction; and (4) the documents placed before them were relevant to the only question before him whether he should or should not accord his approval to the prosecution of the respondent. [100 G] 2. The papers which were placed by the accused were relevant for the purpose of granting a certificate. It was not for Mr. A. K. Sen to judge the truth of the allegations made against the appellant by calling for the records of the connected claim cases or other records in connection with the matter from his office nor did he call for any record therein. [101 G H] 3. The documents which were relied upon by the prosecution showed that the sanction was not necessary in respect of the matters from his Office nor did they show as to how they stood. It is true that Mr. Chatterjee had applied his minds to the fact and circumstances, but he did not call for the connected record from his offices nor did it call for a record in connection therewith. [102 D] 4. The only point which was raised before us and which was the expressed reason for the granting of the certificate having failed, the appeal must be dismissed and the decision of the High court in upholding the conviction is upheld.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenants under section 14(1) (b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The tenant contended that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and reconstruction. The Controller held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction was not bona fide. The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by the tenants against the orders of eviction and set aside the orders passed by the appellate authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the tenant that the landlord had only a life interest in the property, is entitled to evict the tenants on the ground of demolition and for reconstruction. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression landlord ' includes the person who receives or is entitled under the Deed of Settlement as a trustee receiving rents of the premises from the tenants. [776F] 2.1 Section 12(2) of Madras Buildings Act, 1959 provides that "the tenant shall not be evicted except by an order directing the tenant to deliver possession of the building to the landlord before a specified date". The expression 'landlord ' is defined under section 2(6) as follows: ' 'Landlord ' includes any person who has been on his own right under the deed. [771A B] 2 2.2 Section 12 provides that the tenant shall, if he is satisfied (a) that the premises are bona fide require by the tenant for the immediate purpose of demolishing it and such demolition is to be made for the purpose of erecting a new building on the site of the buildings sought to be demolished, pass an order requiring the tenant either to deliver or deliver possession thereof to the landlords before specified date. [ 771A] 2:3 The expression "landlord" in section 12(4) of Act means a person who is receiving or is entitle to receive the rent of a building whether on his personal account or on behalf, of himself and others or as an agent, trustee, executor, administrator, receiver or guardian or who would so receive the rents or profits of the property for his life. [761B] 2 3.3 The words "landlord " include the person whose life interest is in the premises and who actually has been in his possession. [ 762A B; 771C] 4. Section 12 of Act does not provide that a tenant with a life Interest cannot be allowed to demolish the property in order to reconstruct it as that action would, per se, be not bona fides. The words 'landlord " are used in section 13(4). [782A] 4 4. The word 'landlord' in section 2 (6) of Bombay Act, is used for describing a tenant as a landlord.
