It does not contemplate any such construction. [794A B C] 6. In the instant case, the Act with which we are concerned is a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act (See M/s Raval and Co. vs K.

The appellant decree holder filed a suit for recovery of Rs.The respondent decree holder instituted a suit in the court of the Munsif, Allahabad on the ground that certain trees were included in the 'land ' and therefore, he was entitled to the benefit of section 6(a) (i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent decree holders had no right to the benefits of section 3(13) of Act. The appellate court also held that the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force is provided in section 6 (h) of U. P. Zamindari and Land Reform Act 1950, read with section 73 of the , so that nothing more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The definition of the intermediary 's grove under section 3 (13) is wide enough to include trees and a grove. [723C] 1.2 The definition does not include trees but only an inseparable part is always included in it. In view of this very clear legal position, we allow this appeal and set aside the judgments and decrees of the High Court and the Execution Court with costs. S.R. Appeal al lowed. [788B C] 1:3 The definition is wide and comprehensive enough to cover all trees which are parts of the 'lands'. [724D E] 1(4) The definition includes trees, trees and grove land. [789E] 2.2 In view Of this very legal position the only means in which an intermediary could enforce their right against a mortgage or by after the act came into existence is provided therein.

The appellants were charged for an offence under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The trial court convicted accused 2 to 6 under Section 326/149 IPC and awarded sentence of two years each. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Subran had not been charged for the substantive offence of murder punishable under Section 304 Part I against accused 2 and 3, Rajan and Preman, for an offences under Section 307 read with section 149 IPC. [916G H] 1.2 The intention to cause death of Suku was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause his death. It is not possible to say that the injuries inflicted by him were not sufficient in ordinary course or nature to causing death. [1017C D] 1:3 Subran, the necessary intention to commit murder under Section 325 IPC since the injuries caused by them according to the postmortem report were found sufficient in their ordinary course to cause such bodily injury as is sufficient in normal course of type to cause the death of the deceased. The intention was not to cause any bodily injury which may be caused and, therefore, he can certainly be attributed with the knowledge that with those injuries it was likely that death of his brother would be caused. None of the injuries alleged by the prosecution was either individually or taken collectively with the other injuries caused either by blunt weapons. [818E] 1 :4 The intention of causing bodily injury on the deceased as was likely to cause a death of a person is sufficient for the purpose of causing death and, accordingly, he cannot be attributed to him and the medical evidence also shows that the said injuries were not enough in the normal course to causes death. Therefore, the conviction of all the appellants for an Offence under Section 324 IPC is not permissible. [718F] 1.:4 The offence would fall under Section 300 Part I if it is proved by the evidence on record that the accused persons individually had caused injuries with a chopper and those injuries were sufficient in nature to causes such bodily injuries as are sufficient in his ordinary course for cause death. The injury was inflicted by all the four appellants and, thus, he could be attributed only with the intention to causing bodily harm as is likely to result from the act of the accused person though not on any vital part of the body, but looking to the weapon with which he was armed and the nature number and seat of injuries, it is not impossible to say whether all the three appellants had shared the common intention of committing murder under section 302 IPC. Therefore the conviction for an accused under Section 323 IPC read with [918F G] 1:-4 Subran has not been permissible. That apart, according to medical evidence, none of the four accused were charged with the substantive offences of murder under Sections 302/149 and 326/34 IPC also. [820G H; 821A B] 1 2.5 The intention for causing bodily injuries on the person of Sura Ca, was sufficient to cause life of Suhu or were sufficient to Cause death. No charge having been framed against him as envisaged by law, the trial court and the High court committed error in recording a conviction against them for an alleged offence under section 326/147 IPC. The conviction of accused 2 for an act under Section 148 IPC is therefore not permissible and the same would be the position with regard to the conviction under Section 34 IPC also [820C D E] 1 3.6 Subran was guilty of an offence punishable under section 304 Part II against accused No. 1 for an attempt to cause culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

The assessee was assessed to income tax under the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer held that the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash basis for 1967 68 and 1968 69. In appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that even with respect to the accounting years relevant to the assessment year 196768 and 196869, it had been maintaining accounts on cash receipt basis and since it did rot actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax was payable by it. The Revenue contended that though the Indian Company made a credit entry in the account of the assessee in its Books for the relevant accounting years (accounting year for the Indian company was stated to be the calendar year), the assessee did not actually receive the amount and that therefore it had committed a mistake in filing the returns for the assessment years 1967 68, 1968 69 and 1968 70. The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. In the appeals before this Court, it took the stand that even though the India Company was not aware of the true state of affairs relating to the assessee 's accounts, with respect thereto, it did not nevertheless receive any receipts from the Indian Bank. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The method of accounting adopted by the assessee is binding upon the department; on that basis it is immaterial when did it actually receive it in U.K. in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own Books at Coventry. [105F] 2.1 In the circumstances, we do not think it necessary to express any opinion on the question whether there was any conflict or inconsistency between Section 5(2) and Section 145 of the Act nor is it necessary for express ourselves on the view expressed by the High Court that in the case of a non resident assessee like the petitioner clause (a) of sub section (2) cannot apply. [106G] 2:2 The method adopted by an assessee is undoubtedly binding upon him; on this ground, he has received the amount. [107H] 3.1 Section 145 is relied upon by the Revenue to say that when did the assessee have received the royalty amount only when it receives the same in UK. and makes a entry to the effect that it was maintaining its accounts with respect for the said amount. The mere crediting of the said amounts to receipt of income by the Indian Companies does not amount to receipt, clause (b) cannot be applied. [108A] 3:3 In the present case, the assessee had received the money in U..K. on account of its bank accounts for the accounting year 1967 68. The assessee did neither say that the method of calculation adopted by it for all its income was on cash or mercantile basis. His contention that the amount should be treated as a payment or receipt is not correct. [109B] 4.2 In the instant case, it must be held that in view of the above discussion, the method adopted for accounting regularly adopted by Indian Company does not amounts to receipts of income from the assessee. The method employed by the petitioner for the purposes of accounting regularly adopting by an Indian Company is binding on the department. [110B] 5.3 In this view of all the matter, it cannot be said that in this case, there was no conflict or conflict between Section 6(2)(a) and section 145 of Income Tax (Central Excise Act).

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the statement of Santu, brother of Deoba, was not corroborated in material particulars and qua the appellant, the conviction is unsustainable. HELD : (1) The approver 's evidence was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of the first accused upon which he has been charged. [736 A] (2) The conviction of an accused on the testimony of an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal yet the courts nevertheless cannot lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice which in the words of Lord Abinger "it deserves to have all the reverence of the law". [737 B] (3) The evidence of a co witness is admissible in law. [836 A C] (4) The statement of the approver is no corroboration of the accomplice 's story because the knife was got prepared by accused No. 1 and the knife being found blood stained and the unusual character of the knife which fitted in with the dimensions of the injurious caused to the deceased. [820 E] (5) The testimony of a witness cannot operate as a corroboration of his evidence against the appellant. [822 B] In the circumstances of this case, the courts below were right in holding that there should be corroboration of their evidence in material details and qua each accused. [824 C] In re Rajagopal(3) where conviction was based upon the uncorroborated testimony of another co accused, said as follows "Their Lordships. (1)(has become so hallowed as to be deserving of respect" and in the language of Lord Reading C. J. in R. vs Baskerville (2). The rule of law is almost unsafe to convict upon his testimony alone.

The appellant was charged in the Court of Special Judge, Patna for an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on July 8, 1961 a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.W. Chaudhury did not challenge the findings of the High Court on questions of fact but the argument was put forward that upon the findings recorded by the High court the appellant could not be convicted of the charges because he was not a "public servant" within the meaning of section 21 of the Act. Held, further, that the appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21, Indian Penal code and section 2, Prevention of corruption Act. 691 The true test, therefore, in order to determine whether the appellant is a public servant within the ambit of section 81 of the because he is appointed to some office for the performance of certain public duty is: (1)(a) whether he is in the employment or pay or of the Government; and (b) whether his duties are immediately auxiliary to those of any other person who is not directly related with such authority or representative character by the Corporation. The appellant was a person performing duties immediately auxiliaryly to those which he performed as immediately auxiliary or to those who were appointed to certain office for performance of some public duty. The question to be considered therefore is whether as Head Clerk employed under the State Electricity Board and attached to the office of the Executive Engineer, the appellant can be said to be an officer within the definition of section21, Indian penal Code in view of the language of section 51 of the .

The appellant was convicted for contravening cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Declaration of Stock Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. He was further convicted for violating cl. (2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962, and awarded sentence to undergo rigorous imprisonment of six months. The High Court modified the sentences passed on the appellant in respect of contravention of cl. but reduced the sentences awarded by the lower courts to imprisonment already undergone and fine. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order regarding forfeiture of the juar seized from the house of the appellant was legal, and that therefore r. 141 (2), of the Rules is not ultra vires the: Defence of Indian India Act. HELD: The rule is in the following terms: "The provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act." [141C D] In the instant case, r. 138 (2)(i) of Defence ofIndia Rules, 1963 provides that "the provisions of sub rule (1 ), shall have affect notwithstanding anything contrary contained in the Act or in any instrument having effect by virtue of any enactmentother than this, Act". The Rule does not refer to any provision in the two orders mentioned above containing any provision contemplated in r.141(2) which would fall within section 3 because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to. the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34, of the Indian Penal Code for committing the murder of his wife. The High Court acquitted accused 1 and 3 on the ground that it was doubtful whether 682 any one of them participated in the commission of the offence and convicted him under section 304, read with sections 34 and 147, of Indian Penal code. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) When two or more persons named or unnamed are acquitted, the court can convict only one of the accused on the basis of constructive liability. [620 E] (2) The High court was not right in holding that the acquittal of some of the persons named in the charge and tried will not necessarily 686 displace the charge under section 149 because along with the two or three persons convicted were others who composed the unlawful assembly but who have not been identified and so have not yet been named. [613B] (3) The judgment of the High Court cannot be sustained on the evidence that the said accused acted in concert along with some other persons, named or unknown, for committing murder. [686C] (4) The conviction of accused 1, 3 and 4 under section302 read with Section 34, readwith section 149 and section 147, was bad in law, because along alongwith the two accused, who were acquitted, their conviction under section 307, read together with sections 149 and 147 of the said Code, for having committed the offence jointly with the acquitted persons. [688D] (5) The evidence adduced to prove that the accused acted on the common intention was not acceptable or by giving benefit of doubt to them, the result in law would be the same : it would mean that they did not conjointly act with accused 2 in committing the offence.

The petitioner imported a consignment of goods from the Customs Department. The goods were cleared on payment of duty by the order of the Income Tax Authorities dated 11th May, 1983. However, due to circumstances beyond the control of the petitioner, that it could not be released because of the prohibitory orders of the Central Govern ment and the Central Government under section 102 of the . The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court on 16th April, 1988 and on 22nd April, 1989, this Court passed the following order: "Pending notice, there will be limited stay to the extent that the goods name, "MSCR defective sheets/coils" which have arrived at Bombay Port per S.S. It is not permissible to move this Court on the theoretical basis that there was breach of fundamental right for the enforcement of which alone Article 32 of the Constitution is attracted. Article 32 does not apply. Article 226 of the constitution provides that no person shall be entitled to seek recourse to Article 32 or any other remedy except in due process of law. When a person complains and claims that there is a violation of law, it does not automatically involve breach of constitutional right for enforcement of fundamental rights. Article32 does not come to the conclusion that Article 32 applies. Article 31(2) provides that every person shall have a right to move the Supreme Court on any question of the enforcement or of a fundamental fight arising in this case and the petitioner has no fundamental fight to clear the goods on payment o f duty when the goods crossed the customs barrier and were in the process of being cleared, but could not claim recourse to article 32 of t he Constitution. Article 33 does not extend to cases where liability of a citizen to pay a particular duty depends upon adjudica tion or determination of questions of law as well as ques tion of fact without taking any resort to the provisions of the Act, it is not possible for the petitioner to clear goods on paying duty when there is breach of law and determination of facts and the provision of a particular statute for which elaborate procedure is pre scribed, it cannot conceivably be contended that enforcing of those provisions would breach fundamental right. Article 34 does not confer any new right or jurisdiction upon a person to move a Court on his own basis. The petitioner has also no fundamental right to seek remedy under article 32 or 226 of t e Constitution. [675G H; 676A B] In the instant case, the petitioner as such has no enforceable right to claim recourse under Article 32 and the writ petition is not maintainable.

The petitioners in these cases were the guardians of law and who constitute two important segments of society on whom the stability of the country depends. The Committee recommended the transfer of the petitioners in those cases, namely, Ms. Kiran Bedi, D.C.P. (North) and Jinder Singh S.I. The petitioners filed a complaint against them before the Metropolitan Magistrate pursuant to the complaints filed by the respondents under section 178 I.P., which was dismissed on the ground that they were not entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8 B of the Act. In appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate and directed the filing of a complaint in accordance with section 8 C of the , Act. The High Court held that the Committee should send a report recommending suspension of the D.D.CP. Kiran Khanna, Jinder singh S. I. who was also a party to the inquiry as opined by the Committee itself. In this appeal by special leave it is contended on behalf of the appellants that the order passed by the High court directing the filing and prosecution of the complaints and criminal proceedings initiated against the petitioners before the Magistrate pursuant thereto should be quashed and we accordingly quash the said orders of the High Courts. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were covered under section 8B of the . [501E] 2.1 In the circumstances of the case, three persons namely, the Additional Commissioner of Police (Special Branch), D. C.P.(North), who had to be examined at the end of the inquiry, there is no justifiable reason to deny the same treatment to the petitioners Ms. Vasdev Bedi, learned Additional Solicitor General appearing for the Delhi Administration that they never intended to show any kind of discourtsey to the Committee. [502F] 2:2 The Committee must have considered all the aspects of the matter and directed them to give PG NO 523 evidence along with others who were similarly placed at the close of the enquiry. It would have then asked them to produce evidence in their defence : Provided that nothing in this section shall apply where the credit of a witness is being impeached before asking him to be cross examined till the end Of the inquiry. There is no sufficient reason to show that there was a large number of persons who were eye witnesses to the incidents and why could give evidence before the Committee at the beginning of the proceedings. [602G] 3:3 The Committee would have had in the circumstances directed the file of complaint against either of the petitioner for being cross examined at its end of inquiry. If the Committee had found that the petitioners had been covered under Section 8 B then perhaps they would not have been asked to get into the witness box for being crossexamination till the conclusion of the trial. [702F G] 4. The affidavits and other material before the committee show that all those persons to whom notices under section 13 B were issued have to be examine at the stage of inquiry, the Committee may complete its work as early as possible. But if the Committee has found that there are a large numbers of persons in the case direction of the Court directing the file for being crossexamined at the commencement of the evidence is not contemplated under section8 B then obviously they would have been better advised to give such evidence before it. [802F H] 5. The affidavit and other materials before the High Commission indicate that there were a large majority of persons, who were also eye witnesses, to the incident and why should give evidence at the final stage of the proceeding.

The petitioners were the owners of a public carrier. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that it was unconstitutional and ultra vires. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act did not permit an option to pay a lump sum in lieu of payment of tax, but only lays down what the amount of fare or freight is to be fixed by the State Government from time to time by Notification in this behalf. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 is extra territorial in nature and that the levy of tax on fares and freights attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory, even though under the Act it is optional, and involve payment of taxes even when no passengers or goods are transported. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The proviso to subsection (3), in terms, speaks of the charge of the tax "in respect of all passengers carried and goods transported by road or inland waterways". [802 D] 2. The expression 'tax payable under the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1959, means a tax on passengers and goods, and the word 'tax ' is defined in section 3(1) of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959. [803 E F] 3. The words 'tax due under the act ' in respect of every passenger carried or goods transported By road or Inland waterways are not used in the Act. They are used in different senses and it is difficult to see how the intention of Parliament was to make a distinction between the two. [883 H; 803 A B] 4. The word 'rate ' has been defined in the Rajasthan Goods Taxation Act by section 3 (1) as meaning "a tax on goods carried or passengers carried by road, inland waterway or inland waters". It is not necessary to refer to the definition of 'tax' in section 2(2). [804 B] 5. The definition of the word "rate ' in section 1(3) is wide enough to include a tax which is levied on goods and passengers carried or passenger carried by motor vehicles, but it does not mean that the tax is leviable under the Entry, and so, the tax cannot be levied under the entry. [ 804 A B; 805 C] 6. The Act in terms speaks of "tax due" and therefore, the Tax is liable to be levied only on passengers carried in or goods carried by railway or inlandwaterways. [820 E F G] 7. The tax is still on passengers but what it is tobe paid in lieu thereof is not available to the State Legislature. It does not cease to be a tax On passengers and Goods, though what it was to be paid in terms of payment is also, if lump sum payment is made in lieu Of payment of the Tax calculated on actual fares and/ freights. [829 B] 8. The levy of the lump sum compulsory is upon passengers and property, but the amount is measured by the fares and fares and charges payable. It cannot be said to be tax on passenger and goods. [828 A C] 9. The petitioners are not entitled to any relief under article 32 of the Constitution. [824 B D] 10. The State Legislature has power to levy a lump lumpsum payment in lieu or in addition to payment of a tax, even when there is no passengers and/or goods transported through such route. [823 A C; 804 E F H] 11.

The appellant was retrenched from 1st August, 1974. The retrenchment of the workmen was set aside by the Labour Court and the workman was reinstated in service with full back wages. The Labour Court directed reinstatement effective from that date. The appellant challenged the Award in this Court. The question whether the workmen who were retrenched were entitled to the relief of reinstatement effective on the ground that they were 567 entitled to full back salary, HELD: 1.1 In appropriate cases the Court may, in the spirit of labour and management being partners in the industry direct scaling down of back wages with some sacrifice on management 's part too. [569A] 1.2 The question is whether even where reinstatement is found to be an appro priate relief, what should be the guiding considerations for awarding full or partial back wages is the guiding factors for awarding a lumpsum compensation to the extent of full wages or apart thereof. If after such a protracted time and energy consuming litigation during which period the workman just sustains himself, ultimately he is to be told that though he will be reinstated, he will not be entitled to any overriding commission, if there be any, on the turnover of the company since this will account for the pragmatic approach of common sacrifice in the interest of the industry. [570B] 1:3 The question in controversy which fairly often is raised in this court is whether the retrenchment of workmen was invalid for the reasons found by the High Court and that the non availability of raw material or recurrent power shedding and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or a ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon the refusal of the workman to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to be raised(l.4) The question arises whether the nonavailability of raw materials or recattle power shedded and lack profitability is a mere device to toror the workmen 's employer. If during such a prolonged time and effort consuming litigation, the workman does not have any opportunity of explaining why his services should not be terminated and, therefore, reinstatement was justified in the sense that till the loss is totally wiped out the Managing Director and the Directors shall not charge any fee for the services rendered as Director, no dividend shall be paid to equity shareholders. [571C] 1 :4 The question referred to this Court is whether it confers a discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal, inter alia, against the Award of any Tribunal in the territory of India. If the employer is called upon to pay full back Wages in the aggregate amount of Rs. 50,000/- and if he has been asked to pay the same in two equal instalments, it would be wholly undeserved. [572D] 1.:5 The question for consideration is whether in appropriate cases, the Court can, in exercise its discretionary jurisdiction only in cases where awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation and final decision by this Court or discloses such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit consideration of this Court (See Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd., Calcutta vs Their Workman) (1) The High Court was right in holding that retrenchment was not bona fide and that it was motivated and the relief for reinstatement effectivefrom the day on which A they were sought to been retrenched. [573E] 1.(6) In appropriate case, the court may, while exercising its discretionary power, direct scaling up of back Wages with some sacrific on management part too, if it appears that the workman is called to pay his wages which the workmen have been deprived of by the illegal or invalid action of the employer.

The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge for committing murder of his wife Churi deceased. The High Court confirmed the conviction and death sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the confession recorded during investigation of a case by a second class magistrate not specially empowered in this behalf could not be put in evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Code') because the time mentioned by Shri Mahajan of the recording of confessional statement was 11 p.m. while the intimation which was given by Mangat Ram PW 10) to the police regarding a murderer having come to the residence of the accused at about 8 a.m., and that the prosecution had failed to prove beyond any manner of doubt that Joginder had been born to her as a result of her adulterous conduct. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The statement recorded by the magistrate is inadmissible in evidence because it was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [910G H] 2. It is also the case of the prosecution that shortly before the occurrence, the accused enquired from the deceased regarding the father of the boy and the deceased thereupon abused him. The fact that the relations of the deceased with the deceased, ts would be shown hereafter. were strained would, in the absence of any cogent explanation by the accused, point to his guilt. [1010B] 3. It was not the case where the accused suspected the fidelity of Churi, before the visit of the police to the house of Shri Mahajan. The evidence on record establishes beyond any doubt that the accused on the night of occurrence at about 10.30 p. m. went to the village of the complainant and stayed with him without the child. It cannot be accepted because there is nothing to show that the police was aware of the murder of Churu deceased before the visits of the said accused to the place of occurrence. [1110C] 4. The circumstance that the witnesses were not specially empower in this respect, point of time when they were murdered, clearly point to the conclusion that it was the accused and none else who caused injuries, to Churideceased as a consequence of which she died. It would also be difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with him with the Khokhri and the fact that he had gone to see film show at Kotkhai leaving his wife alone at the house. The accused was not in any way responsible for the murder. [1210D] 5. It has also been established by the evidence of Mangat Ram (PW 10) and Shri Mahajan (PW 15) that the deceased was with Churi in the house when she was murdered there with the khokhri, tt is proved beyond any reasonable doubt that he was taken by the appellant to be add insult to the injury by an unchaste wife. The conduct of the witnesses clearly points to the inference that they were aware of murder of the Churi. [1310E] 6. It may also be mentioned that the evidence on the record establishes that the dead body of Churl deceased was recovered after the accused had visited the house at about 7 a. m., while the information given by Shri Thakur was entered in the daily diary at 10.50 p.M. while he was murdered with the Kokhri. The prosecution also proved beyond reasonable doubt the fact of the death of Chruri deceased and with which the injuries on the body of the victim, according to Dr. Besides that it is established by evidence of Shri Mangat Ram that the blood stains were found on the clothes of the dead person. [1410G] 7.

The Judgment of the Court was delivered by KASLIWAL, J. The appellant No. 1 secured 29.50 marks in the qualifying examination thus in all 99.46 marks out of 150. The 2nd appellant obtained 24.83 marks in interview and 66.40 marks in viva voce out of 50 marks kept for this purpose. The Government of Karnataka by notification dated 4th April, 1985 invited applications for recruitment of Asstt. Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) for the Public Works Department. The selection was to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the competitive examination and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the K.S.C.S., (Direct Recruitment By Selection) Rules, 1973. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3 were excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., J..T. On a direction given by this Court on 4th September, 1991 the record of the marks awarded to the selected candidates was declared in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the State also submitted that the selection was made according to the Rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. However, the rules are clearly in violation with the dictum laid down by this court in Ashok Kr Yadav & Anr. vsState of Haryana and Ors., [1988] Sup. S.CR., 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Punjab & Ors.. J.T. In view of the fact that the result of the selection is declared in 1988 and only a large number of candidates have been selected on the basi late of 50% marks kept at 15% of the total marks, the appellants before us were bound to be selected on merits as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants in the eligibility examination thusin all 99,46 marks Out of 150 is clearly in breach of the dictum laying down by the Court in the above referred cases and in case the marks for interview out of 100 are clearly marked in violation to the dictum lay down by it in the aforesaid referred cases. Learned Counsel appearing on his behalf submitted that there was no allegation or any malafides against the appellants who were vigilant in making griev ance and approaching the Tribunal in time. It is not necessary to examine the matter in detail inasmuch as 50 marks for written examination out of 200 are clearlyin violation of dictum laiddown by this cour tions. Learned counsels appearing on their behalf submitted, that the ratio laid down in Ashok K Yadav & Others vs State o Haryana & Anr., J.J.T., was fully applicable to the present case and in view of this fact that there is a large majority of candidates who had secured much higher marks at the viva voce Out of 50 Marks kept for the purpose. Learned Senior counsel appearing for the State submitted that as such the percentage for vivavoce as 33% of total marks was not excessive and, in violation o f the decision laid down therein by this Cour t, the present selection was declared as in 1987. It was also submitted on behalf Of the State that the appellants had filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the validity of the selections on the grounds that the marks allotted for viva lvoce as33.3 and that the Selection Committee had already framed new rules, and as such we do not find it necessary to quash the selection on the above ground.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court, on appeal, confirmed the conviction and sentence. In the appeals by special leave, it was contended that the prosecution has failed to establish conspiracy because Yadav was a Member of the Bihar Administrative Service and was posted as Collec tor and District Magistrate in the State of Bihar on 11th April, 1983 Mahesh Narain went to his court to work in the morning and after he finished his work, both he and his brother P.W.62, who were waiting in the chamber of the victim started going down from the first floor of the Collectorate to reach the portico where the Collector 's car was parked. Yadav was also present when Yadav was taken into custody following the raid on the Ashram. The prosecution has further led evidence to show that P.Ws. 1, 2 and 3 were present when the incident had happened. It is not disputed that from th July, 1982 Sadanand was taken in custody following his raid on a temple at the temple of the deity. Yadav had gone to his office to work for the pourtico wherein the Collector had come to work. The police had also recovered the bomb burst recorded the first information given by P. W.62 and sent him to Gopalganj Police Station. So far as Yadav is concerned, there was direct evidence of his involvement and he had also confessed to his guilt. It was further contended that in view of this fact, Sadanand had continuously been detained in jail till the Collector's murder on 11.4.1983, the prosecution could not be held guilty under section 120B of the IPC. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. [413G H] 2. There is no direct link as defined by section 3 of the Act. The chain has to be completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [414C D] 3. The confessional statement of a coaccused is not admissible against other accused persons. [446G H; 414A] 4. There are no direct evidence in every case but it must begin with other evidence adduced by the prosecution and after it has formed its opinion with regard to the quality and effect of the said evidence, then it is permissible to turn to the confession in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the said other evidence. [ 414B] 5. The circumstance that the wife had been called she would not have supported the version that he met her husband P. Ws. 1 and 2 on that day, the story of brib ing the jail officials has been introduced. It must be established and the chain has lo be completed. If the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has tobe established and it is impossible to accept any part of link as an complete one.

The appellants were employed in the respondent company. The appellants were paid wages and dearness allowance prevalent in comparable concerns which are not comparable. In the year 1957, the appellant company was already paying the highest wages in the comparable concerns revised them. On account of certain circumstances, namely that Greaves Cotton & Co. is the controlling company of the other three companies carrying on the same industry, it has been usual to keep the same scales for clerical and subordinate staff in all these concerns. It has been contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal should have taken into account comparable concerns in the same region while fixing wages and Dearness allowance together as it should have done, for the purpose of finding out whether the total wage packet in the appellants ' concerns can bear comparison with the total wages packet including basic wages and bonus payable to factory workmen. The Tribunal has not specifically considered what the totalakd packet would be on the basis of the scales of wages and other comparable concerns. The way in which the Tribunal had dealt with the matter of competition, wages should generally be fixed on the principle that there will be equality in the matter Of competition. But considering that wage scales fixed by the Tribunal as it was at the time of the application of the industry cum region formula, it cannot be said that the total salary packet would not be equal to 15 months wages. The tribunal has also not specifically consider what the minimum wages for these categories in comparable industries were, though it had made comparison with concerns which were not comparable, but the way in Which the Tribunal has dealt with this matter in respect of deduction from gratuity only to the extent of the financial loss occasioned by misconduct in case of dismissal for misconduct. The High Court was in error in applying the industrycum region formula which is the basis for fixing wages for factory workmen as for clerical staff and other staff including factory workmen and the Tribunal therefore should have followed this pattern. In these appeals, it was urged on behalf Of the appellants: (1) that the tribunal has not properly applied the industry Cum region formula in fixing wage scales and dearness allowances; (2) that Grehes Cotton & Company is the Controlling company of all these three companies; but on account of some circumstances, it could not be said to have been wrongly fixed by it much higher in the case of other comparable industries; and (3) that if there are a large number of concerns in this region carrying on similar industry, then comparison should be made with as similar concerns as possible in different lines of business for the purposes of fixing wage scale and dearness Allowance. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The basic wages fixed by an employer is normally higher than the highest in the near relation to the industry. But if there is a large majority of concerns, it would be open to the Tribunal to fix the same rates of dearness allowance for factory employees as for industrial staff; but in doing so the Tribunal must when making comparisons take into account the total Wage packet including Basic wages and plus dearness allowance fixed by them as well as compare it with the Total wage packet of comparable concerns and thus arrive at a just figure for basic wage, for each category of factory workmen, and thus arrived at a reasonable figure for every category of Factory workmen. [520E] 2. The formula in the region is that there are different scales of dearness allowances for clerical employees and other employees including factory workers and the tribunal therefore should take into consideration what the maximum quantum would be. [621B] 3. In fixing wage rates, the Tribunal does not consider what it should do. It may also consider whether the minimum wage fixed by a employer as well in comparable concern is abnormal or so disproportionate as compared to the total amount of financial loss caused by misconduct.

The plaintiffs 1 and 2, who were the legal representatives of Annappa, filed a suit for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof. The trial Court held that the Rajinama executed by Shiddappa did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property, that he was bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking accounts the mortgages had redeemed themselves. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the District Judge holding that the plaintiffs were agriculturists, that they were bound to Pay the amount only under the equitable mortgage and hence, the mortgagees could not claim redemption of Shiddana 's one half share in the suit land. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had failed to appreciate that the defendants 1 to 4 applied to and obtained from this Court a notice of relinquishment on behalf Of Annaappa, and that as Shiddppa was the manager and karta of the joint family, he could not bind Annappala and Tukaram 's share by the Raj in his written statement and, therefore, operated to extinguish the equity of redemption. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court had failed in appreciating that under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code as Shudappa was the registered occupant, the RajInama executed a transfer of title from the mortgagors to the mortgagees and, consequently, he did not acquire title by adverse possession. [723C] 1.2 The plaintiffs 1 to 3 were admittedly agriculturists, and the defendants could not have acquired title by relying upon the entire occupancy and amounted to a relinquishment of the rights of both the brothers Shiddhappa and Annaiah. [761G H; 723A] 2.1 In the matter of passing the Rajonama, the notice of relinquished on behalf o any occupant must necessarily be a notice on behalfof all occupants or any particular occupant other than the 701 registered occupant. The notice of abandonment on behalf, must necessarily mean a notice upon behalf of all occupants and that in the absence of any specific pleading and cogent proof that a notice given by the registered owner must necessarily have been a notice to the other occupants so as to effect their interest in the occupancy. [758G] 2:2 In the instant case, the defendants did not purport to file, the same on behalf or for the effect of his being the registered tenant and his name shall thereupon thereupon be substituted in the records for that of the previous registered occupant; and, in this view of the matter, he acted as karta was nowhere made by the defendants appellants in their written statement. [759D] 3.1 There is sufficient evidence on record that a Notice of relinquishment given by an unregistered occupant must invariably be a notices on behalf and of all allottees or any specific occupant other to whom such notice may be given by registered occupant and his names shall thereupon thereafter be substituted In the absence Of any specific pleadings and cogent evidence, that a formal notice of transfer given by a registered occupant must mandatorily be a Notice on behalf for all occupants. That does not mean, in the case of passing of the Rajenama, Shiddaiah was the Manager and karta. [763D] 2 :3 The High court having refused to grant leave to appeal against the decision in so far as it upheld the rejection of their claims to Anna arbitration, this case of Shudana did not fall within section 74 Of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1948. [762G H] 3:4 In the present case, there are more occupants than one, the notices of relinquishment must be given to all occupants including the 701 Registered occupant. That is not the case in the instant matter.
