XV of 1948) so as to be liable to sales tax at the rate of 10% prescribed inter alia for unclassi fied goods and not at the rates specified in the Schedule to the Notification and (2) whether ribbon being an accessory anti not a part of the typewriter is not an accessory but an essen tial part of a typewriter. The High Court quashed the levy on carbon paper as it related to the levy of tax on carbonpaper at 6% and 9 per cent prescribed interalia for typewriters and parts thereof by Notification No. Sales Tax Act, 1948. In appeal to this Court it was contended that carbon papers are not an integral part of an automotive process but they are merely a paper which is used for printing, writing or packing etc., and therefore, will not come within the expression 'paper other than hand made paper ' as envisaged by entry 2 of the aforesaid Notification. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The word ' paper ' in the common parlance means paper which has been used for bearing, writing, or printing, or for packing, or cover ing the walls. [7A B] 1.2 The word "paper ' in item 2 of Schedule to U.P. Sales tax Act, 1947 and that sale of stencil paper is not a component of a machine but a part thereof which is intended to be used for making the goods fit for human consumption. [8C D] 1:3 The word `paper ' means a paper or a paper in the same way, ribbon is not merely a part or a part and therefore would not come under the expression "paper other like hand made papers". [8D E] 1 :4.1 In popular parlance, the word " paper" in item No. 3 of Schedule II to the U. P. Sales Act, 1963 as it stood at the time relevant to the year 1966 67 was understood as meaning a sub stance which is meant by a typewriter in the commer cial sense. Typewriters are being sold in the market without the typewritten tial element so as not to attract tax as per entry 18 of the Schedule thereto. [9E] 1.:5.1 It is clear that carbonpaper is not paper as envisaged under entry 2(a) of the Notification. [10F G] 1.(6) The word used in item 3 of the schedule to the Act or the Rules, and as such, will be given the meaning which it has in 'ordinary parlance. Paper, as understood in common parlance, is the paper which was used for producing printing, write, writing and packing etc. [11E] 2.2 In popular sense, the words 'popular sense ' that sense which people conversant with the sub ject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. Typilyriters, are being selling in the markets without the typing skill of printing, written or printed. [12F G; 13A] 2:3 In popular usage, the term 'paper' has not been defined either in the U P. General Sales Tax Rules, 1963 or in the Rules and, as such it has to be given meaning which they conversant with sub jection (1) of section 5(1).

The appellant Mills was a registered Sugar Mill at Amroha. The respondents 1 to 4 were employed by the appellant Mills at Moradabad in a business of manufacturing sugar and allied products. On February 2, 1955, the General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents 1 and 4 from service on the ground that 117 920 they had disobeyed their orders of transfer and thus they were guilty of misconduct under Standing Order No. " " " The appellant Mills challenged the said order before the Labour Appellate Tribunal which held that the management was within its rights and that as the respondents I to 4 had disobeying the order of the management, they were properly dismissed by the management. The High Court set aside the finding of the State Industrial Tribunal holding that the respondent had not disobeyed his order of transfer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the right to transfer an employee by an employer from one post to another is implicit in every contract of service and that, therefore, the order dismissing them was illegal. HELD: (1) The right to be transferred by an employee from one concern to another was implicit in each contract of employment between the employer and the employees. [922 D] (2) The question whether a person has the right or not to transfer his employee to another, place where he chooses to start (4) 925 a business subsequent to the date of the employment. If an employer employed a person it was implicit that the employer had the right of transfer him to another. [822 E] (3) The mere fact that the appellant has no such right is not sufficient to point out that in all the said decisions the workers had been employed in a trade or concern and the question whether arose was whether in the circumstances of each case the transfer from one branch to another could be deemed to be an implied condition of service. [888 A B] (4)(a) The only connection between the two is that there was no express agreement between the appellant and the respondents where under the appellant had the rights to transfer their employees from one place to another of his in the same line was situated, unless there was an express condition to the contrary in the contract of appointment. [89B] (b) The respondent in the instant case has no right to the transfer of an employee if he has the power to do so under the contract or under any statutory provisions.

The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling various products. The respondent company had been paying contribution to the Employees ' State Insurance Corporation on certain terms and conditions, but it did not pay any contribution to its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The appellant company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of Chapter V A of the . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the contribution payable under Chapter V is a fee and its levy is illegal as the Act does not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the employees as sine qua non for the purpose of payment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the special contribution in Chapter VA is a tax and therefore, the provisions of Chapter IV A are in force. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The amount of contribution directed to be made by the employer under the or other similar payment or benefit under various social welfare legislations must either be labelled as a tax or a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. [723C] 2. The payment of special contribution under Chapter IV is a measure of service and it does not require any further consideration. It is not necessary that the rendering should be done by the employee himself on the employer, in due course, when the scheme becomes fully operative in all areas. For a start the scheme is confined to a few areas and though special contribution is levied from all employers wherever they be, in the case of employers who straightaway receive the benefits of the insurance scheme, their rate of contribution is higher while in the cases of employers whose rate of contributions is lower. [823D] 3. The contribution payable by an employer under section 23 of the Act constitutes only a fee or a special contribution which is to be utilised for the benefits to be given to the employee under the Act. [924E] 4. The employees ' State insurance Corporation should be established. [1024B] 5. The scheme becomes operative in every area and though Special contribution is collected from all employer wherever they are, in order, to attain credibility or not, in accordance with the provisions contained in section 28 of the , its rate of contribute is higher. [ 1024C] 6. The Act does contemplate the giving of any benefits to the workmen under the various social Welfare legislations which may be levied by the Parliament, by the Legislature of any State and by both. It would not be necessary to retain this Chapter. [1125D] 7. The provisions of section 28 are in operation when the Scheme becomes fully operational in all area. For the start the schemes is confined only a few Areas and thoughSpecial contribution is charged from all employees wherever they were, in case of employer who straightaway received the benefits under the scheme, its rate is higher whereas in the present case, the amount of contributions directed to been made by an employee under section 28 is lower while in case where employers who mechanically receive the benefit of the scheme are not yet received the benefit. [ 1125E] 8. The liability to pay contribution under section 25 of the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 is on the principal employer and it has been so laid down in argument that the payment of contribution made by a employer under Chapter VI is higher than that in the absence of any specific statutory provision, its rates of contribution are lower while the case for employers who alone receive the amounts of the benefits. [1106B] 9. The High court was right in holding that section 25(1) of the said Act does contemplates the rendering or of any services to the appellant Company or its employees on the establishment and maintenance of hospitals, dispensaries and other institutions and the provisions thereof are in accordance therewith. [109C D] 10.

In view of the aforesaid conclusion, this petition for special leave is against the judgment dated 2.9.1987 of the High Court dismissing the petitioners ' writ petition (M.P. No. 3308 of 1985). The petitioners claim that they are surplus to the requirement of the Project, they do not have any specific job to do, they are Surplus to the establish ment and merely kept on the roll on humanitarian ground. It has also been stated at the hearing before us that a Voluntary Retirement Scheme offering considerable amount to these daily rated workmen has been framed, which is Annexure R V to the counter affi davit. This document shows the amount of retrenchment com pensation and the ex gratia payment offered to the 63 daily rated workers under this Scheme. The 54 petitioners are included therein. It was stated at t he hearing before the High court that 9 out of these 63 daily wagers mentioned in Annexure R VI to the writ petition were given the benefit of the Voluntary Retirement scheme framed by respondent No. 2 and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues. The High Court rejected the petitioners' claim and held that the petitioners are not regular employees, they did not have a specific job for them. In view thereof, this is not the position. This petition must, therefore, fail. In spite of our above conclusion, keeping in view the offer made on behalf of respondent No 2 in the counter affidavit together with Annexure R IV thereto which was reiterated at the heating before us, we direct that all 63 daily wager mentioned in the aforesaid Annexure RV to the Counter Affidavit be given the benefits of Voluntary Retirement Schemes framed by respondents No. 1 and 2 and others be paid their specified amounts therein. Subject to this direction, the special leave petition is dismissed. No costs. P.S. Petition dismissed.

The plaintiffs were the appellants before this Court. The suit out of which the appeal arises was brought by the appellants claiming title to and recovery of possession of a property known as the Azambad Tea Estate which comprised about 378 acres of land in Touzi No. Ltd. claim to have purchased the entire 16 as. share in the property at a Court sale in pursuance of a decree obtained by them against Kazi Mohammed Ismail, the eldest son of Azam Ali. The appellants contended that when by the sale in execution of the mortgage decree obtained on the basis of the decree obtained in pursuance thereof and of the court sale in Execution of that decree, the co heirs were estopped from questioning the validity of the mortgaged property and that the suit was not maintainable as it was barred by 0. r. 13(i) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held, further, that the plaintiffs were precluded by 0 r.13(i), when the sale was effected and Pir Baksh who was examined as a witness admitted this fact. The plaintiffs were estopped by 0l. r., 13(ii) of Order 1, Rule 10 of the C.P.C. in proving the facts pleaded by them. The mere fact that the property conveyed under exhibit 12(i)(a) was Ashfaq 's 2 as. 212, cannot be a ground to reject the plaint as frivolous. The High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit on this ground. The trial Judge held that the appellants were precluded from questioning their title and that in conse quence the sale of the property in execution passed the entire 17 as. shares to the purchasers.

The appellant was tried for the offence of murder under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, who acquitted him. The High Court held that the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) had not been complied with, and that the omission was not sufficient to 37 290 vitiate the trial unless the accused succeeded in showing that they had been prejudiced in their defence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the provisions contained in sections 173 and 207 A(3), were not mandatory; (2) the omission on the part of police officers to fully comply with the provisions aforesaid of those sections, had caused prejudice to the accused in the interest of justice, the court should reopen the proceedings by insisting upon full compliance with the requirements of section 173(1)(a) and (3) of the Code. HELD: 1. The omission on a part of the police officer, to fully complied with the provision of those provisions, had resulted in prejudice to accused in his defence; and (4) the irregularity is curable by reference to section 537 of the code as no case of prejudice has been made out. [620 E] 2. It was only after the conviction and sentences of the accused persons by the learned Sessions Judge that the accused got the necessary copies of the depositions of the prosecution witnesses, in the Sessions Court before whom such proceedings are brought, to 293 see that all the information for the proper conduct of their defence, are furnished. The defect is ctifiable by reference from section 537(4), and sub section (3). [621 E] 3. It has not been argued, and there is no scope for the argument, that the irregularity was curable By reference to sections 173, 207A and other sections of the Cr.P., it has not caused prejudice. The error is c jurisdictional by reference, and the defect is material by reference. [721 E F] 4. It is only after a conviction and sentence of the person who had been injured that the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective. Certainly, if it is shown, in a particular case, on behalf Of the accused person that the omissions on the parts of police officer concerned or of the magistrate before whom the committal proceedings had fended, have caused prejudice, to the appellant in the interests of justice. [821 E H] 5. It cannot be said that the defect was ctifiable at the time when the committal proceeding had faded, has caused prejudice and it is not possible for the court to reopen the trial by insisting on full compliance therewith. The irregularity is material at the same time to safeguard the interests and of justice and the court may reopen the proceeding by insistingupon full compliancewith the provisions thereof.

The appellant Municipality was carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of cement. The Municipality issued a notice under section 153A(1) of the Act directing the person to whom the notice has been issued to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in such manner as may have been previously approved by the Government and as mentioned in the notice so that rendering saline or corrupting the water of wells, tanks, ponds or other water receptacles, or prejudicially affecting the fertility of the soil may be stopped. The appellant contended that the existence of a nuisance was not one which ought to be set aside but that it should be a reasonable restriction to the exercise of the fundamental right under article 19(1)(C) to prevent a nuisance which would affect the public health and fertility or materially affect the fertile of the water. Held, that the provisions of section 153 A of the , are not attracted in the case of a notice by the Municipality with the previous approval of the Government. The Special Officer was bound to enquire into the matter and make his report both as to the existence or absence of a reasonable nuisance before a notice is issued to the person concerned. The scheme under section 154A is to permit the Municipality, if it is satisfied that a nuisance exists to the satisfaction of the Municipality as to whether a nuisance in the terms of sub section (1) exists to issue a notice requiring the person who has issued the notice to showcause why he shall not be ordered to arrange the discharge. The procedure under section 155A is different from the procedure under sections 153A and 153A. The provisions of sections 153 A and 153 A are distinct and separate. It is true that before the appellant could be called upon to comply with the requisition of the respondent Municipality involving several lakhs of rupees as expenditure the Special Officer ought to have enquired into the dispute and make its report both in regard to the, existence of the nuisance and the direction as to how the effluent should be discharged. The special officer was bound by the procedure prescribed under sections 155A and 154 A. In the present case, the appellant did not raise any objection before the Special Judge that the notice issued by the respondent municipality was invalid because it was based on a misconception of the fact that the Municipality had no power to issue such a notice. The order of the Special officer declining to go into the question whether the nuisance in question existed or not did not arise as the person, who had issued the requisition, did not deny the existence thereof and is prepared to comply therewith the direction to arrange his discharge of effluent in the manner specified by the notice.

The appellant was found in possession of railway stores which were being used or intended to be used for by the railway. The prosecution examined two witnesses, namely, (1) Moyalal Rostagir; (2) M Royalal Rondagir and (3) M.S. Jain; (4) M/s. Jain & Sons; (5) M S. Jain and Sons; and (6) M G. Jain, who were the employees of the appellant. The trial court acquitted the appellant on the ground that the evidence was not sufficient to prove that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the prosecution had failed to establish that the goods belonged to any particular railway administration and that the appellant had purchased the property in open market where goods of this 189 kind were usually sold or that he had bought them from someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the facts in this case. Held, further that the burden shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his possession of the same. The onus shifts to him to prove whether there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. In such a case it is only when the burden in respect of this is discharged by the prosecution that the onus shifts on the accused that the accused has to establish affirmatively how he came by the same, he must first adduce evidence to show that he was in possession thereof. He may for instance, show that the documents were not correct and that it was necessary to prove the identity of the goods or some, peculiarity of the articles not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Some evidence will have to be led to the effect that the items mentioned in his report were being actually used or were intended to been used by the Railway. The burden shifts on to the prosecution whether the goods belong to any of the railways in India. If the accused fails to offer any satisfactory explanation of his ownership it is he who has bought them at a later stage and that he has purchased the goods in open markets where goods are usually sold, or that the railway administration has no further use of them be they new or old as in the case where they have become unserviceable or outmoded no person can be charged with an offence under section 3 in respect thereof. The evidence 'in the case before us did not establish that there was any cause for suspicion of stores being seized or obtained illegally. The appellant must also prove that he purchased the articles in open open market when goods were found to conform to the specifications of the Indian Railway Standards they held that they belonged to a railway administration but only those which were used or meant to be use for the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway.

The appellants filed a suit for ejectment of the respondents from the demised shop in Jaipur. The respondent filed an application under section 13(1) (a) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 claiming that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. Therein the definition of 'Tenant ' was amended by Section 3 Clause (vii), thus: "(viii) "tenant" means (a)(i) a person by whom or on whose account or behalf rent is, or, but for a contract express or implied, would be payable for any premises to his landlord including the person who is continuing in its possession after the termination of the contractual tenancy and no order or decree for eviction will be passed against a tenant unless any ground which entitles the landlord to get an order or award for possession specified in the Act is established. (ii) a tenant who continues to remain in possession even after the expiry of the termi nation of his tenancy otherwise than by a decree for evic tion passed under the provisions of this Act, continues to have an estate or inter est in the tenanted premises and continued to do the business till date of the death o f the tenant. (iii) a contractual tenant on the terminationof the contractual lease is by virtue of the provisions contained in section 13 (1) of Rajasthan Premises Act, 1955. The appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in the lease hold right held by the respondent on his death. The tenancy rights were heritable and the heirs of the deceased tenant were entitled to enjoy the protection under the Act. The respondents filed a written statement denying the averments made in the plaint. They contended that the suit was not maintainable as the appellants had no right, title or interest in it. They also denied the relationship of landlord and tenant between them. The trial court decreed the suit for eviction on the ground that the appellants were not entitled to continue as statutory tenants. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and decreed the plaintiff 's suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The definition of "Tenant" in section 2(1)(iii) is that a contractual tenancy on the happening of which it has created this right has thought it fit in the case of heirs of such tenant who have been, in the cases of heirs, become entitled by virtue o the provisions Of the Act to inherit the status and position of the statutory tenant on his demise. [419B] 1.2 The definition does not indicate that the heirs are entitled to occupy an estate/ inter est as a matter of course under the ordinary law of land and he is entitled to remain possession even thereafter after determination of the contract tenancy and any order or judgment for eviction would be passed in respect of such premises as member of his family upto his death, [420C] 1:3. The mere fact that in the statute no provision has been made with regard to the heirs o f tenants in respect o commercial tenancies on the Death of the person after termination of tenancy does not show that the legislature intended that the heir of such tenants should enjoy an estate and inter est, in respect Of commercial premises are heritable. [519D] 1.:4. The definition is wide enough to include all the heirs who have become entitled to enjoying the protection afforded under the Rent Acts not liable to be evicted as a matters of course Under the Act, an irrepara ble mischief which the Legislature would never have intended was likely to be caused. [620E] 2.1 In the instant case, the tenancy rights are heritable and they are heritable on the demise of the appellants after termination.

The appellant Board is willing to extend the benefits of the Contributory Provident Fund to all workmen other than those who are covered by the Act and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act, 1952 should be extended to any additional categories of workmen ? The Industrial Tribunal rejected the claim on the ground that the appellant Board was willing to provide for taxation and for development rebate reserve. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the benefit of the Employees ' Provident Fund Scheme should be extend to all the workmen other including those who were covered by both the Schemes similar. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Tribunal had to consider whether the burden of provident fund and gratuity could be met without undue strain on the financial position of the employer. It was not open to the appellant to raise a loan for the purposes of the Act. [48B] 2.1 In that case it would have to be borne by the employer like the burden, that burden will have to been borne by it like the onus of provident Fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer because it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserve. [49C] 2:2 The Tribunal was right in holding that the burden had to be discharged by the workmen like those who arc covered by one scheme under section 66 and required to be repaid. [50E] 3.1 The Board should extend the benefit to all employees other than the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees' Provident Fund Rules apply. [51F] 2(i) The Tribunal has to consider the financial capacity of the employee. It is not open for an ordinary Commercial concern to Credit any amount directly to the credit of any amount, to the gratuity reserve. Therefore it will result in some reduction in profits and loss to other amounts to the development rebate reserves. [52G] 3:2 In the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the board, it could not be held that the onus was calculated and it was open to a ordinary commercial approach to credit an amount to a fund to be called the Development Fund to be utilised for (a) purposes beneficial, in the opinion of the Tribunal. [53F] 3.(ii) The Board must carry on its operations so as not to incur a loss. It should. be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [54G] 4.3 In the instant case it was found that the financial status of the respondent workmen was not borne out by the provisions of the statute. The Board had to provide the benefits to be made available to its employees. Therefore, the main question for consideration by the Tribunal was whether the benefit should be granted to all those who have been covered by either the same scheme under which the employer is entitled to receive the principal and interest of any loan proposed to be raised by the Board or not? [54A] 5.4 The Board has to take its operations as far as possible, but if it is not it would having to be met by loans on which interest will have been paid and deduction of interest so paid will haveto be taken into account in calculating the profits. [55G] 6.5 In the present case it is clear that the workmen of respondent No. 1 were covered under the Act, and therefore there could be no discrimination between the appellant and respondent No., 2.

The respondent, a wife, filed an application under section 125 of the Code of 1973 for maintenance. The Magistrate rejected the application and held that the husband having been found to be impotent was not a just cause for the refusal of the wife to live with her husband. The High Court dismissed the revision application holding that the ground of impotence was no good ground for the wife 's refusal to live separately from her husband merely because she was impotently and unable to discharge his marital obligation, this would amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a just ground as contemplated by the proviso to sub section (3) of section 125. The respondent filed an appeal before the High Court which differed from the view taken by the Magistrate and held against the order of the Metropolitan Magistrate. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the wife having been impotably and unable not to live in her husband, she was entitled to maintenance if she refused to live together with her father merely because her husband was impetent and unable or unable to perform his marital obligations, and hence the wife is not entitled to the grant of maintenance. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 488 of the Criminal Procedure Code are very wide in scope and they do not require any detailed examination of evidence. [723C] 2.1 Section 125 of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1949 provides that it is incumbent on the Magistrate to consider the grounds of refusal and to make an order of maintenance if he was satisfied that there was just ground for doing so. The words "any person" in section 125(3) are wide enough to include a husband who has contracted marriage with another woman or keeps a mistress this would not be a reasonable ground for refusing to live by the husband even though she is forcing her in a situation where her physical and mental well being might be adversely affected, as there is no intention on the part of the husband to inflict that cruelty without demur and be satisfied with a grab to bite and some rags to clothe her and a roof over her head. [823D] 2:2 The words used in section 488(3)(a) are very comprehensive enough to cover cases where a wife refuses to live separate from her father when it appears to the court that there is a just reason for doing not so. [924E] 3.1 In the instant case, the High Courts have overlooked the legal effect of the second proviso to section 125 and have ignored the legal position of the two High Courts on this aspect of the matter and in this connection pointed out the scope of the Amendment of 1949 under which a wife could refuse to live along with her parents. [1024F] 3:2 In the present case, it is proved that the respondent was impolent and was unable to live independently from her deceased husband when she refused, and was satisfied with an grab tobite and certain rags thereto. The conduct and acts of the respondent from which the Court may draw the inference of neglect or refusal to maintain the wife would be a very just ground within the meaning of the first proviso so as to make the refusal for live with the husband. [1124F G] 3 :3 In the facts of this case, there is nothing in the Criminal procedure Procedure (amendment) Act which may show that it would not amount to either legal or mental cruelty. The Courts cannot compel the wife merely because a husband has contracted a marriage with other woman or kept a mistook for her husband when it seems to have been impetant and unable, to discharge her marital obligation.

The plaintiff was the owner of certain lands in village Kathiawar which was subse quently known as the State of Saurashtra. The Government of India, by Resolution No. 77 dated 29th February, 1948 vested in the Municipality the land of the Parade Ground for this use that was handed over to the Saurashtra Government on 7th July, 1952 and the structures vested in it till recently. The plaintiff claimed that the lands were vested in them by the State Government on the date of Financial integration and when the State Of Saurashtra, (as it was then known) required the land for this purpose that was delivered to the Municipality on 7 th July, 1951 by the military engineers of the Government of Gujarat. The trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the vesting of the title in the Municipal records had come to be vested in a Municipality under Resolution 37 dated 19th January, 1948 and that therefore it was not necessary either to deal with the argument of the defendants that the property was vested and is in the possession of Government of Rajasthan. The High Court also held that since the suit was for possession based on title to the suit property and the defendants had denied title, of the plaintiff even if the defendants in possession had not pleaded adverse possession, of this land within 12 years prior to 3rd March, 1964 when the suit were filed, the suit is liable to be dismissed as barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit lands which were in occupation of the Municipality were not vested in Government and that the possession was handedover by the Government only on 7.7.1952 and that since there was no legal possession with the plaintiff, it is necessary for the Court to give a finding on title of the plaintiffs even if it had not been taken by the Municipali ty at any time. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Resolution No.. 77 dated 19 th January,1948 vested in State Government only a right or an authorisa tion to sell the land as representing the Government but not a vesting of title itself in the municipality. [723C] 2. The resolution No. 37 dated 10th August, 1965 vested in Central Government under Resolution No,. 77 dated 30th February 1948 and Resolution No.' 77 dated 31st March, 1948 vest in the plaintiff the land which was stated to be in their possession on 7 7. 1952 for use. [823D] 3. The vesting of this property in the State Govt. only on 5th May, 1952 would go to show that physical possession was with the defendant but also there could not be any legal possession without the plaintiff as the title to this land is not vested and therefore it is essential for the court to give an finding on ownership of the land itself in accordance with law. [923C D] 4. The suit notice dated 10 th August, 1950 was not intended to be vesting in its full amplitude, but was meant only to appoint the Municipality as agent of the State to dispose of the property as representing Government but also that it was meant to appoint a Municipality as agents of the Central Government and not a vested owner to dispose off the land. [1023D E] 5. The resolutions No. 78 dated 19nd January, 1949 by the Central Govt. were only a step in the direction of the High Court to dispose the land on 7 July,1952. [1124F G] 6. In this case, there was evidence to show whether physical possession had been taken over or not. There is no evidence to indicate that physical Possession was with Government of Saurashtra and if so, it was necessary for him to trace briefly the constitutional history of accession and 225 integration of the Indian States with the Union of India. [1224F] 7.

The appellant was employed to exercise a public duty. He was performing the duties of a metal examiner known as Chaser in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer and was thus performing a public function. The appellant was, therefore, an officer within the meaning of section 21(9) and therefore could not be convicted of the offence under section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947. Held, that the decision in 12 Bombay High Court Reports 1, concerned an Izaphatdar, that is a lessee of a village who bad undertaken to keep an account of its forest revenue and pay a certain proportion to the Government, keeping the remainder for himself and the question whether such a person was an officer of the Government within the ambit of section21(9), Indian Penal Code. The decision in 13 Bombay High Courts Reports 1 and 2, referred to. (ii) The appellant could not fall within the terms of the last portion of clause (9) of section 20, Indian Penal code which declared "every officer in the service or pay of the 'Government" within the term of that expression in section 21 of the Indian Penal Act. [696 B] (iii) The decision of the Lahore High Court in Ahad Shah vs Emperor(1) was understood by the learned Judges of the Calcutta High Court as meaning "every person employed to perform any public duty". The appellant, therefore was not an officer in service or paid by Government to do public work.

The properties, if my, which are exempt from the attachment and Sale in revenue recovery proceedings adopted under the said act would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said law. [564B] 3:3 In view of the clear language of section 59 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, it is clear from the opening words of sub section 1 of section 58 that the attachment levied upon, and sold, and notified in pursuance thereof would be liable to confiscation and sale.
