[561G] 2.3 The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizen to supply information to the Press, such For example, rule 552A provides that every prisoner under a sentenced sentence of imprisonment shall be allowed such interviews and other communications with his relatives, friends, legal advisers and approved religious ministers. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore we do not see any reason why the petitioner could not be denied the opportunity to interview a condemned prisoner. [562G] 3. The existence Of a free press does not mean that they can always and without good reasons be denied opportunity to interviews a condemned person. [565B C] 4.1 In the instant case, the existence of an free Press did not imply nor spell out anything legal obligation upon the citizens, to supply Information to the press, Such for example is rule 552 A also provides that no newspapermen will be allowed. But it does not provide that any newspapermen shall be denied access to a means of knowledge. If it is thought necessary that such a search should be taken, a person who desires to interview an condemned prisoner may have to subject himself or herself to the search in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews.

The appellant was the Receiver of the estate on January 19, 1950. On reorganisation of the Judicial Administration in Tripura, the suit was transferred to the court of the Subordinate Judge, Agartala. The bond was executed both be the Receiver and the appellant in favour of "Sri Ramani Mohan Goswami the District Judge, Tripura. The surety bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the District judge. The appellant filed an application for damages to the extent of Rs. 22 of 1956 which came into, force on December 31, 1950 being the date when the Receiver took possession of the property. On August 26, 1950 the appellant made a representation to the Subordinate judge praying that the amount due under the bond should be recovered from him. The Subordinate Judge rejected the objections and directed that the damages awarded to the respondent be recovered. The appeal was dismissed by the District Court on December 18, 1959. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the surety bond could be enforced only by or at the instance of the presiding officer of the court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The bond executed by the appellant as a Receiver and consequently the surety bonds cannot be enforced merely by or against the Receiver 's negligence in the performance of his duties. [520 E] 2.2 The bond is executed both by the Receiverand the appellant. It is impossible to accept the contention that the Receiver owed no duty or obligation in respect of the tea garden due to the Receiver economically and efficiently. [621 B] 3.3 The surety bonds are a part and parcel of the proceeding pending before him. It was impossible to accepted the contention of the respondent that the bail bond could not be enforced by or by at the behest of the Receiver financially and efficiently, because the surety surety had rendered himself liable as a surety for the fulfilment of the conditions imposed on the Receiver under the orders passed by the court in any suit or in any proceeding J consequent thereon. [721 E] 4.4 The bond could also cover the loss caused to the tea gardens due to his negligence in performance of the duties the appellant is liable to make good the loss sustained to the Tea garden by the 360 fire. [822 C] 5.5 In view of section 150, the Subordinate Judges were entitled to exercise the same powers in the matter of the enforcement of the bond as the District Magistrate himself. The condition imposed on them was a component part of that proceeding pending at the time when the receiver took possession is not an integral part of his proceedings pending in the court and it is impossible for him to enforce the bond. [820 E] 6.6 In view, the surety Bond cannot be executed against the appellant to the tune of Rs 22 of 1955 which rendered itself personally liable under the terms of the bonds. The High Court was right in holding that the order for the recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the receiver could not have been enforced merely because the bond was signed on August 26 1950 being a part or parcel of proceedings pending at that time. [824 E] 7.7 In view the fact that the bond executed on August 25, 1950 relates back to January 22, 1950 and is enforceable only by the or at his instance, it is difficult to accept that the appellant rendered himself personally liable for the loss occasioned to the estate due to him by the fire. The bonds are executed both in favour and in favour by the presiding Officer of the Court. [825 E] 8.8 In view Of the fact, the bond could have been executed only by and at the place where the Receiver had taken possession of it. [828 F] 9.9 In the instant case, the appellant was put in possession of a tea garden which he owed no obligation in relation to the affairs of the Tea gardens.

The appellants were dealers in food grains. They purchased wheat from the Regional Food Controller and supplied to the Regional Supply Controller, who was a dealer in foodgrains. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the turnover of wheat by the appellants. The Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales Tax referred the following questions to the High Court for opinion (1) Whether the sales made to the State Government were sales within the meaning of section 2(h) of the U P. (10) of section 3 means the money consideration for sale of goods, ,and "where under a contract of sale property in the goods is transferred from the seller to the buyer, the contract is called an agreement to sell" [sub section (3) of Section 4]. The High Court held that the transactions of supply did not result in sales and were on that account not liable to pay sales tax. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the sales effected to the Controller under cl. 5 of the Order were sales outside the purview of the definition of the word 'sale' as defined in section 2 (h) and therefore, the transactions could be regarded as a sale. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD : 1. The expression "sale" is used in the sense that it includes every kind of movable property, whether movable or immovable, and also every kind which may be necessary for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act. It is not possible to hold that even if the liberty of contract in relation to the fundamentals of the transaction is completely excluded a transaction of supply of goods pursuant to directions issued under a Con trol Order may be regarded either as a sales or as a contract. [610B] 2. The definition of 'sale ' in section 3(h), does not justify the view that even though the liberty granted by cl. (e) of sub section (2) of s. 3 is completely exclusion a transaction which is totally excluded a sale, but where the liberty is contract between the parties, to the transaction of sale is completely exclude a transaction from a supply of property pursuant to direction issued under an Conciliator Order may also be regarded to be a sale and therefore a sale is not taxable. [710C] 3. The tax payer was under the Control Order compelled to carry out the directions of the Controller and it had no volition in the matter. It had no option in the matters but subject to restrictions, the transaction could be treated as a 'sale'. New India Sugar Mills ' case(1) does not support the view taken by the High court that even when the liberty was contract in respect of the fundamental of the transactions is completely excludes a transaction Of supply of wheat. [810E] 4. The levy order, upon the licensed dealer was imposed a liability to deliver half the quantity of wheat procured or purchased by him every day beginning with the date of commencement of the order until such time as the State Govt otherwise directs. Delivery of the wheat has to be given by the dealer to the Central Government otherwise directs and thereafter fifty per cent of the quantity thereof on hand, and he had also to supply to the Government 50% of the stock of wheat purchased or purchased from him every days beginning with date of the commencement of this Order till such time, as the Central Govt otherwise direct. Delivery was not in any contract but in the statutory order. [910C D] 5. The word 'Sale' is used for the purposes of carrying on business and it includes all kinds which may or may be required for the execution of a works contract.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The report of the Advisory Board is not a sufficient answer to say that the detaining authority can on its own satisfaction detain a person for a longer period than three months unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are or have been qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court, has reported before the expiration of the said 206 period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. [723C] 1.2 The report though not made within three months of the date of detention shows that the maximum period within which the detaining Authority can on his own satisfaction release a person is three months from the date o f detention under the earlier detention order, but it is no answer to saying that the representation made by the detenu was disposed of before the hearing of the case. If the report of such an Advisory board is obtained within three days, it is not answer to the say that there was sufficient cause fo r the detention of the person. [823C D] 1:3 The question whether a reference to an Advisory Boards is to be made within 3 months of its date of the second order of detention, does not arise at all because it is within three weeks from the day of its report. If a reference is made within one month, it would be no answer for saying that there were sufficient cause to continue the detention. The fact that the report was obtained before the hear ing of the appeal and the subsequent order of the High Court dated August 7, 1986 shows that there has been no Advisory Board in existence to which a reference could be made under the Act and whose report could be obtained as required by the Constitution. [923C E] 1 :4. The question to which the Advisory board has to apply its mind is whether on the date when the detention order was made, there was no sufficient cause or for the detention o f the person when the order of his detention was passed, but we see no justification for extending the jurisdiction of the advisory Board to the consideration of the question as to whether it is necessary to continue such detention of a person beyond the period of 3 months after the date on which its report could have been obtained. If there were no fresh facts, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it is outside three months, it being within three month from thedate of detention. If an order of Detention is made before the commencement of the Constitution, it was no answer t o say that it was within 3 days, but if the report is obtained before such commencement, it must be taken to be obtained before that day. [1023C F] 1.:5. The observation of the court to the extent that there are sufficient cause f or the detention, though not so made within two months, is no reason to extend the jurisdiction Of the Advisory Boards to the consider of the questions as to what whether it was necessary to detain a man is three month unless the report shows that on the day when the detained order was passed there was adequate cause for the detaining o r the person to whom the reference could have be secured within three yea. [ 1023C G] 1.(6) The observation in the report though made within four months, but does not mean that the question to be asked as to how the report should be obtained is required to be disposed of within a stipulated period, it cannot be said that the detention must be upheld. If this is so, it will be no end to say whether the representation was made before or after the commencement o r detention under section 3(1) of the Act.

The respondent, a father of the respondent, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of his share in the joint family property. The trial court held that the entire responsibility of solving the dispute was entrusted to him and the petitioner had agreed to such entrustment. In appeal, the High Court dismissed the civil revision application. Hence this petition by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed that both of them should abide by the award dated 20th January 1977 and its interpretation should be left to the arbitrator himself. [723C] 2.2 The conduct, in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case can certainly be construed to be a proper arbitration agreement in terms of section 2(a) of the Act. But in the present context, it is clear that the conduct of both the parties was wholly foreign to its jurisdiction or that the respondent had accepted the award. [823D] 3.3 The conduct and circumstances, of this case can also be construed as a proper Arbitration agreement in accordance with section 2 (a) and (4) of The Act. [820C] 4.4 In the instant case, it was clear that both the petitioner and respondent had agreed not to refer the disputes to arbitration. It is clear from the narration of facts that the petitioner has accepted the acceptance of the award and sought the judgment in terms thereof. Therefore, it cannot be said to be an appropriate arbitration agreement. [829D] 5.4 The conduct on the part of the petitioner that there had been an arbitration clause and by signing the award he could not challenge the award is clearly erroneous.

The appellants were the mortgagees of a property in which the respondent was the mortgagee. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of possession of the mortgaged property on the ground that he had not received the notice dated June 2, 1939, and that the proceedings were barred by limitation. The trial court held that the suit was barred by time. On appeal to the District Judge, the High Court reversed the decree holding that the respondent 's claim to exemption under proviso (ii) to sub section (1) of sec tion 36 of the Act was not an application at all and was therefore not a proceeding in execution within the meaning of section 2(22). The appellants then filed a petition for special leave to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD : 1. A legal interest remained in the mortgagor even when the mortgage was in the form of an English mortgage, and it is not disputed that the interest taken by the mortgagee was not a absolute interest but because a special order was made under Order XXI, rule 57, as amended by the High court. [118 E F] 2. The words "all the rights of the mortgagee" used by their Lordships in the passage quoted above, and they held that in exercise of the powers the Court cannot reopen or otherwise affect a decree of a Court unless such decree is one which was passed in a suit to which this Act applies and ' which was not fully satisfied by January 1, 1939. [119 E F G] 3. The expression "all rights of" used in clause (a) of sub section(5) of section 36 must be construed as including the right transferred to a sub mortgagee under his sub mortgage. [120 A B] 4. The word "all" used is not defined in section 2 (22) of the , and it has to be interpreted in the context in which it occurs. [121 C D] 5. The definition of "proceeding in execution" is wide enough to include a proceeding instituted or pending on that date and includes a proceeding therein. [122 E F; 122 A B].

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The respondents filed O.S. No. 12 of 1954 against one of their sons and another person asking for damages and mesne profits for wrongful trespass on the properties. The trial court decreed O. S. No, 62/54 and decreed O..S. Nos. 63/54, and decreed the suit in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the transfers were made by way of gifts and not in consideration of past cohabitation, and that the subsequent severance of joint status between Venkatacharyulu and his sons could not validate them. HELD: (1) The transfers under exhibit A 1 and A 2 are not hit by sec. 6(h). [446 B] (2) The transactions were made in consideration for past cohabitations, having regard to section 2(d) of the , by reason of the fact that they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubine for her past services. [447 C D] (3) The alienations were not hit under sec.6(h), because they were made without consideration or for immoral purposes, and were by way Of gifts. The transfers were not vitiated by any consideration of cash or delivery of jewels. [548 B] In the instant case, the transfers under exhibits A 1 & A 2 were in reality gift deeds. They were made with consideration of the past cohabitated. [646 C D; 647 E F] (4) The transfer was without consideration and was not hit By sec.2(d). [648 B C] (5) The alienation was without considering or for incor mation, having been made in favour o the appellant, but by way o gift and as such was not vitiated.

The respondent, a widow of the deceased employee of the appellant Life Insurance Corporation, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 issued to her. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the L.I.C. had not made the requisite statement on oath under section 227(3)(vi) of t he Income Tax Ac tation, 1961 and that the order withdrawing the notice was not valid in law. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High court erred in holding that no part of the said amount is due to G.V. Ranade, it was incumbent on the LI.I.,C. to promptly make the requisite statements on oath as contemplated by section 226 (3)(vii) of The Income Tax Officer had not withdrawn the notice issued under clause (vi) thereof, instead of in doing so. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 226(2) of Income Tax, 1961 clearly shows that on a notice thereunder being issued by the I.T.O., in the present case it was obligatory on the part of L. I.C., to make the necessary statement on solemn oath under clause(vi) therein raising an objection on the basis of the registered assignment. It is obvious that the inordinate delay in making the requisite declaration on oath by the L..I. C. cannot be said to be a result of misconstruction of the provision and misappreciation of its liability thereunder. Performance of this statutory obligation by the l.I.'C., in section 226 of the Act lay in its failure to pay to the respondent, instead o n sufficient time without objecting to the demand by denying its liability to the assessee in the manner prescribed in clause (xi) thereof. Performance is not a penalty for delay, but it is a measure of punishment for negligence and misconduct. It may be that the lapse on the face of the record or the conduct of the L.,I.T., in making such an application would have been fatal if the High Curt had not condoned the delay. [623D] 1.2 The mere fact that the notice has been withdrawn by the appellant, does not mean that the amount demanded by the notice is due only to the assignee of the 114 policies to whom the payment thereunder had to be made even according to the stand of the respondent. It would be a case where the lapse was on account of some other reason or the fact that it was on the date when the L,.I.c. made the order, withdrawing the notices under section226(3), the amounts of the matured policies within the time given by the Income tax Act,1961. [723E] 1:3 The mere circumstance that the payment has been made even in pursuance to the Court 's order to enable the L .I.A. cannot justify the inordinate delays in making it. It was not possible for the assignee o f the 114 policy to obtain revocation of the notices by the J.J. and, therefore, clearly shows the intention of the legislature that the delay in filing the statement on r ecordance under section 244(3(vi), should be condoned. [761G] 1.:4 The inordinate delay of making the necessary declaration on solemn affirmation under clause 4 of sub section (3) is the result of misreading of the provisions and mis appreciation of its Liability thereunder. performance of this obligation by L.1.C.. cannot be treated deemed defaulter under clause 3 of section 226, because it involved the likelihood of exposing the L I.I .C. or any of its officers to personal liability has, therefore no merit. [763G] 2.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Civil Service and was appointed as a District Judge in the year 1962. He was promoted to the post of Additional District Judge on January 1, 1963. On February 2, 1963 he was transferred to the State Civil Service. The appellant filed an application under section 29(2) of the Limitation Act for setting aside the order of transfer. The respondent contended that the application was within time and that the period of limitation prescribed by section 12 of the Act had not been extended by the First Schedule to the Limitation act. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that the appellant had failed to comply with the requirements of section 29 (2) and that he had no right to file an appeal under section 116 A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the First Proviso to section 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not apply to a case where the First schedule to the Indian Limitation Act had prescribed any period of Limitation for an appeal and that therefore the application filed by the respondent was within limitation. Held, that in the instant case the Act provides a period of 30 days for an application to set aside an order of the Tribunal under section 115 A of CPC against an order passed by the Tribunal. The proviso to section 25(2)(a) of Code of 1908 does not apply where the special or local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application by any special or Local law prescribes a period for such an appeal. It is only when the special law prescribes that a special or special local law provides for any appeal, appeal and application by a specialor local law it would be attracted by reason of the provisions of section 12(2). The proviso does not prescribe any period for an appeals and therefore it is governed by section 29.

The appellant was a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura. He questioned the validity of the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate declaring Plot Nos. 701 and 702 in the Town Area, Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stand/halting place of Baldev, where the stage carriages were directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get down from the stage carriage vehicles in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. The case of the appellant was that the District Magis trate had no power to appoint any area as a Bus Stand under section 76 of the Act and that he purported to pass the impugned order. It was contended on behalf of the State that the power under section 68(2)(r) of the , Act could be exercised only by the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the district Magistrate. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Regional Transport Authori trate has been authorised by the State Government under section76 of the . [723C D] 2. Section 76 of The , Act confers wide powers on the District Magistrates 'to fix places for the bus stand and to issue a notification fixing a bus stands for purposes of the said Chapter. Such a power should be given specifically by the statute and that the powers to compel persons in charge of motor vehicles to stop only at certain places for purposes o f taking up or setting down passengers was a matter which relating to motor traffic and that there was a specif ic provision in section 68 (2)(i) of . [761G H] 3. The power under Section 76 is confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stand which can only be notified by the regional Transport Authory as held by this Court in T.B. It only authorises the District Judge to exercise the powers under section 71 of the \ , and that power to compel person in charge thereof, which is confined only to the questions of determination o parking places or halting places. [724C D; 723A] 4. The State Transport Authority has been empowered by the Act to fix a bus Stand as a vehicle stand for purposesof the Act. Such an order should be made within the jurisdiction of the Regional transport Authori tion Authority having juris diction under section 78 of the ) . [758G H; 824B D] 5. The District Magiste trate could not exercise the power of fixing a Bus stand under section 77 of the ; and that could be done only by a Regional Transport authority constituted under the Act, which was confined to that question of determining any convenient place or places within the Town area of Baldev ( Mathura) as well as in the State Transport Authorit y. [758C D]. 6. The High Court was, therefore, in error in upholding the impugned orders passed by District Magie trate. [759E F] 7. Section 78 of The . , Act provides that the Regional \ authority shall fix a Bus stands for the purposes of this Chapter. It is not disputed that in the instant case no order has been passed by Regional Transport Officer, Mathura to determine the area in question as a taxi stand and the Dis trict Magistrate cannot be equated with the Regional Trans port Authority constituted under section 70 of the the . The High court was, however, in wrong in upholding that the impugned action was unassailable.

The appellant was driving the truck which was loaded with 75 bags of paddy. The truck was intercepted at Samalkha Barrier along with Head Constable Badan Singh and others. The appellant Malkiat Singh was the cleaner of that truck. As the export of paddy was contrary to law, the Sub Inspector took into possession the truck as also the bags of rice. The trial court convicted all the accused ' persons but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction of the appellant. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there was no attempt on the part of the prosecution to commit the offence of export, and so there was an attempt on their part to commit it. Held, that there had been no attempt at the part or any of the packages, coverings or receptacles in which 'any property liable to be forfeited under the said section is found and all the animals, vehicles, vessels or other conveyances used in carrying the said property shall be forfeited to the Government: Held, further, that the mere preparation on the parts of the truck was a preparation for committing an offence. The sufficiency of the actus reus is a question of law which has led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission of a crime and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt to commit them. In order that a person may be convicted of an attemptto commit an offence, he must be shown first to have 667 had an intention to commit that offence. If any person to whom a direction is given under clause (b) of sub section (4) of section 3 fails to comply with the direction he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year and shall also be liable to fine. The adequacy of the actsus reisus is not a question in law, but an inference of fact depends upon the facts found. In the instant case there was nothing on the record to show that the appellants had knowledge about the necessity or intention of committing an act which constitutes the actu reus of a criminal attempt. The mere preparation for commit an Offence is different from attempt to committing it. In such a case, the sufficiency of actsus rea is a matter of law and not a law. It has been rightly held by this Court in State of Punjab vs Ram Chander Singh, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 896 that there has been no export of rice within the meaning of Para 2(a) of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. The only question which arose for consideration was whether there was any attempt on behalf the part o the appellants to commit an act or not. In this case there had not been any attempt made by the appellant to commit a crime. It was merely a preparation on his part to committing an Offence which constitutes an offence punishable under section 7 of the and the sufficiency thereof is a Question of law arising out of the failure to comply therewith. The absence of such an attempt would constitute an attempt or an attempt at committing it, and as a matter o law a preparation is different form from attempt made to commit offence. In other words, there was not any attempt to export paddy within the ambit of Para2(a). It was only a preparation which constitutes a criminal act.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Company was carrying on business in shares and debentures of the Company. The Managing Agents Agreements were entered into between the two companies. The appellant company claimed that it had earned income from the Company during the chargeable accounting period. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the Sassoons had not earned any part of the Managing Agency commission which had accrued to them under the terms of the managing agency agreements, and that the share accrued to the Sassoonons was not liable to tax in respect of the same. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that the remuneration for the entire year was the income of the assignee and that it was the profits and gains of the business carried on by the appellant company during the relevant accounting period, and accordingly allowed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Sassoon that in any event, what had accrued from the Companies under the term 'business' could not accrue to the Company because the assignment of Managing Agency was merely expectations of earning commission and not any part thereof. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The right of the assessee to receive the entire remuneration did not depend on any specific term between the assignor and the assignee, but on the fact that what was transferred was an income bearing asset which carried with it a right to the remuneration of the year, such a right may arise by virtue of a specific or implied term as between the transferor and the transferee either as part of whole or in part. [345G H] 2. The rights of the parties are not governed by any express statutory provision but by the terms thereof. [346B C] 3. In the instant case, the Managing Agents had been appointed as a Managing Agent only on certain dates in the course of the years by virtue the assignment. It was not necessary to observe that while, it may be, that in the normal run of events the contract for remuneration under the Managing agency agreement is an indivisible contract for a whole year 's work, this clause necessarily implied divisibility of contract and the remuneration in the year of assignment since the assignment necessarily took place with the consent of the principal employer. [347C] 4. The mere clause in the Managing Agent Agreement that the employer is to be responsible only to the assignee for the payment of the entire amount does not depend upon any specific terms between the parties, but upon the fact of that what had been transferred was also an income which carried on with it, and therefore, did not cease to be such notwithstanding the assignment thereof. It may be mentioned in this context that clause 10 of the said Managing Agency Agreement in Agarwals ' case has been relied on by learned counsel for Agarwals to show that the assignors were merely expectations and that on assignment the assignee became the Managing agent as if his name had been inserted in the managing Agency agreement from the beginning, and the continuity of theManaging Agency was preserved thereby and that nobody satisfies the description of the Directors of the company. [348D] 5. The fact that the assignment had necessarily taken place with a right of remuneration not, as per this argument by virtue Of any mutual arrangement between the assigneeor and his assignee, is also the person entitled to the amount by way of remuneration to be paid by the Company or which has accrued to him under the contract terms of his Managing Agency Agreements. [349G] 6. The position in law as between a company and its transferees was that on the date of assignment the assignee becomes the Managing Manager as if he stepped into the position of the deceased Managing Agent, but that the continuity did not dependent on any particular term between them.

The appellant was a resident of Pachperwa in the District of Gonda. He had two sons, Badri and Kirpa Shanker. The deceased and the accused were residing together with their father. On August 13, 1963, Sunderpatti was found with serious injuries in the room of the house where he was sleeping and the appellant was not in the house. The evidence in the case is circumstantial. It is implicit in the concept of confession, whether it is extra judicial or judicial, that it shall be communicated to another. If so much was established, prudence and justice demand that such evidence should be made the sole ground of conviction. [657E F] (2) The accused had illicit connections with the deceased; and he had some quarrel on the Janmashtami day in the evening and the deceased had to be persuaded through the influence of his neighbors, Mohammed Abdullah and his womenfolk, to go back to the house of the appellant. [600C] (3) The evidence adduced by the prosecution is consistent only with the hypothesis of guilt. [60E F G] (4) The circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be consistent only With the hypothesis that they should be such as to exclude other hypotheses but the one proposed to be proved. [61F H] (5) The circumstance narrated by the High Court, which we have stated earlier, lead to the only conclusion that the accused must have committed the murder.

The appellant was appointed as an Assistant Manager in the respondent company. On May 1, 1976, he was transferred to the respondent Company. The appellant was served with a notice under Rule 5 of the Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Ltd. Service Rules (for short "the Rules") for termination of his service. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said notice and also the direction to pay all the allowances upto that date including the period of suspension. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not an employee of the respondent. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board of Directors had no power to terminate the service of a permanent employee by giving one month 's salary including allowances upto the termination of the service or in lieu thereof. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board of Director has to take a decision whether the need to continue the post but also the services of the officer/employee. Once the Board reaches a decision to abolish the post, in consequence the service becomes terminated and the terms and conditions are duly altered by any scheme framed under the Act. [910B] 1.2 The Board may unilaterally and arbitrarily decide that there is no need for the services Of a particular employee, in given facts and circumstances though the post would require. Thereby, the post will be abolished. [1110C D] 2.1 In the event of the Society not having any further need of the employee 's service, whether permanent or temporary, which should be decided by the Board, the Principal Officer shall give 30 days' notice in writing for termination. The other view capable to be construed from the language employed would be that the board may form an objective opinion on the basis of the material, that the post which the employee is occupying may continue and would be put to an end by giving One month ''s salary including allowance upto the period when it reaches a conclusion whether the necessity to continue his service subsists. [1210D] 2:2 The words "in the event" used in Rule 5 are susceptible of two interpretations. The one interpretation put up by Sri Ramamurty is that the Chairman may form a objective opinion, on the ground of material,that the post held may continue or be putto an end. But from the facts it is clear that the appointment of the person was occupying no longer is in need. Thereby the post shall be abolished and the absence of the need for continuance of the post cannot justify to terminate service of an employee or officer. Once a Board reaches an decision, not only regarding the need of any employee ''s service, either permanent or Temporary which should remain decided by Board, but also a direction to Pay all the allowance upto that period including the periods of termination. [1310E] 2 :3. The Board has to consider whether the requirement to continue in office of an officer/ employee is continued and would have been put to a end by give one month' notice or pay in lieu of notice, in the manner prescribed in the Rules. If the provisions of law or the rule are construed in such a way as would make it consistent with the constitution and another interpretation would render the provision or the rules unconstitutional, the court would lean in favour of the former construction. [1410G] 2 4.1 Rule 9 of the Rules gives naked power to termination of service by giving 30 days ' notice in written writing for terminating his service or by paying him such employee a sum equivalent to his one month's salary, including allowances up to the period during which he is occupying no more than once in office.

The appellants were the highest bidder on February 20, 1970 and his name was entered in the bid register. The Collector issued a fresh order dated August 19, 1970 for reauctioning the license and declared that rule 103(1) of the Board 's Excise Rules was ultra vires the Act. The State Government issued a revised order dated September 19, 1971 under section 29(2) of Bihar and Orissa Excise (Orissa Amendment) Ordinance, 1970. The appellants challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court in O.J.C. No. 589 of 1972. The High Court quashed the direction of the State Government dated April 15, 1970 directing reauction of the shops and declared the rule 103 as ultra vires. The appellant contended that section 6 was not made retrospective in operation because the Collector had no authority to issue a notice under that sub section, as the power of the ' State Government in that respect had been delegated to the Board of Revenue. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court erred in holding that section 5 of the Amending Ordinance was valid and the grant of seven ' shops to the appellants for the manu facture and retail sale of country liquor was therefore validated "as the grant had been assigned to the State by virtue of section 6(a) of that Act. [723C] 1.2 The High Courts have also held that as sections 2 to 5 of, the Amending Act of 1970 were not made retrospectively in operation, the effect of section 4 of the amending Ordinance was that the Collector was not concerned and did not in fact issue any public notice for purposes of sub section (1) as the powers of the " State Government under that section had already been complied with by the State. [823D] 1:3 The High ' Court erred in law in holding so. [924E] 2.4 The High courts have also taken the view that what was realised by the Collector, was not a fee or tax, as. had been averted in ' the memorandum of appeal, and that section 4 was therefore ultra vires of the powers conferred on the State under sub section(1). [826F] 1 :5 The High "Court erred in quashing the direction issued by the Government dated March 28, 1974 in OJ. C. No., 589 of 1971 which has given rise to civil appeal No. 1970 Cut tack 777) and the decision of this Court in Jaiswal 's case (supra). [926F G] 2:5 The State had the exclusive right and privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor. [1024G] 3.1 In view of the fact that section 7 was not enacted retrospective in its operation, it is not necessary to deal separately with the judgment of the High court dated April 16, 1971 in OC.No. 589/72 which has been given rise by civil appeal Nos. 2091 and 1970 Cutphasis 777) & the decision in Jaiswal "s case that the amount realised by auction was illegal and that rule103(1)(a) was ultravires the Act and was therefore invalid. [1125A] 2 :5 In view, the High Courts were right in holding the view of this court in Ajodhya Prasad 's cases that section 8 was not retrospective in nature, the impugned judgment of High Court dated March 15, 1971 is set aside and the writ petition No. 2071 of 1972 is dismissed. [1226F D] 2.(6) The High Judge has also held in its judgment dated April 3, 1971 that as the Collector has no authority under section 22(1), as the State had exclusive right, and privilege for manufacturing and sell liquor, he was entitled to license under sub Section (2)of section 22.

The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 302 read with section 34 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court reduced the punishment of accused No. 2 to that of imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no corroboration of the evidence of Dinkar in regard to the connection of accused with the crime and in regard thereto the High Court should have reduced the sentence of accused Nos. 3 and 4. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The prosecution case is that Dinkar was his classmate and through Dinkar he came to know accused No 2 and 3 who were the son of accused NO. 2 and had gone together for sale of cycle carrier to Rupvate. The evidence of the tailor was that accused No 3 called Dinkar and accused No 4 and asked him to take out the key from the godown of Takalkar and he kept that bag in his godown and gave it to accused No 1 who later returned the key and gave the key to accused Nos 2 and 4 and gave them to accused NO 2. The fact that Dinakar was a reliable witness and it was proved that accused Nos 3 and 5 were guilty of the offence, In view of the fact that there is evidence to connect accused No, 3 with murder, the High court rightly came to the conclusion that there had been corroboration of his evidence in material particulars and that Dinker was a credible witness. [623C] 2. There was no evidence to link accused No., 3 with the murder. The discovery of articles in the godown was as a result of a statement by accused No2 and 3. The identity of accused no. 3 is not to be lost sight of. It is only when there is an element of doubt that the prosecution case rests on the testimony of Dinker in material details, that the court can take a view which is more probable than the evidence given by Dinkar. [523C D] 3. There is no evidence that accused no 2 and 5 went together for the sale of articles except the lump of silver which he had seen in the company of accused nos. 1 to 4 and on 27 December, 1967 Dinkar returned the keys and gave him the key. The identification of accused 2 and3 is not of much significance. [525A] 4. There are no evidence about the identity of the articles sold to Gadekar. The recovery of articles from accused No 5 was also not established by any reliable evidence. [500B] 5. There were no material on record to connect the accused with murder.

The appellant was the owner of a plot in which the declaration had been made and published it in the prescribed manner. The Town Planning Officer under section 67 of the Act determined the amount to be adjusted, and he published it on the basis of the market value at the date of the declaration of intention to make a scheme with all the buildings and works thereon at that date and without references to improvements contemplated in the scheme other than improvements due to the alteration of its boundaries. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification on the ground that it was not an order made by the Town Planning officer determining the amount payable as compensation under section 64 (1) (f). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act specifies a principle of compensation, and that the principles for determining the compensation are different from those contained in sections 69 and 70. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Town planning Officer had no power under section 66(1) to determine the amount of compensation in the appellant 's case as the final plot with all buildings and work thereon at the time of declaration of the intention to making a scheme without reference to improvements envisaged in the Scheme other than improvement due to alteration of their boundaries. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Act specifies that the market price of the land at the relevant date is determined on the principles set out in section 69 and that is the guiding rule in respect of all lands covered by the scheme. [775G H] 2. Under clause (xiii) the Town Plan Officer has a duty under clause (viii) to calculate the increment to accrue in respect thereof from the local authority or from any person benefited or partly from such person as the Town Authority may in each case determine. The principle for determining compensation is the same whether an owner of land is given a reconstituted plot or not; compensation is payable on the footing of the value of the plot at the place of the final scheme. In determining the difference between the total of the values of the original plots and the total value of each plots included in the final Scheme, the Town Development Officer under Section 32 (1)(iii) has to find out the market Value of each plot included in a final scheme which is beneficial partly to the owners or residents within the area of the scheme and partly to general public. [774A B] 3. The town planning officer under section 32(1)(ii) has a power under clause(viii) of section 64 to determine compensation on the marketvalue of each Plot included in final scheme, which we will refer to hereinafter as the Final plot for brevity 's sake). Under clause(xiii) of Section 69 the Town plan Officer is required to estimate the amount so determined. [764C D] 4. The principles for determination of compensation are the same as those contained under sections 69, 70 and 71. In fixing the amount the Town Planner Officer under sub section (1), has to take into account the market values of each of the plots included therein in the Final Scheme. [754D E] 5. Under section 64(1), the Town development Officer is empowered to determine a compensation for loss of land and not the final Plot. The amount payable by an owner for loss or damage of land has to be determined on that basis. [784E F] 6. In deciding the difference in between the Total of the amounts payable as damages on each plot, the town Planning Officer is entitled to estimate compensation to be paid to the owner. The City Planning Officer has power under sub clause (ix) to compute the increment. [884A D] 7.

The appellant was the third son of Seetharama Iyer who died in 1934. The appellant filed a suit for partition of his properties and for possession of the remaining properties. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the will did not show that the testator intended to give the selection to his brother, the daughters to make the selection. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the words " he shall deliver possession of any particular one of the properties to the two daughters and stress is laid on the words ' he shall pay the balance of the property to the children as and when they become major. The High Court also held that in India such a bequest would have been valid for uncertainty within the meaning of section 89, for it can be made certain by the selection of the daughters and is not so uncertain that it is impossible to make it certain. Held: (i) The words " the testator" show that it was Seetharamma who was to make a gift which could be made some by the legatee. It is not disputed that if the intention of the testator was to select but the selection failed, the case would clearly be of the third kind indicated by us above and the daughters would have the right to select. (ii) The language in the will shows that it has been expressly stated that "it shall not show any particular person of the lands to be handed over to the three children". The words are different in the case of daughters as compared to the words used in the context of the interpretation of section 87, for they have no express words. (iii) The testator intended that each daughter will select the land devised to them taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. If the intention was not to give a selection but still intended to make an appointment it would clearly mean that the bequest was entirely void for uncertainty.

The plaintiff and the defendants were in joint possession of the plots in dispute. The suit was contested by the defendants mainly on the ground that the defendants had no concern with them. It was also pleaded that though at some time before, the lands in dispute were joint but during the consolidation proceedings the plot in possession of Adhivasi was deleted after 1359 Fasli and there was no order of any authority or court to show the circumstances under which the plaintiff 's name was wrongly deleted. The trial court accepted the allegations of the defendants and dismissed the suit of the plaintiff. The District Judge, however, found that on the admitted facts even after the abolition of zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950 the plaintiff lost her title by operation of law. The High Court reversed the decision of the District Judge and dismissed his appeal. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in law in holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 and the judgment of the High court cannot be allowed to stand. HELD: The High court has committed an error of record because the clear finding of fact was that a clear fraud was committed during the entire consolidation operation either by the respondents or by someone else as a result of which the rights of the appellant were sought to be extinguished. [723C] In view of the clear decision of this Court, referred to above, the High Courts erred in holding the present case to be ousted from possession.

In the affidavit of Respondent No. 1, it is stated that the Constitution of India came into force on April 4, 1950. The Constitution defined a "State" as meaning "the State Government " and "the Union " respectively. Article 173 read with Form VII A was introduced in the Constitution by the President of India. The provisions of the Constitution were made applicable to the Union of India and there is no separate form even for the Prime Minister. It is further stated that under article 173 readwith Form VIIA, a person who has been declared as a "Government" shall be deemed to have been declared a "public servant". Article 173 provided that "the President may by order declare that he shall be declared a public servant". The provisions in the articles of the constitution were made effective from April 4. 1950 and there was no separate procedure for the Union Government to declare a person as a public Servant. The petitioner himself did not press it. He maintained that yet in view of the fact that the form prescribed in the Third Schedule pursuant to the requirement of Article 75(4) of theConstitution is only for a Minister of the Union and there being no separate Form even for his Prime Minister, he describes himself as the Prime Ministers. The affidavit of respondent No. 2 was filed on behalf of the State of Haryana. In the counter affidavit filed by the Respondent No 1 it has been stated that "in view of section 173 read along with Form 7A", the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. And according to him, as long as the substantial part is properly followed, a mere mistake or error in the descriptive part would not vitiate the oath." It was further stated by the petitioner that the requirement under article173 read with Forms VII A and Form VII B were only for the Minister of State Government and there has been no separate forms even for that Ministry. The averments made by the respondent No 1 in his affidavit are vague and general. It was also stated that Respondent No 2 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Prime Minister but the description of him as Deputy Chief Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Ministry, along with his other submis sions, we think the first contention raised by the petition er that Respondent 1 was just a minister and there are no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Minis ter as such. The High Court in the reported decision said: "In view of this statement made by respondent No 2, the essential requirement of article 173(2) read with Rule VII A is that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India." It is also stated in the affidavit that Respondent Nos. 1 and the petitioner himself does not press this petition for the reasons indicated above. The first contention of the petitioner was that the prescribed procedure should be followed, as far as the second contention is con cerned, the petitioner has no force. So far as respondent No 3 is just one Minister like others members of his Council of Minister of Union Government and it contains the words which precede this portion are merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. The words which preceded this portion were merely descriptive and for all purposes he is a Minister and there cannot be any difference in the description or description of the man and of the nomination as such." It has been further stated in paragraph 7 of the affidavit filed on the behalf of respondent Nos. 2 and 3 that the petitioner did not file any objection to the petition.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Railway Establishment and was employed in the Indian Railways. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been guilty of an illegal strike and a break in his service within the meaning of the Factories Act, 1948. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal before the Labour Appellate Tribunal which held that the stoppage of work amounted to a strike so as to amount to a break within the ambit of section 49 B (1) of the Act. The Labour Appellate Tribun al held that there was no break in the continuity of service by the stoppage and that the non permitted absence as a result of concerted refusal to work even for 2 to 4 hours in the course of a working day amounts to an illegal strikes and consequently an interruption of service of a workman for the purpose of section 50 B (2) of The Labour appellate Tribunal held that it was not to be regarded as a strike but did not cause any interruption in the workers service. On appeal by special leave, this Court reversed the decision of the Labour appellate tribunal on the question whether the stoppage was illegal and directed that holidays at full rates as provided for in section 49 A of the said Act will have to be calculated in respect of the operatives concerned on the footing that there had been no break or in the absence of concered refusal to go back to work on the night of 1st November, 1948, and that it would condone the cessation of work on that day. In appeal by certificate, HELD: The stoppage of Work for the period for about 2 to 3 hours in a working days amounts to a disrupt of service and consequently a break of service is not to treat as depriving them of leave by reason of the strike so long as they would have completed a period of twelve months ' continuous service in the factory. [220D] The stoppage was not a concerted action on the part of the workers and that several workers in their own individual capacity wanted leave on that date. [222E] In view of the facts and circumstances detailed in the adjudicator 's award this contention cannot be seriously considered.

The appellant was the proprietor of a theatre known as "A" which was a film which was published in the newspaper 's edition, dated July 1, 1971. The appellant was prosecuted for an offence under section 292 I.P.C. and was convicted by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censors and finding in the prosecution nothing vexatious or vexatious nor any material to quash the proceedings. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the films were not obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals, but that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case, the film having been duly certified for public show by the Board of Censor and finding In the prosecution no material was produced before the court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The trial court when it hears the case may be appropriately apprised of the certificate under the Act and, in the light of our observations, it fills the bill under section 79 I. P.C., driving the producer to satisfy a 'lay ' magistrate that the certificate of the Board is justificatory. [501 E] 1.2 The prosecution has failed to prove that the exhibition had been made by one "who by reason of a mistake of fact in good faith believes himself to be justified by law in committing the act, or alternatively, that he entertained a mistake o fact and in good belief that he was actually justified by Law in exhibiting the film. [602 F] 1:3 The prosecution is unsustainable because section 79 is exculpatory when read with section 5A of the Act. [504 A B] 2.1 Section 79 I P. C. does not apply to a case where the offence committed by any person who is justified by reason o mistake of law in good sense, believes himself or to be justify by law, or who by reason thereof, believe that he is actually justified in committing such act. [506 A B; 507 A] 2:2 The provisions of section 79 are not exhaustive and the purpose of section 80 I P C. is to ensure that the prosecution does not fail on any other ground. It is an antinomy to say that under section 5(A) of the , the producer or connected agencies do enter the statutory harbour and are protected because section 77 exonerates them at least in view of their bona fide belief that the person entertained a wrong of fact and not by reason. [ 507 A B C] 2 2.2 Section 79 is nothing but an exception operates and the bona fide believing, though mistaken, eliminates the culpability. If the offence is done by any other provision, then section 79 exonerifies the doer because the act ceases to be an offence. The mens rea is not a sine qua non for prosecution under section 80 of the Penal Code. [408 B C; 507A] 3.3 Section 79 of the penal code does not operate and it cannot be said that if the offender can irrefutably establish that he has been justified by laws in exhibiting films, the producer and connected agencies did enter the Statutory harbour and were protected because sections 79 exoners them at best in view Of their bona fides, sanctions the public exhibition, the producers and connected Agencies do enter into the statutory portals and are immunity because section 80 exonerces them atleast in view thereof their bona bonafide belief that they entertained a mistakes of fact.

The petitioner was a Government Pleader for the Patna District, including lucrative land acquisition litigation, as part of the professional 'estate ' of a Government pleader. He was appointed as an advocate by the State Government in all the civil cases. The petitioner was also a member of the judicial service of the State of Bihar. On his appointment he was transferred to the Patna High Court and was posted at Patna District. In the year 1971, the petitioner was appointed a lawyer by the Government Pleader. He continued as an Advocate till the disposal of the writ petition. The Government Pleader, Madras was also appointed as a lawyer in all civil cases, including racrative lands acquisition litigation. On the basis of the recommendations made by the High Court, the State issued a notification under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, for acquiring land for the purpose of construction of buildings and other structures. The notification was published in the Bihar Gazette on December 5, 1971. The Collector of Patna District issued a notice to the petitioner calling upon him to file his objections within 30 days from the date of publication of the notice. The petitioners filed their objections before the Collector. The Land Acquisition Officer rejected the objections by holding that the petitioner 's client 's claim as the sole representative of Government in courts is not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviolability of high public office of Government Pleader by politicking men in the Secretariat or by practitioners of favouritism dressed in 'little brief authority ', a deeper issue in which the Bar has a stake and the Bench must also be concerned. The State filed an appeal before the District Judge against the order of the Collector dated December 5. 1971. In his writ petition, the High court held that the Government pleader was not a proper party to the writ petitions. On appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner ' s claim as a sole representative for seeking bureaucratic practice of a single government Pleader is not maintainable in view of the fact that the State has a higher dedication to the people. [690G H] 2.2 The High Court was right in holding that there should be some provision emphasising the need for positive efforts at settlement, in suits to which the Government is a party or a public officer acting in his official capacity is a Party or a Public Officer acting in the official capacity of the Government. [790A] 3.1 In every suit or proceeding to which this Act applies, it shall be the duty of the Court in the first instance, in every case where it is possible to do so consistently with the nature of the circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to assist the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject matter of the suit. [890B] 3:2 The duties of the public nature are also to the Government who are the principal and responsible character, the office must be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. [889A B] 4.1 There should be no provision emphasizing the need that lawyering in India needs a National 768 Commission right now as in England and elsewhere, nor do we subscribe to the U.S. situation on which the President and the Chief Justice have pronounced. The time has come to examine the quality of the product or service, control the price, floor to ceiling, enforce commitment to the persons who are their respective rights in the land of Gandhi is a dignified renunciation of office not a chase for the lost briefs through the 'writ ' route. [990B D] 4:3 The learned Advocate General has a number of other duties to discharge.

The appellants held a total issue of 800 shares of the Bank of India. The Mills exercised the right to apply for the shares of its shareholders in the proportion of one new share for every three shares held by them in this company. The shares were offered by the Bank to its nominees, and the right was thus distributed among its shareholders. The appellants contended that the distribution of the right of the shareholders amounted to a distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Income Tax Act. Held, that the expression "dividend" in section 2 (6A), is an inclusive definition and not an exhaustive definition, and even if the distribution was made by the form of the resolution sanctioning the distribution, the true character of the order could not be altered. The High Court was right in holding that the distributed right to the shareholders was a distribution within the ordinary meaning of that expression and was taxable as income in the hands of the appellants. The Tribunal had referred the question whether the distribution amounted to distribution of dividends within the extended meaning of the expression in section2(6 A) of Income Tax, Act, in enlarging the scope of the question and in answering it in the light of its ordinary meaning. The decision of the High Court cannot be sustained on the ground that it was not justified having regard to the form, of the questions which expressly related to distribution by the forms of the resolutions sanctioning the distributed rights. The appeal must accordingly be allowed. The appeals must be dismissed with costs.

The appellant was a candidate for election to the post of Sarpanch. The respondent contested the election petition on the ground that he had not been given permission to examine. The High Court rejected the prayer holding that the evidence of such witness was not material for the decision of the petition and that the party tendering such witness or witnesses is doing so on frivolous grounds or with a view to delay the proceedings. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in refusing to examine the witness who was present in the Court without the assistance of the Court for the purpose of procuring the attendance of a witness and yet the party was unable to produce him or her on his own under Rule 1A. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of Order XVI is in respect of witnesses to procure whose presence the assistance is t necessary. If mere omission to mention the name of a person in the list envisaged by sub rule(1) would enable the Court to refuse to examine such witness, it is obligatory on the party to file the list with the gist of evidence of witness in the List and yet when the evidence is not closed, and the Court has no jurisdiction to decline to examine any witness. [620B] The only jurisdiction the Court can decline to exercise its discretion under sub Rule (1), of Rule IA of Order XVII. [721C] In the instant case, the High court had erred while refusing to grant permission to the appellant to examine witnesses kept present by him on being summoned through the Court and kept present when the witness was called to produce documents under Rule 2A. The only question which arose for consideration is whether the party who has failed to name the witness in his list could be denied the privilege of examining witnesses kept by him or she? [722D] In order to decide this question it would be necessary to refer to the provisions of Order XVIII, Rule 1(1), and Rule 1 A of Order XV. The proviso to sub rule 1A of Rule XVI confers a wider jurisdiction on the Court which ordinarily the Court would not extend its assistance for procuring the presence of such a witness by issuing a summons through the court or otherwice which ordinarily is the one set out in proviso to Section. [822D E] In view of the clear language of sub rule 2(1)(a) of Order XIX, it was not necessary to provide in Rule 1 that the Court may decline to call any witness to give evidence or to produce document without applying for summons under R Rule 1. But where the party has failed in showing the name and address of such person in his List, the party would be entitled to examine those witnesses who are called to produced documents through the witnesses who were called to appear before the Court.

The appellant was appointed as a Principal of the College by an order dated April 12, 1981. The Committee of Management of the college issued an appointment order on May 1, 1981 to the appellant informing him that the Committee of management had suspended or withdrawn power of appointment of teaching staff including Principal and teachers. The Manager of the Institution issued an order of the State Government in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointments of teaching Staff including Principal, and teachers including Principal. The Director of the School issued an office order dated May 1 1981 to appellant informing that the committee of Management had suspended/ withdrawn its power. The appellant challenged this order by a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed on April 27, 1981 by a Single Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appointment of the Manager of an institution was not valid because the order contained in the radiogram had suspended and withdrawn power from the Committee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order dated March 27,1981 which has been extracted hereinbefore clearly shows that on April 7, 1981 the order containing the radiatiram had suspension or withdraw power of the appointment. Sanghi further contended that the order was never received by the institution and therefore the power of appointing the appellant would be by a body not authorised to make the appointment and hence ineffective though it may not be invalid. [982D] 2. The letter dated May 13, 1981 which has also been extracted hereinafter clearly shows the fact that on June 1,1981 the order issued in the Radiogram was communicated to the Manager. If the order is valid and power to make appointment was suspended it would not be open to the Selection Committee to make any modification or rescind any regulation as also make any other order consistent with the provisions of the Act, the second contention of Mr. (I) confers power on the State Govt. without making any reference to the Board to make, modify or rescind the regulations conferring power on it without making such an order consistent therewith the provisions Of the Act and the Scheme of Administration envisages the setting up of a Committee of the Management and the Committee has the power to set up a Selection Committee for selecting the candidate for appointment as Head of an Institution as provided in sec 16 F. [882F] 3. The power to appoint or withdraw or suspend power of Appointment conferred on the Committee by the regulations is conferred by the regulation conferring power upon the Committee to give such direction consistent with and the provisions contained in section 9 does confer power on State Government without making a reference to it to make modification or rescission any regulation, as also makes such other order inconsistent with the provision of the act. [888A B] 4. The appointment was otherwise valid though ineffective and if appellant under the orders of the High court functioned as Principal, discharged his duties and was paid, no question of recovery of amount paid to him could arise and neither the Government nor the Committee would be entitled to recover any salary paid to the appellants. [898C] 5. The State Government could be said to have rescinded that A regulation conferring powers on the Director to make modify or rescission or rescind or make any order consistent With the provisions o the Act. The question is whether the appointment was in contravention of the provisions ofs. 9 does not arise and if it is not valid, though ineffective, it may be invalid but inoperative though it might not be valid. [90C D] 6. The selection committee had no power to select the appellant nor the Manager on behalf o the Committeeof Management could issue appointment order dated June 1 1981. If that power was riot suspended we would have no difficulty in upholding the appointment order of appellant and we are unable to help the appellant. [1082G H; 990A B C] 7.

The petitioners manufacture "a textile consisting of rayon threads in the warp and cotton threads" in the same manner as in other ordinary textile. The petitioners state that they manufacture " a textile" and also that it serves as part of raw material for what ultimately turn into a fabric in the said way as is being done by the first petitioner. They say that, "tyre cord fabric" manufactured by them was woven by its purchasers "into a fabric In the process of manufacture of a fabric, the petitioners sell their own product which determines the nature of goods which are entitled to exemption, and also because it serves a purpose in the process o manufacture of an article or articles of the like kind. The respondents state that, as some questions were put in the Rajasthan State Legislative Assembly on or about 20th April, 1971, asking for the reason why this particular type of goods of the petitioners were exempted from Sales tax, the Commissioner of Commercial Tax issued a letter to the Commercial Tax Officer to levy Sales tax on the "rayon cord fabric". The petitioners further state that it served as part and parcel of raw materials for what eventually turn into the manufacture of another fabric. They also say that it serve as part or parcel of the raw material in the manufacture, of which "rayor tyre cord fabric", but that it does not, therefore, seem propel. for us to finally decide whether the goods under consideration constitute a fabric entitled to the exemption. The question is whether this product constitutes a fabric which is a textile? It requires careful consideration of the technical processes of manufacturing, of the composition of the "tyle cord fabric." The petitioners allege that it serving as part, parcel or parcel for what purpose ultimately turn out of which 'rayon band fabrics" was made and its composition, the petition sets out item 22 of the first schedule of the Central Excises Excise and Salt Act, 1941, as the applicable entry covering the goods manufactured by it. They further say that they sell their "textile" fabrics and also the product is a fabric consisting of a rayons in the cotton fabrics. The case of the Delhi Cloth Mills was that, on admitted facts, it could be decided whether the "tiesre cord fabrics" manufactured were more correctly capable of being described as a fabric or not in the final manufacture of any other fabric was quite irrelevant. It is then stated that, so far as the Delhi Textile Mills are concerned, the goods sought to be taxed are not the "end product". The case for the petitioners is that, since the statutory remedies had not been exhausted, leaving some "error apparent on the face of the record" still to be determined whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabrics entitled to exemptions. It does not appear from the record and 503 that it is the stage reached by this product, in the case before us that, after the statutory procedures had not exhausted, left some "ersror apparent On the face thereof, to decide whether this particular kind of goods was more correctly valued as described as an fabric or as merely cord pretending to pass off as ar textile fabric. Having indicated the nature and substance out ofwhich "rayil tyre cord" is a manufactured product which is entitled to Exemption, but it is not so much the point of manufacture at which the Mills sell their product which determine the nature thereof. It also does not seem propels. for the reasons given above, we think that the High Court should have interfered as the question whether the tyre cord fabrics was more appropriately capable of be described as "textiles" or not.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal washeries on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied and incidental work. The respondent was a Senior Supervisor in the company 's establishment at Dhanbad. When the matter was thus pending consideration the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour Court, Patna. In exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of Section 33 B of the , the Governor of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the petitioner Shri Shivajee Prasad Sinha wherein he has prayed for the transfer of the case from the labour court, Dhanbad and transfer the said proceeding to the Labour Court,. Patna, regu larly due to his residence at Hajipur is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure 'A ' pending before the Labour C ourt, Dhanbad. The Government accordingly acceded to the request of the respondent and without opportunity to 294 the management transferred the case to Labour court, Patna for speedy disposal from the stage at which the case was transferred. In view of the above, the appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality of the reasons given by the Government for transferring the case. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Government was misled by the representation of the workman and transfer of it to Labour Cour t, Dhanbad was illegal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had written to his employer stating that he would be able to attend the labour courts at Dhanbad since he has been residing at Hajapur and it would not be difficult to attend Labour court Dhanbad because he has already written to him stating that the case would be trans fered to Labour Courts, Patna, without hearing the petitioner. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Government was induced by the representations of the workmen. The representation of Shri Shivendra Prasad Sinha was accepted by the High court and it was not open for the appellant to contend that the government was misled in refusing to an assessee a reasonable oppor tunity of representing his views when any order to the prejudice of the normal procedure laid down in section 64(1) and (2) of the Act is sought to be made against him, be it a transfer from one Income Tax Officer within the State to an Income Tax officer without it, except of course where the very object of the transfer would be frustrated if notice was given to the party affected and he is afforded a reasonable opportunity of representing their views when no order to that prejudice of normal procedure lay down in Section 64(2) and(2). [415E] 1.2 The Government had not acceded to this request of ShriShivendra Prasad Singh, but it was made obligatory to record reasons in making the order of transfer after affording a reasonable opportun tunity to 294the management.
