[416B] 2.3 The Government has accepted the request and transferred the matter from Labour Court Dhanbad to Labour cour t. The order of transferring the said case is quashed for not communi cating reasons to the assessee, be It a transfer by way of an administrative officer within the meaning of section 5(7A) of Income Tax Act, 1961, which now makes it obligatory to records reasons in writing. [404C] 3. The power vested under section 33 B is not so much to act judicially as to act fairly has been explained by Lord Pearson in Pearl bergg vs Varty, ,547: "A tribunal to whom judicial or quasi judicial functions are entrusted is held to be required to apply those principles (i.e. the rules of natural justice) in performing those functions unless there is a provision to the contrary. [402E] 4.

The appellant was a hotel operator. The respondent, a hotel employee, was employed in the hotel. He was dismissed from service on October 7, 1955. On appeal by the management, the Additional Industrial Tribunal held that the reference was incompetent and two grounds were urged in support of it. The High Court held that (1) the union could not be made a party to the reference under the , (2) the Union could not make a party thereto; and (3) the reference did not indicate how many of the 480 workers of thirty different categories working in the Hotel were involved in the dispute. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The words "as represented 36 282 by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi " which appear in the order of reference make it incompetent merely because it is mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by some officer, such as its president or secretary and it is that officer who will actually represent the workmen before the tribunal, but mentions the union itself. [283E] (1)(a) The fact that in the application the words " as represented 36 281 by the hotel Workers ' union, KatraShahanshati, Chandli Chowk,Delhi " have been added for the sake of convenience as to where the notice to the workmen should be sent would not in our opinion make the reference incompetent merely since it is stated therein that " the workmen shall be represented through some officer". [283F] (b) The words 'as represented36 282 by Hotel Workers Union, Amritsar " which appears in the Order of Reference do not indicate that there was a dispute between the hotel and its employees. It is therefore obvious that the union was not a living person can only be served through some officers, such like its president, secretary or secretary. [284G] (c) The mere fact that the workman was entitled to be represented in by an officer of a trade union of which he is a member, does not affect the competence of the order.

The Collector rejected the claim holding that the appellant is entitled to the benefit of the Notification. On appeal by the Department, the Appellate Tribunal held that the goods imported by them are parts and accessories of the engine and not a few parts thereof. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Customs authorities should have followed the procedure prescribed under the Notification for claiming exemption from duty in terms of paragraph 2 of column (2) of the Table annexed to the Notification, irrespective of the fact that they or any or some of them have already been included under Heading 84.6. The Tribunal held against the Department and dismissed the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to avail of the benefit under the notification, it has to be proved that the parts in respect whereof the exemption is claimed, are parts or accessories thereof. [227G] 2.1 The Notification exempts also parts of engines mentioned under Heading Nos. 84.2006 and 84.07. [228B C] 3.2 In order that the Notification exempts all parts of machinery specified in column (3) of Table annexed thereto, it provides that the articles specified in Column (2), shall be those parts which must be all the parts constituting the engine or engines, as mentioned under Item No.84.06 and not any few parts therefrom. [229H] 3:2 The Notification does not, however, contain or refer to the parts of internal combustion piston engines falling under Heading no. 8405. In view of our finding that the bushes imported are parts parts of such engines, it includes the parts thereof, but also the parts which are included under a Heading other than Heading No.. 8406, will get the benefit as provided by the Notification irrespective of fact that those parts have alreadybeen included under heading no.8406. [226G] 3 :3 The Notification provides that all parts constituting a engine or part thereof. It includes parts of Chapter 84.05 and not every few parts of a engines, such parts will get exemption as provided in the Notification regardless of the facts that they/any or some other them have been included in Heading 8406 or under any other Heading. 8404. [230H] 4. The Notification is not intended to cover parts of engine or parts thereof falling under heading 84.04. It merely provides that parts of those engines, mentioned under heading No. 85.05, will be excluded from the benefit. In order for the reasons aforesaid, it excludes parts of Heading 8405 and in the context of the notification. [231H] 5. The Notifications are not intended only to parts of vehicles falling under Chapter 84 but also to parts thereof and not to parts or any of them. It is clear enough to provide that the Parts of the machinery mentioned under headings No.

The plaintiffs claimed through female members of the Dargah and even if they were entitled to any right in the management or share in the offerings in the Dargah, that title was denied. The defendants filed a written statement on 22.4.1972 stating that the plaintiffs claiming through female were not entitled to claim any right of Mujawar as the right was given only to the male members and not to the females. The trial court held that the rights of Fathima Bee had become barred by limitation by ouster and as such the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathim Bee were also not entitled for any relief. In appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court and dismissed the suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The right of Fafima Bee to the share of the plaintiffs and on the ground that they had claimed through Fothima Bee was a Mujawar and was also ousted from the enjoyment of any share in it, the plaintiffs were entitled in the right and management of the offerings. [116B] 1.2 The only question is whether the High court was right in holding that the right of FAafim Bee to Fathiman Bee was barred by Limitation by ouster. [117C D] 1:3 It is clear that neither in the written statement nor in reply to the notice of the plain tiffs any stand was taken that the defendants were claiming ouster on the basis of expressed denial of Fatima Bee from the fight or management of any right or claim in the hundial collection or offerings in a Dargah and on that ground they were pleading an ouster of Fothim Bee as well as the plaintiffs. [118D] 1.:4 The only controversy now left to be determined is whether there was really no dispute now as regards the period of 27 days falling to the shares of the defendants. [119E] 2.1 In so far as there was absolutely no evidence whatsoever to show at any point of time till her death in 1957 that Fathum Bee had no right or title of interest in the Wakf property and was therefore ousted from enjoyment of such share in any share, the defendants who were claiming through FAafimaira Bee were entitled only to a right of succession. [120E] 1 :4 The plaintiffs were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under the Muslim Law were not entitle to any rights of management or posses sion in a Wakf. [121F] 2:2 The female members were entitled, in the rights and management o f administration or possi sions in a wakf. [122G] 3.3 In order to make out a case of ouster against Fathyam Bee, the daughter of Sayed Gulam Dastagir had no title according to Muslim Law. At the risk of repetition it may be stated that neither Fathiliya Bee nor the plaintiffs had at any time received a share in her hundial collections or offerings nor had posses y right, the same was lost as she did not claim any rights till her lifetime. [123F] 3:4 The female member were entitled under the customary law to get any right, title or interest in a mosque and on this ground they are claiming ouster of the Wakf properties. [124G] 4. In order that Fafum Bee was an independent wakf, the provisions of section 123(1) of the Act would be applicable. [125H] 5. The plaintiffs had not at any stage received a right or interest of whatsoever nature in the mosque and even though they were claiming some rights in the Wakfs, they were asserting hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoy ment to the knowledge of Fayima Bee as such was not entitled. [126G] 6.

The appellant was employed as a railway employee in the respondent 's house. He was allotted railway quarters of a suitable type and as he had refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowance. The appellant filed a claim for house rent allowances on the ground that there had been no illegal deduction from the respondent's wages inasmuch as the respondent had been allotted railway quarter of a similar type and that he refused to vacate those quarters, he was entitled to withhold the house rent Allowance. The Authority held that the house Rent allowance claimed by the 1st respondent was "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act because it was not payable under the terms of the contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one 173 1352 of the specified places will cease to be entitled to the allowance if either the Government provides accommodation to the employee in question or the employee refuses to occupy the quarters so offered to him. The respondent ' appeal to this Court by special leave was dismissed on the grounds that there was no absolute right in the 1 st respondent to claim the house salary allowance being admissible, namely, that the employee should be posted at some of those places, like Bombay, Calcutta, 1350 Madras ' etc., before the claim for House Rent Allowance could arise and that there is a condition subsequent, namely that the employees posted at any one of those place will cease not to be so entitled. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The definition of "wages " contained in the Act does not create any absolute right or interest in the employee to the house allowance accrue as soon as he has fulfilled the terms Of the contract of employment including regular attendance, good work or conduct and his other behaviour in terms of such contract. [1353C] 2. It is equally clear that the rules which must be included in the terms o the contract are inconsistent with some of the terms contemplated the grant of house rent Allowances to every employee of a particular category but the rules do not make the grant in such absolute terms. Once an employee of the description given above has been offered suitable house accommodation and he has refused it, he ceases to be a entitled to that allowance thus cease to being so entitled., whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarter allotted to him, is not the same thing as the value of any house accommodation referred to in the definition in the act. [1256F] 3. The rules which are included in "wages", are inconsistent With some of them as the values of any House accommodation referred thereto in the Rules do not constitute a part of the term of the agreement between the parties including that of regular attendance and good work. That being so, there is no valid reason for holding that the appellant was not entitle to withhold house rent claim allowance. [1056F G] 4. The rule 3(i) quoted above is inconsistent with any of the clauses of section 7 and 1 of the act because it is no more payable under "wages". [1257A B] 5. It remains to consider the last argument advanced on behalf of the appellant that there has been a breach of contract between him and the employer requiring him to pay house rent at the rate of Rs. 500 per month. The question whether rule 3 (i) aforesaid is 1353 inconsistent with the provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the , Act, because it does not make any grant in respect of house accommodation allotted to every employees of a specified category but merely provides for payment of house Rent Allowance at the rates mentioned therein. [ 1256F H] 6. The contention on behalf Of the 1nd respondent that rule 3 is 1354 inconsistent with section 7 of the, Act cannot be sustained.

The detenu was one Indru 's father, Ram Chand Bharvani. On February 16, 1980, an order of detention, purporting to have been made under Section 3(1) of the (for short called COFEPOSA), by the State Government, was served on the detenus. The detenu received a letter from the State government requesting him to furnish the detenus with the material relied upon in the grounds of detention. On March 14, 1980 copies were supplied to the detenus on April 3, 1980. On April 3. 1980, the wife of the detenu, Ramchand Bharvani, addressed a letter to the first respondent (Under Secretary to the Government of Maharashtra), requesting him not to supply the copies of the statements and documents relied upon by the detaining authority in the ground of detention but to enable them to make an effective representation against his detention. The detenus made a written request to the State Govt. that the contents of those documents had been incorporated in those 'grounds' which were entirely in favour of the detenus and the full texts of which have been supplied to them by the detenus, that in such a situation, the "grounds" served on them should be more than sufficient to enable him to make effective representation at the earliest. The State Government refused to supply these copies and conveyed rejection of this request by a letter dated March 14 1980. Thereafter, the detenu made a request to this detaining authority on February 18, 1980 for supply of copies to the detenu. On May 3, 1981, the detenus made an oral request to supply them with the materials relied upon or referred to in those "ground" of detention and that rejection was communicated to him by letter dated April 3 1980. The detaining authority, however, calledously and deliberately refused to furnish them. In reply to this request, it seems, that within three days the copies 349 were put in a course of communication to the petitioners on April 4, 1980 and were actually received by the detenu on April 5, 1980 respectively. On the direction of the Central Government that the StateGovernment supplied the copies to them on April 2, 1980 the detenus refused as desired by the Collector, to supply those portions of statements after undue delay on the direction that the detenus would make an adequate representation against their detention. In the grounds for detention, it was stated that the detenu had received a written letter from Shri Salvi, Secretary to Government, Home Department, to the effect that he had acquired gems in question from those persons. It was further stated that after undue delays on the part of the officials, the appropriate authority could, after due application of its own mind, make an order under clause (6) of Article 22 of the Constitution withholding the supply of those portions after satisfying itself that their disclosure would be against the public interest. The grounds of challenge were: (1) The detenus had made a oral request for supply to the detaining authorities on February 14,1980; (2) The detenu was not supplied with the copies and the documents relied on in the "public interest" of the detention; (3) The statements of those persons which were allegedly sent to the Central Govt. under their covering letter, dated March 31, 1980 by the petitioners were not supplied; (4) The detaining Authority had no authority to pass the order of preventive detention. It is obvious that in addition to the supply, the copies were asked for by the Petitioners on April 03, 1980; and were subsequently received by them on May 4, 1981. In this view, there was an infraction of the constitutional imperative that in order to enable the detenu to make a full and effective representation, the necessary authority could after due consideration of its request, make such an order.

The appellant was tried by the trial Court for offences under sections 120B, 420 and 423 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted all of them. On appeal to the High Court it held that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 is against the maintainability of a joint appeal against an order acquitting several accused persons tried jointly. The Division Bench of the High court reversed the decision of the Single Judge holding that the Full Bench decision in Mahadeolal Ranodia vs The Administrator General of West Bengal(1) was wrong, instead of following the usual procedure in case of difference of opinion with an earlier decision of another Division Bench and holding that it was difficult to distinguish a previous decision of two judges of the same High Court. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD : 1. The Full Bench judgment of the Gujarat High Court is correct in law. [620 E] 2.1 Section 419 of the Criminal Procedure Code on which the High Courts are based is against section 419 of that Code and therefore not legally prohibited. [720 G H] 3.2 In order to be valid, a joint application by all the accused persons for joint trial has to be made in writing signed by all or any of them and signed by each of them together with their respective signatures. The object of section 419 was to give effect to the decision on the merits. [820 E F] 3:3 In order that a joint petition can be filed, it is necessary for the court to decide whether there is sufficient ground for proceeding against all or some of the accused. If the court finds that there are no grounds for proceeding, then it has to consider whether there are any grounds for presuming that the case against the accused person is one which comes within the purview of section 417(1)(a) of the Cr. P.C. and if the evidence against him is one in which he has been acquitted, then on principle it is difficult to negative the maintainability. [820 G] 4.3 The Full bench decision of this Court in Mahaddeol Malodia vs State of Gujarat (1) does not militate against the locus standi of a Joint appeal by the State against several accused person. It merely lays down that the Appellate Court hearing an appeal cannot admit it only on a question of sentence and that such a restricted order of admission being invalid, the appellant would be entitled to insist that his appeal should be heard on the merit. [824 A B] 4:4 The Full Benches of the Bombay High Court were wrong in holding that when the earlier decision was wrong it gives effect to that view, the result would be utter confusion. [825 C D] 5.5 In order for a joint trial, there must be some bar as is suggested by the order of the Appellate court. If one Division Bench hearing an appeals cannot admit the application only on one question of fact, but if an appeal by persons jointly tried and convicted is competent, then upon principle it becomes difficult to accept the maintainability, the appellants would be bound to insist on that their appeal should not be heard On the merits, the competency of a single Judge of the said High Court cannot be upheld. [828 A B C] 6.6 In order, however, to be effective, there is no bar as regards the joint appeal by any accused person against whom an order has been passed in a criminal case, and therefore, not legally barred.

The assessee was a firm called O.R.M.SP. Firm which was registered under section 26(A) of the Income tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter called the ' 1918 Act') and was assessed to tax under the 1918 Act. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim holding that in the case of business carried on in foreign territory the assessee was liable to pay tax under section 3 of the 1918 act because it was discontinued in the year of account. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that in view of the provisions of sub section (4) of section 25(3) of 1922 Act, income derived from business activities could not be deemed to have been charged under the provisions Of the 1918 and therefore the foreign business of the assessee could not claim exemption under section 25 (3) as it was only taxed on remittances received from the profits of the foreign company. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant commissioner who dismissed the appeal holding that the foreign income was chargeable to tax in respect of his activity styled ,foreign business and that the Indian Income tax law did not apply to the foreign trade. The High Court held that the assessee had been only taxed under the 1922 Act because what was taxed was the remittances received by the assessee from the foreign firm which was discontinued. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in order to claim exemption from liability to pay income tax in regard to interest on securities as well, the assessee must be held to have incurred expenditure for the purpose of the exemption from tax under s 25(2) of The 1922 Act and therefore he was entitled to relief under section 23(3). HELD: (1) The foreign business was not charged under section 14(2), but only received by an assessee. [912 E] (2) Where any business, profession or vocation on which tax was at any time charged under this head is discontinued, then unless there has been a succession by virtue of which the provisions o sub section(4) have been rendered applicable no tax shall be payable in respect thereof. The exemption under s. 25(1) is general. [1012 E F] (3)(a) Where income is received by a assessee from foreign business and as the income received by him was derived from the Foreign business, it must be taken that there was an assessment to tax on the foreign asset. [1113 B] (4)(b) The exemption is general in nature. It must therefore be taken, upon the facts found by the appellate Tribunal in this case, that the entire income of the Indian business was remitted to the assessee and tax imposed on that income under the 1920 Act was charged upon the assessee in respect for his activity titled ,foreign trade. [1312 C] (5)(a). The exemption was general. It is obvious that by section 3(4), the charge was made on the receipt of income in British India and as there was no succession by reason of which it could be deemed that the income, profits and gains of business, Profession or voltion was transferred to the Indian company.

The assessee entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said Department for construction of the Capital Project, Ghandhinagar. The contractor was required to give notice to the Executive Engineer or his Assistant of his intention of making delivery of materials and on the materials being approved, receipt shall be granted to him by the Executive engineer or his Assistants and no materials which is not so approved shall be considered to have been delivered. Clause 17:No claim or claims made by the contractor for increased rates on the grounds that the market or other rates included in the contract, have risen during the period of his contract, will be recognized that is to say, the contractor would have to complete the work and or to supply materials at the rates mentioned in the Schedule and accompaniments hereof and the contractor hereby guarantees that the said articles would continue to conform to the description and quality aforesaid for the period shown in the schedule from the data of delivery of the said Articles to the purchaser and that notwithstanding that fact that 163 the purchaser may have inspected and approved, the said items will continue to comply with the specification and the contract. Clause 18:No claims or claims for increased rate on the ground that the Market or other rate included in th contract, has risen after the date of final delivery. In Chandra Bhan Gosain`s case (supra) dealing; with those very common features this Court observed as follows: "The property in the bricks was entirely of the assessee. The property in this bricks was wholly of the appellant. The possession of the bricks after manufacture was not disputed by the department. It was also not disputed that the goods were sold by him to private parties or other bodies, but it was admitted that the bricks were manufactured and supplied under the contract and the assessee had received payment for such materials only as are approved and passed by the competent authority. The Department was therefore bound to complete all rejected materials, stacked or placed in such position as may be pointed out to him. In the event of the material being considered by the officer in charge OF the work to be inferior to that described in the specifications, the Contractor shall have no claim for any compensation for any loss that may accrue on account of the collection of the materials or engagements entered into. The materials shall remain at the contractor`s risk till the dateof final delivery." Clause 17(2):In the event, however, it is found that the materials have been sold by the assessee to private party or other body, he shall have to pay to Department at the rate of 10% of the value of materials at tender rates. In view of the special features and characteristics of the contract with which we are concerned, this Court held as follows:- "Clause 17(3):In consideration of the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the property in question shall remain entirely of The assessee."

The petitioner was a member of the Legislative Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir. He was elected as a Member of the Lok Sabha on 4th February, 1972. The Proclamation of Emergency issued on 3rd December, 1971 by the President of India was either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased to be in operation on April 1, 1972, because the resolutions passed by both Houses of Parliament approving the said Proclamations of Emergency as required by clause (2) of Article 352 of the Constitution were not published in the official Gazette of the Government of India. The petitioner contended that the duration of the House of the People could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of emergency was in force under the proviso to clause (4) of article 352 of Constitution and since the two Proclams had ceased, the House had no effect and consequently all Acts passed by the House during the extended period including the Finance Act, 1976 were ultra vires. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Proclamation of Proclamation of AMENDMENT was not in operation as it stood during the relevant time had not been published in accordance with clause (1) of Art. 352 of 'the Constitution and therefore Parliament was entitled to extend the period of the said House for a period not exceeding one year at a time. The State has filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The two ProClamations had been validly issued by the Houses of the Parliament and approved by the resolutions of both Houses. [523C] 2. The resolution of the Rajya Sabha approving the Proclamation dated 25th June, 1975 was not published as required under clause (3) of section 2 of the first of these Acts. [624D] 3. The existence of the two proclamation of Emergency had also to be established by the Parliament before it could be said that the twoProclamators of Emergency were validly issued or not. [725E] 4. The duration of House of People was extended for a further period of one year and on the 25th day of June, 1976 when the Proclamation was passed both the Proclimations of emergency as required to be published in official reports of the three Houses of parliament and Rajya Sabha had not become in operation by virtue of the resolutions dated 3rd January, 1972 approving each of them had not ceased to operate before the expiration of two months from the date on which each of the them was issued. [825B] 5. The period of five years in relation to the then House of Parliament could have be extended for one year " while the Proclamation Of Emergency issued by both the Houses were duly revoked by the two Vice President acting as President of the India in the year 1977. [926C] 6. The second question is whether each of these Proclayations had ceased or not to operate after the expiration period of two years from the commencement of the extended date. [1025D] 7. The first question is, whether the two Proclamation of proclamation of Emergency dated 3th December, 1972 and 25th July, 1975 were either ultravires the Constitution and had ceasedto be in force by virtue Of the resolutions issued by Parliament approving each one of them having not been publication in the Official Gazette. [1125E F] 8. The real question in this case is whether the resolutions adopted by both House of Legislature approving the two resolutions had to be duly published in a official Gazette. It is clear that the existence of these proclayas was not disputed before the High Court and it was only contended on behalf of the petitioner that the resolution of Parliament approved by both of Parliament was invalid because the said proclayamations had not continued to operate even after the expiry of two days from the day on which the resolutions were passed.

The appellant was the owner of a temple. The said property belonged to the Thoguluva Thirumalayyan, the appellant 's ancestor, for a sum of Rs. 20,000/ and that it was an alienable private property of the family. The appellant claimed that the property belonged not to him but was incapable of valuation as it could have in either case no market value or was capable of being valued. The Trial Court decreed the suit in favour of the appellant holding that the said premises did not constitute a temple and set aside the decision of the District Judge. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court and dismissed the application for leave to appeal to this Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The property in question was a public temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951. [157 G] 2.2 The appellant did not have to pay court fees as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on a valuation made by him therefor. That being 157 the dispute between the parties, the question whether the property was a private or a public religious temple could have no market Value and therefore capable of a valid transfer. [158 A B] 3.3 The appellant ' s case was that in execution of the decree in Suit No. 650 of 1882 passed against the said Kuppaiyan the property fell within the ambit of Madras City Municipal Corporation Act, 1949. [159 C] 4.4 The High Court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that the subject matter of dispute was a Private or a private temple and therefore incapable of Valuation. [160 G] 5.5 The appellant could not have claimed that he had to pay Court fees as he would in his plaint and since according to the respondents the property did not involve directly or indirectly a claim or question resecting property of value of Rs 20, 000/ or more and (c) that the appeal did not involves any substantial question of law. [161 C] 6.6 The appellant was therefore entitled to leave under article 133(1)(a) and (b).

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the respondent company. The appellant was reemployed by the respondent Company and he urged that the practice started by the appellant of re employing retired persons should be discontinued. The Tribunal held that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for tiffin to its employees, but there was no obligation on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tiff in its employees. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court set aside the award and directed that the clerical staff should be paid As. /8/ per day and the subordinate staff as well as the subordinate employees should be given cash allowance in lieu of tiffins. The State Government appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The Tribunal has erred in law in making an award in respect of the cash allowance to tiffout allowance for the purpose of giving them a cash allowance. [815 A B] (2) The appellant 's grievance against the direction in the award that 572 As./8/ and As. 6 of the agreement between the parties, the appellant should stop the re employment of retired persons was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations. When it appeared to the appel lant that some employees who had retired found it difficult to maintain themselves and their families, the Tribunal took the view that it is not obligatory on the appellant either statutory or otherwise, for providing any further facility to the employees by way of giving him a cash Allowance for turtin. [915 C D] (3) The question posed by the Respondents ' demand must be considered. It may be conceded that some of the re employments may have been actuated by humanitarian reasons and the appellant cannot, therefore, be blamed on that account. But there are some other factors in relation to this problem of re employment which cannot be ignored.

The respondent Radha Kissen Agarwalla had obtained a money decree against Browne and he applied to the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge at Alipore for execution of that decree. The High Court held that the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the amount standing to his credit in the Provident Fund Account be remitted to the Westminster Bank, Birmingham. The respondent RadhaKissen Aggarwalla had not authorised the Reserve Bank to receive payment of the money on his behalf and that therefore the attachment could not be sustained. Held, further, that the order of attachment of the amount into which the two cheques were drawn by the Railway Administration was contrary to the terms of section 3 of the . The High court was in error in holding that the sum lying with the Reserve bank as agent of the Railway administration was exempt from attachment. The order of attach of the amounts into which both the cheques were issued by the railway Administration were contrary to law and therefore, liable to be attached. The appellant could not have been deprived of his right to claim immunity from attachment on the ground that he represented provident funds money and had applied for removal of attachment. [713 G] In the instant case, the amount lying with Reserve Bank as agent was not legal tender. The Union had clearly an interest to maintain the application for removal. The appeal is accordingly allowed and the order passed by the High Court is set aside.

The appellant was employed as a pump manufacturing enterprise, issuing a notice ending the ,employment and offering one month 's pay as authorized by the relevant Standing orders. The appellant submitted his tender on the ground that he had merit on his side, judged by the social conscience and judicial construction of the law in this branch of discharge simpliciter versus disguised ' dismissal. The Labour Court held that the motivation for the termination was the suspicion which lurked in the mind of the Regional Manager that information regarding tenders was being passed on by the workman '. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the action regarded as punitive it was bad, there having been no enquiry whatever with liberty to the employee to meet the charge. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : 1. The order of termination is not conclusive and the tribunal can go behind the form of the order look at the substance and set aside what may masquerade as termination simpliciter if in reality it cloaked a dismissal for misconduct 'as a colourable exercise of power by the management. [819D] 2.1 In the instant case, the action was held to be bonafide and the ground given that he was a cantankerous person undesirable to be retained was good. The form of order in such a case is not decisive and the Tribunal can go into the question whether the termination is a colourable or mala fide or an act of victimisation or unfair labour practice. [820E] 2:2 In the present case, it has been admitted before the Labour Court that the appellant had no merit on the point that he did not even file a counter affidavit and the counsel for the Union agreed that the order of retrenchment was not a camouflage to cover up what really was an order (1) 496 of dismissal. [828F] 2 :3 In the circumstances, it is difficult to accept the contention that the termination of service was a colourable act or an arbitrary exercise of the power vested in the management or as a result of victimisation and unfair labour practices. [829G] 3.2 The appellant had not even filed a counteraffidavit and the Counsel for the respondent submitted that he has no material and if so advised, to proceed against the appellant departmentally and, in the circumstances it was the duty of this Court to interfere and set matters fight. [827B] 4. In the facts and circumstances, the Court was satisfied that order of discharge was not an disguise or cloak for dismissing the employee and the grounds given that the same may be tested judicially. It was also necessary for the management to disclose to the Court the grounds of his impugned action so that the said same may not be tested judicial. [823A] 5. In view of the fact that the employer had lost confidence in the appellant, it was not open to the Labour court to interfere with the finding of fact recorded by the trial court on this point. [822B] 6. The power of the Court to go behind a form of an order is reaffirmed there. For instance, Vaidialingam J., speaking for the Court observed that if the exercise of such power is challenged on the grounds that it has no evidence, or is the result of a misreading of the material evidence, and is so unreasonable or grossly unjust that no reasonable person would judicially arrive at that conclusion, it can be the dutyof this Court. [824C] 7. In order to find out whether the action is justified, the employer must disclose to him the grounds for his impugned actions so that he may be examined judicially.

The Club, Pottery Town at Khurja in Uttar Pradesh arranged and conducted, as part of its social service programme, an "Eye Camp" intended to extend facilities of expert Ophthal mic surgical services to the residents of the town. The Committee deliberated on the issue and its recommendations in regard to the norms for the conduct and management of eye camps. It was submitted before us that persuant to the results of the inquiries conducted by the Deputy Director (Eye Treatment) and the Sub Divisional Magistrate, appropriate follow up action is contemplated by the Government against persons concerned and that, indeed, a criminal case has been regis tered against Dr. R.M. Sahay and his team and also against officers of the Government who, according to allegations, committed serious breaches of duty in sanctioning permission for the conducting of the 'eye camp ' without ensuring a strict compliance with the conditions prescribed in the Guidelines prescribed by the State Government in that behalf and in not effectively dis charging the duties enjoined upon them to over see the satisfactory and safe functioning of the camp. The learned Senior Counsel also sought to rest the right of the victims for damages on the footing that the persons who organised the 'Eye camp ' were acting pursuant to and under the 255 authority of Government and that on the doctrine of State action, the activity must be reckoned as that of the State itself which must, accordingly, be held vicariously liable. The amount shall be deposited in the District Judge who shall arrange to dis tribute the same in accordance with the procedure adopted at the time of administration of the interim relief.

The petitioner No. 1 was the President of a Board constituted under the Asom Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (Taking over of Management and Control) Act 1984, which was an Act enacted by the Legislative Assembly of Assam and received the assent of the Governor of Assam on 15.12.84. The petitioner No 1 filed a suit for temporary injunction restraining the respondents from taking over management and control of the affairs of the said Samiti. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the petition ers were not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution as they had been appointed by the Board and all the functions, properties and affairs of t he Samiti were taken over by this Board and the same was also confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order passed by the Governor under Section 3 of the Asam Rashtrabahasha Paonta Sabha (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1984 was a temporary measure and therefore the Samiti was being run by nominated members and the rights of the members of the Samiti under Article 19(1)(c) of the constitution were taken away. HELD: 1. The right to form an association, in our opinion, necessarily implies that the persons forming the Association have also the right to continue to be associated with only those whom they voluntarily admit in the Association. [912G] 2. It is not therefore possible for us to decide whether the petitioner No1 was a permanent measure or not. The period of the Karyapalika Sabha which was functioning in 1984 has come to an end though from 1984 till today they were not allowed to function. [ 913A B] 3. In view of the fact that the Act does not provide for as to how when the temporary measures comes to an d end the elected Byabasthapika Sabha and Karyapalka Sabha which were 176 functioning in 1985, it is clear that the Karyaprada Sabha which came into existence in 1984 had come to a end though after the new elections and a new Government came in power in Assam the Act was replaced by the Act and therefore we are restoring the Samiti and therefore it is made clear that this all was the mala fide action of the then Chief Minister of Assam. [1013C D] 4. The question whether the petitioners were entitled to an order of temporary injunction or not, was a matter which could be decided in a suit under Article 32 of the Consti tution of India. [1113F] 5. The Act does provide for temporary transfer of the management and affairs o f the Samiti from the Board imme diately but it is also clear that when the Act talks of a temporary arrangement in fact, the Act itself does not specifically provide for how when a temporary measures come to any end though there was no intention to restore them back to its elected authorities and office bearers inspite of the clear fact that they were never allowed to work.

The appellants and the respondents were married on May 10, 1938. The gift was made at the time of the marriage itself. It was accepted by Nand Lal Sao on behalf of Kamala Devi. The deed of gift was later confirmed on the occasion of the Dwiragaman (Gowna) ceremony which took place in December, 1938 and possession of the houses was also given to her. Thereafter Sumitra Devi felt ill and the deed of Gift was actually executed and registered on March 10, 1940, some two years after the marriage. The plaintiffs respondents claimed that Sumitra Devi was competent to execute any document of gift in favour of Kamala Kumari. The trial court held that the gift being of a reasonable portion of the estate of her husband to her daughter as a marriage dowry in pursuance and fulfilment of an ante nuptial agreement, it was not necessary for them to make a gift at the relevant time. On appeal by special leave, this Court reversed the findings of the trial court and held that it was competent for a Hindu widow governed by the Mitakshara law to make such a gift. In the instant case, however, the plaintiffs respondents were not entitled to the reliefs which they claimed. The High Court also held that in view of the said provisions the plaintiffsrespondents were not competent to make any gift at all and that the deed was made some two year after the death of Kamala. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The gift being a religious duty and the promise to make an ante muptial promise made by her father in law of giving a portion of his joint family property for the benefit of the daughter and the son in law, and a gift made long after the marriages may be supported upon the ground that the gifts were not in fulfilment of the moral obligation flowing from the ante n uptial agreement. [620 E] (2) The plaintiffsrespondents had no right to make gift at any time. It is further contended that Kamala Devi was not competent under the law to execute a deed of marriage in favour o the daughter as her marriage portion created a moral or religious obligation in fulfilment Of which it was entitled for the father to execute an ante deed of gifts in favour thereof. [613 A] (3) The mere fact that the mother had the limited right of 458 disposal, as in the case of a Hindu woman governed by Mitakshara law, would not make a valid gift at her time of marriage but it may be made afterwards in fulfilment o the promise.

The appellant was elected to the Baghapurana Constituency (District Faridkot) in the State of Punjab. The election petition was filed by Tej Singh alleging that he had got circulated pamphlets and posters among the voters of the constituency wherein he had mentioned that Ruplal had withdrawn his candidature and any vote given to him (Tej Singh) would be deemed to have been cast in his favour. The appellant contested the election on various grounds, namely, (1) that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices; (2) that the election petition did not contain a statement of fact as required by section 123(2) of the Act and (3) that no particulars of corrupt practice were given to the appellant in his nomination paper. The High Court dismissed the election Petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practices were clearly proved. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 123(1)(a) of The Representation of People Act, 1951 provides that every vote cast in favour of a candidate shall be deemedto have been casting in his own favour. [723C] 2.2 Section 123 (2), therefore, clearly lays down that every votes cast in the favour of the candidate shall not be deemed be a vote for Ruplals and the said posters were printed not by Ruplar but at the instance of Tej Singh. The effect of the posters was that all the voters who would have voted for Ru Plal would now cast their votes in favour, of Tej singh. [823D] 2:3. Section 123 of the Representation of the People Act provides that no person shall vote or be deemed as a candidate for any election to the Legislative Assembly unless he has been duly elected and has given notice in writing of his intention to do so within one month from the date on which he is required by the provisions of section 123 to give him a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken. [923C D] 2 4.1 The appellant had, proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh was known to him and that Exs. P 5 and P 6 were taken by him from Bhum Raj. In these circumstances, it is clear that Tej singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing of the poster by TejSingh was very small viz. 123 votes, if such a misrepresentation was not made, in all probability the votes would have gone to Avtar Singh. [1023C E] 2 5.2 The appellant has also proved beyond any reasonable doubt about that the payment of the vouchers .(Ex P 1 and P 2) were made by him along with the return of expenses incurred during his election campaign which was verified by him to be a true and correct statement. In other words, the effect of posters was to mislead the voters so as to make them believe that one of the candidates, viz.; Ruplad had withdrawn and any votes given to Tej Singh would be considered as a vote given for RuPlal. [1123C G] 2 6.3 The appellant is entitled to succeed on the ground of corrupt corrupt practices (referred to above). [1024D] 7.1 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour Of Rup Lal would have go to Avtar singh cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result of the election. [ 1024E] 2 7.2 In view, the irresistible inference and inevitable conclusion that can be arrived at is that TejSingh had indulged into corrupt practices specially when the Printing of the pamphlets by Tej singh was very large, viz.123 votes, it would have doubtsless materially changed the result thereof of the elections.

The appellant was a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal. The respondent, who was then Chief Minister of the State, filed an application for contempt against the appellant alleging that one Shri Devinder Sharma was a forest Minister in his Council headed by Sri Bhajan Lal and that he had been falsely implicated in a criminal case. The High Court dismissed the application on the ground that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have exercised their jurisdiction or power as conferred on them by Article 215 of the Constitution when it imposes a punishment for contempt. [893B] 1.2 The High court does not exercise its powers or power to punish for contempt under Article 215. When an order or decision is that of a single judge, to a Bench of not less than two Judges of the Court, the High Court cannot be said to be exercising its jurisdiction or powers as conferred by Article 216 of the constitution. [889C] 1:3 The High 'Court has exercised its jurisdiction and power only by punishing for contempt also includes the jurisdiction to decide whether such punishment should be imposed on the alleged contemnor or that no contempt has been committed by the alleged contemner and acquits him, such decision of the High court acquitting the contemnor is made in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punishfor contempt. The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the , cannot be exercised by the High Courts exercising their jurisdiction and the power will involve the acting in that particular manner and in no other. [899D] 1.:4.1 In a contempt proceeding there are only two parties, namely, the court and the contemnor. It may be one of the reasons which weighed with the Legislature in not conferring any right of appeal on the petitioner for contempt, but it must always be borne in mind that in a contempt proceedings there is only two party, namely the Court and the contemner. [994E] 1 :4.2 In a proceeding there is no right of Appeal under section 19(1) of the Act, as there is nothing to indicate whether such an order was passed by the competent authority or by any other competent authority. The aggrieved party under section19(1), can only be the contemnor who has been punished for contempt of court. [1094F] 1;4.3 In a case where the High ' Court does not impose any punishment on the allegation of criminal contempt, the petitioner cannot move this Court under article 136 of Constitution. [1009C D] 2.5 The High "Court" in section 19 is to punish the contemnor for contempt and it must be borne In mind that when the High' Court acquits a contemnor after hearing the parties and after considering the facts and circumstances of the case, theHigh Court does so also in the exercising its power or jurisdiction to dismiss for contempt by punishing him. [1019E] 2:6. The right of appeals under section 20(1)(a) is provided for. After giving such information he may still assist the court, but he must always keep in mind the fact that in contempt proceeding it has imposed punishment for Contempt also includes also the jurisdiction of disposal of the cases either by punishing the contemnor or by acquitting him. The exercise of jurisdiction or the power would involve the act in that manner and/or the power to decidewhether such punishment shall not be imposed upon the contemnor, but when theHigh court comes to the finding that such punishment will not be inflicted on the contemnor and acquir him,such decision of High Court acquitting the contemner is made In the exercise Of its jurisdiction/jurisdiction, the jurisdiction or authority conferred by article 215 of Constitution cannot be invoked by the courts.

The appellant was the tenant of a building in which he had been let out to the defendant for a period of three years. The lease was determined under section 111 (g) of the , and the lease was therefore determined under sub section (g). The plaintiff filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of possession of the building on the ground that the tenant had not paid rent as required by section 111(g) and that the lease could be terminated only if notice in writing to the lessee of his intention to determine the lease by the lessor bad been given. The trial court held that the provision in the rent note that on non payment of rent the rights of the tenant would come to an end was a clause of forfeiture and that no notice as required under section111(g), was necessary for terminating the lease in suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In second appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the amendment made in 1929 to section 111 of the Act is merely a procedural and technical rule introduced in the section by the legislature and is not based on any principle of justice, equity and good conscience and that therefore the principle of equity applied is the one contained in sub section(g). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The rule laid down in sub sections (g), (g ) and (g)(i) of section 111 prior to its amendment in 1929 and which still governs leases executed before 1st April, 1930, OD the reasoning of the decision would also be a rule of justice equity and justice or notwithstanding section 2 of the . [923 C] (2) The principle of law embodied in sub Section (g(i) is not applicable to leases made prior to 1st March, 1930. [924 D] (3) The rules laid down by the Master of Rolls in the present case are useful maxims in general and that in general they reflect the point of view from which judges would regard (1). equity and fair play. [1025 E] (4) The principles of justice and equity are not such a variable commodity, that they change and stand altered on a particular date on the mandate of the legislature. [ 1026 F] (5) The provisions as to notice in written writing as a preliminary to a suit for ejectment based on forfeiture of a lease are not based upon any principle or law which must be held to govern even agricultural leases.

The respondents were dismissed from service by the appellant on the ground that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the Respondents of showing cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of the dismissal order as required by the Standing Order No. Rauf (fourth charge being held not to have been proved) the punishment of dismissal in respect of Rama Shanker and Barmapradhan was erroneous while another writ petition (Misc. 17 as requiring a second opportunity being given to a workman at the conclusion of the enquiry into his misconduct and before inflicting upon him the punishment awarded by the learned Arbitrator was erroneous. The High Court held that the order of dismissal passed against Rama Shanker, Barmapsradhan and Baramapradhar was vitiated since no second chance was afforded to the respondents of showing any cause against proposed punishment after the recording of finding that the delinquent was guilty or the opportunity spoken of is the opportunity to meet the charges in the domestic inquiry. The Court, however, held that on proper construction of the Standing order it should have been held that no second notice was required to be given to an employee at the end of the period of probation and therefore the finding that enquiry was vitiated by not affording him such opportunity must be set aside and according to the High Court if the enquiry was valid and was not vitiated the punishment imposed on Rama Shanker was erroneous and consequently the order passed by the Arbitrator was set aside. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High court erred in setting aside the dismissal of Rama Shankar and Barchapradhara, while allowing the writ petition filed by the Management and directing the reinstatement of Rama Prasad and Bar chamapras for a period of two years with effect from 9th February, 1970. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in setting it aside. No question of law much less any substantial question of fact arises in this case. [209E] 2.2 The High Curt has confirmed the view of the Arbitrator and by the High C Court is correct in holding that the first part of the standing order deals only with punishment of dismiss inflicted upon Rama Shanker but does not warrant any such assumption and, therefore, it must disappear. [210G H; 210A] 3.3 The language used in the last part of Standing Order is clear and unambiguous. It is true that the words "all dismissal orders shall be passed unless the Manager gives an opportunity to a person to show cause against his proposed punishment of dismissing after he has been found guilty or, the opportunity afforded to him". [210A] 4. The language employed in the first portion of Standing order is clear. It does not require any such inference and therefore, the interpretation placed on Standing Order cannot be sustained. [212B C] 5.1 In the instant case, the Arbitrator had taken the view that the opportunity given to Rama Shanker & Barma pradhan while fomenting the strike was distinguishable from the more serious mis conduct of fomenting or inciting the strike and all the respondents were found guilty by the Learned Arbitrator of such serious mis practice and as such no distinction on the basis indicated between the two sets of workmen should have be made in the matter of punishment, on the other hand coun 367 sel for the Respondents urged that Standing Order NO. 17 provides for second opportunity to show explanation against the graver punishment of dismissed after he had been found innocent or the chance spoken of was the opportunity offered to him. [213F] 5:2 The language in which paragraph 3 of the S.O. says "all dismiss orders shall, be passed by Manager or Acting Manager who shall do so after giving the delinquent an opportunity of showing his explanation".

The appellant was a tenant of the land in question. The respondent 's father had been cultivating the land for not less than ten years to be deemed tenants under section 52A of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963. On the basis of an oral permission granted by the competent person, he continued in possession to be a tenant. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for eviction on the ground that the respondent was a lessee and had been inducted as a tenant by the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 7D of the Act. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree holding that since the lease was granted by a person who had no right over the land or who was not competent to lease the land, he could be deemed to be tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was in occupation of such land for non payment of rent. The High Court held that the lease granted by him was on the basis o an oral agreement and therefore the appellant could not be deemed tenant under section 7 D of the Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since there was no express provision in the Kerala Rent Control Act, 1961 for eviction of a tenant from his land, the respondent could not claim the protection under section 6D of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The lease granted to a person by a competent authority is valid and effective only if he has paid amounts for occupation of the property on the 11th day of April, 1957, and was not actually transferred possession of the same to the landlord before the commencement of the Karnataka Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1968, but had not actually transfer possession of such property to the tenant before the coming into force of the said Act. [620G H] 1.2 The lease deed executed by a lessee in favour of a person on the 12th day o f April, 1958, is valid only if it is shown that he has no right to continue in occupation after the 11 th day of May, 1957. [721B C] 1:3 The lease was not granted by any competent authority and the respondent had not lawfully transferred possession thereof to the appellant before the date of publication of the Madras Land Reforms amendment Act, 1970, but continued in occupation to be in continuous occupation of that land till the 11rd day of June, 1957 when the possession was handed over to him. [821B] 1.:4 The lease is valid for a period of ten years from the date on which it was granted and not for any period thereafter. The lease executed by the lessee in his favour is valid even if he had no rights over the property or had been lawfully cultivating the same before the 11 st day of July, 1957; [722C D] 1.(5) The lease has been granted by incompetent persons to be treated as invalid and such person shall be deemed not to be tenants. [921D E] 2.1 In the instant case, the lease deed was executed by an unregistered document purporting to be an oral consent or an unregistered deed purporting to have been a lease deed granted by an person who had been in occupation on the 13th day from the 12 th day o of April 1957, on the date when the appellant became a tenant and continued in his possession till the commencement o f the Kerala land Reforms ( Amendment) Act 1969, was applicable on the 10th day. [1021B D] 2:2 The respondent had paid amounts towards occupation of land to the respondent before the 12 st day o April 1957; and that he had not been actually transferred to the owner before the expiry of the term fixed under the varam arrangement.

The appellant was prosecuted under Section 135(b) (ii) of the , and sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,000/ . The prosecution evidence was that the cigarette lighters and flints were imported into India without an import licence and in contravention of provisions of Government of India, Ministry of Commerce & Industry, Import Control order No.17/55 dated 7 12 1955 (as amended) issued under Section 3(2) of Imports & Export (Control) Act, 1947, which was to be deemed to be an order passed under Section 11 of the Act. The appellant pleaded that he had not given any evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there, or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. The defence was that he did not produce any evidence before the Magistrate and that the goods were illegally imported into the country without an Import licence and that he was dealing with them knowing them to be smuggled goods. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under Section135(1)(ii) read with Section 114 of the Evidence Act, and sentenced him to six month rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the appellant had not produced evidence to prove that he knew that the articles were smuggled or imported in contravention Of the law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The mere possession by the accused of such goods could not enable the prosecution to apply Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act when the appellant could not know where the goods came from or when the goods are imported or that duty, if leviable was not P d on them. [529 E] 2. It is immaterial that the person who has been found in possession of the goods can not be said to be in possession with full knowledge of what the goods actually were. The very appearance of the accused indicated that they were newly manufactured and brought into this country very recently from another country of their assumed origin after a time when the restrictions on their import had been imposed. [629 E F] 3. Section 106, read with section 114 of Evidence Act is sufficient to enable the Court to come to the conclusion that the accused knew that goods must have been smuggled or brought into India. It was contended that mere possession of such articles could not be allowed the prosecution under Section 111(d) (i) of The Indian Evidence act when the person from whose possession the goods had been seized, for proving the place from where they came, or when he were imported, were questioned. [729 F] 4. It would apply only to goods seized under the Act in the reasonable belief that the article was being smuggled or import into the territory without payment of customs duty at a time. If the goods with which we are concerned here were not seized under Section 108 of the Customs Act, it is contended on behalf of the State that there could be some evidence which could enable the Courts to come conclusion that they are not smuggled goods and the manner in which they were packed indicated that them were newly procured and brought to this country. [765 G] 5. The appearance of ' such goods without knowing that they have been illegally imported or smuggled, is very significant. It may be true that the words "any goods to which this section applies" are not used in Section 116 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. But it would apply to goods arrested under the provisions of the Sea Customs Act and those arrested under a warrant issued by the Magistrate. [773 G] 6. The word 'or' is not defined in the Code. It has been used in section 116 of Evidence act.

The appellants were the President of the said Association from January 1946 to June 26, 1946. The suit was instituted by respondent No. 1 in the court of the District Judge, who reversed the finding of the learned District Judge and came to the conclusion that the other members of the Association were not entitled to participate in the profits made on the sale of 284 bales of Gwalior cloth and inasmuch as Nagar Mal had rendered accounts with regard to all other transactions, the suit for accounts must fail. The appellants filed an appeal before the Judicial Commissioner of Vindhya Pradesh, who set aside the finding and held that the suit was not maintainable by reason of the provisions of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935; and that the appeal was dismissed. On behalf of respondent No 1 it was contended that on the analogy of section 69(3)(a) of The Partnership Act, 1932, the purpose of the association was not illegal and a suit for recovery of contributions made by the appellants and also for accounts was maintainable for recovery. Held, further, that the High Court was in error in holding that the plaintiffs had a right to bring a suit against each other for contribution or apportionment in respect of the partnership dealings and transactions. The appeal must therefore be allowed. In the instant case, the High court was in wrong in holding the appellants had a legal right to bringing a suit on accounts of an illegal association which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the company association or partnership or by the individual members thereof unless it is registered as a Company under the RewaState Companies Act 1935.

The appellant was convicted by the Magistrate under section 9(1) read with sec. The allegation against him is that on 8.6.1986 at 2.0 P.M., he along with two others named in the complaint, shot and killed an elephant in compartment No. 6, compartment No 6, situated at Chaibasa, taken by the police along with three others named therein named in a complaint, fired from a rifle and killed one person named in his complaint, who was also injured. The High Court quashed the proceedings of the Magistrate on the ground that the allegations made in the article constituted an offence under sec. 9(i) readwith sec. 50(1)(a) of the Act. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that as an investigation by the Police was in progress in relation to the same offence, the learned Magistrate would be justified in quashing the proceedings and ordering issue of process against the accused. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The words "where such contempt is an offence punishable under the Indian Penal Code" are not defined in the Act but they have been used in the sense of being a part of the same transaction. [912C] 2.2 The expression "any person" in sec. 2(3) of 'Act' means any person who, by virtue of section 2(1), is an officer or servant of Government or a local authority or a corporation owned or controlled by the State Government or any other authority or body established by or under any Central or State Act or any local authority. [1012D] 3. The expression 'any person' in sec.(2) of Sec. 2 of the Contempts of Courts Act, 1953 is not defined either in the Indian Criminal Procedure Code or in the Code of Criminal Procedure. [1113E] 4.1 In the present case, the allegations and the complaint as they are, without adding or subtracting anything, if no offence is made out then the High Court will be justified In quashing the proceeding of the police on the facts of this case, is impermissible as an exercise under Sec. 50 (1) of The Act in its ingredients and content, is the same or substantially the same as Sec.2(3)(a). [1112F] 4 3.2 It is not possible nor advisable to lay down any inflexible rules to regulate that jurisdiction, one thing, however, appears clear and it is that when the High court is guided by the allegations, whether those allegations, set out in the FIR or the charge sheet do not in law constitute or spell out any offence and that resort to criminal proceedings would, in the circumstances, amount to an abuse of the process of the court or not. [1312F G] 4 4.3 In the instant case, there was no prior conviction and sentence for an offence u/s. 429 IPC e en assuming that the two offences are substantially "the same offence" and do not say 'There the act alleged to constitute such contempt being an offence '. ." [1313G H] 5.4 The High court was justified in exercising its powers under sec.(50) of Cr. Procedure Code, in its ingredient and content. [1412F; 1413A B] 6.5 In regard to the first ground, presumably, certain provisions of the "Act" in regard to cognizability and investigation of offences against the act, relevant to the matter, had not been placed before the High Courts.

The petitioner was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to six months rigorous imprisonment. In appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The law is that the accused should ordinarily be released on bail or on his own recognizance unless it is shown that there is substantial risk it is appearance or there are circumstances justifying imposition of conditions on release . [885F] (2) The object of granting bail is to secure the presence of the accused before the Court for further proceedings. If a Magistrate is Satisfied after making an enquiry into the condition and background of the complainant that the release on one 's own recognizances with punishment provided for violation will go a long way to reform the bail system and help the weaker and poorer sections of the community to get equal justice under law, he can safely release the accused on order to appear or on their own recognization. [886F] The language used in section 389(1) is clear and unambiguous. It is not intended to be exhaustive but it is intended to give a wide meaning to the words used in the section. [889A B] (3) The Magistrate must always bear in mind that monetary bail is not a necessary element of the Criminal process and even if risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against fleeing from justice, it is not the only deterrent and there are other factors which are sufficient deterrents against flight. [879B] (4) The language employed in section 390(1), as well as in section 391(2) of the Code is clear enough to cover both release on bond without bail, i.e., surety, cannot be conditioned to attend at the appointed place. If an accused released on his personal bond without sureties or financial security and release on his individual bond without surety will automatically lose his job if he has one, and is deprived of an opportunity to work to support himself and his family with the result that burden of his detention falls heavily on the innocent members of the family, (5) The socialist republic must always be in mind while interpreting bail. [ 889C] (6) The words used are "bail bond" in section 392(1)(a) of Code. It means a bond with or without sureties. If the accused is in confinement, actual or potential, may be released by the court to appear and on his/her own recognizence unless it was shown that he has been released on order for appearance or on her own recognizings. But if risk is of monetary losses, it can safely be release on order. [899D] (7) The word "bail" in Section 392(2)(a), means a person who has been arrested or imprisoned, upon receipt of security to ensure the released prisoner 's personal appearance or that he be released thereon. If any Magistrate is satisfied after making such enquiry into his condition and circumstances of the case that the releasing on bail included release on the accused 's his own bond without arrest or on His own recognizment, it cannot be said that an under trial is worse of than a convict or that the power of the court is not merely a penalty but also a measure of punishment. [909E] (8) The provision in section 394(1A) of Criminal Procedure Code may appear to be a safeguard of presence in court for further proceeding. But, if a Magistrate has been Satisfied before making an order under sub section (2), the power is not only the same as that which is contemplated by section 389 of the Cr.

The assessee was a branch of the assessee. The assessee claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, exemption from tax in respect of 6% of the capital employed in 'Eldee ' as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of the Capital so employed Rs. 3,21,460 advanced to 'Castle '. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that no question of law arose out of the order of the Tribunal. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to "Castroly established undertaking 'Effee Velvet and Silk Mills called for the sake of brevity '. In the appeal before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the finding of the Appellate Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on some evidence ignoring other essential matters, and that the factor taken into consideration by the Appellate Board in coming to its conclusion was a relevant factor. Held: (i) The finding of fact recorded by the Income Tax Officer was not based upon any material extraneous or irrelevant considerations; (ii) The Tribunal had failed to consider the other questions whether the constitution and ownership of the two businesses 'were the same, and it could not be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. The Appellate Assistant commissioner had rightly rejected the appeal. Held, further, that the decision of the Incometax Officer was based upon some evidence on which its conclusion is founded and ignores other relevant matters on which the Appellate Asstt Commissioner had relied in support of his conclusion. The Tribunal has not misdirected itself in law in arriving at its finding, and in refusing to require the Tribunal to state the case and refer it, the High Court was in error.

The order of the High Court is set aside. The Minister in charge sheet dated February 18, 1975 was issued by the Secretary of the Department to Duggal respondent. In the writ petition filed by him, Dugdgal respondent challenged notification dated January 29, 1974 fixing the seniority of the engineers n the Irrigation Department of the Punjab Government. During the course of the heating of the writ petitions, an order was made by the High court on November 18, 1974 whereby the Minister concerned had heard the parties and passed the necessary order in the matter. The High Court directed that the Minister should file his personal affidavit in regard to the allegations made in the petition and also to give him an opportunity of controverting those allegations if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of facts and circumstances of the case, we do not feel persuaded to interfere with the order made by this Court insofar as it has directed that Dugodgal respondent should file her personal affidavit. The other part of the order whereby the Secretary was directed to file his Personal affidavit is setaside. The appeal shall stand disposed of accordingly. M.R. Appeal partly allowed. (1) The High court was in error in directing that the Secretary should file an affidavit in respect of the allegations contained in the amended petition. (2) The Minister concerned should file a personal affidavit before him. The remaining part of order whereby DugDgal respondent had raised a grievance against the Minister. Direction was also issued that the Ministry should file its personal affidavit and thereafter pass the necessary orders in the case.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The rent was due as arrears of rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent. The respondent filed an application under section 259 of the Act for realisation of the amount. The magistrate ordered that the amount be recovered from him and directed the respondent to pay the same within one month. The appellant challenged the jurisdiction of the magistrate to realise the amount by suit. The High Court held that arrears of the rent due under a lease cannot be recovered under section 260 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and that it was not a "claimable" by the Board under the Act or the Rules framed thereunder. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The words "rent on land and buildings" which appear between the words "any tax" and "any other money recoverable by a Board etc." must equally be governed by the words 'recoverable by a board etc.". [347G H] (2) The section provides for recovery by suit also and as such it wilI not be possible for the Board to recover rent of land and building only if such rent is recoverable by the board under the provisions of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911.
