[348B C] (3) Section 259 does not empower the Board or the Military Estate Officer to let out the land or buildings upon the ground that it cannot be said to be claimable by the respondent in respect of rent directly claimable under any express provision of the statute or the rules framed thereunder thereunder. The section is intended to give protection to tenants against eviction and to protect them from eviction. [349D] (4) Section 258 does not confer power on the Board either to recover arrears of any tax, rent or fee which could be recoverable under summary provisions of that Act or Rules.

The appellant was employed as a section salesman in the respondent company. The appellant was appointed as a Section Salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. The Company had sold its product to various dealers appointed by the company in the area of each section salesmen and local travelling salesmen. The company had sold their products to various dealer appointed by it in the areas allotted to him. The respondent company was also engaged for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sale of the product of the company. In the year 1973 when the appellant 's service was terminated, the appellant was paid a sum of Rs. 1,000 as compensation. The Labour Court held that the termination itself was illegal but dismissed the application only on the ground that the appellant had left the company 's services of his own account. On appeal by the respondent the High Court set aside the order of the Tribunal and directed the management to pay an amount equivalent to three years salary at the rate he was drawing when the services were terminated. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Labour Court had given findings in favour of the appel lant on the question whether the termination of the services of the employee by the management was legal and justified and if not to what relief he was enti tled to. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Labour Courts have given findings on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour court. It is seen from the facts found that the Tribunal had noted that the appeli lant is required to supervise the work of the other local salesmen appointed in the place of their operation. [446G H] 1.2 The Tribunal was right in holding that the finding of the Tribu nal on the nature of the work is a finding on a questions of fact. It was also borne Out by the documents produced before it and it was also bear out by evidence before the labour Court. [547C D] 2.3 The Labour court had given finding in favour o the appellant on that question. The finding of fact has been recorded in favour Of the appe lant. It cannot be said that the findings were perverse or based on no evidence. [648B C] 3. In view of our holding that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. The question whether an employee is a workman employed for manual, skilled and/or clerical in nature cannot be gone into by the Labour Courts on the questions whether the appellant is aworkman or not. [748C D; 749A] 4. In order to come within the definition of workmen under the Industrial Disputes Act as it stood in the year 1972 when the respondent 's Service was terminated the employee has to be under the employment to do the work for one of the types of work referred to in the Section i.e. manual, clerical and/ or clerical in character. The employer had to supervise work of other local salemen and the supervising work of others were part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the Area of his operation. (749E F] 5. In these circumstances, the Labour C ourt was right. [848B D] 6. The Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act was not applicable to the termination in the instant case which was long prior to the enactment of this Act and it being long prior thereto had come to the conclusion that the employee was employed to do canvassing and promot ing sales for the company and to collect the amount of sale. [948C E] 7.

The Company was a Government lessee under section 181 of the M.P. Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007 (Act No 66 of 1950) and was holding land from the State Government after it had been acquired by the Government for a public purpose of the State. The Company filed an application before the Additional Collector alleging that the land admeasuring 495.05 acres was held by the Company in terms of the lease granted by the State and the Company was not a "pakka" tenant under section 185 of the Code. The Additional Collector dismissed the application holding that the Company had not become a `pakKA ' tenant under Section 54(vii) of Part II of Act 177 No. 66 of1950 in respect of the land in question. The High Court held that the company was not an occupancy tenant under sections 185 and 187 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue & Tenancy Act Samvat, 2007 ( Act No. 67 of 1950), as it had never become a "a Government lessee" under section 178 of the said Code. In appeal to this Court by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Company that the High Court had erred in holding that since the Company failed to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the agreement, the proceedings were initiated by the 178 Additional Collector by his Order dated 1.10.1977. Dismissing the Appeal, HELD: (1) The Company was entitled to remain in possession of the lands as a lessee under the newly stipulated terms of lease, the Company has been holding the land 180 from the date on which it had acquired the status of a " Gair Maurusi tenant" and that it had not been an ordinary term as defined in the Madhya Bharat Act No 66 Of 1950. [419D] (2) The High court was right in holding, that the Tribunal had erred by holding that there was no evidence to show that the original lease was obtained from the predecessor State and that the fact that the appellant Company had never acquired the character of a 'pakata' tenant under the old lease or holding under the new terms agreed upon between the parties to enable the Company to remain In possession of that land as a lessor. [519E] (3) The Additional District Collector was well justified in having recourse to the proceeding prescribed under section 182 of the Indian Penal Code.

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands in the State of Orissa. They had been cultivating the land for a period of about five years prior to the coming into force of the principal Act, and they were paying rent regularly to the Government. The petitioners contended that the provisions of the Travancore Act 14 of 1965 did not apply to them as they were not law in force when the United State was formed. Held, that section 47 incorporated by Act 13 of 1965 which provided for compulsory acquisition of any land in an estate under the personal cultivation of a person is guaranteed by the second proviso only where the land is within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force or any building or structure standing thereon or appurtenant thereto, unless the law relating to the acquisition of such land, building or structures, provides for payment to the landholder for extinction of his interest, the market value of that part of the surplus land which is within "the ceiling limit" under the principal act. The right to compensation which was not less than the market price under any Act providing for the acquisition by the State Government was never made operative by a notification and was repealed by Act 15 of 1965. The power to bring into force the provisions Of the Travancore Cochin Act 14, was exercisable by the successor State. The proviso was not applicable to the landholders under any statute for the purpose of determining compensation. The second proviso was in operation on July 1, 1949 and since no notification was issued before Ch. IV of the Principal Act was repealed, there was no ceiling limit prescribed to the petitioners under any other law for that purpose.

The widow 's estate was in the hands of a Hindu widow. The widow ' s estate was not in existence at all and the widow ' had no interest left in her, which she could make a surrender of her estate to the reversioner. The suit was filed by the widow for possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that as the widow herself was in sound disposing state of mind and was not competent to execute the sale deed, she had no right to claim any interest left by her deceased husband 's property. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that as a widow herself is in possession of a limited interest of a widow ' and that as such surrender could not prejudice the rights of persons, acquired by grant from the widow or by prescription against her prior to the date of surrender and that the right of the widow to make a surrendered in favour of reversions was not an alienation but merely a transfer of property. Held, further, that if the effect of surrender is to destroy the widow "s estate" it could not be surrendered to the reversioners. The fact that the widow had made a surrender by the Hindu widow to her husband or his spiritual benefit, did not affect the right and interest of the alienee or of the person who has acquired interest by adverse possession against her. Instances do arise where an alienee has paid valuable and substantial consideration for a property on the expectation of enjoying it so long as the wife remains alive and his expectations have been cut short by a surrender on the part of the husband, which no doubt benefits the reversioner in the sense that he gets the inheritance even during the entire period of the deceased 's lifetime. The reversioners could not, subject to any question of fraud or collusion that might arise, be in a position to recover possession of property from (1) Vide Vaidyanatha vs Savithri, I.L.R. [1955] Mad. 892; referred to.

The appellants, who were the Directors of the Polytex Company, had been appointed as a Receiver in respect of certain shares of the Cotton Mills Company. The company was a registered company under the Indian Companies Act, 1956 and it had been established by the Central Government under section 3(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of the amount due to it from the respondents on the ground that the notice issued under section 169 of the Act was invalid as the provisions of the U. Thapar (Control) Act, 1958 were not applicable to the Cotton Mill Company and that the proceedings before the Collector were without jurisdiction. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the order of the Collector being an order in the nature of a charging order the Receiver had obtained an equitable right in the shares pledged in favour of the Government of Uttar Pradesh against a loan for the purpose of meeting the dues payable to the employees of the cotton Mills Company and he made a further order under section 149 of the Land Revenue Act read with section 5 of the Uttar Pradesh Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act 1958 appointing a Receiver. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that since the order was an order passed in the exercise of its powers under the English Law, it had no bearing on the case before us. In this appeal by special leave it is contended for the appellants that the High Court was wrong in holding that when the order is an order made in the discharge of its statutory functions, the Receiver has no power to appoint a Receiver and that therefore the order passed by the Collector was without jurisdiction as the proceedings were not maintainable under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The order of a Collector being a charging Order the Receiver having obtained an enforceable right in favour, the Cotton mills Company had lost its right to vote at the meeting or to issue a notice under section169 of the Indian Income Tax Act and could exercise its rights under section 170 of the said Act. [520E] 1.2 The order passed under section 17AA(1)(a) of U.P. Government Electrical Undertaking (Due Recovery) Ordinance, 1952 taking over six industrial units of the yarn Company held by the Cotton Corporation Company was not an order under the law but a charging provision order under which the Receiver was appointed in respect thereof and there being no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, the cotton mills Company continued to be the member of the polytex Company. [620B] 1:3 The order dated February 1, 1985 clearly shows that it had not been validly passed since the Cotton mill Company had ceased to have the rights of a member under section 167 of the Income Tax Officer. It was therefore not open to the appellants to contend that the attachment of the shares in question was an act done by the Receiver and could be enforced only if he had been attached by the collector. [720C] 1.:4. The order was passed under the provisions contained in section 169(2) read with Section 190 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [821B] 2.1 In view of the foregoing the shares were pledged in their favour and the ownership of the share in question had vested in the Cotton Textile Mills Company by reason of the appointment of a Receiver by the Government. The sale deed executed by the appellants was not a valid document. It could be said that the sale deed was a sham transaction. [820C] 2:2 In view Of the foregoing, the High court was wrong holding that it has no bearing in the case of the appellant and other connected cases. [824D E] 3.3 The High court had erred in holding the order dated March 1, 1986 to be an order as a charging section under the Land Tax Act.

The plaintiffs were the owners in posses 833 sion of the suit land along with some others. The Gram Panchayat, Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala, District Sangrur in the State of Punjab had no sort of right in the suit property and that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. The plaintiffs filed a suit against the Panchayat for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering their possession. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that since the question involved in the case was merely one of title to the suit, it had jurisdiction to try the suit. In appeal the High Court reversed the judgment of the trial court and held that the civil courts had no jurisdiction to entertain or adjudicate upon any question whether any property or any right to or interest in any land vested or deemed to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Act or in respect of any matter which the Commissioner or the Collector is empowered by or under the provisions of the Act to determine. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since there was no question involved as regards the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner, the jurisdiction of civil court had not been taken away by virtue of section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in holding that the question whether the property in question belonged to the Gram Panchayat or not is shamlat deh vested or not and whether it belonged to a Panchayat. [833C] 2. Section 13 of the Haryana Village Common Land (Regulation ) Act,1961 provides that no civil court shall have jurisdiction to decide any question Whether any property has been or is not shamlat Deh vested or otherwise than as a Panchayat, may submit to the Collector within such time as may be prescribed, a statement of his claim in writing and signed and verified in the prescribed manner and that he shall have Jurisdiction to decide such claim in such manner as may been prescribed. [820D] 3. The question whether a suit land belonged to it as shamlat was not a civil court by virtue o section 13 of Act which had been inserted by the Haryana Legislature into the Act. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil Court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question Whether the property belongs to the Panchayat or whether it belongs to that Gram Panchayat. The Collector only under section 11 of the act has jurisdiction to determine such claim. [828E] 4. Section 12 of the Land Act provides that every order made by the Collector or the Commissioner shall be final and shall not be called in question in any court by way of appeal or revision or in any original suit, application or execution proceedings. No civil court can have jurisdiction (a) to entertain, adjudicate upon a question whether an property or a right to interest in such land has not so vested in the Panchayat; or (b) to question the legality or of any actions taken by him under the act or under this Act. [829G] 5. The civil courts have no jurisdiction in respect to any matter arising out of any transaction which the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be shamlat land vested in it. [827B] 6. Section 11 of Act provides for a declaration that the land in question belongs to it or is being shamlatted deh vested in Panchayat under section 13A of the said Act and such order cannot be called In question in an original suit application or executing proceedings. The Civil court has jurisdiction (i) to decide whether the suit is not maintainable by virtue Of section 13(B)(ii).

The appellant Board had been granted a licence for the supply of electricity to the respondent Board. The respondent Board had issued a notice under Section 49(1) of the Electricity Act, 1910, requiring the consumer to deposit in cash security for one month 's estimated consumption charges and bank security equal to two months estimated charges as contemplated by Regulation 20 read with Schedule. The appellant Board filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the supply on the ground that there was no commercial transaction governing a bank deposit, and that the Board had not been conferred statutory power under Section 50(1)(c) of Electricity Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there is no legal obligation to pay interest to the consumer proceed on the assumption that the board is keeping the security deposit and deprived the consumer of the money which is alleged to be earning interest with the Board. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. There is no statutory obligation to Pay interest to a consumer who may become due and payable to the Board for violation of any conditions of supply in the context of wide scale theft of energy, tempering with the meters and such other methods adopted by the consumers. The obligation to make payment of consumption charges is such that it represents the moneys of the Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. [529G H] 2. There are no statutory obligations to pay Interest on a deposit made by the consumer with the Electricity Board against default in payment of interest. The duty to pay the interest to its consumer proceed is not only a deposit in money to safeguard recovery of electricity dues for the energy supplied to the consumers on credit but also a security towards payment or satisfaction of any money (For example, theft), which may become payable by the Consumer to the Electricity board against default. [629G] 3. The condition of supply requiring a consumption security deposit has a direct bearing on the operations of the board which are To be conducted In such a way as to ensuring a surplus, it is liable to be appropriated for the satisfaction of the concerned authority for violation by any conditions Of supply in that context of wider scale theft. [613G H; 613A] 4. The Board has been conferred power under section 49(2) (g) to determine the conditions on the basis of which supply is to be made. [429C D] 5. There can be no doubt that if there is a revision in the rate of tariff there must be an upward revision in consumption security deposits since it has direct bearing to the level of supply, in consumption of electricity. The measure of interest is such as to shock the conscience of the Court. [ 613A B] 6. The Electricity Board has not been given any power under the provisions of Section 49 (1) (c) to fix the conditions for supply of energy by the Board as to how it represents moneys of its Board. It is only a security for payment of electricity and the conditions subject to which it is supplied are statutory, the provisions under the conditions of Supply that the Electricity Boards shall not be defeated a law is enacted which operates somewhat harshly on a small section of the public taken in conjunction with the position that without a law in that form and with that amplitude smuggling might not be possible of being effectively checked, the question arises whether the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by article 19 (1)(f) & (g). [613C D; 613F] 7. The power under sub section (2) is subject to the condition that there are special reasons why interest should not be allowed namely: (a) where money or other property has been deposited as security for the performance of an obligation imposed by law or contract from the date of deposit.

The petitioners were appointed as Deputy Directors in the Telecommunication Research Centre under the Semyian and Technical Officers Grade I. The petitioners were promoted to the post of Assistant Director by way of promotion from amongst the direct recruits who were working in the telecommunications Research Centre. The respondents, who were directly recruited to the Telecommuni cation Research Centre, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the rules of promotion contained in the Recruitment Rules and the petitioners contended that the impugned rules are violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution by not granting them the same special pay which is granted to the trans ferred officers who are working in that centre with effect from 1.1.1973. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were not competent and were not able to discharge their duties. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belong are not entitled to any Special Pay but the transferred officials have to be paid extra amount by way Of Special Pay in addition to their scale of pay which was the same as the scale ofpay of direct recruits because the transferred official had to perform in the Telecom Research Centre duties which are not in their general line. [13097H] 2. The Government has virtually admitted that all relevant things such as qualifi cations, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same between direct recruits and the transferred employees and that the transferred Officials have to work throughout the Tele Communication Research Centre duty which is not in his general line and that they are given only the pay at the same rates at which it is paid to the transferred officers working in this centre with retrospective effect from the date on which the transferred officer commenced to draw the Special Pay upto date and to continue to pay it in future also as long as the transferred Officers have to perform their duties in future. [10097B] 3. The discrimination between the direct recruit and the transfer officials regarding the payment of Special Pay is attempted to be justified by the Government in the Counter affidavit filed by Shri C.L. It is not the case of the Government that the petitioner are not competent or are not able t o discharge their duty. All the direct ent recruits are graduate engineers and have been working throughout in the Telephonecommunication Research Center duties which arc not in the general line, that is, the same post and discharging the same functions as between direct recruitand the transferred personnel and that th e transferred officials had to be pay extra amount at the pay scales prescribed for them. [ 10097C] 4. The arrears of the Special pay upto date payable to the direct recruited shall be paid within four months from today. [910D] 5. The arrear of the special Pay uptodate payable to all the direct recruitment shall be payable within four month from today and to continued to pay the same in future further as long As the transferred Official has to performin the Tele communication Research Centre functions which are non in their normal line, it is not possible to deny the Special Allowance at the higher rates to the petitioners according to the Recruitment rules. [1110B] 6. The question relating to the denial of promotional opportunities to the petitioner according to t he Recruitment Rules is left open to be agitated before the Central Administrative Tribunal after a rigorous competition examination need to be adjudicated by the Central Government in accordance with law. [1210C] 7. The petition ers (direct recruits) who are specifically recruited to posts and Telegraphs Research Centre discharge same functions, responsibilities and responsibilities as the posts of Deputy Director, Assistant Director and Scientific and Technical Officer Grade I respectively with effectfrom 1.2.1973, are entitled to the Special Scale at which they are drawing the SpecialPay upto date. [ 1210D E] 8.

The appellant was an employee of an industry governed by the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The respondent was dismissed from service on account of certain dispute relating to change in respect of certain industrial matters. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court contending that he had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application under section 42(4) of the Act which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Court and prayed for setting aside the order of dismissal, discharge, retrenchment, termination of service or suspension. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42 (4) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour court for relief under section 7 8(1). In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The scheme of section 78 (1) seems to be that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all the same by a direct reference to the labour court. [723C] 2. The Scheme of section 8(2) appears to be very clear and unambiguous. It is not necessary that an employer intending to effect any change in regard to matters covered by section 42 must give notice of such intention in the prescribed form to the representative of the employees. If an employee desiring a change in his respect of any order passed by the employer under standing orders which would of necessity include an order of discharge, to see whether it was possible to come to any agreement and an application to theLabour court could only be resorted to after efforts had been made to settle the dispute and no agreement had been arrived at. [761D] 3. The object of section 79(1) is that disputes must be settled between the employer intending, to effect a change or in respect thereof. If within the period prescribed under the proviso to sub section (4), no agreement is arrived at in respect Of an order matter or change referred to in the said proviso, it cannot stand to ground that an application should be resorted only after efforts have been made by the employers more than six months prior to the date of such order. [763F] 4. The purpose of section 78(1), therefore, is that a Labour Court must first take steps to settle all disputes covered by paragraph A. As the scheme of the act is that dispute should be settle as far possible and ultimately through conciliation, it did not stand on reason that no agreement was arrived at between the parties to the dispute etc. and an applications to the workmen seeking relief under sections 7 8 (1), 42(2), 42 (3) and 43(4). [763D] 5. The provisions of section 77(1)(a) are very clear. It does not mean that disputes falling under clause (a) of paragraph A should be decided as far in possible and only primarily through arbitration and agreement it does so. [762B] 6. In the instant case, the scheme is that all disputes should have first arisen if within the prescribed period under the Proviso to sub Section (4). The object is that the dispute should not be settled without reference to any of the parties concerned to the disputes covered in section 4. If a Labour court is to decide, all the disputes falling within clause A must be commenced on an application made by any of them to the employer. [758G] 7. In other words, effort must first be made by an employer who intending to affect any change or dispute in respect o matters covered under section 4 and that an employees desiring a changed in respect to any order issued by the employee under standing Orders which would include an application for relief before the Labour Courts.

The respondents, who were occupying the property under a registered lease for a period of 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971, filed an application under section 12(3) of the Act before the Munsif praying that the appellants ' application under sections 12 and 12 be dismissed. The Munsif allowed the application and directed the appellants to make another application under [section 12(1)] of the Bihar Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The respondents filed an appeal against the order of the Munsif before the District Judge which was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner, Ranchi. The appellants ' revision application was also dismissed by a Division Bench of the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question is whether the petition filed by the appellants as an application for eviction under section 11 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, is maintainable before the Civil court. [910B] 1.2 The question whether a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term lease is entitled to move the Court by an application Under section 12 of the , is whether he has any other good and sufficient cause for terminating the lease on the expiry Of the period limited thereby, he may, within fifty days of the delivery of such notice, appeal to the court in that behalf and the Court after hearing the parties may termi nate the lease or extend the same for such period as it deems proper in the circum stances. [1010B C] 1:3 The question does not affect the substantive right of the parties as the controversy is concluded by the first appellate court in favour of the appellants. If it is assumed that an application filed under section 13 of the . Act before a civil court was maintainable and the judgment of the learned Munsif as a decree therein. [1110D] 1.:4 The question arises whether the petitioner 's application under Section 12 of .the Act before Civil Court was maintainable in the facts and circumstances of the present case, there is no point in asking the appellants t o choose which course to follow. If the matter is covered by section 12, and as we have made an assumption in favour o the respondents that section 12 has no application to the presentcase, there would be no question in asking them to file such an application. [1210E] 1 :5 The question of whether a petition under section 10 should be treated as a plaint and the impugned proceeding as the one in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeal. If that is not so, the proceeding has to be treated to be a suit and the decree therein as a result thereof. [1310F] 1.(6) The question also does not arise where the matter was covered by Section 12. [1410G] 2.1 In the present cases it is the Civil Court, Ranchi which is the appropriate court either for filing a suit or proceeding followed by a appeal and an second appeal, but that should not come in the way in construing the correct nature of the proceeding. [1512E] 2:2 The occasion for filing an applica tion under section12 of the -Act because even on assuming the argument of the respondents to be correct the appellants would succeed. The occasion fo r filing an application before the civil court, Ranchi was concluded by a first appellate Court either for filling a suit for eviction or making an application in accordance with law and the present appeal is a most appropriate one for exercise of such power. [1612F] 2.(6)(a) In the instant case it is not the Civil Courts, Ranchi who are the appropriate courts either for entertaining a suit under section11 or making any application under that section.

The appellant Society filed a suit against the respondent for a declaration that the election of the Secretary of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as the Secretary. The trial court after holding that the appellant had consented to it, dismissed the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court set aside the order of the trial court and allowed the appeal filed by the appellant. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court has erred in holding that a suit for restoration of the suit was not maintainable and the error committed by the trial judge while recording the finding on the merits of the case was such which the High court ought to have rectified. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court had rightly dismissed the appellant' application as not maintainable. [723C] 2.1 In the exercise of inherent power under section15 1 of Code of C.W.P. Bey pointing out that it has no jurisdiction to do so, the trial Court was justified in dismissing the appellant's application as being maintainable. The courts below were, therefore, not right in holding the application filed by Hari Narain Swami on the ground that the trial Judge had failed to exercise a jurisdiction vested in him by law. [761D] 2:2 In the instant case, the High C ourt was, therefore wrong in dismissing appellant ' s application as non maintainable. If the appellant did not give his consent, the court has the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set aside its decree if it is satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree on a fraudulent repre sentation made to it that the party had actually consented to the compromise petition filed in the case but his consent has been procured by fraud, the Court cannot investigate the same. [763D] 3:3 The High Curt was also wrong in holding so because it had no jurisdiction, and the only remedy to the party is to institute a suit. [762B] 4. In the view of the High Courts that the only remedies available to the parties are to institute an suits were to institute fresh suit. If a party makes an application before the Court for setting aside the decree, the prayer for withdrawal of the same cannot be made on behalf o the appellant at all and the mere fact that the court had not jurisdiction to entertain the suit is no ground to refuse the prayer.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Civil Service and was appointed as an officer in the Indian Police Service. He was promoted to the post of Additional District Magistrate, Jammu on April 1, 1946. On June 27, 1940, he was confirmed as an Additional District Judge. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Ordinance. The High Court dismissed the writ petition and held that the Ordinance promulgated by the Governor General under section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, did not cease to be in operation after April 1 1946, because it was repealed on April 2, 1946, and that as soon as the declaration that the emergency was at an end was made on April1, 1946 by the Indian Legislature without any limitation on its duration, the original position was restored and the Ordinance in question which had been promulgated in exercise of the emergency powers ipso facto lapsed when the emergency became declared to have ended. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation " were omitted from section 72 by section 1(3) of the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940. [656 C] (ii) The Ordinance having continued in operation even after the declaration of the Emergency having come to an end, it continues in force until it was superseded. [757 D] (iii) The word " for " the space" in section 72 was not to be read with the omission of the words restored to their original position after April1 1946, but was merely a temporary measure which could have been validly made applicable to the State of Jammu and Kashmir as stated above. [856 E F] (iv) The expression " for" in Section 72 is not to mean that the period of duration of the ordinance in question should be determined having regard to the provisions of section 72. [957 D H] (v) The Act having continued, it was not limited to Ordinances which had already been promulgated between June 27 1940 and April 1 1947, but would have the like force of law as an Act passed by the State Legislature without limitation on their duration.

The appellant, who was a member of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and was convicted by the trial court for an offence under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death on the ground that he had committed murder in the course of his employment with the Government of India. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that the death sentence should be awarded or not, because the accused had committed an offence within the meaning of section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and that the sentence imposed on him by the High court was not proper or uncalled for. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The right to life has been regarded as 'very valuable', sacrosanct and fundamental ' therein, though in Jagmohan Singh 's case (supra) it is not permissible for this Court while hearing such an appeal to lay down any law ' within the ambit of article 141 of the Constitution to limit or circumscribe the scope of death sentence under section 354 (3) Cr.P..C., 1973, nor is it constitutionally or legally permissible for the Court while dealing with an appeal confined to sentence under Article 136, to curtail the scope and ambit of death penalty under section 307, as a rule of universal application, be substituted by a sentence of imprisonment for life, irrespective of the gravity of the clime as the surrounding circumstances i.e., virtually abolish the extreme penalty. [1077 H; 1078 A] 2. The question whether the death penalty should be imposed or not must, in my view, be left to the discretion of the Judge trying the accused and the question of sentence must depend upon the facts and circumstance obtaining in such case. [100B C] 3. In the instant case, the High 'Court was justified in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a) of Cr. P.C. 1973, I would say that on the facts before them they commuted the sentence of death to a sentence lesser than that imposed by the Trial Court and confirmed the death Sentence. [101B C; 101D E] 4. The decision in Rajendra Prasad 's Case (supra), therefore, cannot be construed as laying down a ratio decidendi. [102A B] 5. In view of the principle laid down in Rajendra Singh Prasad ''s case (Supra) it must be held that it does not lay down many legal principles applicable to any legal problem disclosed by the facts or circumstances obtaining in the said case. The guidelines given are that the 'special reasons' must relate not to the crime as such but to the criminal" for which there is no warrant in section 354 of the Cr. PC., 1973. [103C D] 6. In order to determine whether a death sentence can be awarded, it is necessary to consider whether the accused has committed an act which constitutes an offence punishable under section 304 I. P..C. and whether he has committed such an act or omission as would render him liable for punishment under section 498A of the IPC. [104D E; 1077 A] 7. The expression 'special reason ' occurring in section 376(3)(a) is so great that an interdict against it is impossible to define nor legally permissible, but the guideline given is that the "special reasons ' must relate to the Crime as such and the criminal". For this purpose, the pendulum has swung to 1076 the other extreme and the guideline giving is that a special reason ' must relates not to "the crime assuch but to" the criminal." [1078 E] 8.

The appellant was a partner in a firm called Gautam Cycle Mart, Meerut. He entered into partnership with others under the name of Gautam Cycleolla Mart, in 1939, in contravention of the Government Servants ' Conduct Rules. The appellant was exonerated of the allegations and imputations made against him on each occasion. The Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., Lucknow, reduced the appellant 's rank from the post of an Income tax Officer to that of an income tax Inspector, and that he had been subjected to trial on allegations which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries overlooks that no charge was framed as a result of any previous enquiry. The order passed by the Commissioner of Incometax, U P., Lucknow reducing the appellant from the rank of an Assistant Income tax Inspector to that post was void and inoperative. He was also placed under suspension on 30th September, 1953, by the Deputy Director of Investigations, who was appointed by the commissioner of Income Tax as Inquiring Officer. That first charge was that the appellant had entered into a partnership with other persons, under the style of Gautam Auto Mart, Agra in 1939. The question whether the appellant was subjected to a trial on allegation which had not been proved, could only be raised before the High Court. It was only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural justice that it can vitiate the whole departmental trial. In any case, this could not be material. Unless such a point could be raised, there could be no declaration that the departmental proceedings were null and void. The plea that the order passed was invalid and inoperative, was also raised before us in the departmental appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court did not deal with a number of submissions made because they had, apparently, been forgotten. [696B] 2.1 In any event, it is possible that the appellants may have been emboldened by the failure of officers to report earlier that charges should be framed and fully inquired into by Officers whose integrity and sense of justice is not challenged. If such a contention could be made, there would be no question of revocation of special leave at this stage after hearing arguments. [796C] 2:2 The High court did not consider the question whether any rule was cited in support of such an objection to the nature of charge which would cover the starting of the Gautam Cycle Return at any time subsequent to 1939 also. [597E] 3.1 There is no provision in the U. P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, for revocation of grant of special Leave to appeal by this Court on the ground that some material 586 facts were suppressed or misrepresented for the purpose of obtaining special leave. The High 'Court did not decide whether a rule was relied upon in support thereof. [643E] 4.2 In any view of the matter, it could not have been said that all the points sought to be raised by the appellant which had gone into the case upto its final stage were not argued before the Division Bench. The mere fact that some materials 586 facts are suppressed or over misrepresented cannot be a ground for revocation. [641B] 4:3 In the instant case, it was for the appellant to satisfy the Departmental authorities, which had looked into the matter upto its stage, that he has suffered some injustice which to be set right. The point on which special leave was granted is not enough to merit cancellation of the special leave to appeal which was granted by this court. [651B C] 4(a) In the case before us, it had not even been shown how the witnesses whose production was said to have been disallowed could also help the appellant. The departmental proceedings are null and invalid.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The contracts between the appellants and the M.M.T.C. were entered into by the S.T.,C. on board the ship named by the Corporation. The appellants contended that they were not the last purchaser within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Pradesh) Sales Tax Act, 1957. The High Court held that the contracts between them were integrated and that the contract of sale was integrally connected with the contract entered into between the parties. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the agreements between the M/s. F.O.B. and the foreign buyers were inter separate and independent con tracts of sale, and therefore, the M..M. T.C., was liable to pay the tax. HELD: The contracts entered into with their foreign buyer on F. O.B., are distinct and separate transactions and it is the S tatement which determines the question whether the contract between the merchants and the Corporation is integrated or not in the course of export. [412 E] In the instant case, the contracts were inter independent and con tracts and therefore the purchase by the State Trading Corporation from the merchant was the last purchase in the State. The agreements between them are distinct. It is true that the transactions between the appellant and the S T. C. were inter part of the same transaction. [427 G] In F.I.R. 1957 Mad. 864, referred to.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi 521 Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. The respondent was appointed as Salesmen in the year 1974 and he was confirmed in the post of Salesmen on probation for one year. On October 19, 1974, the appellant was not on probation and assuming maximum in favour of the respondent that he was a temporary employee, constituted retrenchment within the meaning section 2(oo) and in the absence of strict compliance with the requirements of section 25F, termination was held to be invalid. The appellant filed an application before the Labour Court under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act for setting aside the order of termination and for reinstatement. The Labour Court dismissed the application holding that the termination was illegal and inoperative. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the termination of service of the workman was invalid as he had rendered service for a period of 240 days in a period preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually worked under that employer for not less than 240 days; and (2) the order terminating his services was illegal. HELD: 1. The termination of the service of an employee constitutes retrenchment within section 2 (oo). [515E] 2. If a workman is in employment for a certain period he shall be deemed to be in continuous service for the purpose of Chapter VA. October 19 1974 Commencing from that date and counting backwards, admittedly he has rendered service during a period Of 12 calendar months preceding the relevant date being the date of retrenchment. [516F] 3. The conditions are that commencing the datewith reference to Which calculation is made, in case of retrenchment the date thereof being the relevant day. If he has, he would be deemed not to be In continuous service within the ambit of sub section (1). And if that service is continuous service throughout the period of 12 calendar month, he shall, be deemedto be in uninterrupted service for one whole year. [616B] 4. The condition is that commencing of the date With reference towhich calculation is required to be done, in cases where a workman has rendered services for a periods of six calendar months, he should be deemed as in continuous Service for a further period of one year for the purposes of Chapter V. [717C] 5. If the termination is illegal especially where there is an ineffective order of retrenchment, there is neither termination nor cessation of service and a declaration follows that the workman concerned continues to bein service with all consequential benefits. [816F G] 6. The provisions are that where a person has rendered continuous service in the sense of his employment for not more than 240 day during the period he has been in continuous employment for one full year, he will be deemed be in regular service for another period of two years for the same purpose. If that service was continuous service before the date on which calculation was to be effected, he could be deemed only to be 'in continuous service under an employer for a duration of one month for the reason that he has not rendered uninterrupted service during the periods of 12 months and, therefore, his case falls within section 25B(2) (a). [716F H] 7. The order terminating the services of the workmen was ab initio void and inoperative and a declared that he continues to remain in service with effect all consequential reliefs, namely, back wages in full and other benefits, if any. [758G] 8. If there is no termination or cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of the employee, it would be a retrenchment within Section 25B (2).

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. The appellant submitted his explanation to the charge sheet and contended that he had received Rs. 150/ as illegal gratification from one Darbara Singh and bad demanded Rs. 30/ as unlawful gratification from another Ude Singh. The Enquiry Officer held that the appellant was a temporary servant and had no right to hold the post he was occupying and by the impugned order the appellant 's services were terminated. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order dated March 17, 1955, was in contravention of article 311(2) of the Constitution as no reasonable opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him was at all given and that the provisions of article311 had not been complied with by the Enquiry Officer. HELD: The order dated February 5, 1955 was not the order pursuant to which employment of the petitioner was terminated but it appears that in the written statement filed by the State in the High Court it is expressly admitted that the employment of appellant was terminated on March 17. 1955. [723C] In the instant case the enquiry made by the Settlement Officer was made with the object of ascertaining whether disciplinary action should be taken against the appellant for his alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the Settlement officer with 719 which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed, the misdemeanor was proved. [823D] The order of termination of employment was passed without affording him an opportunity to make his defence and it appears from the record that in this case the appellant had been given an opportunity against the enquiry. In the written statements filed by both the parties before the Settlement Office the appellant admitted that he was a probationer or a temporary employee but, in the reply filed by him, it was specifically admitted that his employment had been terminated on February 5 1955. The order passed by the Deputy Collector on March 30, 1955 is not of that nature and therefore, there was no stigma affecting the future career of the public servant by the order terminating his services for unsatisfactory work and conduct. [820E] In view of this clear admission of the fact that the appointment of the respondent was terminated without giving him an (1) (1958) S.C.R.828. (2) (1960) S C.R..828. termination of service or discharge of a probationer following upon an enquiry into allegations of misconduct or inefficiency with a view, if it put a stigma on his competence and thereby affects his future career by the orders terminating his employment for unsatisfactory worked and conduct, the termination of services is by way of punishment. [829F] In that case the order of dismissal was passed with the purpose of ascertaining who should be confirmed. The termination of the service or discharging a probationer in an enquiry on charges of misconduct cannot be said to be an order pursuant thereto.

The appellant was promoted as Professor in the Department of Science and Technology, Government of Jammu and Kashmir. He was promoted to the post of Professor in a college on November 28, 1978. The State Government made rules for selection to posts of Professors in the colleges. The appellant was selected by the Selection Committee. The Selection Committee recommended his name for promotion as Professor. The respondent was appointed as Professor on November 15, 1977. On December 1, 1979, the State Government issued a notification under section 133(2) (b) of the Constitution inviting applications for selection and appointment to posts in the college. The Commission published a list of selected candidates for the post. The list was approved by the State Govt. on January 28, 1981. The name of the respondent was included in the list of successful candidates. The Government issued an order dated December 1., 1979 appointing him as Professor with effect from November 15. 1977. The respondents challenged the validity of the said order before this Court. It was contended that the Selection committee had not consulted the Commission and that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The State Govt., at first framed rules on November 14, 1968, for selections to be made to posts for Professors in colleges. [873 H] (2) On the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions from one service to another, and on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers, from one Service to another and on suitability of candidate for such appointment, promotions and transfers, the Governor may make regulations specifying the matters in which either generally or in any particular circumstances it shall not be necessary for the Commission to be consulted. [888 A] (3) The High Court erred in holding that the requirement for consulting the Commission was mandatory and not does not arise in this case because it is not disputed, and is in fact the case of the appellant State, that the Commission had consulted the Public Service Commission under section133 of the constitution, and as the writ petitioners have not ventured to take a plea to the contrary, we have no hesitation in holding on the facts which has been brought on the record, that it was not necessary for them to undertake a plea that the State was consulted. The High court erred in observing that the Government was consulted in regard to the principles regarding be followed by making appointments from one services to another. [898 B] (4) On a perusal of the record and we find that the High Court has erred in law in holding, on the basis of the minutes of the Commission dated July 22, 1969, which makes it quite clear that the Public Services Commission for the State of Jammu & Kashmir, hereinafter referred to as the Commission, was consulted on the eligibility of candidates to promotion as Professors.

The petitioner was a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly. He was elected to the Bihar Legislature on May 30, 1957. The Speaker passed an order under section 7(1) of the Representation of People Act, 1951 declaring that the House of Commons had been declared as a "public assembly" within the meaning of article 194(3). The petitioner challenged the validity of the said order before this Court in a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition and held that the Speaker had no power to make an order for removal of the House from its membership, and that the provisions of article 105(3) on the ground that they were ultra vires the Constitution were not violative of article 19(1)(a). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the freedom conferred by article 19 (1) (a), having regard to the nature of the fundamental right and the rules of interpretation, this Court should so construe the provisions as to give force to both the provisions. [682 E] (ii) Even if the privilege was not expressly made subject to Article 19(3), having due regard to its nature, the Legislature has also a similar privilege or power and it can exercise it notwithstanding the fact that it infringes the fundamental rights of a citizen. [643 F] (iii) The privileges conferred on a House of the Legislature by article 194 (3) are only those of the members and committees thereof and by the latter part of article 195(3)(a), the Legislature had also a corresponding privilege or jurisdiction and it cannot exercise it, notwithstanding the facts that it infringe the fundamental Right.

The private college in the town of Behram pur, Ganjam District was established by the name of Khallikote College. The Government of Orissa took over the management of the College on and from March 9, 1971, and a formal agreement was executed between the managing committee of the college and the Governor of the State. The College after taking over was administered as a Government College. In the year 1971, each of the respondents were drawing a salary of Rs.600/ per month or more in the scale of pay Rs.61080/ whereas the Government scale for Reader was Rs. 60000/ . On July 30, 1970, each one of them less by only Rs.60/ . The last two Readers in the list who. were lucky to draw salary of the amount of Rs,600/ and Rs.510 860/ respectively as on the date of take over were treated differently by the Government from the eight Respondents on the sole ground that they were drawing as Reader salary of more than Rs.100/ . In the meantime, the Government prescribed qualifica tions for appointment as Readers in different faculties in the said College on the basis of liberal endowment under a trust deed from the then zamindar of Kujangpur District. The Director of Public Instructions (Higher Education) Orissa, which appears to supersede the earlier circulars on the subject, issued a formal order dated July 19, 1971 directing that the Gov ernment shall take into account as experience, the service of the Respondents while they were in the private college since, according to him, the necessary qualification is eight years experience in Class II, Orissa Education Serv ice (O.E.S.). The Government also prescribed qualif ions for appointments as Readers was Rs,.600/ . It is further stated that at the time of reference to the P.S.C. for determina tion of suitability for appointment, the Director of public Instructions ( Higher Education)Orissa, which appear to supersede earlier circulars dated the subject. The Respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order and praying for a direction to the Government to take into consideration the recommendations made by the Public Service Commission for consideration of their suitability for appoint ment as Readers. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since under the aforesaid terms of the take over they were working as Reader before the takeover was administered, the only differentia was, therefore, the salary drawn by the Readers on the dates of take ing over was a highly different matter. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that though the Respondents had all requisite qualifications for the appointment as Reader and they were all holding the posts of Reader before taking over their names, they will not be even eligible on the plea of absence of teaching experience in Government service, for consideration for appointment by the public Service Commission. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The condition of draw ing of Rs.,600/ or more on thedate of takeover is arbitrary and discriminatory. [675G H] 2.2 The condition regarding drawing of Rs,.500/ or less on the d date of taking over, which has been laid down in the aforesaid circular as a particular qualification for eligibility for appointment to the post is arbitrary, discriminatory and violative of Article 16 in the sense that it will not only be more than one but also all the Readers in Class I, Orissa Educational Serv ice(O.F.S.) but also amongst the Readers who on the day of takei ng over were in receipt of pay of Rs..600/ on the eve of takingover.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1) of the . The State Transport Authority granted temporary permits to them on certain conditions. On appeal by the Corporation, the High Court held that in respect of the route a scheme has been prepared and published under section68C of Chapter IV A of . The Corporation applied for only 3 temporary permits and therefore an application for temporary permit was made by the appellant. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that in view of the provision contained in section 68F(1A) the Corporation alone is entitled to apply for temporary stage carriage permits and if such application is made by a person other than the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled, to obtain a temporary permit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The scheme in question provides that even though there are 7 vacancies and the Corporation applied only 3 Temporary permits, once the Corporation made an application under section 66 F(2) of .the Act for grant of temporary permits not for the full strength but something short of it there was no power left in 985 the State Transport authority to grant temporary permits. [782F] The scheme is published by the State Government under section 67C of .The Corporation will have to consider the applications of the present appellants for the remaining 4 vacancies and grant four permits according to law. [882G H; 883A] In that event the State transport Authority or the Regional Transport Authority as the case may be, in exercise of power conferred specifically upon it by section 68 C(1 A) can grant temporary permit to any person in respect thereof till the approved scheme is notified and, therefore, the Corporation will be entitled to all the temporary permits, if such applications are made by persons other than Corporation. [888B] The State transport authority or the Appellate Tribunal cannot grant a temporary stage Carriage permit merely because there are seven vacancies and one of them is entitled for a temporary permits only. If the Corporation applies for all the permits but only for some, the inevitable conclusion is that for the balance strength the Corporation has made no application for the temporary permit which was published in respect Of the route under section 65F(I A) to the exclusion of others. [982C] The High Court fell into an error by interpreting section 68A. If a scheme is prepared and, if the Corporation is willing to operate vehicles to the maximum strength undoubtedly the State Roadways will have power to grant permits to any other person willing Jo obtain temporary permit and ply vehicle because in respect the remaining strength there would be no application by the corporation and section 68 E(1 C) would be squarely attracted. [898D] The Corporation is entitled only to temporary permits till the scheme is finally published, but if the State is unable to provide services by obtaining all requisite temporary permits it will have also to grant permit to anyone else if the corporation is unable not provided service by obtaining any requisite temporary permit, the State may grant to any one else if it has applied for all of the permits. But if the Government applies for only three temporary permits then the State can grant to a person in regard of the area or the route or part thereof specified in the scheme and the permit so granted will cease to be effective on the issue of a permit to the State. [878D E] The decision of the State Tribunal is upheld both by the High court and the High Courts.

The appellant was the son of Sarup, respondent 10. The father of the appellant died leaving behind his widow, two sons and three daughters. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the property inherited by him from his maternal grandfather. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the property in suit was ancestral property qua the appellant and so it allowed the appeal preferred by respondents 1 to 9 and dismissed the appellant 's suit. In appeal, the High Court held that the properties inherited by respondent 10 were not ancestral property but that the ancestral estate in which under the Hindu law, a son acquires jointly with his father an interest by birth, must be confined to the property descending to the father from his male ancestor in the male line. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the decision of the trial court. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit in question was not ancestral properties as the appellant had no right to bring the present suit. HELD: (1) The doctrine of stare decisis is applicable and should present no obstacle in holding that a custom differed from the Hindu Law on the issue before their Lordships. [1107 C] (2) The principle of stare judicata is in applicable and cannot apply where the property has come to a person by descent from a lineal male ancestor, or in default of, heirs male, to property which if the descent had been through a son, would be ancestral property. [1007 D] (3) The decision of this Court in Narotam Chand 's case (1), should not be accepted as correct. In dealing with the point as to whether the property acquired by a Hindu from his paternal grandfather is ancestral property or that such property in the hands of a daughter can be given that description. Mahajan J., as he then was, who delivered the main judgment of the Full Bench, held that this decision was wholly unsustainable. [1108 E] (4) The question as to what whether property inherited from a maternal grandfather is not ancestral qua his descendants under the customary law of the Punjab; but it was not suggested that the custom differed with the Hindu laws on the point before their Lordship. In deciding the question as whether the suit was joint property or not, the Court has to consider whether the properties which were inherited by a son can be described as ancestral property and that raised the same old question whether property from maternal grand father in the hand of a grandson can be said as ancestral Property or that Such property in his hands is given that designation. [1008 E F] (5) The decisions of the High Courts are wholly unsustainable as a decision on the question of law which has been followed by the community since 1895.

The appellants were charged under section 449 and section 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted them under sections 449 and 302 read with sections 149, and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for two years under section 307/34 and to rigorous rigorous imprisonment each under section 448 of the Code. In appeal the High Court held that there was no evidence against them and that they were not guilty of murder. Held, that the conviction of the appellants under section 302 readwith section 34 is not sustainable in law. The charge under section 324 read with s 34 of Indian Penal code is not based on any evidence. It has to be noticed that the object of the house trespass was to commit theft if it is committed "in order to the committing of any offence punishable with imprisonment". Section 452 of the Criminal Procedure Code runs thus: "Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge and under such circumstances that, if he by that act caused death, he would be guilty of offence of murder." The words "inorder to" have been used in section 449 of the Penal Code are not intended to refer to an act done by a number of persons in furtherance of the common intention of all of them to kill Ebrar Ali. There is no reason why the purpose in committing the house assault must be the commission of an offence punishable under section 450 of the Act. The object of house trespass is the commission or offence punishable as provided in section 451 of the criminal Procedure Code. If the purpose of committing the murder is the act of a person when that individual has a particular intention or know and under the circumstances, it will be proper to say that he has committed the house offence in order to committing theft. The words 'in order lo" have to be understood in the context of the object and purpose of the section. The word "in Order to" has been used by the legislature not only in section 450 but in section 457 of the Evidence Act. It is quite clear that each of the other three who did not use the dagger must in law be considered to have done this act of using the dagger. The intention or possession must in fact be gathered from the circumstances and the surrounding circumstances. The purpose of house assault is the offence punishable by section 452 of Indian penal Code. Section 457 of Indian Evidence Act runs thus "Whoever commits a house trespass with the object or knowledge of committing theft but has failed to accomplish the purpose, it shall be lawful for him to commit an offence under section 451." The word 'in" has not been used either in section 448 or section 457. It must be understood that each person shall be held to have committed the entire criminal act. If he by such act caused a death, the offender would be liable either to imprisonment for life or to suc h punishment as is hereinbefore mentioned. The offence under Section 451 read with Section 34 of Criminal Procedure code is punishable under Section 452 read with [section 457] of the IPC. The second contention that no charge under Section 307 readwith s 34 was sustainable in Law, must therefore be rejected.

The appellant was a Sarswat Brahmin, resident of Pathankot in the district of Gurdaspur and the last male holder of the properties in suit were non ancestral. The respondent filed a suit for declaration of his title as collaterals within four degrees of Gurdial. The trial court held that the suit for a mere declaration was not maintainable (ii)that the appellant was not a collateral of Gurdial at all, (iii)that there was no custom whereby the collaterals of one Harnam Singh were excluded from inheritance by the collateralS up to the fourth degree with respect to ancestral as well as self acquired property of her father. The High Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the appellant had failed to discharge the onus that was placed on him by producing in evidence the Riwaj i am of 1913 and, therefore, the appellant could not be held to be a collateral or a collateral. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) that the respondent had not produced any evidence showing that he was a collaterals; (ii),that the properties were ancestral while the rest of the lands in suit are non ancestral and (iii). that there was a custom according to which daughter was excluded from succession to the self acquired properties of her husband. HELD: 1.1 The respondent has not produced a single instance of a daughter having excluded the collateral or self acquired Property of her deceased father. [153 A C] 1.2 The appellant had fully discharged the onus by producing evidence showing the custom of the Punjab being that a daughter excludes the collateral from succession, to the ancestral property of his father. It was enough for the Court to say that irrespective of whether the properties are ancestral or selfacquired the collateral is not a record of the wishes of the persons appearing before him as to what the custom should be. [154 A C D] 1:3 The respondent had failed in discharging the onus which was cast on her by producing the RRiwaji am and which has been discredited in judicial proceedings and held tobe incorrect cannot, in our opinion, be regarded as a reliable or trustworthy document and cannot displace the initial presumption of the general custom recorded in Rattigan 's book so as to shift the onus to the daughter who is the res pondent. [156 A C E] 1 :4. The appellant has fully discharged his burden that was on him. [157 D F] 2.1 In the last case, the collateral's were beyond the fourth degrees and it was enough if the presumption as to the correctness of the RRC was rebutted by the instances collected and set out in Appendix 'C ' of the same Riwraj i am and who have, therefore failed to discharged the burden that is cast on the respondent. [158 B] 2:2 The respondent did not now dispute the appellant 's right to succeed to her father 's ancestral propertie 'section These cases, therefore do not throw any light on the present case which is concerned with the question of succession to self acquiredproperty of her mother. [159 G H] 3.3 In the third case, it was sufficient for the court to say whether irrespective of either the properties or in dispute the collateral has been carefully prepared and does not contain within its four corners contradictory statements of custom and in the opinion of the Settlement Officer is not an record of a wishes of a person appearing before them as to how the custom could be, it would be a presumptive piece of evidence in proof of the special custom recorded therein. [160 C] 4.3 The appellant ' s right to succeeded to her husband 's self acquired estate of her son has been varied by a special local custom excluding the daughter which is binding on the parties.

The appellant was the Managing Director of Messrs Bird and Co. Ltd., and of Messrs F. W. Heilgers and Co., Ltd., who were acting as managing agents of various companies registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The respondent 's case was that the different capacities of the executant were distinct matters for the purposes of section 5 and that the instrument was chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty payable if separate instruments were executed in respect of each of those capacities. Held, that the document in question does not comprise distinct matters and therefore requires to be 855 stamped with the total amount of stamp duty payable in respect thereof. The fact that the donor of the power of attorney executes it in different capacities is not sufficient in my opinion to constitute the instrument one comprising distinct matters or in respect Of each of such matters would be chargeable under the Act within the meaning of section 3(a) (1) (d). The fact, however, that he, as trustee, executor and administrator is also comprised within the instrument and are not separate matters but comprises one matter only and that matter is the execution of a general power of Attorney by the donor in favour of the donees constituting the doneies constituting the same. The words "distinct matter" must be construed as distinct categories. It is within the very nature of the general power conferred thereby. If every capacity of the donor is to be considered as a distinct matter, it is but logical that whatever acts the donor are capable of performing whether in his individual capacity or in his representative capacity as trustee or as executor or administrator are also comprised in the instrument, and therefore require to be included within the expression "distferent matters" in section 5. The word "distinction" must mean all acts which can be done by the donee himself, whatever be the capacity or capacities which he enjoys and cannot be split up 857 into individual acts which the donor was capable of discharging whether in their individual capacity as trustees or as an executor or Administrator are also included within it. If that is the position, it would be logical that what constitutes the instrument is one comprising different matters in so far as the different functionaries of the donee are concerned. The mere fact that a person executes a power of power in favour to act for him in all the capacities which his attorneys were enjoying and cannot therefore be split into separate instruments each comprising or relating to a distinct Matter in so insofar as the various capacities of his donor are concerned, would not constitute the offence under section 5(a)(1) of the Act. The High Court was right in holding that the instruments in question do not comprise different matters and thus requiring to be855 stamped.

The assessee was a Mahalaxmi Mills Ltd., in the other two appeals, and it had filed the appeals before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner as also the Income tax Officer. The Appellate Assistant commissioner held that the depreciation availed of by the assessee under the Bhavnagar War Profits Act was not allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, because it was a fit case for appeal to the Supreme Court under section 66(1) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1961. In appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words "any law relating to income tax and super tax or any law relating thereto" did not permit the Income Tax Officer to make any deduction under this bead. Held: (i) The words "or which would have been allowed to him if he had been in force in the past" in section 13(5)(b) of Indian Income Tax Act, 1923, do not require "all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to Income tax and Super tax or a law relating To tax on profits of business which was law of a part B State before it became included in the Part B States before it become included in Part B state. The words 'any law pertaining to income Tax and supertax or any Law relating to tax on profit of business" are apt and sufficient to express the intention that if the Incometax Act, 1948, which was not in force, the depreciation that would have be allowed if proper claim had been made should be deducted in ascertaining the written down value. The word "or" is a term of art. 286(1)(a) of Constitution. It does not mean any law which has been passed by Parliament or State Legislature but which has come into existence after it became part of the Constitution. (ii) The expression "or to which would be allowed to he if proper application had been filed" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order, 1949, means that if a proper claim has been made and substantiated, assuming the Indian income tax Act 1922, then depreciation actually granted under any law or rules relating thereto, should be excluded in ascertaining its written down Value. (iii) The word 'or' does not require any indication to indicate that it would have to be included in computing the written up value. It is only a provision which has to be made for the purpose of determining the written off value under section 13 (5)(a).
