The words used, in our opinion, are apt to express and give effect to this intention.

The appellant, a contractor of the Mysore Construction Co. (M.C.) was awarded a contract by the Karnataka Power Corporation Ltd., in favour of the respondent No. 1 for construction of a building on the land belonging to the respondent Nos. 2 and 3. The respondent No 1 had also executed an agreement with the appellant for construction and execution of the work. The appellant, however, did not execute the work within the stipulated time. On the other hand, the respondent authorities issued a notice inviting tenders from intending contractors for supply of tender forms to various intending tenderers. The respondents were called upon to submit their bids on or before 31st March, 1985. The appellants submitted their bids and the appellant was also informed that the pre conditions mentioned in para I of the N.I.T. and other documents referred to in para V could be supplied at any time before the final award of the contract could be made. The first respondent rejected the bid of the appellant on the ground that the appellant had not fulfilled certain preliminary requirements which, under the Notification Inviting Tenders (N.I.)T., had to be ful filled even before the forms of tender could be submitted to any intending contractor. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the requirement for supply was only the three conditions set out in para 1 of the notification and that the details called for in para VI could be met before consideration of the tenders. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that there is no difference between the requirements in paras I and V and that only para I and not para V sets out the preconditions and that all the documents referred thereto were intended to verify the fulfilment of the condition in para l. The contention was that even if there is some difference between para I, V or VI of theN. I.T., it is open to the K.P.C. to decline to consider the party for the contract and if a party comes to Court saying that the rule was likely to be relaxed, he will not be able to produce the document by the time stipulated but would have applied had it known that the rules were likely to been relaxed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The preconditions of eligibility to submit tender forms are only the two conditions set forth in para II and not the general procedure which the KP. C. was following in regard to N. I.,T.s issued by it from time to time. [237E] 2.1 In order to assess the value of the certificates furnished in this regard and if the K P.C., considered them sufficient to warrant the issue of a tender form to the applicant, no injustice can be said to have been done to the appellant by the consideration of its tender side by side with that of the M.C..C. [238E] 3.1 A court may place on the NI. T.s issuing the tender documents only because it thought it would not be possible to produce a document by way of evidence before the time fixed but would require application of mind and that it has been understood and implemented by the K..P.c. [239B] 3:2 The pre conditions and that every document referred to therein must be intended to verifying the fulfilment thereof before the tender books can be supplied, are all necessary requirements in para III, V and VI of N.1. [240C] 4.3 In order that the tender papers issued by the appellant should satisfy the K C.P.,C. is also found to have satisfied the K Public Works Department. The K. P.

The appellant was a displaced person. He had been allotted certain land in the East Punjab Act XIV of 1947, and he was declared to be evacuee property under section 5 B of the EastPunjab Act XIV Of 1947. The Custodian General issued a notice to him on the 10th March, 1952, asking him to show cause why his order should not be reviewed. He did not comply with the notice. On the 11th March 1952, the appellant filed an application before the Additional Custodian General for revision of the original orders of the Custodian General and Additional Custodian in 1953. The Additional Custodian dismissed the application on the ground that the application for confirmation was not maintainable as he had no jurisdiction to entertain the application. The appellant preferred a revision petition against the order of the Additional Deputy Custodian General which was rejected by the Additional Commissioner, who held that the order passed by the Custodian was not an administrative order and it was not open to him to file an appeal in this Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the revision petition filed by the appellant was incompetent as he did not have jurisdiction to hear the revision application against the orders passed by Custodian General under section 27 of the Act and that the revisional order of Additional Custodian was an administrative one. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order under appeal is one passed by virtue of the wide powers of revision vested in the CustodianGeneral under section 56(2) (q) and that clause (c) thereof must be construed as referring to matters ejusdem generis with clauses (a) and (b) but in the view we propose to adopt, we do not wish to express any opinion on the merits of the revisional application. [1139F] 2. The High Court was right in holding, that the applications for confirmation pending on the date when the order was passed by a competent authority were not open and became final and conclusive. [1040B] 3. Section 58 of the Ordinance provides that anything done or any action taken in exercise of any power conferred by or under the Ordinance shall be deemed to have been done or taken in the exercise of the powers conferred by this Act as if this Act were in force on the day on which such thing was done or action was taken. [ 1040C] 4. The provisions of section 40(4) of the 1947 Act, viz., sections 5 A and 5 B are not applicable to an order passed under the Act as they apply only to purely administrative matters and that their case falls within the scope of the first portion, viz. "anything done" or any act done or anything taken in exercising of the power conferred under or under this Act.

The appellant company was a registered concern. The respondent company claimed bonus for the relevant four years in respect of its practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 and that the claim for bonus for those who were either excluded or exempted from the Act, was founded on tradition or custom or 596 condition of service and in that light, the Tribunal made short shrift of the workmen 's plea in these words: "In my opinion, the demand pertaining to the practice or customs prevailing in these establishments before 1966 is not such a matter as has to be adjudicated and it also does not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act." The Board referred the dispute for adjudication to the Industrial Tribunal. The Industrial Tribunal made an award on March 31, 1965. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the demand relating to the practices or custom prevalent in the establishment before 1965 was not such as has been raised by the workmen and so, the bonus could be claimed as a customary bonus. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal was called upon by the terms of reference, to go into a different claim. [605B] 1.2 The question whether the subject matter of the statute is 'the question of payment of bonus based on profit to employees employed in establishments '. The question of profit may or may not arise at all and such customary and traditional bonus will depend on the content and terms of that custom or the tradition on which the claim has been made. [0605C] 1:3 The Tribunal is called upon to go through a different method of claiming profit bonus de hors the Bonus Act. If, therefore, Parliament wanted to retain the right to claim bonus by way of industrial adjudication for those employees who are either excluded and exempted from that Act, it would have made an express 612 saving provision to that effect as it has done for employees in Coal Mines. [ 0605B C] 1 :4 The question regarding the policy of the Parliament that was agitated in that case turned on the availability of the as an independent method of seeking profit bonus, does not detract from the claim of customary bonus or those based on custom or usage. [ 605C D] 2.1 In the instant case, the dispute related to the procedure followed by the Tribunal in making short shruft of workmen ''s plea in this regard. The Tribunal has taken the view that so long as that award stood, the same claim under a different guise (the Shops Act) could be subversive of the rule of res judicata. [ 601D] 2:2 In the present case, there was a binding award of the Industrial Tribunals relating to this claim. It is true that so far as customary and customary bonus are concerned, the codification may be of everything relating to profit bonus in which case other types of bonus are left untouched. But it is quite conceivable that the codifications may beof everything relating thereto to profit Bonus in which cases other kinds of bonus were left untouched, but it is very unlikely that the rules may be more than what they have been put an end to, and so long that awards are not of things relating to profits bonus, there may be a bar, but this Court took the view in that context. [ 602E] 3.2 In order to appreciate the question whether a claim for customary bonus is barred by the general principles of resjudicata, it will be necessary to examine the scheme of the Act and its scheme. The object and reasons of the Bonus (as it stood in 1965) was to allow an invasion from the flank in that manner.

The petitioners were appointed to the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab and Haryana and were confirmed in the service on or after December 31, 1976. The petitioners who were promoted as District Judges from the cadre of District Judges were promoted to the Higher Judicial Services of Punjab. The High Court held that the rules regulating the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed, inter alia, to the Judicial Service were valid and the Governor was not justified in applying the rule of rotation at the time of confirmation so that, after every two promotees are confirmed one direct recruit has to be confirmed and until that is done, promotees cannot be confirmed even if vacancies are available within their quota in which they can be confirmed. The State Government filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the validity of the rules on the ground that it was not open to the High Court to give an arbitrary date of confirmation to the promotees. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The rule of seniority is concerned under the aforesaid amendment the inter se seniority of the members of the Superior judicial Service who were appointed or promoted to a post in the Service irrespective of the date of their confirmation. It may be recalled that after every several promotees are confirm one direct recruits has to have been confirmed and till that is so done, promotee cannot be confirmation even if vacancy is available within his quota in that particular year. [422C D] 1.2 The High court will re draw the interse seniority (i) of such of the petitioners and respondents as were promoted or appointed to a service irrespective of their date of appointment. [427F G] 1:3 It may also be recalled, that after some time the Governor of Haryana amended rule 12 by the Haryana First Amendment Rules 1972 providing that the seniority of members of Superior Judicial Services who are confirmed shall be determined by the length of continuous service (in a post) irrespective of whether the direct recruits or promoted officers, shall be fixed by the High court according to the criterion of the dates of confirmation. [321A] 1.:4. The seniority list will be drawn by the Governor on the basis of the respective dates of confirmed appointments and in the light of the directions given by this Court in the Punjab Writ Petition, in so far as it confers the power of confirmation on the Governor. In so far the rule regarding seniority is concern, under the said amendment the seniority list shall be drawn up by the State Government according to criterion of seniority. [333B] 1 :5. The question as to whether the Governor, in the exercise of powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309, has the power to frame rules regulating recruitment and condition of judicial officers of the State is to be determined with reference to the dates from which their appointments are made or promoted. It will be recalled at the stage in which the Rules of the Higher Administrative Service have been amended by the Government of India. [332C D; 334A] 2. The power of appointment conferred on the High Courts by article 235 is thus expressly, by the terms of that Article itself, made subject to the law which the State legislature may pass for regulating the Recruitment 1054 and service conditions of judicial officer of the state. In view of this clear position, it is clear that whatever amendments are going to be made hereafter to the Rules will be made in consultation with the High Commission. [ 335F G; 334C D]. 1.6 The High Courts will re drawing the inter-se seniority of such petitioners and respondent as were appointed on or before December 31 1976, on the date when they can become confirmed even though vacancies are not available within its quota in accordance with the amended rule. [336D E] 2:7.

The appellant was the auction purchaser of a plot of land in village Kokra, District Burdwan. The respondent 's father executed a lease deed on December 14, 1939 for a period of 20 years. On January 1, 1939, the appellant sold the property to one M/s. B.K. Banerjee and others. The appellant filed an application under section 65 A of the Transfer of Property Act for recovery of possession of the mortgaged property so as to bind the mortgagee. The trial court dismissed the application on the ground that the decree which had been passed in the mortgage suit was binding on the parties, that the lease rendered the mortgagee 's security insufficient and that the Patta being subsequent to the plaintiff 's mortgage thus came to an end and he was entitled to recover khas possession from the defendants. The High Court dismissed the appeal of the appellant holding that the appellant had no power to grant the permanent lease in question to the respondents, that he was subrogated to the position of the Bank, that it was not competent to grant a lease unusual terms or authorise the use of land for a term. Mukherjee J. held that the mortgagor could grant leases which were not wasteful in their effect the mortgagee had no right to disturb the graves of those who had been: buried the land while the mortgagor continued to hold it. The Court further held that as the object of the burial ground was to grant rights of burial, this 's right could be rightly deemed operative against the mortgagee.' On appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The mortgagor in possession having the authority to deal with the property in the usual course must rightly be deemed operative under the mortgagee's security. [1112 E] (2) The question whether Wazir Narayan Singh had got such power or not has been decided in other cases which laid down a different rule, viz., that a mortgagor was not restricted in the management of the property by making a mortgage and that so long as nothing took place to impair the value, or impede the operation of the mortgage the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for a Term. Mukherjee, in Madan Mohan Singh vs Raj Kishore Kumar(1) , 119 any such plea we are of the opinion that there was no answer to the appellant 's claim and the permanent tenancy granted by Wazir Narayan to the defendants could not prevail against the plaintiff. [1312 F] (3) The High court was right in holding that as a result of the enactment of section 65A of the Act in 1929 a mortgagor who had taken a mortgage of a burial ground and it Was held that he had ample opportunity to@ redeem the mortgage if they so desired but did not choose to exercise their right of redemption, that there were no answer thereto.

The petitioner entered into an agreement with the respondent for execution of certain works. The respondent agreed to execute the work within 9 months from the date of receipt of notice and the petitioner was required to execute it within 15 days from the receipt of the notice. The petitioner filed a suit in the Court of Civil Judge, Junior Division, Delhi praying that the respondent be appointed an arbitrator and on its failure he is entitled to appoint an arbitrator. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that clause 68 of the Contract provides for appointment of an arbitrator or umpire who has entered on the reference or a sole arbitrator or all the arbitrators, the Court should exercise the power sparingly, cautiously and with circumspection to permit a party to the contract of a arbitration voluntarily entered into to relieve the party from dispute or difference. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit as it applied to actions in the High Court and the making, after a claim has become statute barred, of a submission of it to arbitration, does not prevent the statute of limitation being pleaded. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the provisions of section 14 of the Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations as they apply to actions under the Arbitration Act and not to proceedings in the court within the meaning of section 15 of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of sections 5 and 12(2) (b) to permit an arbitrator to be appointed by a Court are like construction which is to be removed, in effect from the jurisdiction of the court, by including an arbitration clause in the contract providing that any arbitration under it must be commenced when one party to such arbitration enters into to relieved the party. [656B] 1.2 The provisions contained in sections 5 & 12(3) (a) to (d) are not applicable to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in the agreement, a cause of action accrued to the party in respect of any such matter at the time when it should have accrued but for the. contract. [756C] 1:2 The court has been given power in given circumstances to grant leave to a contracting party to have the arbitrator or arbitrators removed and the arbitration agreement entered into with other contracting part revoked. [758G H; 957A] 2.1 Section 14 of Limitation Act applies to arbitrations, as it applies to actions outside the High Courts and the filing of the suit is not to be brought after the expiration of a specified number of years from the day when the cause of arbitration accrued, so in the case of arbitrations, the claim is not barred. [957B] 2:2. The provisions relating to arbitration are like sections 5, 12(1) (d), 14(3), 14 and 15(4). Section 14(5) of Limitation is applicable to proceedings before the court in which the cause for action accrued, that is to say, from the commencement of the Arbitration Amendment Act, 1976. [759E] 2.(i) The provisions under sections 5(1)(d) to(e) are inapplicable to arbitrations under section 14(4) of the Code. [761G H] 3.2 Section 14 applies to proceedings under the arbitration Act and is not applicable in arbitrations as it apply to proceedings pending before the Court within the ambit of section 5 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. [763D] 4.3 The provisions in sections 15(1), 15(5)(a) and (b), are not attracted to arbitrations which are governed by the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. [762G H, 963A] 4.(ii) Section 14 is applicable only when one of the parties to the arbitration dispute or differences has arisen after the commencement.

The appellants were the tenants of the lands in question. The respondents filed a suit for recovery of possession of the mortgaged properties on the ground that the execution was barred under section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 (to be hereinafter referred to as the Act). The trial court decreed the suit holding that the objection raised by the judgment debtors is barred by the principles of res judicata and further on July 23, 1960 for default of the judgment debtor. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree holding that it was 'so barred. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions contained in section 16 in regard to the executability of a mortgage decree were not applicable because the execution proceedings had been filed by the decree holders and the objection was overruled by the executing court on two different grounds namely (1) that the objections raised by them are barred by principles of Res judicata; (2) that, as the Bakasht lands which form part of the property mortgaged had not vested in the State, the execution can proceed against those properties. HELD: The provisions contained therein indicate that a mortgage deed is an estate and there can be no doubt that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions of the Act do not fall within the protection of the said Act. [916 B] (2)(a) It would be reasonable to confine the operation of section 4 (d) only to execution proceedings in which the decree holder seeks to proceed against the estate of the debtor. [1017 C D] (b) The language of section 16 is clear and unambiguous that a mortgagee deed can proceed with the execution of a document only if it is proved that the property is mortgaged or charged on, such estate or tenure and all suits and proceedings for the recovery of any such money which may be pending on the date of vesting shall be dropped. [1117 C] (c) The words used in section 4 are not intended to convey an intention to exclude the operation from the operation. It is only when a mortgage document is executed that it can be said that the interest of the creditor affected by it will fall within section 4.

The appellants who were allocated to the Indian Civil Service, Group 'A' and who had appeared in Civil Services Main Examination, 1988 or 1989 under the interim orders of the Tribunal, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4(1) of the C.S.E. Rules, which was dismissed by the High court on the ground that it did not apply to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes candidates who had been allocated to any of the Central Services Group ' A ' or I.P.S.' and who were within the permissible age limit and had succeeded in their selection to higher civil service. The appellants contended before the Tribunal that the second Proviso to Rule 5(ii) of C.C.E., Rules did not extend the benefit of the proviso to sub rule (1) to Rule 17 of the Rules, as it did away with the effect of excluding those candidates who were otherwise eligible and had failed to join either of the services, their allocation based on one or both the examinations, as the case may be, will count as attempts for this purpose. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the proviso was not applicable in the case of Scheduled Castes & Scheduled Tribes candi dates who are otherwise eligible; and that the Tribunal had erred in holding that it had no application to Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe candidates who have been allocated from any of their Central Services, Group A 'A ' and who joined Group 'B ' service subsequently on allocation either on the basis of the results of the previous Civil Services Examination. The appeal by special leave was dismissed. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The proviso to rule 4(i) of Rules does not extend to Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Castes candidates who are allocated to a service subsequent to the main Civil Service Examination. [1123C D] 2.2 The second proviso appended to the said rule does not restrict it only with regard to the preliminary examination as now contended by the learned Additional Solicitor, according to whom those candidates are not eligi ble to sit for the main examination since the Tribunal has upheld the validity and that if he fails to join Either of the Services, his allocation based upon one or either both the examination, as t o be, would stand cancelled. [1023C] 3.3 The proviso does not limit it only to Scheduled castes and Scheduled tribes candidates who on the date of the commencement of the Constitution of India but who expressed their intention to appear in the next Civil Services examination, can either join that service or the service to which he has been allocated, nor will they lose their original seniority in the service. [ 1023C E] 4.4 The proviso is only for the purpose of determining whether a candidate who on his own behalf is entitled to sit at the next civil Service Examination subject to the provisions of Rule 17 and that he has already been allocated or not. If he fails, his allotment based on either of these two examinations will stand cancelled but he will lose his original seniority if he is unable to take training with his own Batch. Those candidates who having been allocated in Civil Service Main Examination of a subsequent year under the Interim orders of this Court for the Civil Services Examinations in 1988 or1989 and have succeeded, are to be given benefit of their success subject to t he provisions of rule 17. [923C F] 5.5 The Tribunal has allowed the candidates who appeared in civil Services Main examination for competing for IAS, IFS, IPS and Central Services under the orders of Tribunal for the CSE (Main) for competing with IAS, Group "A ', and who have succeeded in his Civil Service examination. [0923C G] 6.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) Act, 1974 by the Central Government. The grounds of detention were served on him and he was informed that he is not a friend of the detenu and because of his professional experience he liked to help the detenu. On 25th November 1986 while the detaining authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise, the appellant was denied the assistance of Sundararajan as a friend. The Advisory Board considered the representation of the appellant and rejected the same on the ground that it was admitted by Mr. Sunderarajan before the Advisory Board that he was not a relative of the petitioner and because he had no statutory right to legal assistance in the proceedings before the Board through a legal practitioner, the Advisory board did not consider it proper to allow him to represent the case of the respondent detenu. The appellant challenged his order on the grounds that (i) the detaining Authority was not very much acquainted with them and (ii) the detention was vitiated. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The detaining authority or the Government should have the facility of appearing before the advisory Board through an advocate. [792C] 2.1 In the present case, the Government merely informed the detenu that he had not been able to appear before the board through a lawyer. The detaining Authority or the Board did not permit the appellant to be represented by a legal adviser. [893D] 3.2 The refusal of such assistance to the appellant is not justified. [994E] 4.1 There is no question of any estoppel against law. [1094F] 5. In the instant case, there was no denial of the fact that if Sundararajan had been permitted to assist the detenu before the Central Board could have, if he was so minded, made a request to the Advisory Boards for permission to be heard by a lawyer and a legal Practitioner or a legal aid was also granted to him.

The appellants were owners of certain lands in the State of West Bengal. The requisition was made for the acquisition of their lands under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The appellants contended that as the goods requisitioned and acquired were subject to pucca delivery orders they were not entitled to claim ownership through the mills. Held, that the requisitioning authorities had no power to acquire the property on September 30, 1946, as provided in 0. XXIX, r. 2 of 0. XXI, r., 75 A (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure and as the provisions contained therein did not apply , to the case, there was no acquisition following on the service of the notices in this case. The notice of acquisition in this suit was served on the appellants on September 31, 1946. It was not in dispute that the notice of requisition was served upon the appellants by endorsement and were sold and dealt with in the market as absolutely representing the goods to which they relate and as there was a schedule attached and that schedule mentioned that acquisition was of goods held by the jute mills under the managing agency of the corporation to which the notice was addressed and the names 837 of the mills whose managing agents the addressed corporation was also included in the schedule. The service of notices of acquisition on the owners as owners for the purpose of r. 75 A(2) would apply and the property in the goods passed to the Government of india on September 29, 1946 for the goods were not ascertained till then, whatever may be the position of the holders of the pucca delivery order in a suit between them and the mills to enforce them. The Act did not provide that the requisition should be brought to the knowledge of the person whose interests are being affected by it and that this was not done in this way, for neither the holders were apprised of the orders of requisition on September 15, 1946 nor the mills were informed of the order of requisition so in the manner provided in a. XXX, r 2 of the Rules.

The assessee was a Private Limited Company. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken up for hearing, another appeal preferred by it in the East Punjab High Court. In so far as the item in question is concerned it held that it was a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the said sum of Rs. 4,50,000 was a reserves and should not be included. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that no action can be taken against the assessee under Section 23A. [111B] In the circumstances of the case it must be held that the provision made by the assessee in its Books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23 A) was indeed a provision and not a reserve. The assessee itself called it a provision. It did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve, but appropriated as an appropriation. [112C] In other words, reserves are appropriations of profits, the asset or assets by which they are rep resented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. The balance sheet is therefore conclusive. [113D] Commissioner of Income Tax vs Metal Box Company of India Limited, , relied on. The distinction between a provision made against anticipated losses and contingencies is stated in the following words: "The distinction between an appropriation and a reserve is stated In commercial accountancy fairly well known. Provisions made against apprehended losses and contingency are charges against profits and, therefore, to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P.& L. account." [113E] Commissioner Of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh vs Sri Venkateswara Rao, , followed.

The petitioners were appointed to temporary posts on the basis of competitive examinations and those that were recruited by selection, but both by Union Public Service Commission. The petitioners were not given weightage in seniority "on the basis Of half the total length of continuous service" as temporary Assistant Officers subject to a maximum of five years. They filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the validity of the action taken by the Railway Board and the order passed by the President of India on the recommendations of the Union Public Services Commission. This Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the classification of temporary Assistant officers was neither discriminatory nor violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution, for the reason that it had nexus to the object sought to be achieved, which mainly was efficiency of service, and that both the services had started separately and never became one. The Union Public Commission filed a writ petition in this Court claiming that Officers were appointed on temporary posts as temporary officers on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the principle of "equal pay for equal work". This Court while dismissing the writ appeals held that the petitioners were entitled to weightage in the seniority " on the ground that they did not concede that in any given year, the candidates appointed as Engineers on the strength of selection by the Union Government would be given weightage. The State was directed to consider the case of the petitioners for promotion to the post of Assistant Engineer from the date of their absorption into the Indian Railway Service of Engineers Class I and to give them weightage in accordance with law. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The classification of Temporary Assistant Officers is neither discriminatory or violative of Article 14 nor it provides for promotional avenues reasonably, because of its being questioned elsewhere. [912D] 2.2 The petitioners are not entitled to any relief under Article 32 of the constitution. [1013B] 3.3 The petitioners have spear headed the claim of the temporary Assistant Officer subject to the maximum of 5 years, because they conceded that in some given year the vacancies arose and that they were recruited on the same basis. They conceded that there was complete absorption of the personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority had been reckoned from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of half the length of service subject to maximum of seven years. [813C] 3:4 The petitioners cannot claim any relief on the assumption that they had conceded that the persons appointed as temporary Officers on the posts of Engineers were placed above those appointed on the date when their absorption was made possible and its pace quickened with weightage, it is difficult to find fault with the scheme at this point of time to look for a substitution at our end, as that would unsettle a settled position, established more than a decade ago. [713C D] 3 :5 The petitioners had spear headed by the Federation of Directly Appointed Officers (Suppressed) of Indian Railways and a few others in a representative capacity across which stand arrayed the Union of India and the Railway board as respondents. Garg, learned counsel for the petitioners has spear headed this claim at our close, as also in the rule of constructive res judicata. [613E] 3 5. The question of equality was once for all settled. When there has been complete absorption, it would otherwise be imprudent now, at this stage to dig up old issues. It needs mentioning that the appeals being decided instantly are against the judgments and orders of the High Court rejecting writ petitions of the petitioner 1027 before it on the grounds that it has nexus to both the service and create discrimination by making one as an isolated one, and not providing for promotionalvenue reasonably, which basically was efficiency in service. [1413G] 3 6.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 9 and 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance, which provided that "all offences under the Indian Penal Code shall be investigated, inquired into, tried or otherwise dealt with according to the provisions hereinafter contained". The Special Judge framed charges against the appellant. The appellant contended (i) that sections 9 and 10 were not ultra vires because they were violative of article 14 of the Constitution; (ii) that section 5(1) of the Ordinance was void as offending against the provision of the equal protection clause in article 14; (iii) that the notification issued by the State Government under section 5 (1) was beyond the competence of a legislature and was, therefore, void. Held, further, that section 11 of Ordinance which empowered the State Govt to direct any class of cases or classes of offences or such cases to be tried by the Special Court constituted under the Act did not offend against the equal Protection clause of our Constitution; and (iv) that in so far as it authorised the State to make a classification, the authority given by section 5 was beyond its competence. The notification issued under section 11 was therefore valid. Held: (i)(a) The words "any offence" or "classes of cases" in section 11 were wide enough to include offences which were grouped together from other offences and that part of it, with which we are here concerned, authorises the State government to direct "offences", "cl classes of cases". [457 C] (b) The notification under section 10(1)(a), was not ultra rites because it did not infringe article 14. It was not a valid notification and could not be held to be invalid or ultra vires.

The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 1,000 in default to undergo further rigorous imprisonment was confirmed by the High Court. The High Court acquitted all the accused but maintained their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the evidence of P.W. 8 is not reliable because he had not sustained any injury during the occurrence and had not mentioned the name of any of the accused to other villagers who entered the house immediately after the culprits left the place. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The evidence of the witnesses lend assurance to the evidence that all the 9 appellants were in the western kotha of the house at the time of occurrence and they had got up on hearing the noise and that P.Ws. 1 and 7 could not identify them. [723C] 2.2 The evidence given by the eye witness is corroborated by the evidence given in the tin shed at the instance of the appellant. There was sufficient moon light at the place of occurrence which had gone on for about 15 20 minutes. It is not improbable that all these appellants were seen by P. W. 1 immediately after he left the house and that it was not improbable whether these appellants could have been in a position to identify them during the course of the occurrence which took place and must have had sufficient opportunity to indentify with the help of the lantern which was burning, the appellants who were previously known to her and not strangers and she has received as many as 19 injuries during the night. [823D] 2:3 The evidence on record is consistent and reliable. There is no reason whatsoever for not accepting the evidence adduced by P W. 8 altogether because he has intentionally made improvements in his version about the occurrence. It was not unlikely that all 9 appellants would have seen any of them during this occurrence which might have had a sufficient "glimpse" of the miscreants so as to be in a situation to identify those persons who entered into the house soon after the dacoits left the scene. [923C D] 2 4. The evidence adduced on behalf the appellants lend assurance that all of the 9 accused were seen together and not stranger and they have got up at the spot. It cannot be said that P W 8 had no opportunity to confentify, with the aid of the lamp which was burnt in the verandah of the houses. [1023C E] 5. The learned Sessions Judge has rejected the evidence on the ground that it is admitted by PW.8 that he had never seen any accused to others who entered their house immediately before the occurrence could have seen some of the offenders and could not be identified. There were sufficient moons light at that time when the incident was taking place, it is not possible to agree with the learned Sessions judge that no reliance can be placed on the evidence Of P. Ws. 1 & 7. [ 1023D E] 6. The prosecution has proved the case against the appellants satisfactorily and beyond all reasonable doubt and that the appellants were found guilty of the offence under section 395 I. P.C., and the sentence awarded to them by the learned Judges of the High court is correct. [1124A D] 7.8 The evidence regarding P.w. 8 does not lend assurance for the evidence being corroborated by other circumstances of the case namely that it has been admitted by the appellants lends assurance to their evidence. It may be difficult to accept the evidence as it goes to prove the presence of the Appellants lend assurance, with help of lantern which is burning, and the appellants have gotup on hearing of the noise.

The appellant Corporation was a State Road Transport Corporation created under the State Act entitled the Transport Corporation to the Transport Undertaking Act, 1950 ( 'Corporation Act ' for short) is in appeal by special leave. The employer Corporation contended that the employees were probationers and the order of discharge in every case was on account of unsatisfactory service. The Labour Court held that termination of services while on probation on ground of unsuitability amounted to retrenchment and for non compliance with the provisions of section 25F of the ( 'Disputes Act ') for short), the termination is bad, but set aside those orders and gave appropriate relief to the workmen. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the services had been terminated on the ground of unsatisfactory services, the order passed by the Labour Court was not bad and consequently it upheld the Award of the Labour court which set aside the order. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The expression 'retrenchment ' must include every termination of the service except those not expressly included in section 25FF or not expressly provided for by other provisions of the Act such as sections 25FF and 25FFF. [793A] 1.2 The definition of 'ret retrenchment ' in section 2(oo) of the , includes every termination by the employer of the services of a workman for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf. [893B] 1:3 The expression "retrenchment" in section 3(oo), means the termination by an employer of his service except as a penalty inflicted by him way of punishment inflicted upon him by way Of disciplinary action. It means only the discharge of surplus labour or staff by the employee for any reasons whatsoever is no more good law and in fact the decision of the full Bench of Kerala High Court in L. Sundara Money 's case was approved in the aforementioned three cases. Once the conclusion reached that retrenchment as defined in section2(oo)(i) of The covers every case of termination by act of employer even if such termination involved is a consequence of transfer or closure of the undertaking, is to be treated as 'retrenched in the definition, discharge from employment or termination of service of a probationer would also amount to retrenchment. [994C] 1 :4.1 In Hindustan Steel Ltd. vs Bharat Electronics Ltd., it was held that the expression 'termination of service for any purpose whatsoever' must include all termination of his services except those which have been embodied in the definitions, discharge of retrenched labour or Staff by the employers for any such reason whatsoever is nothing more good Law and in law. [1094D] 1.:4.2 In the instant case the services have been terminated by act o the employer even though such termination was not a consequence ' to transfer or termination or termination. The order of retrenchment was on the basis that the employee had been appointed as a probationer. Once it is held that retrenchment was bad and illegal, the question of reinstatement would also arise. [ 1094E] 1.(i) In Hindustan Steels Ltd. case 'Sher Singh vs Bharat Electrical Industries Ltd., , it was in terms held that in these cases the order dated 14th July, 1979 terminating the services was bad. The decision in Sundara money 's Case was not at all inconsistent with the decision in Chandara Money's case and not only required no reconsideration but the decision therein was approved by the Constitution Bench in Lan Sundara moneys 's cases. [1194F] 1;4.5 In Hindustan Corporation Ltd.

The question raised in these two appeals is directed against the questions:The assessee South Eastern Railway disposing of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. On 1 April, 1952 the assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of registration of the assessee as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the appellant 's activities, and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not a " dealer" within the meaning of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1940. On appeal by the Revenue to the Board of Revenue, West Bengal, the High Court dismissed the revision application on 27 January, 1960. In these appeals the question is whether the assessee in each case is a "business" for the purpose of as sessment under the Bihar Finance ( Sales Tax) Ordinance, 1941 and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. It was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the activity of so disposing of the goods did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying on business as a dealer liable to tax under the Act and that consequently the assessee could be treated as a 'dealer" within that Act; Held, that the transaction of sale of goods by the assessee were sales under the provisions of Section 56 of the Railways Act. In the instant case the assessee had purchased the goods from it of unclaimed or uncon nected goods. The question whether the activity was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods is involved in the auction held by the appellant and that accordingly the assessee became a "assessee" within t he meaning of Section 2(c) read with C1. (g) of the Bihar Sales Tax Ordinance, 1940 and therefore could not be treated to be a " Dealer" for purposes of as Sessment. The High Court was in error in holding that the activities of so disposal were adjun tioned to the main activity of sale. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the Goods. It seems to South Eastern Railways was a "goods" for purpose of Section 55 of the Indian Railways Act, 1939 and therefore a sale of such goods took place. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. In C.A. No. 1069 of 1975 arising out of a suit for specific performance of contract of sale, it was held that a transfer of property was involved in auction held on the basis of an activity of purchase or of manufacture for sale. The decision of the High court in each appeal is set aside and the questions referred to the High Courts are answered in each cases in favour of the revenue and against the assessee.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling securities. The appellant was a director of the Company. On September 17, 1954, the appellant issued a notice to the respondent for the payment of the losses, presumably because necessary steps to be taken both in connection with the fictitious purchase of securities, in order to pay money to Bhagwati Trading Company for being made over to the Union Agencies when funds were needed and also or providing funds in the Insurance Company 's account with the Chartered Bank, Bombay, in case the 810 balance was not sufficient to meet the losses. The respondent filed a complaint against the appellant under section 409 I.P.C. alleging that the appellant had committed an offence punishable under section 477 I. P.C., and that the respondent had misappropriated the funds of the Union Agency. The Magistrate acquitted the accused, but convicted him under section 420 I.PC. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the prosecution case was established beyond reasonable doubt and that it was not possible to believe that the amount which his company viz., Bhagwati Trading Co. Ltd., received from the Insurance Companies must have purported to be on account of securities sold to the Insurance company unless he was authorised by the Chairman. The High Court also held that there was no evidence to show that the money had been paid in cash and not through transfers which transactions had to be adjusted. On further appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The reasonable conclusion can be that they mentioned Bhagwati Trading as that represented the true state of affairs and Chokhani had to inform the Delhi Office of the Bharat Union Agencies about the source of money he was receiving for the Union agencies to meet its losses. [815E] 2.2 The reasonable inference can be drawn from the entries in the books of the company, which did show the receipt of the amounts from Bhagwati Trading Corporation, but the prosecution evidence was that the amounts were received in cash, and not by transfers which transaction had tobe adjusted. [ 816B] 3.3 The reasonable conclusions can be arrived at only on the basis of the entries and not on the mere ipse dixit of the accused. [820G] 4.4 In the circumstances the reasonable conclusion cannot be that the appellants mentioned Bhagwati trading Company as that representing the true real state of affair and Chokhani, had to intimate the Delhi office of theBharat Union Agencies regarding the source from which money was received for the Insurance Corporation to meet their losses. It is not possible, in law, to believe, that the funds were purchased by the Insurance Co., but on the other hand, it was for them how to direct the necessary entries to be made in the advices prepared by Lakhotia on behalf of the Bombay Office at Delhi and on the evidence adduced before the Magistrate. [824G] 5.5 The reasonable presumption can be raised that the accused had committed the offence under section misappropriation I.p.C, and that therefore Chokhani did not include those securities in this letter. [825A B] 6.6 In the instant case, some of the cheques issued on behalf Of Bhagwati Trading company were deposited in the bank by Vishnu Prasad himself, but he was a Director of the latter as he never issued instructions regarding the activities of the InsuranceCompany to meet his losses. He also denied that Dalmia had said that the investments had either been sold or pledged and that he knew that most of this amount was passed on to the Bank of India, which Dalmia did not know that the securities had either actually been sold nor pledged. The prosecution case is that the sum was received in Cash and not from Bhagwati trading company, but from the evidence produced before the Court it appears that the moneys were paid in the Bank by Vishnu.

The appellants were appointed as ministerial staff in the ministerial service of the State of Gujarat under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act. The services of the appellants were transferred to the Secretariat of the Gujarat State Secretariat and the State Government was directed to treat their services as permanent posts in the Secretariat. The State Government filed a petition before the High Court for an order directing the State Governments to treat them as servants of the "Secretariat cadre" and to forbear from enforcing its orders treating the persons whose names were specified in the annexure to the order as servants. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the transfer of the former Saurashtra and Kutch States was not open to objection. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellants had been transferred to their Secretariat by virtue of sub section (7) of section 115 of the Act, and that the State was competent to transfer and did transfer them to perform ministerial duties in the subordinate offices performing ministerial duties. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court has rightly held that when the ministerial services were posted and assigned duties in various districts in Saurashtra and Saurashtra, after they were allotted to the State, it is not open for the officers of the Secretariat to challenge the authority of the Government of Gujarat either to transfer officers from the Districts and to post and assign them duties in accordance with the rules made under article 309 of the Constitution. [419D] 1.2 The High ' Court has rightly observed that when a ministerial service personnel in the States of Saurashtra and Bhuj and Kutch were posted, their right to be absorbed in equivalent posts in their Secretariat will not, in our judgment, affect the right of the personnel to be appointed in connection with the affairs of another State and on terms notexceedingvanta geous to those they were already entitled except with the previous approval of the Central Government. [519E] 1:3 The High "Court has rightly dismissed the writ petition holding it not open, to the appellants to challenge an authority of their Government of India either to make a final decision or to fix their pay and seniority among the officers in the Subordinate offices performing the ministerial duties, that is, before embarking on varying the conditions of service, the State governments should obtain the concurrence of the Union of India. [619G] 1.:4 The High Courts have rightly held against the appellants. [720B] 2.5 The High" Court has also rightly observed in deciding the case against the appellant. [613A] 3.1 In the absence of determination of equivalent posts under the orders of the central Government, the States were competent to make appropriate decision. [413C] 3:2 The State of Saurashtra was competent as a matter of provisional arrangement to absorb the former Kutch and Kutch State personnel in their ministerial establishment of theGujarat State Secretariat. [414D] 4.1 There is no distinction between the posts in which the members of the ministerial staff were posted or assigned duties. It is difficult to hold that when there has been an equivalence established between the post in which they were posted between 1956 and 1960, the Central government does not make a Final decision, it being not open open to the officers to challenge their authority either to transferred officers from them or to fixing their pay or seniority among them in the administrative establishment of Gujarat State. [416B] 4:2 In the instant case, there has riot been any equivalence established by the Government Of Gujarat to which the appellants acquired under the Absorption Rules. The transfer of personnel from the States concerned with the administration of the successor State to the ministerial Service of the erstwhile Saurashtra and Gujarat State was complete and no transfer thereafter to the office of the Chief Secretary was made, disadvantageous.

The petitioners in these writ petitions were dealers of cotton and sold them. They claimed deduction under section 5(2)(a) (vi) of the Central Act on the ground that they had purchased cotton and sells it after the period provided for in section 5 (2)(b). The Sales Tax Officer rejected their claim. In appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the petitioners contended that the sales tax was levied at a rate higher than the prescribed limit and that the tax could not be collected at more than one stage. The Appellate Assistant Commission held that the levy of tax was illegal as it was beyond the prescribed limits and therefore the tax was liable to be refunded to them. In revision, the High Court held that section 5 of the Act did not indicate the stage at which the tax can be levied and because under section 15(1) of Central Act there could be no liability for payment of tax unless this stage was so stated in the Act or the rules thereunder thereunder. Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1. The normal rule under the Act is to levy the tax on the first purchaser. If a person has purchased cotton or sells it before the date of sale by him, that party is liable to pay tax and would also claim refund at a later stage. [723C] 2. In respect of the same item of declared goods, more than six naye paise in a rupee as the State Government may by notification direct. The difficulty however, remains that the Act itself did not specify the stage when the tax is to be levied. If the Central Legislature makes it mandatory that the Tax can be collected only at one stage and that stage shall be (i) in the case of goods liable to purchase tax, the stage of sale is purchase by the last dealer liable to paying the tax. [761D] 3. The discrimination is also between the first purchase in the cases of imported goods and last sale in the State and last sales in the Case of local goods. If this stage is so stated, in the statute or rules thereunder there can be no obligation for payment thereof at a subsequent stage. In the case where the tax has been levied, whether on sale or purchase inside the State of any declared goods by the first dealer liable, the point is that the dealer could always claim exemption under section 10(2) (a)(vi). [724E] 4. The tax can also be collected even at one time and then claim refund, at a latter stage. If it was so pleaded in the writ petitions that the discrimination was between the two first purchase, the question of discrimination would not arise. [758G H; 925A] 5. In view of the amendment brought about by section 15 (1) (b), the tax cannot be said to be higher in the nature of tax and therefore it is not enough for the State to say that a person, who is not liable to payment tax must nevertheless pay it in the first instance and then claiming refund, when the goods are sold by the next dealer liable. [925B] 6. The question whether the tax should be collected on the purchase or sale inside the state of any declare goods is a matter for consideration of the Court. If that stage was not so stated there could have been no liability to pay the tax unless it was otherwise stated in section 15. [759E] 7. In order to determine whether the levy can be said higher in nature, the Court has to consider the provisions of the statute and the rules therein. The Court is required to examine the scheme of the law relating to imposition of tax on goods manufactured or produced in the state.

The respondent, who was defendant No. 1 in a mortgage suit and the appellants were declared entitled to have the debts scaled down under the Agriculturists ' Relief Act, but as no application had been made on behalf of defendant No, the proposal, which seems to have been accepted by the Receivers, was that the amount payable by him under the decree was to be settled at Rs. 3,215 and put in a petition under section 47 and 297 Order 21, rule 2, Civil Procedure Code praying that as the amount thus deposited together with the payments already made completely wiped off the amount due under the decrees as scaled up by the High Court in favour of defendants 2 to 7, full satisfaction of the decree might be recorded exoner ating the mortgaged properties and also the defendant No 1, in substance was entitled to avail himself of the benefit of scaling down the debt. The trial court decreed the suit against defendants 2, 3 to 7 only and the appeal filed by them was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf on behalf the appellants that the High court was wrong in holding that the decree contained no such clear directions but reading the decree as a whole and having regard to the actual decision in the case, this must be taken to be its plain implica tions. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding, that by virtue of the principle of Judicisibility of the mortgage decree, a non agriculturist debtor, whose debt has not been scaled off under the provisions of the Agriculturists' Relief Act may indirectly get the benefit which had been granted to his agriculturist co taintiff under the provision of the Act. [520 E] 1.2 The High court erred in holding against defendants 3 to7 separately and by allowing the application of defendant Nos. 2 to 6 only and that by adding a proviso, it was not possible for the defendant Nos 2 to 5 to 7 separately but should have expressly directed ,that on payment of the amount directed to be paid by them proceeds clearly on the assumption that the mortgage debt and the security had been split up, and in our opinion it is not possible to the defendant no. 1 and that even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the whole of the mortgaged property including their interest would be sold for the entirety of the loan for which defendant No.. 2 was entitled. [620 E F] 1:3 The High ' Court erred in not interfering with the finding of the trial court and that the view taken by the District Judge was right and should not have been disturbed. [721 C D] 1 :4. In the present case there is no question of the pur chaser, who is not an agriculturist himself, being entitled to the benefit under a decree which has been schedaled down in favour o defendants 2 t o 7 only. The further direc tion should have been that in case they did not pay this amount, the entire of the pledged property including its interest would stand sold for entirety of th e mortgage debt for which defendants 2 and 3 were entitled to get their debts scured down under this decree. [821 E F; 822 A B] 1.:5.

The appellants, who were the tenants of the premises in question under the first defendant, filed a suit for declaration that the first plaintiff was a tenant of the defendants and was entitled to protection under the Act. The City Civil Court dismissed the suit on the ground that there bad been no lawful subletting by the first appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was not one between a landlord and a tenant because the relationship of landlord and tenant subsists between the parties, and that the second and third plaintiffs were lawful subtenants of the first respondent and were entitled to possession, use and occupation of the property as sub tenants thereof. Held, further, that the City Civil Courts had jurisdiction to entertain and try any suit relating to possession of premises to which the provisions of Part 11 of the Act apply and in that suit claims and questions arising out of the said Act or any of its provisions were to be determined by the courts specified in section 28 and no other court could have jurisdiction to try such a suit, proceeding or application or to deal with such claim or question arising out o f the Act or the any of their provisions. The provisions of the Bombay Rents, Hotel Rates and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bombay Act No. ") do not contemplate the filing of any suit in respect of possession of any premises to a tenant even though he may be in possession of the same premises. In other words, the City civil Court could not decree the suit of the plaintiffs unless their claim to remain in possession was established under the provisions Of Part 11 and no such other court would have jurisdiction if it had ordinary jurisdiction. The section does not contemplate filing of a suit relating exclusively to possession. It merely provides that all claims or questions arising from the Act, or any its provisions, even though they may be outside the purview of section 28, shall be determined only by the Courts specified in sections 28 and 29. In order to determine whether the plaintiffs were the tenant of premises within the meaning of the section, it is necessary for the court to decide whether the suit should be entertained by that Court or not. The jurisdiction to deal With any claim or questions arises out of a statute or any other its provisions. It does not mean that all disputes arising out or arising out Of the Act are to be decided by the City Court alone. In the instant case, the plaintiffs had established their claim only to the effect that the premises had been lawfully sublet to them and under section 14 of the , they must be deemed to be tenants of such premises. The question whether the appellants were the landlords would be a claim or dispute arising out from the provisions in Part 11.

The appellant was appointed as the managing director of the Company by the will of Dadoba. On July 7, 1955, Dadoba transferred his business to the Company. The appellant was a managing director in succession to him and in exercise of that power he had appointed the appellant Govind as the Managing Director. The appointment of the appellant was not to be included within the word "assignment". The appellant filed an application under section 66(1) of the ,of the , of the . The High Court took the view that the words "assign" in the main part of section 312 were intended to render void a transfer of his office by a director for, the old Act contained in section 83B, 340 provisions substantially similar to those contained in sections 255 and 256 of the new Act. It further held that the word 'assignment' in the section included "appointment" and so, such an appointment would not be an assignment. The High court also took the same view. In appeal by certificate, HELD: (1) The proviso to section 86B does not indicate that it was intended that the expression "assigned director" in section 312 of the old section should include an appointment by a Director for his successor. [341 D] (2) The word 'resignment' is used in the sense of giving a meaning to the words used in section 313, and includes a person who has been appointed otherwise than by the company in a general meeting. It would therefore be legitimate to infer that the proviso to the section was intended to give an interpretation to the word only restricted to the extent mentioned therein. [342 E] (3) The rule of construction on which the High Court relied in arriving at the conclusion that it did, was put in these words: "It is a well established principle of construction that when one finds a proviso to a section, the presumption is that but for the proviso the enacting part of the section would have included the subject matter of the proviso." [342 G] (4) The High Courts were not justified in holding that the appellants had conceded that an appointment was not made by a directors.

The appellants were tenants in the premises situated at No. 6 Kasi Chetty Street, G.T. Madras. They filed an eviction petition against the respondent landlady under clause 13(3)(iv) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and 419 Rent Control) Act, 1960 on the ground that they had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the said shop to M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart and were liable to be evicted forlivered possession under the provisions of Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of The said Rent Act. The Trial Court held that the appellants had committed a breach of the terms of the lease deed executed by them in favour of the landlord and that they were liable t o be evicted from the premises on the grounds that they have unlawfully and with the consent or connivance of the respondents sublet the same to M /s. J.J. Glass Mart, and that the respondent subletting was unlawful sub tenants. The Appellate Authority dismissed the said appeal. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that the application against the partnership firm was not maintainable without joining its partners as re spondents. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure are not applicable to the proceedings under the said Rent Acts either and hence, the ratio laid down in the aforesaid decision is directly applicable to t he eviction petition. [620G H] 2.2 In the instant case, no such objection has been raised at any stage till the stage of Special Leave and it is certainly open to the appellants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. It was next submitted by Mr. Nayar that there was no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that had the account books and ledgers been produced, they would have shown that rent was received by the appellants from M/ s. Adeswar Glass Mart which would justify the finding of subletting. In these circumstances, this contention of Mr. Sethi must fail. [ 620G] 3. The respondent landlord had sublet the shop to the appellant a partnership firm under clause 12(3) (iv) and (vii) of Order 30 of CPC. There was no material to show that M/S. Adjeshwar Glass stall was carried on business in the said premises even for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the business there. [864A B] 4. The High Court has erred in not appreciating this contention and wrongly held that it is only by virtue of the provisions contained in order 30, Code of C.P.C. that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. In view of the clear language of section 12(1) (a), the respondent landlord cannot raise this contention at any time during the pendency of the eviction petition and join the partners as respo ndent. [ 864A C] 5. The provisions contained under order 30 are not attracted to the facts of the case. [876B] 6. In order to come within the purview of section 13(1)(a), it is necessary for the Court from these circumstances to come into the conclusion whether the partners of the firm are before the Court though in a wrong name, they will have shownthat rent was paid by them from M / s. J Glass Mart. [886C] 7. In this case, there was evidence to show the fact that M /S.

The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1950 was enacted to provide for imposition of ceiling on land situate within the urban agglomeration and for matters connected therewith. The Andhra Pradesh Act came into force on 1st January 1975 and it was with reference to this date the surplus holding of land in excess of the ceiling area was required to be determined as on 1 st January 1975 under the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Pradesh) Act. The State of Andhra Pradesh enacted the Andhra Nadu Land Reforms (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961. Section 2(n) of the Act provided that every individual who is not a member of a family unit shall be an extent of land equal to one standard holding. The ceiling area in the case of every individual was required for being determined and if there was any surplus it was to be surrendered to the State Government. The Act provided for imposition on land situated within the rural agglomeration under section 2(m) (A)(ii) of that Act. Section 3(f) of this Act provided, inter alia, that every person who is a member or a family Unit shall be liable to be assessed as on the 1st day of January 1975 in accordance with the provisions of the Andhra Act and only land within the ceiling limit would be allowed to remain with him. The expression "family unit" was defined in section 2 (n) (a) (ii) to mean, inter-alia, a family consisting of persons who are not members of a joint family unit or whose father is not member of any family unit and whose property could not be clubbed together with the land held by the other members of the family unit. The definition of "family" in section 3(m)(A) was amended by Act No. 13 of 1972 on 22nd April 1972. Section 4(1) provided that where a person is not an urban agglomeration under section 3 (f), he shall be assessed to land revenue for the purpose of applying the ceiling. The proviso to section 4(3) provided, that if there is any surplus area which comes to the share of a divided minor son, the whole of the State ofAndhra Pradesh shall be surrendered immediately to the Government and the provisions contained in the Andhra Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1972 would apply if and when the area in question is notified to be an urbanisable Area under section 4 (1) of Act. In the case before this Court it was contended on behalf of the landholders that the Andhra State Legislature had legislative competence to provide with imposition of a ceiling on lands situate within these urban agglonies, the entire of theAndhra Pradesh Act would apply and only such land within its ceiling area would be liable for payment as part of joint family property. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Andhra State Land Reforms Ordinance, 1972 was enacted by the Andhra Legislature to provide that every member or family unit in a urban agglisable Area shall be entitled to remain in possession of such land and he shall not be liable under any other provisions of this Ordinance. [423C] 2.2 The Andhra Act would not apply but it would be fully applicable in respect of land situate in the urban area. [427D] 3.1 Section 4 of the Ordinance provided that if a partition effected prior to 2nd May 1972 is not invalidated by theAndhra State Legislature, the Central Act would continue to be applicable if and at any time after such area is notified as an urban precinct under section 1(n)(A)(i) of Central Act.

The respondents were workmen in the appellant Company. The dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that all the workmen who turned up on or before October 2, 1953, must be taken back in employment without condition and of the two men who came later, one was ill of typhoid fever and had sufficient reason for reporting himself for duty on October 9, 1953. The Company challenged the order of termination before the Tribunal. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the workmen were entitled to be taken into service without condition, and of their services as of right without any condition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Industrial Tribunals had in each case considered the justification for absence without leave and that the decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. HELD: (1) The Industrial Tribunal had in every case considered whether the workmen could be taken away from their employment as of rights without any conditions; but it found that the decisions were mala fide and amounted to harassment. [656 E] (2) The Tribunal had not interfered with what really is a finding of fact. If, on the contrary, the Tribunal proceeded on the footing that the employer was guilty of such activities then on being satisfied that the action was mala fides or amountedto victimisation. [613 C D] (3) The workmen themselves were admittedly near Burnpur and might have joined earlier, some claimed to come back to their services. In view of the circumstance that the men were in custody, the Company was not justified in refusing leave. [557 F] (4) The employer had decided to terminate the services of Chattoraj on the ground of his prejudicial and subversive activities thenon being satisfied with the decision of the Company. If a large number of workmen are arrested by the authorities in charge of law and order by reason of their questionable activities, as in this case, the work of the company will be paralysed if the Company is forced to give leave to all of them for a "more or less indefinite period. [457 F H] (5) The mere fact that some of the workmen are brought back to employment without any reason and without any explanation does not mean that the employees were guilty of misconduct. If on the other hand, the employer is forced by his doctor but was engaged in doing some " public work", it is for the Company to decide whether the charges have been proved and the Industrial Court unless it found otherwise, would have interfered with the finding of facts. [558 G] (6) The industrial Tribunal had also taken into consideration the circumstance of the case that the workers were not taken back by the Company but failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence, and that was the reason why they were not taking complete rest as " advised by his doctors but were engaged in some essential departments, with effect from August 24, 1953 and the notice dated September 17, 1953,. and therefore, they were entitled for compensation.

The University of Rajas was invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under Sec. Urea Kant was mentioned in the reserve list by the Selection Committee. Dr. Nathawat, who was already selected and kept in the reserved list was appointed as Professor in Botan. Dr Nathaikwat, a selected person joined the post on the ground that the Selection committee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection raised that once a selected candidate joins the post, the reserve lists exhausted itself. The Syndicate in its resolution dated 10th July, 1978 decided that the reserve List recommended by the selection Committee shall be valid upto six months from the date of approval of the Syndicate as per the resolution passed in its spe cial meeting on 3.12.1983. Dr Urea Kumar who was earlier selected and appointed as professor in the University of Rajasthan was appointed a Professor in a department of the Bot any. Dr M. Nantik, who joined the service on the basis that the selection committee was constituted in compliance with law. Dr K. S. Gupta, who had been already selected, was appointed to the post by the duly constituted Selection Committee and he kept in reserve list for six months instead of six months in a resolution passed on 3rd December 1983. The appellant Dr. M.Nantik and Dr. A.K. Sharma were appointed as Professors in the Department of Botsany. Dr R. N. Sharma, who is already selected by the University was appointed by the Committee constituted for the selection of a teacher in the university. Dr A. K. Gupta and Dr A P. Gupta were appointed to that post on a vacant post caused during the validity period of the reserve pool. The appointment of Dr. Sudhu Kumar was approved and recommended by Dr. R.N. Sharma. Dr C. Nhaikwat was appointed in the post. Dr D. K Gupta, the appellant Dr N.D. Sharma and Dr M P. Sharma who were already selected were appointed on a non vacant post. The University ofRajas were appointed by Dr A Nathayikwat on the recommendation of the Selection Committe constituted under Section 5(1) of the Act of 1974. Dr B.Natakanta, who has been already appointed as Reader in the college was appointed on the post and he was kept in waiting for such a long period of one year. The selection committee approved and forwarded the main list alongwith its recommendations to the University. Dr H. Nathiikwat filed an appeal before the Syndicate against the decision of the High Court which was dismissed by the Syndicate.
