In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that once the selected person joins the posts then selection made by the committee is exhausted and the reserve panel is of no avail and becomes extinct. It was further submitted that once an appointment made by a duly constituted selection Committee has joined that post then selection makes it quite clear that the procedure adopted in preparing a reserve list would be defeated if the view taken by the High court is accepted that once again a selected teacher has joined the same post then Selection made by it is exhausted, and becomes substitutable. It is further submitted on behalf for the appellant University that once another person selected by a selection committee has joined another post then the reserve s list is of No avail and become extinct and thus no fault can be found with the view of the learned Single Judge. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The very purpose of preparing a reserved list would not be defeated unless the view taking by theHigh Court is accepted. [417C] 2.

The petitioners in these writ petitions were owners of certain lands. They had been allotted plots by the Municipal Commissioner for development of a park and green belt by the first, second and third respondents in the development plan finally adopted on January 9, 1964. The petitioners contended that their lands were earmarked in the Development Plan originally published on January 7, 1964 by green colour without assigning any purpose and the reservation and re designation of these lands for recreation centre and green bel belt was illegal and void as they had been reserved for the benefit of the owners of the land for recreation centres and green area. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the petitioners were not entitled to the relief claimed in the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the lands were allotted by the State Government under section 17(3) of the Act and the notification issued thereunder was illegal as they did not have any title or interest therein. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The provisions of sections 4 and 11(3)(a) of section 3 are borne in mind and the rules framed thereunder complied with as far as they can be made applicable, apply in respect of such revision of development plan including all parts if sanctioned separately and the provisions of Sections 4 to 16 (both inclusive) shall, so far as it can be making applicable, applied in respect thereof. [723C] 2. The preparation of the tentative plan or the final development plan was not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the local authority. If the provisions were borne in view and the Rules framed thereunder, as appears to have been done in these cases, there was little or no scope for the local authorities acting arbitrarily under section 13 of the act. [823D] 3. The preparing of the draft of a section of the development plans for K, P and R Wards was not an offence which could be tried by a court of law. If resort was had to power,% under section 11(2) of revising the existing development plan at the end of this period of 14 years, there would be little or nothing else but a mere possibility that some other authority might be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. [923C D] 4. The publication of the final Development Plan was not a violation to the development scheme and the rule framed thereunder did not comply with the provisions thereof. If section 17 were borne out, as appearing to have happened in these matters, there could be no justification for the State Legislature to protract the acquisition of any land designated for a public purpose under section 7 of the Land Acquisition Act at least for 14 years and if resort was having to power. [1023C E] 5. The submission that by the combined operation of sections 3 and 11 (3) the local Authority could protract or alter the development Plan at the close of this year, without doing any violation to it is difficult to accept what other authority could be entrusted to the work appeal or Revision.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Kutch. The State of Gujarat had a sovereign right to establish and administer a new territory, but the Union was not competent to make any law for the purpose of establishing a new State. The appellants contended that the Great Rann of Kutch was part of India and had always been so from the establishment of the two dominions, that the area was in different state at different seasons in the year, for part of the year it is water and for the remaining part it is land; and that the existence of a cession of Indian territory was not necessary. Held, that there was no evidence to show that the inlets were territory over which the Maharao of Kutch exercised sovereign rights and which by merger of the territory became Indian territory. The claim made by the claimants that in imple menting the award of the Tribunal an attempt is made to cede Indian territory before 1948 or was in de facto occupation and in respect of which sovereign authority was exercised by the Maha Rao of Kutch, cannot be accepted. The existence of an cession of India with a Dominion of India was not a condition precedent for making any law. It was not evidence of the fact that it was territory over where the Mahazdar of Kutch had sovereign rights but that it is part of Great R Ann of Kutch and is now Indian territory, and apart from the survey maps there is no evidence that it has been so declared foreign territory. [475C D] The existence or absence of an express provision in article 19(1) (d), cannot be said to be a condition for making a law. The fact that the Maha n of Kutch vested with the Dominion of Indian, and therefore, the existence or non compliance of any such provision would not make the award void.

The mortgagor 's interest in Mauza Bansjora was sold on January 16, 1937, and after th sale was confirmed, possession of Mauza Bahaldih was taken by the auction purchaser on April 7, 1937. The plaintiff filed a suit on July 12, 1946, in the Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhanbad for enforcement of the two mortgages by sale of the mortgaged properties. The trial Judge rejected the defence raised by the contesting defendants and held that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the mortgage deed dated June 14, 1922, was not barred by the law of limitation because the mortgagor ' had lost his interest in Mauzas Bansjor lands at the Court auction and that the claim to enforce the mortgage was within 12 years from April 14, 1925, by the sale under the money decree passed against the mortgagor, a cause of action accrued to the mortgagee to enforce that mortgage and the plaintiff 's suit filed within twelve years from the date of dispossession was barred. Held, that the right to sue where the mortgagee is deprived of the mortgage security or where he is not secured in his possession of the property or where possession is not delivered to him as agreed, the mortgagor having lost his share in Mauza Bansjecora prior to the payment of Rs. 600 by the mortgagor on April 14 , 1925, the plaintiff was entitled to enforce a mortgage and that under section 68(1) (b) of the Transfer of Property Act dispossession of the mortgagee from Mauza Bahaudih by virtue of the sale was governed by article 120 of the Limitation Act from the day when the mortgage money is repayable. The right to claim compensation and the period of limitation for a suit to recover the mortgage amount is governed by Article 120 of Limitation Act, from the very date of the dispossession of a mortgagee to secure the mortgage property. The mortgagor ' s interest in the mortgaged property was transferred to extend the period for which the mortgage debt was repayable.

The appellants were charged at the rate of Rs. 2 per month for transport of employees from Chinchvad Village to TELCo factory at Pimpri and back. The appellants contended that these amounts were realised by the appellants only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in the supervisory grades. In the course of the arguments it was pointed out that when the company was prepared to grant free transport facilities to the supervisory staff there was no reason why the same amenities should not be extended to the other employees and Mr. Nariman, learned counsel for the appellants frankly conceded that in future no charges would be realised from the employees and they would he provided free transport as in the case of supervisory staff. It is manifest that if the appellants had not levied any charge at all for the transport facilities granted to the employees it would not be liable to passenger tax. The Commissioner appears to have dismissed the appeals of the appellants 5 978 SCI/78 362 as he felt bound by the judgment of the Bombay High Court which had held that the transport vehicles provided to the appellants could be a public service vehicle carrying passengers for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers, either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey. The appellant further averred that the Transport Vehicles provided to them was reserved for them only and no other member of the public even if he wanted to pay full charges could be carried on the said vehicle. In view of our finding that such a transport vehicle is not a public Service Vehicle within the meaning of the provisions of the Act, it cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the Public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. The transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within the ambit of the aforesaid definition. Hence, it is not necessary for us to go into the question whether the transport service provided to these employees could be said to include employee of a public company who were given facilities by the appellant to pay the full charges. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the appellants were liable to pay passenger tax as also the penalty. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that transport vehicles did not fall within the purview of the definition of 'public service vehicle ' and that the appellant was liable to be taxed only if the passengers were carried on a public services vehicle which fell beyond the ambit Of the charging section. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The term 'public Service Vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules but that too does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the enactment we are of the opinion that the tax can be levied only on passengers who are carried on public service vehicles falling within the scope of the said definition. [360G H; 361A] 1.2 The expression 'public transport vehicle ' has been defined by section 2(7) of the , and that therefore does not creating any difficulty, because having due regard to its Preamble the Act we areof the opinionthat the tax could be levied on passengers carried by a stage carriage which is of the nature of a Public service Vehicle. [361C D] 1:3 The word 'public ' has also been defined in section 2 (7) and that too did not create an difficulty, since having regard of the Preamble and the Act it cannot By any processof reasoning or otherwise, be deemedto include employees or individuals of a company who have been given facilities for not as member of public but as held by the BombayHigh Court.

The appellants were granted a licence for a quasi permanent cinema to respondent No. 3 Prem Narayan son of Ganpatlal Chouksey, proprietor, Chitra Talkies, Lalbagh, Burhanpur (M.P.) against which a petition under 795 Article 226 of the Constitution by the petitioners was dismissed in limine by the High Court. The appellants filed an appeal before the State Government challenging the order granting licence for quasi permanent cinemas to respondent Nos. 3 and 4 Prem Narayan and others. The State Government did not give any opportunity to the objectors and decided the appeal at their back and thus, it is not a fit case for the interference of the High court under Article 226. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellants who had objected to the grant of a "no objection certificate" to the third respondent and had succeeded in persuading the licensing authority to refuse the grant, were rightly heard and the decision arrived at by the State government was violative of the principles of natural justice and the order passed by the Government is invalid. [696B] 1.2 The appellants not being entitled to challenge the grant or refusal of a cinema licence, the local residents, who had opposed to the granting of a no objection certificate and whose objections had prevailed with the licensing authorities and, therefore, they cannot now be permitted to plead a right to oppose the grant. [796C] 1:3 The appellants were not entitled to raise any objection certificate before the licensing Authority. They did not file any objection or were they entitled to be heard. [897D] 2.1 In an appeal filed by an applicant, who has been refused a cinema license, the State Govt. did not grant any objection certificates nor were the appellants entitled to file objections and nor were they entitle to be represented. The order granting the no objection Certificate is without prejudice to the right of the licensing officer to refuse a cinema Licence. [997C] 2:2 The High Court was in error in holding that there was no statutory obligation on the licensingauthority to invite objections or if any objection had been made by the applicant, the application for grant of such a licence could not be allowed. [1097D E] 3.1 Rule 6 declares that the grant granted shall without prejudice, to the rights of the licensee to oppose or oppose the granting thereof. The grant of an "noobjection certificate" is without jurisdiction and cannot be challenged on any ground whatsoever. [1006C] 3:2 In an application for a licence, which has been granted by the licensing authori ty under rule 101 and 102, the licensing Authori ty must invite objections and if such objections are filed, it would not have applied for a cinema. The question whether in an appeal preferred by an appellant, who is aggrieved by the grant o f a " no objection" certificate or a licence as the case may be, is a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the State authority. [1016E] 3.(3) The licensing authority must invite objection and decide the appeal after hearing the objectors. If there was a statutory obligation upon the licensing body to invite objection or if no objection had arisen, it was not the stage for grant o licence. [102D E; 1017A B] 4.2 In the instant case, the appellants were entitled to have an opportunity to oppose and decide their claim of the application. The High court was in wrong in holding the order of the Licensing Authority that there is no objection to the location of the cinema at the site proposed by the appellant. [103E] 5.3 The State Govt., did not furnish any reply or representation to the appellants before granting a "No objection" Certificate and, accordingly, turned down the request for "temporary cinema licence".

The plaintiffs filed a suit for specific performance of the contract. The Trial Court decreed the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that there was a contract as alleged in the plaint and that the service of a copy of the plaint along with the writ of summons was a communication of the acceptance. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 was not an acceptance. It is not usual to communicate an acceptance by serving a copy thereof through the medium of the Court. Nor is it usual to intimate an acceptance of the application for shares and the acceptance is communicated to the applicant, see In re: Pellatt 's Case(4) . The mere filing of a bill in a suit to enforce specific performance was regarded as sufficient acceptance of a defendant 's offer unless the offer had been withdrawn before, the filing of the suit, see Boys vs Ayerst(1), Agar vs Biden(2), article 306, page 142, Pomeroy on Specific Performance, 3rd ed., article 307, P.omeroy, on Specific performance of contract. [657 E] 1.2 The plaint was not a acceptance. The suit was not merely an acceptance but was a document made by the plaintiff. It was not usual for communicate an acceptation by serving copy of a plaint through the media of the court. [613G H; 613A B] 2.3 The communication of an acceptance is not an accepted contract unless there is an acceptance thereof before,the filing of it, see in re: M/s. Bloxam 's case a contract to take shares and to obtain necessary consent of the central government to assignment the mining lease. [557C] 2:4 The plaint did not allege any concluded contract between the parties. It only alleged that the contract was concluded on September 2, 1957. The letter dated September 2 was not communicated to,the plaintiff. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that there had been a concluded contract. In the peculiar facts of Bloxum 's cases a contract for taking shares and acceptance is communicating to the plaintiff before hi withdraw the offer. [457F] 3:5 The letter of an oral application for letters was not necessary. It did not disclose any acceptance by the plaintiffs. There was no concluded, contract or the acceptance of an application for share and the receipt was communicated to him before hi withdrew the offer and that as the governments concerned could not be compelled to accord the necessary sanction and approval, the contract to assign the mining leases could not have been specifically performed and on this ground the High court dismissed the appeal. [757F H] 3.6 The letter in question did not contain an acceptance or communicated to them before hi withdrawal of the offer, but it was only a communication from the plaintiff to the defendant before hi withdrawing the offer at any tune before,its acceptance by him. It could not therefore be said that there were no concluded contract and the suit for Specific performance was instituted. [857F G] 3 :7 The High court held that the plaintiffs accepted the offer of September 2. 1957 by their letter dated October 31, 1957 and that they reserved their right to file a suit in enforce specific Performance. It also held that in breach of the agreement the defendant failed to apply for and obtain the necessary consent before execution of the conveyance of the mining area. [820G H] 4. The contract was not concluded by an oral order. The plaintiffs did not accept the offer either orally or by any letter sent to them. They were entitled to remain in possession of the Mining lease even though no notice of allotment had been given to them and that there could be no estoppel against their claim.

The appellants were the owners of sugarcane in the State of Bihar. The appellants were prosecuted under section 3(1) of the Act on the ground that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of the sugarcane purchased by them, within the time prescribed. The trial court acquitted the accused and convicted them for an offence under section 7 of the (to be hereinafter referred to as the Act). On appeal the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence and directed their acquittal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the investigation which is being carried on against the appellants under sub rule (3) of rule 3 of Sugarcane Control Order, 1955, could not be said to have been in accordance with law because the complaint made before the police did not disclose a Cognizable offence and as such the police could not have taken up the investigation of that complaint. HELD: The provisions of section 11 of the Cr. P.C. are clearly covered by the Act. [767 E] In view of the provisions of article 372 of the Constitution which empowers the Parliament to legislate in respect of production, supply and distribution of foodstuffs, it is idle to contend that the regulation of the price at which sugarcane may be bought or sold must have been 677 altered in view of article372 of the constitution. [867 F] The contention that in view Of section 11(2)(c) of Rule 3 of the Sugarcane Control order 1955, no cognizance could have been taken of the offence alleged is premature. There is no substance in the contention that the complaint was not disclosing a Cognizrable offence and therefore the police should not have take up the Investigation of that case.

The appellants were engaged in the manufacture of various types of misuse and the Government of Karnataka issued a notification dated 30th June, 1969 exempting certain categories of misuse. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th September, 1966 when the order dated 12th January, 1977 was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given to them by the former order as the said grant of concessions constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the basis of which they had acted by starting new industries requiring investment of considerable funds and the State was not entitled to go back or that promise as it had sought to do by the order of 12th May, 1977. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government that the concessions granted under the said order dated 30 th June, 1968 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The doctrine ofpromissory Estopport is not applicable where a statute provides for a refund but can be found on examination of the relevant Act, the exercise of the power must be attributed to that source. [417C D] 2.1 There is nothing in Section 8A which indicates that any refund could be granted if it is made payable by a new industry on raw materials purchased by it for the first five years from the date the industry goes into production as set out in the order. The mere fact that the order was issued will make no difference because such a power is clearly there in Section8A and where the source of power under which it is issued is not stated in an order but can also be found On the examination of relevant Act the exercise Of the power should be attributed, to that sources. [517E] 2:2 The doctrine must be regarded as good law in view of the recent decision of this Court in State of Bihar and Anr. vs Usha Martin Industries Ltd., [1987] 65 STC 430 where a Division Bench comprising three learned Judges of this court upheld and applied the doctrine as to whether the doctrine should be regarded good law or not. The only submission made on behalf of the appellants is that even the second order of 30th May 1969 did not specify the power under Section 8 A. [617F] 3.2 The question whether the Doctrine of Prom promissory Estopports could be regarded in view Of the recent decisions of this High Court in Bihar and Ors. vs East India Commercial Co., Ltd., , [1987], 65 STC, 430 where the Government had no authority to provide for the grant of refunds was by way of refunds. It is clear that even if the said contention of learned counsel is correct, the result would be that even though in a more limited manner and that is not even the case of the appellant. The exercise of power must also be attributed by way Of refunds, although in a very limited manner, but can find on the examination o the relevant statute, the exercises of the powers must be attributable to that Source. [717G H] 4.3 In view of this, there is no substance whatever in the contention that the Doctrine was not good law now, it is clear from Section 8(A) and where it is granted by way thereof refunds, though in an more limited sense and that are not even a case of any statutory provision but can only be found upon the examination. [817G] 4:4 The doctrine should also be regarded to be regarded if good law is shown on the examining of the facts and circumstances of the case.

The appellants were tried for the offences under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegations that they caused the death of Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogudem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted A 3 to A 6 but found them guilty under Sections 148 and on applying 149 I P.C., convicted them for the offence punishable under Section 302 readwith Section 34 I. P. C. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A6 under Sections 302 read read with section 34 I P P.c. The appellants preferred an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 In view of the fact that the appellants were only three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 I.PC. [815E] 2.1 The non applicability of Section 149 is not a bar in convicting the appellants under Sections148 and 302 I.p.C.. [816B] 3.2 In view, there is force in the contention of the learned counsel for the appellants that the conviction of the appellants Under Section 148 read with Sec 34 I I.A. was illegal. The non application of mind by the High court to the facts and circumstances of the case does not warrant any interference. [916C] 3:3 In view the fact, there has been a long standing enmity between the parties. The evidence discloses commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of the unlawful assembly. A 4, A 5 and A 6 were armed with spears, A 2, A 3 and A 4 dragged the dead body from the field of A1 to A3 on his heals and chest and A 3 chopped off the fingers of left hand of the deceased with their respective weapons. The manner in which the attack was made on the deceased is satisfactorily established. The method in which A 1 to A 3, A 4 and A 5 were attacked by the accused party is clearly established. [716G] 4.3 In so far as the presence and partic ipation of the accused in the attack on the victim is concerned, there are as many as 18 injuries on the person of the victims. The number and nature of injuries, we have no hesitation in holding that the Appellants made the mur derous attack on them with their weapons. Keeping in view the manner of attack as disclosed by the eye witnesses and the number and type of injuries found on the persons of the group of the appellant, all the accused juveniles are guilty under Section 148 I.C.' [717G] 5.4 The non absence of any question of his forming an assembly within a definition of Section141 I.R. is, therefore, no bar in conviction of A 3 under Sections 149 and 34 IP.c., for convicting them under 7 Section 302 I read with 8 Section 34 IPC read with [718F] 5 5.5 The non existence of any element of unlawful assembly in the commission of offences in furtherance o f the common object of the assembly is, thus, no ground to interfere with the conviction under Sections 14 and 149 I I P C. The appeal fails and is dismissed.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family. The assessee was assessed to tax on the income of the family consisting of himself and his wife, two sons and one son. The Income Tax Officer assessed the sum of Rs. 48,500 to tax relying on section 52 sub section (2) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer but reduced the amount of Rs 48,000 to tax under section 52(2). In appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the assessee was not entitled to claim any deduction from the gross value of the consideration declared by the appellant. On behalf of the Revenue it was contended on behalf of it that the Income tax officer assessed the sums of Rs 24,500 and Rs. 54,000 respectively as capital gains taxable under the Gift Tax Act, 1958. Held: (i) The assessee is not entitled in law to claim deduction from its gross value for the purpose of assessment of income tax. [523C] (ii)The Income tax Officer assessed a sum of about Rs. 24,000 and Rs 54,500 respectively as revenue expenditure under section 53(2)(a). The assessee has actually received more than what is declared by him in respect of the transfer and sub section 2(2) provides that where an assessee transfers a capital asset and in respect thereof the consideration has been declared or disclosed and in such cases it is very difficult, if not impossible, to determine and prove the exact quantum of the suppressed consideration, sub section(1) provides the statutory measure for determining the consideration actually received by the Income-tax Officer. If therefore the Revenue seeks to bring a case within sub section 1(2), it must show that the fair market value of consideration has accrued to the assessee or been received by him and which from no view point can be rationally considered as capital gain or any other type of income. [623D] (iii)The true position in law is that where a full value of a consideration declared in respect to the transfer is correctly declared by an assessee, sub Section (2), provides the legal measure for determination of the amount actually received and the burden of proving such under statement or concealment is on the Revenue. [723C D] (iv)The real test for determining whether the transaction was effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of liability of the assessee to tax is whether the consideration had been declared by a person directly or indirectly connected with the assessee and it would have no application in case of a bonafinde transaction where the full value thereof received in respect the transfer has been understated by the Revenue, but if the construction of sub section is literally construed as applying even to cases where the real consideration received for the transfer, it would result in an amount being taxed which has neither accrued to him nor been received from him and it must be confined to caseswhere the actual consideration received is under stated or in other words, shown at a lesser figure than that actually received. [823D E] (v)The assessee has not been able to prove that the transaction had been effected with a view to evade tax on capital gains. The real test is whether there was under statement of consideration in respect Of the transfer. If it is found that the consideration received by an employee is more than the full amount of consideration declared, then the benefit of section 52 would be available to him. [923D F] (vi)The mere fact that the entire consideration received has been over and there is no understatement of the value of such consideration, it cannot be said that the real transaction had not accrued to it or was received by it and it could not be rationarily considered as a capital gain.

The appellant was charged with the offence of adulteration of "food" meant for human consumption. The Food Inspector 's evidence consisted of the testimony of the Food Inspector and the Food Inspectors. The appellant denied that he had only black Tils in his shop, but not on the packets, though he had deposed in his examination in chief that Tambe was probably not present at the time when the samples were sold by him to the Food inspector. He also stated that the food inspector did not know about the purpose for which the Til seeds were kept in the accused 's shop. The learned Magistrate after finding that it was more probable that there was talk about the object for which articles of food covered by the Act were manufactured, distributed or sold and that the Til plants were unfit for human use, held that the appellant had committed an offence under sec. 10(7) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The High Court on appeal reversed the finding of the Magistrate and convicted the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there is such vagueness and apparent contradiction in pictures conveyed by Tambe and the food Inspector that Tambbe was perhaps not present when the sample were sold. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The evidence of the prosecution witnesses produced before the Magistrate who said that Tamasbe was never intended for human purpose but an article kept for a special use could be used as food only if reasonable doubts arise this fact. [723C] 2.2 The appellant had no knowledge about the actual purpose for sale. He did not have any knowledge of the contents of the packets nor did he know that the Food Analyst 's version or the accused were sold it in an adulterated condition ? It is also true to say that the whole object of the Act was to prevent adulteration of 'food' meant for Human consumption. [823C D] 3.3 The evidence on record does not establish that the quality of the food was not necessarily food intended for a human consumption but an item kept for pooja and not for human purposes. It is further true that, when the case of the accused supported by his cash memo, is that the particular black '`Til' seeds were used as a food also. [820C D; 823A] 4.4 The evidence produced before this Court does not support the prosecution case that the sample was meant for poojy and not human food. It cannot be implicitly relied upon in this case. [824D E] 5.5 In view of the above, it is clear that the entire object of Section 10(8) of The Prevention ofFood Adulteration Act was only to prevent sale. [825C D]. 6.6 In the instant case, the evidence of P.W. 2, who said in his cross examination that the contents were not meant for personal consumption and that it is presumed from the nature of the article itself or the circumstances and manner of offering it for sale, cannot be impliedly relied on in this behalf. [823A] 7.7 The prosecution case was that the price of the Til bags at his shop was Rs.1,000/ , and that there were no other evidence to prove that what he had sold was not really food meant for a particular human consumption or, they were sold without giving such information to theFood Inspector. [828B] 8.8 The prosecution has failed to establish that what was stored or sold in a shop was neither "f Food" meant to be so used could a person be prosecuted on the ground that he sold it at an adulterated price ?

The plaintiff was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January, 1966. The order of dismissal was communicated to the plaintiff on 19th September, 1960. The plaintiff 's suit was one to obtain a declaration that the order of dismiss was bad and he continued to be in service. In the appeal to the Divisional Commissioner, the appellant contended that the period of limitation had not been computed from the date of the original adverse order but from the expiry of six months from the dale of filing of the suit, the plaintiff ' s suit was barred by time. The Divisional Commissioner dismissed the appeal on the ground that the suit was within time and as such the suit could be said to have been filed within time. In second appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the application for review was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether the order passed by the State Government had merged into the order or was it one pending at the commencement of the Constitution and the revisional order being after the Constitution came into force, the writ petition would be maintainable. [419D] 2.1 In every such case only when the appeal or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of action shall first accrue and where such order is not made, on the expiry period of six month from thedate of preferring of the appeal/revision, the right to sue shall first accrues. [519B] 2:2 The remedy has been availed of, a six months ' period from the commencement date when the cause of actionshall be taken to have first arisen. Reliance was placed by appellant 's learned counsel on a recent decision of a Two Judge Bench in the case of Raghubir Jha vs State of Bihar & Ors., [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 865, referred to.

The appellant was a tenant of a building in which the respondent had constructed a house. The respondent filed an application under section 110 of the Code for variation in the decision of the trial court and the High Court allowed the application and set aside the decree passed by the trial judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the appellate decree did not mean the whole of the decision but the grounds stated in support of the said decision were not sufficient to enable the appellant to go to the Privy Council in appeal; (2) if the appellate court makes a variation in regard to the order as to costs, then there is a right of appeal not only to the person against whom the variation has been made, but even to the party in whose favour the variation had been made. Held, that the word "decision" in article 133(1) means something more than what is actually proposed to be brought to this court under section 35 of the Civil Procedure Code; (3) if an appellate decree confirms the decision on a part of the judgment or the grounds given for it but merely makes a difference in respect of the award, of interest that would affect the character of the appellate suit and not against the party who has filed the appeal. The word "judgment" in section 35 is not defined in the Code but is used in its wide sense as meaning something more. It is a well settled principle of law that an order as a whole must be construed to mean that in determining the character or the ground given for the variation it is necessary to consider only that part of it which is actually sought to be made to this appeal and not by reference to the whole, of the appeal; and if that be so, the clause could be harmoniously construed to include that part. The words "decision", in article133(1), are wide enough to cover all cases where a variation is made in favour of one party or the other. In order to determine the value of the subject matter it is essential to consider whether only part of a decree and subject matter which are actually proposed should be brought into this Court under section 34 of the C.P.C., that part must be considered which is proposed tobe brought to the attention of the court in appeal, and not any other. The decision of this Court in that case construed the relevant provisions of section 110 literally and held that if an appeal court makes any variation in a decision of a suit it is not a decree of affirmance but variation in question is made by the appellate judgment as (1). A.I.R. (5) I.L.R, 499. 473 would not affect the nature of the decree which would be passed if the appeal court make a variation or variation in its decision. The position with regard to a claim for interest before the date of the suit is entirely different; for instance, in regardto a claim by the intending appellant it may also be necessary to make it clear that even the test of affirmation should be applied by reference only to that portion of the order which is allegedly proposed to been brought to it in appeal and (2). If an appellate court confirms the decree of the lower court it is a decree, of affirmence and this position would not be affected either by the extent of the variation made or by the fact that the variation is not made in respect thereof.

The petitioners, who were the respondents in the two revision petitions filed under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, challenging the orders passed by the District Court under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, was dismissed. The High Court held that the revisional order of the District Judge under section 24 of the Provincial Small Causes Courts Act was not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 115 of Code of Criminal Procedure and that the revision petition filed by the respondents was incompetent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High court had exclusive jurisdiction under section115 of the CPC in a case arising out of an original suit of the value of Rs. 20,000/ and above, and that as such the revisional power of the State Government under section 5(2) of the Act could not be revised by the High Courts under section 35 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, the revision petitions should be dismissed. Dismissing the appeals, HELD : 1. The revisional order passed by a District Judge exercising the jurisdiction of a Judge of Small Causes Court is not amenable either to the Revisional power under section 125 or section 115, Code of C.P., 1973. [975 D] 2. In respect of cases decided before 20th September, 1972 and also all cases arising out from such suit was decided by the said date, irrespective of the valuation of the suit out of which the case arose : (a) in the District Courts, the case would be amenable to revisional jurisdiction under Section115 of Code, Civil Procedure. No. 9752 of 1979, the High Curt had exclusive Jurisdiction under section 114 read with section 115 and no question could have arisen of invoking the revisional powers of the Court under that section. [875 E] 3. The revision petition under section 116 of the , Code of civil Procedure is not maintainable against a revisional order under section25, Provincial, Small Cause Court Act. No question could arise of invoking revisional power under Section 25, the appeal and the associated special leave petitions must be dismissed as such. [775 D E] 4. The District Judge had exclusive powers under section 235 in respect of an order of a District Court exercising the revisional Jurisdiction of the said High Court. [76 A B] 5. In view of the clear language of section 115(1) of Code and section 115 read with Section 115, C. P., it is not open to the High Judge to exercise revisional power in cases arising from original suits of the nature in which a District court would exercise revisional jurisdiction. [774 E F] 6. The question whether a revision petition against an order passed under section 29 of the . , Code or section 30 of the. U. P. Urban Building (Regulation) Act by a High Court is maintainable against an appellate order made by a Judge exercising jurisdiction of another Judge of a Small Causes court, is not a matter which can be decided by that court as if the amendment Act of 1978 were in force at all material times ; [776 D E F; 774 A B]. 7. The power under sections 115 and 115 of C P., 1973 to revise an order made under section 30 or section 31 of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings(Regulation of Rent and eviction) Act is a discretionary power conferred on the High Civil Court in cases where it has been decided by a subordinate Judge exercising original jurisdiction of that court. [784 E] 8. The provisions of sections 115, 115 and 116 of C, P., Code of Code are not applicable to the present case. [795 D E; 776 A B B]. 9.

The respondents, who were the owners of certain lands belonging to them required by the Urban Improvement Trust , Jaipur for a public purpose namely for implementation of a development scheme viz. for implementation a development plan viz. the Civil Lines Extension Scheme, The State Government issued a notification under section 52 (1) of the Act for acquiring the said land admeasuring more or less 44,770 square yards under section 53 (2) of Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act , 1959 for a purpose namely, for implementation the development scheme at public expense viz. "for implementing a development Scheme viz. It is stated that the respondents had acquired their lands at Jaipur and wanted to take immediate steps under sub section (6) thereof to secure such possession. The notification was issued on February 8, 1984 under section 51(1) read with section 52 of the Rajasthan Urban improvement Act , 1961 for the purpose of implementation of the development schemes viz. 'for implementing the development plan etc. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification issued by the State Government under section52 (1). The Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the notice was duly served on the respondents and they had no objection as to the power and authority of the State government to acquire the notified land. In appeal, the Division Bench held that the service of notice under sub Section (2), of section 52(1), or his jurisdiction to proceed with the inquiry under section 55 of the , was sufficient to invest the Calcutta High Court with jurisdiction to entertain a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the notification dated February 8 , 1984. The State of Rajasthan preferred an appeal before this Court, which was dismissed by the Division bench on March 13, 1984. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the writ petitions filed by the respondents purporting to be under article 227 of the constitution were not maintainable as they had been served on them by the Special Officer , Town Planning Department , Jaipur and the Land Acquisition Officer, Jaipur and that the rule nisi thereon and the ad interim exparte prohibitory order obtained by them on the basis of such petition from the learned Single Judge on March 12, 1984 when there was total lack of inherent jurisdiction on the part of (1 ) ; , 602 the Calcutta high Court to entertain such a petition. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The service of notices under sub sections (5) and (6), of Section 52(2) for the grant of an appropriate writ, direction or order under article226 of theConstitution is not necessary for the respondents to plead the service by the special Officer , town Planning Department, Jaipur under section 54(1). [605F H; 605A B] 2. The notice issued by a Special Officer, Town Planning department , Jaipur was duly sent to the Secretary to the State of Raj, Town planning Department , Rajasthan for issue of requisite notification under Section 52 (2). [ 602C D] 3. The entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition of the land under section 50 of the . Act arose within the State and was therefore sufficient to invested the CalcuttaHigh Court with power to entertain an application lay before the Rajasthan High Court , Jaipur Bench, where the cause of actions wholly or in part arose. [606F G] 4. The whole cause of the action culminating into the acquisition is within the territorial jurisdiction of the High court , Jaipur bench , where the causes of action wholly or partly arise. In view of this , the appeal succeeds and is allowed with costs.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant from the premises in suit. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the building was constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to s.2(2) of the new Rent Act and that it was covered by the new rent Act. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree for arrears of rent and remanded the case to the trial court for deciding the question whether the building in question had been constructed substantiallyout of funds received from the source mentioned in sub s.(2) and (3) of s.39 of the Act. The appellant landlord challenged the order of the High court before this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The new Rent Acts will not apply to a building during a period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. [419D] 2.2 The new rent Acts will apply to buildings constructed after the commencement of the old Rent Act. [520B] 3.3 The new Act will not be applicable to a case where ten years expired during the pendency of the litigation. [621C] 4.1 In the present case, the building had been purchased by a co operative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, there was no question of giving the benefit of s 39 as the building has not become more than ten years old on the date of assessment which was 1st October, 1971. [721D] 4:2 The building in dispute was constructed by a cooperative society and that the landlord purchased it through the society. It was not at all necessary in that case to deal with the question as to whether the appellant would be entitled to the benefit under s. 39 of the New Rent Act after first determining whether any amount is due from the tenant towards rent for some period prior to April 7, 1976 and if so, the appellant will be entitled only to the benefits of s39 as the house had not become ten years ' old on that date. [821B] 4 3.4 The building was subject to assessment therefore it will be deemed to have been completed on 1st November, 1971 and not on the basis of any such report, record or assessment, the date, on which it is actually occupied (not including occupation merely for the purposes of supervising the construction or guarding, the buildings under construction) for the first time. [820G] 4 4.5 The building will be treated to have become morethan ten years' old on 1 st October, 1972. [822C] 5.6 In the case in hand the building is subject to Assessment and assessment the date from which the first assessment thereof comes into effect and where the said dates are different, the earliest of the said date, and in the absence of any report, Record or assessment the Date, onwhich it is finally occupied (Not including occupation simply for the purpose of supervising construction or protecting the building under construction), for the second time. The earliest of such report record or assessments, the dates, on where it is allegedly actually occupied(not includingoccupation merely for purposes of supervised the construction)for the first lime. [823D] 5:7 In the instant case, there is no reason why the benefit Of s.41 of the Old Rent Act be not given to the appellant.

The appellant entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings, stores and other works at Ranchi, the first of them being contract No. 21 of 1942 dated November 5, 1942, and the other two contracts Nos. 21 and 26 of 1942 respectively. The respondents entered into two contracts for construction of theerodromes, buildings stores and works at Patna, the second being contracts Nos 21 and 22 of 1942, which were contracts Nos 20 and 26. On the first question, the appellant contended that the agreement for reference to arbitration did not comply with the requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the Constitutional provision in force at the relevant date, and it was therefore void, that no decree should be passed thereon; and that the award passed in proceedings founded thereon is a nullity and that no order could be passed therein. Held, further, that the document in court which was a copy of an instrument cannot be validated: That the copy of the instrument cannot, in our opinion, be validated and "acted upon" and that it fell within item 2 and that accordingly it fell outside item 12 of K Lall, the Executive Engineer had in fact been specifically authorised to execute the arbitration agreement. The law does not provide for the levy of any penalty on lost documents, but only provides for the imposition of any penalties on lost document, and that law does no provide for a levy of penalty on loss documents. It is therefore clear that the copy which was sent by the arbitrator to the court must fall within item 12, in which case he would not be competent to execute it. The question whether the award which was received from the Legal Remembrancer could be validated or invalid cannot be answered in the absence of a copy thereof.

The appellant was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. He was prosecuted and punished for various offences under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471 and 120B IPC. The trial court acquitted all the accused persons. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court reversed the order of acquittal and convicted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the said Rule placed an embargo on initiating judicial proceedings for prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years from the date of cause of action or event mentioned therein. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The third proviso to clause (b) of Rule 2.2 is in the nature of a beneficent legislation and in case of doubt has to be interpreted in favour of the person for whose benefit the Rule has been framed. This purpose can be achieved if the said proviso by adopting the rule of reading down is interpreted to mean that even if a government Servant is prosecuted and convicted in judicial proceedings instituted in respect of cause or event which took place more than four years before such institution the government will not be entitled to exercise the right conferred on it by substantive provision contained in clause (a) with regard to pension of such a government employee. A similar submission as has been made by the learned counsel for the respondents in the instant cases was also made in the case of Des Raj singhal and did not consider other grounds, if any, that may have been raised by him for quashing of the prosecution on grounds, when he had already been considered earlier. [419D] 1.2 The third Proviso to clause(b) is in nature of an exception to the power of the government in the matter of withholding or withdrawing etc. of pension of a retired government servant contained in clauses (b), (b). [421B] 1:3. In view of what has been said above and keeping in mind the scope of the power to frame a rule under Article 309 and the purpose of Rule2.2, there is no doubt with regard thereto that even though a government officer is prosecuted or punished in judicial proceeding instituted in connection with cause of actions which arose or an event which taken place morethan four years prior to such institution, as has already been held by the High court can be treated to be a rule regulating the condition of service of such retired government servants contained in Clause (b)(i) of rule 2.1. The third provisos to clause 2.3 are in the form of an embargo against prosecution of government servant if the conditions stated therein are satisfied. [427C D] 1.:4. In the instant case, there was no doubt that even when a government official is prosecuted for commission of offences under sections 420, 468 and 471 IPC before such commencement, the government would not be liable to pay pension of the retired government employee contained in sub clause (i) with respect to pension. [321C] 1 :5. The fourth proviso to Rule 2(2) of the Punjab Civil Service Rules has been issued for a different purpose namely to provide an exception or to the powers of the Government in the matters of withholding etc. and virtually incorporates the principle underlying Article 21 of the Constitution by fixing four years as the limit for initiating prosecution.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3 preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to a fixed dividend of 71 per cent on the face value of the shares. The respondent company had been floated as an public limited Company under the Companies Act 1913, to acquire & carry on business of manufacturing and sale "Amritanjan". In September 1936 the respondent company started its business in the trade name of " Amrutanjan" which was marketed by the company in the Trade name of 'Amrut Niranjan'. The authorised Capital of the Company was 7000 ordinary share. The preference shareholders who were entitled to fixed dividend were not directly interested in such accumulation. The shares yielding a fixed rate of dividend were held by the public and shares belonging to the controlling group were held, by the parent company or by the nominees thereof. The result of the partition between the two groups was that the respondent Company was one in which the public were substantially interested, and there fore the income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to pass the order under section 23 A. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 23A were correctly applied for the three relevant years. Held: (i) The Explanation to sub section (1) of section23 A is in substance a clause which defines what a company, in which case the public are substantially interested and to a subsidiary company of such a company if the whole of the share capital of such subsidiary company is held by a single individual or group of individuals acting in concert, the company would be regarded as one in whom the public is substantially interested. The definition of "public" in section 23(A) is not exhaustive of the meaning of the expression "public". It only provides that where a shareholder holds or a group of shareholders acting in association with others acting in combination hold fifty one per cent or more of the voting power, the question is one of fact to be determined in each case whether it is a company in which such public are not substantially interested or having regard to the purpose for which the holding of fifty one percent or more is utilised. The total voting power is 5,500 one vote, for each share, ordinary and preference alike and twenty five per cent of that voting power has been allotted unconditionally by or is beneficially held by both shareholders as well as the controlling groups. The entire voting power was 5,000 one vote. [775 C] (ii)The Explanation to section 23 does not refer to any company in whose case the shares are vested in persons other than the controlling members and not by shareholders entitleci to a specified fixed rate. It only makes a conclusive presumption in those cases where shares not entitled to any fixed rate or dividend have been allotted partially to, or acquired unconditionally by, or is interested partly by the Public. The words "public", in section 22(A), are wide enough to cover all companies in which public are being substantially interested but not by the shareholders entitle to a fix rate of dividends. [76 D] (iii)The definition of 'public ' in section 21(A)(i) is in itself exhaustive of all the provisions contained in sections 23 and 23 A, as it stood at the material time, no order could be passed in respect of any company which the Public are substantially concerned with.

The appellant was a del credere agent of the first appellant. The goods were delivered to him on behalf of another quota holder Beharilal Bajirathi, and he paid them to Dharsi Moolji on account of the 13 bales. On the same day, i.e., on 21 st February, 1947, the first respondent sent a notice under section 6(1) of the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949, to show cause why the goods should not be delivered to the appellant. On receipt of the notice, the appellant filed a complaint against the first and second respondents alleging that the bales remained in the physical possession of the appellant at all material times and were not physically delivered to Messrs. Dwarkadas Khetan & Company on behalf Of another quota holders Beharilal. The Magistrate took cognizance of the complaint and issued summons to the first respondents. On appeal, the High Court held that the goods were not delivered to them and directed the first accused to deliver them to the Mills. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf the appellant that (1) the sale agent bad informed the first plaintiff that he had effected a sale, (2) the selling agent had paid the first defendant for the goods, (3) the goods had actually left the Mills ' premises, and (4) they were in the Dady Seth godown under the control of Dwarkadash Khetan. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The entry in column 3 is not intended to be confined to quota holders or their agents but means what it says, namely the person to whom physical delivery of the goods has been made whoever he may be. [833C] 2. It would not be correct to say that this godown belonged to Dwarkadalas Khetan and Company. The record amply bears it out, that this shop belonged to Chankadas Daga. So, even if there was a technical breach of the law it was not one which called for the severe strictures which are to be found in the trial court 's judgment and certainly not for the savage sentences which the learned Magistrate imposed. [733C D] 3. The entries in column 2 are not intended only to be restricted to quotaholders but means What it says that "the person to who delivered the name of Dwarakdas Khetan has refused to deliver him, (4). It is clear that this godowns belonged to ' Dwarkadasa Khetan & Co., and not to Dwarkotas Khetan. [633C E] 4. The fact that Dwarkada Khetan had control over the godown, the control was exercised on behalf and as the agent of Mills. So even if it be assumed that the entry in Column 3 is meant to be limited to quota holder or his agents but actually what it means, it is clear from the record amply borne it out that this storage belonged to the Dwarkadars. [533C F] 5. The appellant had been authorised to take delivery of goods on behalf, and as he did not receive them, they were handed over to Dwarak Khetan for delivery in the same truck as the 13th bales. But the learned magistrate imposed a penalty of Rs. 1,000 on the first two respondents. [433C G] 6. The order imposing penalty was passed by the Magistrate after considering all the relevant facts and circumstances. [525A B] 7. In view of the fact that the appellant had not made any attempt to obtain delivery of these 13 bales on behalf or on behalf either of them, the order imposing the penalty is vitiated.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5(1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was appointed as an Examiner of University which, it is alleged, had no connection with his being a Government servant. The appellant was charged under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed offences punishable under sections 161 and 165 of the I.P.C. and section 5 (1) of Prevention of corruption Act. He pleaded that he had been falsely implicated in the case. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that he was a Government Servant within the definition of "public servant" as defined by section 21 of the Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was not a public servants within the ambit of the Ninth clause of section 21 and that the ninth clause of s.21 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not cover the case of Dwivedi as he had no relation with his having been a Government employee. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (1)(a) The word "obtains" on which much stress was laid does not include an element of effort on the part of the receivers one may accept money, that if offered or solicit payment of a bribe, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion; in each case, lie obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position as public servant. [446C D] (b) The use of the word "subtains" in clause (d), (b), (c) and (d). is clearly implied. It would, therefore, be reasonable to put on clause (a) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. [546E F] (2)(i) The abuse being either by corrupt or illegal means or by other means of the nature mentioned in Narayanan Nambiar 's(1), case. [647B] (ii) The misuse being either through corrupt or unlawful means or otherwise, it would be the necessary ingredient of the offence; the abuse being neither by corrupt nor illegal means. It is wholly immaterial in what capacity he has committed the offence under sub clause (b). The abuse was either by indirect means or through other means. [747C] (iii) The expression "obtaining" on whom much stress is laid does Not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element Of effort on a part of it. [848E] (iv) The abused word " Obtains" does not exclude the idea that if offer or solicit money was made by corrupt means or any other means, it should be accepted as a public Servant.

The petitioners were engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the Construction Department of the Signal and Telecom Construction Organisation under which the petitioners are working, according to the Railway Administration. The petitioners were initially appointed as casual labourers on temporary basis for a period varying between 2040 and 2100 respectively. They were later absorbed against permanent vacancies in the regular cadre in the Permanent category. On completion of 120 days of service as against 180 days they were asked to be absorbed against a permanent vacancy in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondents. The Railway Administration, respondent herein, rejected their applications on the ground that they are not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, City Compensatory Allowance, Casual Leave etc., after attaining temporary temporary status. The Railways passed an order of absorption against a temporary vacancy in regular cadre. The petitioner filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the order of the Railway Board 's order dated 1st of June, 1984 and the High Court dismissed their writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Administration that the Railway administration had not treated them as temporary servants and has applied discriminatory rates of wages. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The petitioners should be entitled to the same pay as is 1) admissible to others either in the project or in the open line. [144A B] (2) The Railway Board had issued directions on January 1, 1984, to absorb the casual labourers who acquire temporary status for the conferment of attendant benefits like regular scales of pay, increments etc., they are now entitled to be regularised against permanent posts which mostly occur in open line as well as willing project casual labour. [145C D] (3) The scheme formulated under orders of this Court, steps have been taken. It is not disputed that on eventual absorption in regular employment half the service rendered with temporary status is counted as qualifying service for pensionary benefits. In the Signals and Telecom construction organisation under which they are working the petitioners were combined for the purpose of screening and forming of panel on the basis of seniority depending upon the days of work put in. This Court changed the existing practice for reckoning seniority and directed that seniority of project casual labourers should be combined and prepared departmentwise and category wise and in terms of the directions of this court, steps has been taken to screen such of the petitioners who have not yet been tested for the purposes of regularising their service. [146A B C] (4) The Railways Administration had to take appropriate steps to remove difficulties faced by the casual labour but there is perhaps slackness in enforcing them. Several instructions issued by Railway Board and the Northern Railway Headquarters were placed before us to show that the Administration was anxious to take necessary steps to screen those of the petitioner who have been denied the benefits like House rent Allowance, city Compensator Allowance, casual leave etc., while there is no break in such continuity the previous service is also taken into account. [147C D E] (5) The object of the scheme formulated by the Railway Boards was to take prompt steps to scre such of those petitioners who had not yet completed 240 days of continuous employment previously. This is evident from the fact that the Railways Administration has been anxious to remove such difficulties facedby the casual labourer but there are perhaps stiffness in enforce them.

The Forward Markets Commission, in exercise of the power conferred on it under section 12 of the Act, framed bye laws 52AA and 52AA. The said bye laws provided for the framing of bye laws by the Central Government for the Association as its bye laws. The relevant provisions of the bye laws were: (1) "The Forward Market Commission shall be a proper recipient of the powers conferred on the Forward Markets Committee under section 11 or 12, as the case may be, of the Central Govt. for the association as its Bye law 52AA; and (2) confirmed prohibit, as from the date of such confirmation or from such later date as may be fixed by the Board in the resolution referred to in sub clause (1), (a)trading in the Hedge Contract for any delivery or deliveries notified under section 13 or 14. The Forward Markets Act, 1952, was amended by the Forward Contracts Commission (Amendment) Act, 1956, and it was provided that "the Forward Markets Board shall be competent to exercise a power assigned to it under a bye law made by the Government under section 3 of the , and (b)that the Forward Market Committee may, either on a request in writing received by it in this behalf from the governing body of a recognized association or if in its opinion it is expedient so to do, make bye laws for all or any of the matters specified in section II or amend any bye laws made by such association under that section. The Act was amended in 1956 and it provided that the Forward Marketing Commission may exercise a, power assigned by or under the Act." Section 12(1) of the Forward markets (Amendment), Act, 1957, provided for a byelaw made by an Association under section 4 of the . It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the power of the Government to make bye law with retrospective effect is not competent to confer any power on the Central government by necessary implication. Held, further, that the provisions of section 12(i) do not confer a power on a Central Government to frame bye laws with retropective effect and, therefore, the new bye law framed by an association under section 10 of the Indian Contract Act is invalid. The power of making bye laws under section 14 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, was not competent for the Central Legislature to make a bye legislation with retrospective operation.

The assessee, a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. was a shareholder in a company called the Ukra Estates optical Ltd. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ for the year 1358 B.S., and Rs. 21,822/ for each of the three years in respect of which they were received by it as consideration for grant of long term mining lease, the entire amount for each year was income in the hands of the assessee. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amounts to tax declared as dividend for each three years under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the Company for the grant of lease was not taxable as dividend but income of the company from other sources. The High Court also held that the entire sum for each years was income within the meaning of section 2(6A) of Income tax, 1922 and as income of assessee from "other sources" (not being dividend), within the ambit of section 12 as dividend income liable to tax under section 12. In second appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the whole amount for the three year in question was not capital gain, because it was not a receipt of income in its hands and therefore, the distribution to the assessee of the entire money was not exempt from liability to tax. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The expression "other source" is wide enough to include all sources which are statutorily payable on compensation. [775F] 2.2 The word "income" in section 2 (6A), is wide and comprehensive enough to cover all kinds of income which are not included in the definition of "income". [776B] 3.3 The expression 'income" is wider than the words "other Source" in Section 2(4) of Act, 1961. [771C D] 4.2 In the instant case, the amount for which the assessee was entitled to receive was not part of accumulated profits but only a part of it being dividend income. The expression used in section 12 is wide in amplitude and includes all kinds which are included within the definition. [764D] 5.3 Section 2 (7A) is wide as wide enough, and covers all types of income including income from "any source". [772B] 4:4 In the present case, it is not a part or whole of the capital gains arising after 31st March, 1948, but only one type of income. It is an inclusive definition. The word 'income' in section 3(7A), therefore, includes all types which are excluded from the definition and all kinds thereof. [773G] 5:5 In the context of the form of the questions, it would be clear that the receipt by the assessee for grant or lease of longterm leases after the 31st day of March, 1949 was a receipt received by him of dividend within the connotation of section 3 (7 A). [774C D; 771A] 6.6 The word used in Section 12 is wider enough to exclude all kinds from liability. It includes all categories which are covered by the definition but not included within it. [782D] 7.7 In the case before us, the receipt of compensation for land compulsorily acquired which forms part of its fixed assets of a Company is of a capital nature: Senairam Doongarmall vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Assam(1), and other references, decided by this Court on July 25, 1969, the only question of law raised was whether any amount of salami was capital gain.

The appellant, who was the owner of Sandalwood Oil, was engaged in the manufacture of wood oil. The forest produce was being used for manufacturing wood oil and rosewood. The wood oil is a natural produce of the forest directly derived as an exudation from living trees in the forest belonging to the family of the Dipterocarpucoae trees while sandal wood oil was a bye product from sandalwood (Santalum Album) by industrial process. It is further contended that Sandal Wood Oil is not a wood oil as defined under section 2(f) (1) of the Act and therefore, it is a forest produce which include wood oil in the definition of forest produce. The timber was being manufactured from rubber trees while sandalwood oil is also a bye products derived commercially manufacturing process. The Forest Range Officer, who issued notice to Sandal wood Oil, found Sandalwool Oil as well as roots of sandalwood and rocewood, held that Sandals Wood Oil are not wood oil but are wood oil which include, that is to say, the 'enumerated items in Clauses 1 and 11 "wood oil" is one of the enumerate items as well and roots of trees therein. The learned Single Judge had rightly construed the meaning of the word 'wood oil ' and held that sandal wood Oil being the bye product derived commercially manufacture process is not wood Oil as defined in section 2 (f) of The Act. The Division Bench also took into consideration the definition clause of the inclusive definition of the term "wood Oil" and held, from the context and purpose the Act seeks to serve and the family to which sandal wool oil belongs being an essential oil would include wood oils. It must be noted in this context that there are several types of essential oils in India, the important being Sandal trees, agar wood oil derived from exudations from living tree in the forests belonging to family of Dipteroocarcoae and while sandalwood oil is an essential commodity which includes wood oil, agari wood oil obtained from exODation from residing trees in forest belonging https://hcservices.ecourts.gov.in/hcservices/ the family. The definition of 'forest produce' in section 3(f)(1) (i) of Act would require purposive interpretation drawing the context in which it is used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. In view of the clear language employed in the inclusive definitions, Sandal tree Oil is a species of wood oils and as ideas and concepts change, as they are bound to do in any country like ours with the establishment of a democratic structure based on agalitarian values, the meaning and content of the statutory provision undergo a change. The expression being technical and being part of an inclusive definition has to be construed in its technical sense but in an exhaustive manner, it cannot be restricted in such a manner so as to defeat the principle object and purpose of the enactment. When there is nothing in the context or the subject matter to the contrary, to be applied to some things to which it would not ordinarily be applicable. But to enable the word as used in the Act, when there is anything in the statute sought to serve the tribals in theforest area, the interpretation and purpose will have To be discovered Having regard to its meaning, the words not defined may be construed In the context of the definition will haveto be discovered with reference to the object and purposes which legislature seek to subserve; while there is no nothing in context or subject matter thereto to which they would not normally be applicable, but to enablethe word as use in the act, sought to be interpreted.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. The High Court set aside the judgment of acquittal on two grounds: (1) that there were no compelling reasons for reversal of the judgment; (2) that the prosecution was producing Bega merely I 858 because the village diggi (pond) which was empty had to be filled up; and (3) that it would not be dangerous to accept his testimony as being of any great value which is still more diminished by the finding as to the guilt or innocence of the accused. HELD: The High court should not set aside an acquittal unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons justifying interference with the findings of the trial Court. [858 D] (1)(a) The High Courts have held that the evidence in the present case is of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt could properly be drawn. [ 858 E F] (b) The judgment of the High Court does not disclose any such reasons justifying interfering with the conclusions of the Trial Court. It is a well settled principle of law that the High Courts should not interfere with the finding of the Sessions Judge unless there were " substantial or compelling reasons" for setting aside the order of acquittal. [888 F] In the present cases, the High court has set aside only one conviction and that too in appeal by special leave. The judgment does not indicate any such reason justifying interference. [ 889 E] (2)(a). The High courts have held on the evidence as to what the accused is guilty. The learned Judges of the Rajasthan High Court were, therefore, in error in accepting the testimony of these witnesses in support of the correctness of the two dying declarations. [898 F G] (3)(b) In the instant case, the prosecution has not been able to prove that there was no compelling reason for reversal. The second point on which the judgment is challenged is the lack of compelling reasons justify interference with findings of acquittal unless it discloses any such grounds justifying interference therewith.
