The appellant company was a private limited company having establishments in different parts of the country. The company was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act, 1947. In the year 1963, the appellant company entered into an agreement with the Indian Oxygen Workers Union for a reference under section 10(2) of the . 'Act, 1947, to the Government of Bihar for adjudication under section 11(1)(a) of . The dispute was referred by the Central Government to the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the union 's constitution was duly amended on January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963, i.e., after the said purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company and Indoxco Labour Union does not materially affect the position that the dispute raised by the union is in respect of the employees of the appellant 's factory at Jamshedpur and the workmen represented by their aforesaid union the Indox co Labour Union. The appellant company challenged the award on various grounds, namely (1) that the reference was barred by limitation; (2) that as there was no agreement between the management and the Indian oxygen Workers Union to pay for overtime rate allowed by the Tribunal in respect o those disputes, the reference extended to them also and (3) that since the dispute was not referred to the Central government under section 5(1) of , the reference did not materially affected the position as it had amended its constitution so as to extend its membership to the company 's other workmen in its other establishments. The High Court dismissed the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal was justified in obliging the appellant Company to grant special leave to attend the meetings of the federation and the conventions of the I.N.T.U.C. over and above the various types of leave available to the appellant also and the parties who had agreed to refer those disputes for adjudication. [501B] 1.2 The Tribunal 's extension of that award to workmen in the company's other establishments was clearly without jurisdiction. [602E] 2.1 In view of the fact that the appellant has not made any difference that the name of Indoxex Industries Union as representing the workmen concerned was mentioned in the agreement and the said statement and not that of the Indian assured workers Union, it could operate only in respect thereof. The reference extended by the appellant to the workmen of the company which represented also workmen employed in the appellant factory at Ranchi and represented by its aforesaid union. [702F] 2:2 The dispute raised between the appellant and the employees was only those set out in the said agreement and not as regards the claim of the Union that it had changed its constitution on January 21, 1963. It made no difference whether the name was mentioned or not. If the overtime exceeded 48 hours per week, 48 hours of work being the maximum provided by the Bihar Factories Act, 1948, the company would be liable to pay at double the ordinary rate of wages as provided in that Act. [802F G] 3. The dispute referred to it was only one set out and was actually referred to and was finally referred to a Tribunal by the said notification. It was clearly between the employees and the appellant having practically to finance the administration and management of the union, the members of the executive committee of that Union could be attended by the Union 's delegates by availing themselves of their earned leave. [902F H] 4. The question whether the dispute referred as a " dispute between" the management or the workmen was in respect Of those disputes was not one which arose out of the agreement. It is only when the dispute is referred to an Industrial Tribunal that the Tribunal 'is justified in refusing to grant Special leave to the parties.

The assessee firm was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The firm was dissolved on March 31, 1939 and on that account the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the firm Messrs Hakam Mal Tani Mal was dissolved by a deed dated April 1, 1939, before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 came into force and that the assessee had no right to claim relief under s 25(3), or in the alternative under section 24(4). Held: (i) The assessee was carrying on business at the commencement of the Act. The business in timber which was carried on by the firm was taken over by the assessee. The assessee started doing business immediately after the dissolution of the firm from April 1 1939, and it could not be said that the business of Messrs Hakams Mal Tati Mal was discontinued before the expiry of the period of six months from the date of dissolution. (ii) The partnership therefore came into being at the time when the assessee commenced doing business, and there is no other evidence in that behalf. (iii) The firm of Messrs bearam Mal was not dissolved by any deed signed by the partners of the assessee, and the business at Abdullapur was takenover by the Income Tax Officer. (iv) The business of the partnership was taken into force on April 1., 1939, when Act 7 Of 1939 came in force and it was found that the partnership had been brought into force before the commencement. (v) The income tax (amendment) Act, 7 of 1942 was brought into operation on April 31, 1988, by the Indian income tax authorities. The High Court was right in holding that the assessment was not carried on business after March 31., 1939 and that it could be said to have been carried on at the date when the dissolution took place. (vi) The Income tax Appellate Tribunal held that the appellant was carrying business at a particular point of time at which the IndianIncome tax Act had come into force, and that there was no other material evidence in this behalf.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Act, 1963. On April 25, 1967, the State Transport Appellate Tribunal passed an order granting the permit to the appellant. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order and also the order of the State Government refusing to grant the permit. The High Court dismissed the writ application holding that the issue of the permit was made beyond the prescribed period of limitation under rule 119 of the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Rules, 1945 (old Rules) after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of the permits. It was contended by the appellant before the appellate authorities that there was no period of Limitation under rule119 of the Bangalore Motor Vehicles rules, 1945, after a period of nearly six years from the commencement of the Act and therefore the issue was made within the prescribed time of limitation. The State Transport Tribunal held that the question whether any appeal lay under section 64 of the , was not competent under section64 of the . The High court dismissed the appellant 's writ petition on February 27, 1967. In this appeal by special leave it is contended by counsel for the appellant that the High court was right in dismissing the writ petition of the appellant which ought to have been allowed. It may be mentioned that at the time of the granting of the permission the Mysore State Transport Authority granted the permit on April 25. 1967, and the order passed by the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal was affirmed in appeal by the State transport Appellate Tribunal. The question whether a writ application under article 226 of the Constitution is maintainable against an order issuing a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional Transport Authority granting the permits, or by any condition attached to a permit granted to him, is only a ministerial act necessarily following the grant. It is not necessary to consider the other clauses of section 64(1) which are admittedly not relevant. The appeal before the State Appellate Tribunal and the further appeal to the Mysore revenue Appellate Tribunal are, therefore, not competent.

The appellant contested the election to the Lok Sabha from Hapur Parliamentary Constituency in the year 1967. The respondent was a sitting member of Parliament. He alleged that at the meeting held on 7 February, 1967 there was no discussion of the entire evidence and, secondly, there was rejection of the evidence on behalf of the appellant on consideration that the appellant 's witnesses belonged to particular castes and sects. The appellant also relied on the oral evidence of Shamshad Elahi P.W. 18 said that there was a meeting on 6 February, 1968 at the Town Hall Maidan, Hapur. The High Court rejected the election petition holding that no meeting was held in support of respondent Shastri 's case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf on behalf the appellant that (1) the publication Exhibit 22 was an instance of corrupt practice and (2) there was an allegation that the supporters of Prakash Vir Shastri were alleged to have chased the appellant and threatened his workers. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The publication Exhibit 23 is an appeal on behalf o the appellant. [797C] 2.1 The publication in the newspaper named 'Vir Arjun' does not mention or refer at all to any meeting on behalfof respondent Prakash Vir Acharya. The allegation that there were no discussion on the entire material and, thirdly, the reports did not mention the name of the petitioner as having been assaulted or chased and fourthly, the news item in the Patriot was not proved as to the truth of the contents therein. [897C D] 2:2 The publication does not refer at any meeting any meeting held by respondent Prakashvir Shastri on 7 Feb, 1967 or in the Hindustan dated 8 February,1967 at the town Hall Majan, Meerut. [8897D] 3.1 In the present case, annexure KK has not been established to be published with the consent of the respondent Prakash Chand. The alleged incident at Chhajjupur is unacceptable because, first there was nothing in the news report to show that the members of Prakash Singh Vir Shastri and his 899 supporters were allegedto have chased him. [997C E] 3:2 In the instant case, the publication does no mention or reference at all either in the Vir Arjun of 8 February 1967 or at all. The allegations are that on 2 February, 2021 an election meeting was organised in support thereof and the appellant was denied the opportunity of meeting that case. [1097C G] 3 :3 In the absence of any allegation by the appellant to the Election Commissioner, secondly there was neither any police case nor no investigation, thirdly or the reports do not mention even the name or names of the parties as havingbeen assaulted or apprehended and fourthly. the news items in the LIBERTYot was published with consent of respondent Prakash Singh. [1006C D; 1097A] 4. The newspaper publication Exhibit 21 is an election petition filed by the respondent. It does not contain any allegation that respondent Prakash had committed any corrupt practice in relation to personal character and conduct of the appellants. The news item does not disclose or refer to any meetings on behalf or of respondentPrakash Vir Shastri. [1016C E; 1098A] 5. In the circumstances, there is no evidence that the incident at Chajjuapur was a result of the influence of respondent Parkash Vir Shastri or his election agent. [1106B] 6. The printed news item did not contain the name and address of the rival contentions, namely, whether the Jatav voters would be allowed to vote and the supporters were allegedly assaulted or convicted.

The appellant, who was the auction purchaser for delivery of possession of the property auctioned by him was resisted by the respondents. The trial court held that in view of Article 136 of the .the Limitation Act, 1963, Article 136 will apply and not Article 134 of the Limitation Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sale became absolute after the sale was confirmed, as provided in clause (b) of Explanation II to section 47 read with Article 136, and that even though the application for setting aside the sale on the ground of fraud was made after the disposal of such application, the sale becomes absolute after its disposal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The sale became complete only under the circumstances as mentioned in Rule 92, and therefore, the period of limitation prescribed by Article 136 would be computed from the date of the order disallowing the application to set aside the auction on the grounds of fraud and not from the dale of sale. [620 E] 2. The amendment of section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure by Section 20 of the Act is a complete code in itself, and it cannot be said that the application was within the period prescribed by article 136 of .the . [621 G H] 3. The application for delivery must be made before the sale become absolute after disposal of the application on July 21, 1979, and by virtue of clause (a) of proviso to section47 read with article 136, an application for set aside sale can also be made within a period of 12 years from thedate of the decree irrespective of the date when the sale is confirmed. [721 E] 4. The provisions of Rule 92 of Order XXI of the Civil Procedure Code are not exhaustive and they cannot be construed to have any retrospective effect. [822 D] 5. The provision of Explanation I1 of section47 of the old Limitation Act would apply only in respect of an application under Order XXI Rule 95, and not in respect o f a decree. [921 E F] 6. If an application is made within one year of the dismissal of the second application for execution of a decree, an order for settingaside the sale can be passed and the period provided by Article 134 will apply. The period of Limitation as prescribed by clause (c) of Rule 95 cannot be computedfrom the date on which the first confirmation was confirmed. It is submitted that even if the application is not one as contemplated by Rules 89, 90 or 91 of Order 21 of the C.P.C., the sale would become absolute only after the completion of the period for limitation as prescribed under Article 136. [1021 E G] 7. The Full Bench took the view that the period o f 12 years mentioned in clause(c) to section 48 read with Rule 92 will be computed From the date fixed for delivery, which is absurd on the face of it. [1122 D E] 8. In view of the discussion made above, we are unable to accept the contention made on behalf by the respondent decree holder that the order for delivery was quite within the time prescribed by Articles 136 and 137 of the , Limitation Act cannot be equated with an application to setting aside sale on grounds other than those mentioned in the said Rules. [1222 E] 9. The learned District Judge took a similar view that even after the insertion of ExplanationII to section 50 read with section 47, an applicant for setting up a new auction purchaser can file an application before the Court within the prescribed period of one year from the expiry of 12 months from the dismissal o f the second or confirmation. [1322 E F; 1323 A] 10.

The appellant 's election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattancherry Constituency No. P 14 was declared void on the ground that the said wall poster was pasted on a wall at the instance and with the consent of the appellant ' s election agent. The appellant filed an Election Petition under section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act') for setting aside the election of the respondent No. 1 to the Legislative Assembly. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the publication by a candidate or his agent was not defamatory or that it is then true of the plaintiff. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the printing of exhibit P 1 was intended to create an impression and did create an believe and did creating an impression that the incident of murders had taken place a day prior to the election, and that it did so. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The contents of this wall poster directly named the first respondent as the murderer of the four victims, and if it is proved that the words complained of were reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospects of the election the appellant would be entitled to know that meaning of the statement on which the plaintiff relies so that he is able to argue either that the statement in that meaning is not defamatory. [776F] (2) The publication by the candidate or their agent or by any other person with the knowledge and consent of a candidate, being a statement reasonably calculated To prejudice the prospectus of the defamed candidate 's Election, it may be necessary to prove that the statements on which he relies so far as they relate to the personal character or conduct of any candidate or in relation to the candidature or election are concerned. [771A] (3) The printing by a person or his election agent of any statement of fact which is false and which he either believes to be false or does not believe to be true, in relation thereto, it might not be necessary for him to prove such facts, for the defendant is entitled to have know that meanings of the statements complained of in a defama tory sense in an election action, it can not be possible to do so and all that is necessary is to prove whether the words spoken of are reasonably calculated or to prejudice his prospects. [ 771B] (4) The mere fact that he had taken the photographs in question on 25th and 26th March, 1987 but at a much later date and just prior to that filing of the present election petition would not support the case that the newspaper was affixed prior to or after the election. [782A B] (5) The statement in exhibit P1 being pasted near the wall poster together with exhibit P I being pasted on one week prior to election, it is difficult to understand as to how this witness could have seen the actual pasting of exhibit p 1 being pasted at the place where he had allegedly taken the photograph in question.

The respondent No. 5 submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay for the construction of a five star hotel. The Municipal Corporation, however, rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said land under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the respondent No 5 filed an appeal before the Minister of State for Urban Development, the Respondent No. 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner and directed 924 sanction of the revised development plan to be submitted by the respondent NO. 5. The respondent No 1 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the resolution on the ground that the property was proposed for earmarking the said plot under reference, as a recreation ground with adequate internal network. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Municipal Commissioner had not taken into account the relevant factors and had rejected the application for approval of the draft revised development plans submitted by respondent No 4. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The impugned order of exemption granted to the respondent Nos. 5 and 6 is quashed. [929G] 2.2 The Municipal Commissioner would be entitled to rely upon the same in rejecting the plan submitted by Respondent No 5 and conditioned by the Respondent NO. 1. [1030B] 3. In the circumstances, there is no merit in this appeal challenging the order granting exemption to the respondents No. 4 and 6. [729G H] 4.1 There is, therefore, no substance in the appeal challenging that part of the impugned order. The question whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved for park and recreation ground has been adequately considered and taken into consideration by the High court. [830B C] 5.2 In the instant case, however at the time the Municipal Council had prepared the draft modified development plan in accordance with the direction of the respondent no. 2 sanctioning the development plans, the Municipal Commissioners were not justified in rejecting it on the grounds that there was a proposal for revision of draft development plan or that such a revision is under contemplation. [820C] 5 3.3 The Municipal Council which is the Planning Authority, had prepared and published on April 30, 1984 a draft revised Development Plan. The plan submitted before this Court by respondent no 5 and undertook by respondent NO 1 to prepare a draft modified Development plan in conformity with the directions of the Municipal council, was not published and the plan filed by the respondents no. 4 to 6 and conditioned upon by the Municipal corporation, which is a Planning Authority. [829G] 5 4.4 The Municipal Committee had prepared revised development Plan on April 29, 1984 and thereafter submitted the draft Development Plan for approval before the respondent Council. It was not open to the petitioners to challenge the order passed by the Council on April 31, 1984. [828D] 5 5.5 In the absence of any material, it will be improper to reject the plan after considering the application of the respondents for grant of exemption to them. There is no substance also in this Appeal challenging the legality or otherwise of the order allowing exemption to respondent No 2. The petitioners are only interested in seeing that sufficient area is kept reserved and taken for a park or recreation ground for the benefit of the members of the public. They are not, in our opinion, concerned with the question as to the legality and otherwise of whether or otherwise sufficient quantity is kept reserve for a playground or recreation grounds for the benefits of the member of the community. They were not, therefore not, entitled to challenge that order on the basis of the validity or otherwise.

The appellant union was a registered trade union. The workmen were employed by the employer for short) under an agreement dated April 8, 1980. On the basis of the said agreement the employer terminated the services of the workmen on the ground that they had committed unfair labour practice. The Industrial Court held that the employers were guilty of imposing and continuing a lock out as provided in Item 6 of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971 (Act ' for short). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant union that the employer had committed an unfair labour practices by imposing and terminating a lockout or has closed down the business. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Industrial court while rejecting the complaints filed by the appellant Union which does not command to us and to avoid any such error being repeated in future, must consider all the relevant circumstances at the time of closure decide and determine whether the employer is guilty of unfair labour Practice. [67 H] 2.2 The correct approach ought to be that when it is claimed that the workmen have committed an illegal lock out or has closing down the industrial activity, the Industrial Court before which the action of the employer was questioned must keep in view all the irrelevant circumstances at that time of the closure and decide whether the closure was a device or a pretence to determine 69 the services. [68 E] 2:3 The true test is that when the employer has resorted to closure, bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activities he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a deviceor a pretence. [69 F] 3.1 In case of a lock-out the employer refuses to continue. to employ workmen. The duration of the closing down of the industrial undertaking is normally a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employers at the relevant time. To accept the view taken by the Industrial court would lead to a startling result in that an employer who has resorted, bonafide needs to re opened, revive or re start his industrial activity he can neither do so nor has closed the industrial establishment it is necessary to approach the matter from this angle that the closing off of the business itself permanent and irrevocable. [70 E] 3:3 In case where it is alleged that the employee has resorted a closure bonafide wants then revival and re started the industrial enterprise, the industrial court before which an action of employer is questioned must keeping in view the relevant facts at the stage of closure deciding and determine if the closure is a device, or pretence to decide whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employee. [71 E] 4.2 In case it is contended that the employees have imposed a lock Out or has not closed down their industrial activity and that as resumption of production was gradually expanded, the old workmen will be re inducted in service. The mere fact that the business activity was not closed cannot be a ground to hold that the new workmen are being re inducted into service and that the lockout is necessarily temporary or for a period. [72 F] 4:3 There is no evidence on record to show that the workers had committed any unfair labour Practices by imposing or continuing alock out which under the law was illegal. The employer has failed to prove that the old employees were being re employed. In such a situation there is only closure of the factory itself permanent, irrevocable and permanent and that lockout was necessarily temporary and for a duration. [73 E] 5.4 The true criterion is that if it is shown that the workman had resorted to the closure, fide wants to continue, revive, and re commence the industrial process he can be not guilty of imposition or continuing an lock out but has closed his industrial undertaking.

The assessee company was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company. The objects of which are set out in el. III of the memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cl. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that clause. The Memorandum of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but the case of the assessee company all along in the past was that it was a dealer in shares, securities and immovable properties and that it incurred losses or made profits and losses arising from sale of shares, security and immovable property of the Loyal Mills. The Income Tax Officer held that the assessee Company was a "dealer" within the meaning of section 66(1) of the Act and dismissed the appeals. On appeal by the assessee to the Appellate Tribunal under section 66 (2), the High Court held that in the case it was not a dealer, the assessee was a 'dealer' within the definition of section 2(15) of that Act and therefore the profits and gains arising from the sale of share, securities or immovable properties of the company could be taxed as business profits. The Appellate Tribunal also held that there was material on the record to support the finding of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner that the appellant company was a trader in shares and securities and that the question as to whether it incurred loss or made profit and losses arose from sale, of shares and security properties of E.D. It further held that even if the assessee had claimed to be a dealer under section 2 (15) the profits or losses arising out of the sale transactions were taxable as business income. The High Court also held in favour of the appellant. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question as regards whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the assessee could be termed a dealer or an investor was itself a question of pure fact but was a mixed question of fact and law. [520B] 2.2 The question is not a question which can be answered by the Tribunal in reaching its decision on the point; but it is because the question involved in this case was not one of pure question of mixed fact and Law, that this Court allowed the appeal on the last occasion and set aside the judgment of the Bombay High Court dated June 15, 1952. [620C] 3.3 The question whether the profits & losses arising therefrom are questions of fact but were a mixed questions of law and facts and what was the legal effect of the facts found by the Appellate tribunal can be challenged on a ground of law. It is because of the existence of some mistake or inadvertence the actual questions framed by this Court seem to assume that the questions framed are questions which of fact could not be answered in view of section 65(1). [621B] 4.4 The question involved was a pure question and mixed question, of fact & law. That question was a question Of pure fact and it was therefore a question whether this Court permitted the appeal to be disposed of by the High court on the ground that the enquiry made by the Income Tax officer was not competent on the questions as framed by the appellant in its .petition under section 65 (1) because it was an error or inadvertence. [721C] 5.5 The question referred to the High Courts is a mixed one of fact, and law and that this question was decided against the assessee. It was therefore expedient in the interest of justice that the Appellate Court should be asked to make a fresh statement of the Case on the aforesaid questions of facts. [821B C] 6.6 The question framed by it seem to assumed that the relevant legal principles have been mis applied by the appellate Tribunal in arriving at its finding on the question.

The appellant was appointed to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. He was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On October 1, 1953, the appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954, on the grounds that (i) the enquiry into the conduct of Government servants on a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above in respect of matters involving corruption on the part of such Government servants in the discharge of their official duties and (ii) that the proceedings of the High Court were without jurisdiction, and secondly, that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the constitution. The appellant contended that (1) the order passed by the High court on January 28 1954, was not one of dismissal or removal from service within article 311(2), and (2) the Government was bound to hold a fresh enquiry and decide for itself whether the charges were well founded. Held, that in view of the provisions of rule 4 of the Madras Civil Services (Classification Control and Appeal) Rules, 1953 it was only a Tribunal constituted as provided in Rule 4 (1)(a), which could enquire into the charges, and that the Government could dismiss or remove him from service, and such an order is neither one of dismissing removal from Service within article 310 of the Code. The order passed on January 13, 1954 is merely one of suspension pending enquiry into grave charges under rule 17(e) against the Members of the State Judicial Service.

The appellant company was a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company. The liability to pay tax on the dividend so deemed to be distributed is of the shareholder, and not of the legal representative. The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant 's income in respect of those years. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the assessment order. The Appellate Assistant Commission confirmed the assessment but reduced the amount of refund from Rs. 1,000 to Rs. 2,000. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not liable to pay any tax on receipts by the legal representatives after his death in that previous year became assessable to income tax in the relevant assessment year and therefore the claim of the Income tax officer to make an assessment under section 23(4) must fail. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The expression "assessee" in section 2(2) as substituted by the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act 25 of 1953 with effect from April 1, 1952, means a person by whom income tax is payable and not any other person by whose estate income tax was payable. [523 C] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City I vs Amarchand Shroff, , followed. The expression 'assessee " in section 24B does not include a person who dies, his executor, administrator or other legal representative shall be liable to tax under the Act if he had not died. [624 D] In construing that expression the expression "person by whom Income Tax is payable" cannot be deemed to have supplied the machinery for taxation of income received by a legal representative which would have been payable if such person had not expired. The Legislature has not provided that the income received before death of the deceased, is to be regarded as extended to the end of the year in which such notional income must be deemed as having been received by the deceased person and therefore he could still be taxed as his income. [643 E] Commissioner Of Income tax Bombay City 1 vs Amar Chand Shroff, ; , followed; Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay city I vsAmarchand Shroff & Company, Bombay, ; referred to.

The appellant was a Ruler of the State of Baster. He was a permanent Ruler and an absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. The appellant was the Ruler of a State. On the basis of the evidence led by him, the High Court held that the villages mentioned in Schedules C and D were not assessed to land revenue but no evidence had been led to this effect. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was an ex Ruler and therefore a Ruler could not conceivably be a maufidar. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The definition of 'maufidar ' in section 2(m) of the Act has no application to a Ruler or to a private property of a Ruler which is not assessed as such by the President as the successor of such Ruler. [505B] In the instant case, the appellant had given no evidence to establish that the village in question was not assessed or assessed to lands revenue but only some evidence had led to it. The High Court rightly held that even if he was regarded as a mahafidar it was not entered in the wajib ul arz with respect to any of his maufi villages that he had a right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such village. [605B C] In view of the clear language of article 366(22) of Constitution, the definition of the word 'proprietor ' in the Act does not apply to a person who by or under the provisions contained in the Wajibul arz applicable to his village held by him it was for the appellant to establish whether he had any right to receive rent or Revenue from persons having holding land on such villages. [504D] In order to determine whether a Ruler is an ex- Ruler, it must be shown that with reference to any village held in such villages, the person who for the time being is recognised by the Government as the successors of such holder as the Ruler. The effect of the Merger Agreement is clearly one by which factually a Ruler ceased to be a Ruler but for the purposes of the constitution and for the purpose of the privy purse guaranteed, he is a mahaufter.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. The respondent submitted that he had been served at Shillong for a longer period, having been allowed to continue at Shillong. He submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. tie complained that some other officials who have been serving at Shillong have been allowed/ continued at Shillong and that they are posted at different places. The Administrative Tribunal quashed the order of transfer on the following reasoning: (1) The guidelines contained therein do not permit the posting of both at one place without sacrifice of the requirements of the administration and needs of other employees; (2) The administrative authorities do not consider it feasible. They can only consider this aspect along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the transfer policy does not permit posting of either at one location without sacrifice or the requirement of other employee; (3) The Administrative Tribunals are not Appellate Authorities sitting in judgment over the orders of transfer. In this case the Tribunal did say so merely because certain guidelines issued by the Central Government are not followed, with which finding we shall deal later. Who should be transferred where, is a matter for the appropriate authority to decide. Unless the order is vitiated by malafides or is made in violation of any statutory provisions, the Court cannot interfere with it. While ordering the transfer, there is no doubt, the authority must keep in mind the guidelines issued on the subject. Similarly if a person makes any representation with respect to his transfer, the appropriate authorities must consider the same having regard to the exigencies and transfer policy do not allow the posting Of both at two places without sacrifice; (4) If such an order is questioned in a Court or Tribunal only where it is passed malafide or where it has been made in contravention of any statute, the court cannot interfere With the order o transfer. There is no dispute that the respondent was posted at Shillong as far as practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do neither consider it advisable nor allow the post of right; (5) The Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order passed by transfer. The order of the Tribunal reads as if it was sitting in appeal over the order dated 3rd April, 1986. The Tribunal does not say that the Court or the Tribunal can quash the order if any of the administrative instructions/guidelines are not adhered to; much less can it be charactrised as malafide for that reason. To reiterate, the order impugned is vitiated because some guidelines issued are not strictly followed, much less could it beCharactrising as malafide. The only thing required is that the departmental authority should consider this issue along with exigencies of administrative needs & transfer policy doing not permit any spouse thereto; (6) If the administrative authorities does not consider this factor along with other employees, the question of posting of two spouses cannot be transferred to the place of the other 's posting. After giving preference to the career prospects by accepting such a promotion or any appointment in an all India service with the incident of transfer to any place in India, subordinating the need of the others employee cannot be challenged in a court or Tribunal merely where it being possible without detriment to his administrative needs; (7) The Court or Administrative Tribunal can interfere with the orders passed by the authorities if it passed malafide and where it was made in breach of the statutory provisions.

The conviction and sentence of the appellants under Section 302 read with reference:The prosecution case was that Al, A2, A4, A5 armed with sticks, A6 armed with aruval (bill hook) and A6 along with A3 armed with stick (spear stick), attacked Jawahar at about 8.30 A.M. on January 2,8, 1977 and caused him multiple injuries as a result of which he died on the same day. The third charge related to rioting wherein A1, A3, A 6 armed with vel stick (bil hook), attacked Manali @ Velladurai, Karuppaiah, Nagasundaram and four others were acquitted by the learned Trial Judge. On appeal the High Court set aside the conviction and sentences of the accused persons under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34, I.P.C. and convicted them under Sections 147 and 148 I. P.C., read with section 149, I P. C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder. The High Court while setting aside the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect. of A1to A3 was found guilty under Section304 Part I, IP. C., readwith Section 34 I.p.C and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. This appeal by special leave is against the judgment of the High court. The appellants have been convicted under Section 307 read with [Section 34], I.A.2, I, P.c. and were sentenced to undergo imprisonment already undergone by them. The prosecution case is that Al was a member of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly. He was convicted under Sections 302 readwith section 34, IPC for instigation A1 and A3. The appeal by A1 was dismissed by the High Curt. The State has filed this appeal against the order of acquittal passed by the Trial Court. It is contended on behalf of the appellant that the participation of the appel lants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar had been proved beyond doubt. It was further submitted that keeping in view the nature of injuries on the person of the deceased and the facts and circumstances of this case the 3 offence committed by them came within the mischief of Section 325 read with 34,I.P.,C. read with Sec tion 34, Cr. P C. and as such the offence committed was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The learned counsel for the appellants submitted that the presence of A2 in the incident which resulted into his death was established beyond doubt and therefore the conviction under Section 325 Part I is liable to be set aside. It has been further contended that keeping the nature and circumstances o f the case the three offences committed by the appellants came within th mischief of section 325 readwith 34, C.P..C. as well as Section 325, I PC.C, read with Sections 34, and 149, IPC. The other charge under Section 324 read with sections 34, i.e., attempt to commit murder was proved beyond all reasonable doubt and the appellants were convicted under section 304 Part II read with s ection 34, Indian Penal Code read with sec tion 34 I P,C. for abetting A1. It had been further submitted on behalf o the appellant State that keeping this in view of the nature o f offence committed against Section 325 I.PC., Thirteen external in juries were found on the dead body of Jawahar and assuch the offence was not attracted under section 325, IPC read with Sect ion 34, Code, and therefore, the conviction of the Appellants under Section 326 Part I cannot be sustained.

The Banking Companies Act, 1949 was enacted by the British Parliament to protect the British economic interests and for matters connected therewith. The Banking Companies (Acquisition) Act, 1970 was passed in the year 1969. Section 4(e) of the Act provides that the expression `special Indian law ' shall include any law made by an Indian Legislature or Legislature of a State. Section 3(27)(a) of that Act defines `special law' to mean a law made under the Constitution and not by any other law for India. The appellant Bank was constituted under the Ordinance VIII of 1969 and not under the Banking Companies ' Act, 1948. It is submitted on behalf of the Bank that as the words `any special Indian law " refer or relates to a law enacted by an Act of Parliament or Legislature, it must be held in view of the setting that the expressions `specialIndian law ' refers or relate to a special law enacted under the Constitutional Scheme of the 1953 Government of India Act. It was submitted on their behalf that as a corporation has been formed by or under a special Indian Law and not in pursuance of any `special laws, it will not come within the purview of section 4(a) (i) of The Banking companies Act, 1951. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 4 of the Banking Corporations Act is a special code enacted by Parliament for India and not as an enactment of Parliament. [969H; 969A] 2.2 The words `in pursuance of ' and the words 'any specialIndian law or Royal Charter or Letters Patent ' are offensive to Article 14 of the Constitution. It will be highly unreasonable and illogical to think that as an Act may apply to a corporation which is the creature of a specialIndian Law, it would not come under the purview Of section 4 (e)of the Act. [ 969B] 3.1 The words 'in pursuance or ' in section 4 of The Act are placed after the words "any special law" refers and relates to any law enacted in that behalf by an act of Parliamentor Legislature. It would be highly unfair and illogical if not, it can never but be held to have become void as making invidious discrimination in favour of corporations created or constituted by any special Indian laws which, in the instant case, is the Banking companies (Acquisition and Transfer) Act. No other point has been urged by either party in this appeal. [969C] 3:2 The expression `any Special Indian law' refers and pertains to a legislation made by the Indian Legislature and not to a statute enacted by any Legislature of our country. [970D] 4.3 Section 4 (a) is applicable to a banking company which is an autonomous body under the Central Act. The words "in pursuance" in section 3(e)(i) are placed before the words ''any special foreign law '" refer or relate only to a general Indian law, but not to any other special Indian statute which, by using the expression 'special Indian Law ' refers and is related to a particular law. [971G] 4:4 The words of `in pursuant of ' or under ', but by using ' the expression "by or under" in Section 4 are placed on the same footing as making a discrimination in respect of corporations formed or created by any Special Indian Law which, according to the setting, is offensive to Articles 14 and 15 of the constitution. [973G] 5.4 The provisions of section 3 (27)(b) of Act are not applicable to the appellant Bank and, therefore, there is no question of scaling down the debt due to the Bank by the respondents. [974C D] 6.5 Section 4 does not refer to any special law made or by the Provincial Legislature.

The petitioners were manufacturing sugar in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The price fixed by the Government was Rs. 1,000 per quintal and the petitioners were entitled to fix ex factory prices at the rate of Rs. 2,000 for each of these three regions. The petitioners contended that the impugned notification is violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it imposes an unreasonable restriction on the right to trade under Article 19 (1) (g), inasmuch as the Act and the Order do not authorise the Central Government to fix the price arbitrarily, and (2) the impugned Notification merely fixes ex factory price. The High Court held that the fixation of ex factory rates is bad as it fails to provide for a fair price for the ultimate consumer which must be done under the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the notification fixing ex factory Price at Rs. 3,000 was not violative of Article 19(1) and (g) inasmuch as there was no commitment in this press note by the Central Govt., that if prices are fixed for factories only in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar, in effect they would fix prices separately so far as factories in other States which are said to be mainly deficit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned notification merely fixes the ex factory rate and is bad, firstly on the ground that it compels factories to sell sugar at a loss, (ii) it fixes the wholesale or retail price. [135 E] 2. It does not follow from this that if fair prices for the factories in the other areas are fixed, there is no reason why the Government should go on further to fix wholesale and retail prices. There is, therefore, in our opinion no discrimination after the control of sugar 136 prices in these three region and the contention that the factories were left uncontrolled with the result that there was discrimination after they fixed prices below that level or even below the level at which they were at the end of May, 1958, cannot be accepted. [136 F] 3. The object of the Act is to secure equitable distribution of the commodity to the consumer at a fair value; but if fair price is fixed in this area, it is not necessary to fix prices differently far as factory in other areas is concerned. It is said that the press note issued by the State Government on July 30, 1958 shows that the Government has gone on to fix rates separately so long as the price is controlled in Punjab and North Bengal. [137 G] 4. The contention that there is discrimination in effect by the fixation fixed by it on July 31, 1958 and that there are no reasonable basis for such clasSification cannot be sustained. [138 E F] 5. There was, however, no commitment made in this Press note by Government that if they intervened they would fixing prices separately So far as Factories in other parts of India are concerned, once the production of these two regions is controlled, there can only be achieved if retail price is fix and that it is also not necessary for fixing wholesale or wholesale price. There are, therefore in our view no discrimination by the fixing of prices at any price is permissible after the Control of sugar in, this country. [139 G] 6. The question whether the impugned order is violative Of article 14 is a matter which can be determined only on the basis of the economic factors which control the price of sugar. [140 C] 7. There cannot be discrimination without the control or supervision of sugar and commerce in these two areas and the contentions that there has been discrimination after this control of Sugar in, the other regions are left uncontrolled.

The Company was a registered trade union. The workmen of the Company were employed in the factory of the company. On April 26, 1951, the previous award made by the Tribunal between the same parties on April 26 and 1951, had not been terminated in accordance with the provisions of section 19(6) of the Act and therefore the present reference was bad in law. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the working class cost of living index stood at 344.1 in August 1954 up to March 1957. On appeal by the Union before this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the award dated June 21, 1951 was not terminated under section 19 (6) and therefore there was no question of the reference being made to the Labour Appellate tribunal constituted under section 7A of the Amending Act. HELD: The Tribunal wrongly relied upon Exhibit 3, corrected on the basis of the information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal for ascertaining the working classes cost of labour index since August 1954 upto March 1957 up to march 1957. [696 B] In regard to matters covered by it, the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore, the date of the agreement is the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the workingclass cost of live index by dearness allowance could not be permitted and therefore allowed them only 75 per cent. of the increase in the dearness allowance to which they would have otherwise been entitled on the ground that there was a rise of 56 points, a substantial rise in the cost of lived index by Dearness Allowance could not possibly be permitted. [796 C] The Tribunal rightly relied upon the document Exhibit 3 and corrected on that basis. [897 F] In the instant case, the Tribunal wrongly held that there had been a fall in the rate of working class costs of living Index by dearness allowances could not therefore be permitted to be challenged under section 33B.

The appellant was a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The said management continued as before and the fact that an Executive Officer had been appointed under the scheme made no difference to the actual administration of the Mutt. It was no doubt urged before the learned Judge that the appellant 's writ petition should not be entertained because he had a definite adequate alternative remedy under the latter Act, but this plea was rejected by the Division Bench with the observation that where the fundamental right is clearly infringed, it is the duty of the Court to interfere in favour of the citizen, unless there are reasons of policy which make it inexpedient to do so. The appellant contended that since the scheme had been framed as early as 1939 under the relevant provisions of the earlier Act, he must be modified so as to make them consistent with the said provisions. Held, further, that the scheme having been framed and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed in courts of law. It is true that section 103(d) provides that a scheme settled or modified under the provisions of this latter Act shall be deemed to have been settled or modify under &a former Act; but the effect of this provision merely is to make the schemes in question operative as though they were framed under the said Act without examining whether all the provisions are necessarily justified by, or consistent with. the provisions. It would thus be clear that when the scheme was framed and an appeal made against it to its legality failed in court of law, his property rights had been taken away. Sastri 's argument is right, because the deprivation of his property right is taking place for the first time in 1952 and as such, it was open to the appellant, to challenge the validity of the scheme by legal proceedings and partly because he has otherwise obstructed the said implementation.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in the school on July 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986 save for misconduct or. . The appellant continues to serve as Hindi teacher in the School under the orders of the Managing Committee yet his appointment after 1986 has not been approved by the educational authorities. The appellant continued to work as such teachers with repeated spell of 89 days appointments and two day break between the periods till May 26, 1986 except for misconduct and. . . . The State of Orissa filed a writ petition before the High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi Teachers with effect from July 12 ,1982. The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation on the ground that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Validation Act because his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. The State Government preferred an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court erred in denying the benefit to the appellant on the grounds that his initial appointments for 89 day were conditioned by condition that he will continue until replace by a person from the selected list. [912D] 2.1 Section 3 of the Validating Act does not arise because of the vice of discrimination. It is only when the State Government takes a decision that it decides to regularise the services of any particular employee, that the question of issuing any direction to regularise his service in a substantive vacancy does not arises. [1012E] 2:2 The High Courts erred in holding that the appointment by the managing authority of the School on ad hoc basis must be on or after the 1st December, 1976 but not later than 31st December 1984. [1113F] 3.1 In response to the notice issued in the Special Leave Petition the managing Committee through its Secretary cum Head Master has stated that the teachers have been appointed regularly and they would have been entitled to salary and allowances for the period of summer vacations and other breaks which must be taken as non est, from the date of his regular appointment i.e. 31st March, 1984 save for offence or misconduct or otherwise. [1213F G] 3:2 In response, the notice was issued in Special Leave petition the managing committees through its secretary cum Head master has stated in their reply that the appellants are still continuing to serve in the schools under the order of the management for almost 4 years with short breaks and in the process denying them their rightful dues and other service benefits. The case of the appellant is, thus fully covered by Section 3(1) of the validation Act. [1313F D] 3 :3 In response thereto the managingcommittee through its Chairman cum Headmaster has stated, that they are still utilising his services though there is no approval by the Educational authorities for the periods subsequent to 1986. The contention of the appellants is, therefore fully covered in Section 3 (1) and the High court rightly held that the case of appellant is fully covered under Section 3. [1413F E] 4.

The appellant was elected as a member of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being a candidate was based on Rules 3 to 7 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads, Non official Members (Payment of Allowances) Rules, 1965. The respondent filed an election petition under section 100(1)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the election of the appellant. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that the allowances paid under rules 3 to 6 of the Rules did not convert the office of Chairman of a panchayat Samiti into an office of profit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under r. 3 to7 made the office an office which was outside the district, including attending of meeting, supervision of plans, projects, schemes and other works and also for 'the discharge of all lawful obligations and implementation of Government directives; (1) that the Chairman must be making gain out of the payment to him of daily allowance; (2) that in view of the provisions contained in rule 7(b), the Vice Chairman and Member must not be entitled to mileage allowance under clause (b) unless the journey for such work or supervision has been approved by the Panchayat Samiti or Zila Parishad, as the case may be, and the number of Members deputed for supervision does not exceed five on any one day; (3) that there was no evidence from which an inference could be drawn that out of expenditure received by a Chairman for travelling allowance or daily allowance is in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have to incur for 'he purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : 1.1 The appellant has failed to establish that out o the amount received as daily allowance the Chairman will in fact make a sense of profit; (4) that out Of the amount paid as daily allowances the Chairman would in fact be making profit out of such payment and out of pocket expenses of the Chairman, he will in himself be entitled for mileage allowances. [723B] 1.2 The appellant failed to prove that outo pocket expenses were in excess than what was received by him; (5) that he had been made gain out from the payment made to him by the Chairman for traveling allowance or Daily allowance, and that there is no question of any disqualification arising under rs. 3(1) of section 7 of Act. [823C] 1:3 The appellant was not entitled to claim mileage Allowance under r 8 of the rules because in his case he had failed to show that outof the amount receipts received as Daily allowance were in addition to the payment for travelling allowances and daily allowances under r, 3 to 9 made the Office an office o profit; and (6) that even if the payment was made at a higher rate to the Chairman of Panchayat Samiti an office not of profit, it cannot be held that this payment would result in gain so as to make the office profit. [923D] 1 :4 The appellant had failed in establishing that out from his own pocket expenses he would in himself make gain out the payment and therefore, there is a question of disqualification arising on account of any pecuniary gain to a Chairman of the Panchayat Samitis or Zila Parishads as the nature of the work done by him does not warrant such a conclusion. [1023C D] 1.:5 The appellant having failed to established that out-of the sum received as monthly allowance the respondent would in itself make gainout of the payments made to the appellant of daily allowances, he cannot be allowed to claim any mileage or allowance for journeys performed by him outside the District.

The appellant was tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The respondents filed an eviction suit against the appellant for eviction on the ground that the partition wall did not constitute material alteration as the construction had been made with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin shed marked with letters CDGH had been constructed by the appellant with the permission of the former landlord. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal, the High Court set aside the judgment and decree of the first appellate court and decreed the eviction suit. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that the tin sheds marked by letters ABHG had been erected by the respondents without consent, which materially altered the accommodation and on that findings the trial court decree decreed the plaintiff 's suit for eviction without obtaining permission of District Magistrate but the second appeal was allowed by the High court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The construction of a partition wall does not provide a ground for eviction; instead the constructions complained of, must be of such nature and character as to materially alter the accommodation. [77 A C] 1.2 The construction carried out by a tenant in the building does not give rise to any damage to the accommodation, it being temporary in nature, did not affect the question as to whether the constructions materially alter or not. [78 E F] 1:3 The character of the constructions and the extent to which they make changes in the front and structure of the accommodation is a relevant consideration in determining the question of 'material alteration '. The nature of construction and the effect of altering the front or structure of a building does no affect the questions as to what material alterations mean, as such, the alteration must beof such nature as to substantially alter the structure. [79 E] 1.:4 In determining the questions of ' Material alteration ' the Court must address itself to the nature, character of construction carried on by the tenant. The essential element which needs consideration is as to when the construction has been made, and if so, whether the construction materially altered or not, whether such constructions are sub stantial in nature and they alter, the form, front and structures of the building. [80 E] 2.1 In determining whether the structure materially alter a building is a material alteration, it must mean material alteration. The character, character, of the construction and extent towhich they make alterations in the accommodation must be considered in determining whether such changes are necessary for effecting any change in the form or structure. If so, how, whether those constructions are permanent or temporary, is a matter which can be determined by the Court. [81 E] 3.2 In deciding this question the Court has to address itself whether the structures materially alter,the form, rear and structureof the accommodation; having regard to the purpose for which the accommodation may have been let out to the tenant ; and if necessary whether such construction is of such substantial nature which make material alterations in it. [82 E] 4.3 The Court must consider whether the structural alterations made by a landlord in the shape of kitchen and bathroom do not materially alter that structure or not; and if such changes affect the character as To materially alter its structure, it is free to file suit for tenant 's eviction without seeking permission of Rent and Eviction Act. [83 E] 5.3 In determining this question, the Court should address itself on the nature of constructions and/or alteration made by an tenant in his building does neither affect the determination as to how the construction may have materially altered nor is it likely substantially to diminish its value substantial ly.

The respondent firm filed a suit against the appellant company for setting aside an ex parte decree passed in favour of the respondent firm on 22 4 1975. The Trial Court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975 about the passing of the ex parte order. The High Court allowed the revision, set aside the judgment of the Trial Court and upheld the exparte decree. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 2 is not an exhaustive provision providing for all modes of service on the defendant in the sense as to what is meant by service of summons on the Secretary, Director or Principal Officer in Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. and another vs The Union of India and others it was held that the words "Principal Officer" in clause (b) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. [723C] 1.2 Rule 2(a) is an exhaustive one providing for service of summon on natural persons. The meaning of clause (c) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the Code in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of notice on natural person. In Rule 17 of Order 5 it has been provided: "Where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or where the serving officer, after using all due diligence, cannot find the defendant, and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving Officer shall affix a copy of the notice on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain, 1032 and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued, with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the copy, the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed. It is not the case of the appellant that the service of such summons as effected in accordance with the first part of clause(b) was not due service on it itself. [823D] 1:3 Rule 2 has got no meaning because it is meant to issue and serve a summons by post to the registered office of the company. In rule 17 of order 5 it is provided that where the defendant resides or carried on business, or personally worked for gain , 1032, and shall thereafter return the duplicate copy to the court from which he was issued. It has been further provided: "(a) Where the defendant personally works on business in or personally work for gain; (b ) by leaving it or sending it by post addressed to the corporation at the registered Office or if there is any registered office then at the place where the corporation carries onbusiness or personally Work for gain. " [824E F] 1(a)(ii) The words " Principal Officer" occurring in Rule 2 of Order 29 of C.P.C. are not an inclusive provision providing that all modes, of service by summons on a secretary, Director, Principal Officer, Jute and Vanny Broker Ltd. shall include managing agent and it cannot be regarded as due service or on any other persons on whom the service can been made, The meaning in clause(c) is meant only for issue, and service or of summons to natural persons who are entitled to be served on their behalf. [820G] 1.(b)(ii).

The appellant was the owner of a land in dispute. The respondents filed a suit for possession of the land in question on the basis of a police report. The Magistrate passed an order on 17th July, 1978 declaring the appellant to be in possession of that land. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court set aside the order and remitted the case to the Magistrate. In the revision petition filed by the appellant, it was contended that as there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the final order that there was an apprehension of breach of peace existed at the time when the order was passed, therefore, the final orders were bad and the High court should not go into the sufficiency or otherwise of the materials on the ground that there had been a breach of the peace. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court in revision cannot go into an sufficiency orotherwise of the material which has satisfied the Magistrate regarding existence of a dispute likely to cause a breach or of the disturbance of the order under sub section (5) of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [723B] 2.1 In the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, would not go in the question of sufficiency of material which had satisfied the Court that there is an apprehension about breach of law existed and such a finding was implicit in thefinal order passed by the High Magistrate so it was not necessary for the Magistrate to repeat what he had said in the preliminary order. [823C] 2:2 The High court, in the exercise o its revisional power, would certainly not go to the question whether there was a breach on the part of the Magistrate or not. If the Magistrate has given a finding on this aspect of the matter also but in the circumstances as mentioned above, it can be safely presumed that apprehension of violation of peace exists and such an order is implicit in every final order. Once he records his satisfaction in the Preliminary order, the Magistrate would continue or exist. [923D] 3.1 The enquiry under section 145 is limited to the 95 question to which he was satisfied on these two conditions the section requires him to pass a preliminary order under subsection (5). If at the stage of passing the final judgment the apprehension of the breach of disturbance of peace is not necessary, then it is not possible that the Magistrate should give a finding again about the existence of such a dispute. [1023C D] 3:2 In the instant case, the enquiry under Section 145 was limited to only the 95 questions to which the satisfaction of the magistrate was based. The enquiry Under section 145 was confined to the 94 final order and not to the 96 question of adequacy of material. [1124E] 4.3 The Magistrate had no jurisdiction to mention in his final order any ground for holding that there existed a breach. [1223C E] 5.4 In the present case, it is well settled that under section 146(5) Cr. P.C., if a Magistrate finds that there exists a breach o the peace exists, he can proceed under section 144 Cr.P.C. and thereafter to make an enquiry under sub Section (1) and thereafter, to make a final order under section It is not essential that at the first stage of the proceedings the apprehension should continue or existed. The question of existence of breach on which the opinion of the police is based cannot be said to be a manifest defect so as to attract the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Courts under section 482 of Cr. Procedure Code. [1323D E] 6.5 In the facts and circumstances, it cannot be held that there has been an omission on the face of the record or that any prejudice was caused to any of the parties who had the full opportunity to produce their evidence before the Court.

The appellant was a resident of the State of Bombay. He was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, and was assessed by the Income Tax Officer on the basis of the assessment made by him. The Appellate Tribunal held that the transactions were benami for the purpose of section 14(2) (c), and that the profits had accrued to it both in the business and in the legal sense and that under these provisions, the appellant was liable to be taxed on such portions of the profits as were apportionable to the manufacture of the goods in British India. The Tribunal held against the assessee but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, the Revenue contended that the finding of the Commissioner was correct in law and that it was not open to review under section 66(1). Held: (i) The decision of this Court in Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co.(2) was not even so much as referred to in the (1) [1955] 1 S.C.R. 869, (ii)The question whether a finding on a question of law is open to appeal under section 64(1) or not must depend upon the true interpretation to be put on the agreement and that actually was a question which could be referred to the court under section 65(2). The decision in Commissioner Of Income tax vs Ahmedabhai Umarbhai & Co.(1) was, therefore, not even an authority for the proposition that sections 42 (1), 42(3) and 42(4) applied only to non residents and that section 42(5) applied both to residents as well as nonresidents. The decision was not a pure question of fact or mixed question of Law and fact. [776 H; 776 A] Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay City vs Ahmed Bhai Umarbhai, I.L.R., Bom. 892, referred to. (iii)The finding of fact on the application of the proper principles of law was a pure finding of facts and it could be reviewed under section66(1), even if it is not supported by any evidence or perverse but that where there is evidence to consider, I the decision of the Tribunal is final, its decision as to the legal effect of those findings cannot be challenged in a reference under section 67(1); (iv)The decision in Com Missione; of Income Tax vs Ahmedubhai Umarbhai was not therefore open to challenge on any of the grounds on which such a finding could be challenged.

The assessee was a partner in the firm of M/s. J.P. Vaish, a partner of the firm. The assessee claimed deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to the General Manager and the assessee claimed a deduction of the amount paid to Shri Vaish in excess of tiffs amount. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the amount of Rs,. 55,465 was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee and was wrongly disallowed by the Income tax Officer. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the commission paid by the assessee was not a capital receipt but was merely a fixed salary of Rs 1 lakh and therefore the commission payable to Shri J. P. Vaish was an allowable deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act. The Appellate Tribunal also rejected the view of the Appellate Tribunal that the rate of 121/2 % commission was reasonable and the allowance was accordingly restricted to half of the sum claimed by the appellant. On reference, the High Court held that in the circumstances of the case, the amount laid down or expended entirely for the purpoSe of business, profession or vocation as required under section10(2) (X.v) of Income Tax, 1922 was an expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for or for the purposes of the trade of the appellant and therefore it was rightly disallowed by that Tribunal. The High Court also held that there was no material on record to show that the alleged payment was not made by the employer in the past and that the assessee had taken over the mill at a time when it was old and dilapidated and in the first 14 months the mill made some profit. On further appeal, this Court, HELD : (1) The principle of commercial expediency for determining whether an expenditure is wholly or partly for the business purpose of carrying on business has to be adjudged from the point of view of businessman and not (2) [75 E] (a) In applying the test of commercial fairness for determining how an expenditure should be paid to an employee of the company, the nature of duties to be performed and the special aptitude of the employee, future prospects of extension by the business and a host of other related circumstances. [76 D] (b) The principles of this decision apply to the present case and it must accordingly be held that as in the present cases, both the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner and the Appellate tribunal rejected the contention of the Revenue that the sum of Rs., 75,464 paid to him was not laid out fully and exclusively towards the purpose for which the business was carried on, the entire amount of commission was laid out and expended wholly and solely for the benefit of the General manager for accomplishment of the task entrusted to him.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. On March 7, 1957, the appellant filed a fresh petition stating that he had not authorised Fateh Singh to enter into any agreement in his case and praying for an issue of an appropriate writ or direction quashing the Tribunal 's order of February 26, 1957. The Tribunal rejected his application on the ground that it related to the appellant 's case and to give its award without reference to the settlement and on proper adjudication of the matter. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD: (1) The scheme of the Industrial Disputes Act does not contemplate that the machinery provided therein should be set in motion to settle only disputes which involve the rights of workmen as a class and that a dispute touching the individual rights of a workman was not intended to be the subject of adjudication under the Act when the same had not been taken up by the Union or a number of workmen. [901 B] (2) The Tribunal committed an error in rejecting his application for separate representation, because it did take up this appellant ''s case against his dismissal as its own. It was not unreasonable to think that section 36 of the Act does appear to contemplate that when an individual workman becomes a party to a dispute independently of the Union which he is a member, as 200 a matter affecting workmen in general and on that basis a reference is made under the Industrial Dispute Act unless it is taken up either by a Union of the workmen or by a considerable number of workers. [ 901 C] (3) The appellant ' s case against Fateh Singh was not an 201 industrial dispute as defined in section 2(k) of the, Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1957 unless it was taken up for hearing by a union of which he was a member. It is not unreasonable that section36 of the said Act does contemplate that where a dispute between an employer and a single employee arises under the provisions of the [Industrial Disputes Act, unless it has been taken into consideration by a Central Government or a State Government or any authority or body constituted by or under any law for the time being in force, such a dispute shall be deemed to have arisen within the meaning of section 2 (k) and the Tribunal shall not be bound to record the compromise in so far as it related with the appellant.

The appellants were the tenants in the suit premises. The respondent No. 1 was a tenant of the appellant 's father who had sub let the premises to defendant No. 2.
