The appellants filed an application for ejectment against defendant No, 1 on the allegation that defendant No., 2 was the tenant inchief who had no interest in letting out the property to defendant Nos. 1 and 2. On appeal by defendant No,. 553 At the hearing of the appeal, the Court held that the surviving appellants were competent to continue the appeal in view of O.XLI, r. 3 of O.,XXII applied and the appeal of Kedar Nath had abated. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the deceased appellant was not a joint Hindu family and the surviving plaintiffs could have continued their appeal in spite of O.'XXXIII applied and that they could continue the appeals even after the death of Kedarnath and the abatement of the suit so far as he was concerned, that the Court could have reversed or varied the whole decree in favour of all the original plaintiffs and could have granted relief 'with respect to the rights and interests of Kedar Chand as well. The appellant preferred an appeal against the judgment of the High Court dismissing the appeal. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions of O'XXXIII apply to an appeal which was not competent in the circumstances of the case and, therefore, the provisions of 0. XLI, r 4 of O,.XLI are of no greater help to the contention of the appellants that their appeal could continue even though the appeal against defendant Nos, 1 and 3 was filed by all the plaintiffs jointly, and, consequently, the provision of O.(VI) r. 33 of O,XXII) r., was not intended to apply to a case which was a competent appeal against a party under the Code or under the Letters Patent 'of the High court. [966 D] 1.2 The provisions Of 0. XLIII apply only to an appeals filed by any one or by even some of the plaintiffs as he wants the reversal or modification of the decree in respect of the rights of KedarATH, deceased, as well as against all of them. [1066 E F] 1:3 The provisions o O. XLI r. 4 of 0 XLI, R. 33 are of a greater help than to an application under the Civil Procedure Code and may be exercised in favour Of such a party. [1166 C D] 2.4 The provisions contained in O.XXII, r., 33 are not intended for apply to appeals which were not filed by either of the parties as well, in view o O.'XLI overriding the provisions o r.3 of O..XXXIII, r, 33 is of no less help to defendant to continue as tenant of one of the landlords and not as a tenant or of the others when all of the defendants had a joint interest in let out the premises on the basis of the decrees holding that Kedar Nath, deceased was entitled to remain in occupation of the premises. [1266 D E] 2:5 The provisions under O. XLI are not meant to apply only where there are more plaintiffs or any one of them, but are filed by some of them as an appeal from the whole judgment and may also be exercised if such respondents or parties may not have filed any appeal or objection against the entire decree in certain circumstances. [1366 E] 3:6 The provisions relating to O.XXXIII are not applicable to an Appeal which was filed under O,XLI. III, r 3 of 0 XLIII.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for ejectment based on forfeiture of the tenancy under section 111(g) of the TP Act, as amended by the Amending Act of 1929. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section111(g), because the TP act did not apply to the present lease and the principles of justice, equity and good conscience were not applicable, did not, ipso facto, extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right if he so chooses, to determine the lease by giving notice in that behalf. The High Court held that the tenant had accepted the application, not of the Act as such, but on the application of the principles embodied in section 111 (g) and no notice terminating the tenancy was needed and further that the forfeiture of tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111 of the said Act. The tenant appealed to this Court, on the ground that the provisions of sections 106 and 111 of TP Act did not extend to the cases covered by section 112(g). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Section 111(h) of TP act does not apply in regard to notice to quit and notice of forfeiture. The only question for consideration is whether the particular provision introduced in sub section (g), of section 111 in regard thereto applies to the lease of 1952 executed in Delhi and, secondly, if it does not whether its present provision, as modified in 1929, has to be treated as a rule of justice equity and justice, justice and good law. [920 E] 1.2 The question for determination is whether a particular provision inserted in sub sections (g ) of section111 of the Transfer of Property Act by the amending Act of 1930, has any application to the facts of this case. [820 F] 1:3 In the instant case, no notice was sent to the tenant of the application for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the grounds that no such notice was necessary because the tenancy stood determined either by efflux or by forfeiture following the breach by the tenant. The mere institution of legal proceedings for ejectment would not tantamount to an act evidencing the intention of the lessor to avail himself of the forfeiture clause and sufficient to satisfy justice, Equity and good justice is the alter ego of section 112 (g). [821 E] 2.4 In regard to notices to quit, notice in writing was no part of equity. The crucial principles, not the technical rules, of the Rent Control Act form part of justice. equity and fair play are the changes made by the legislature and the legislative intent is clear that the intention is clear from the language used in section 112 of the new Act. [820 E] 3.1 In regard, notice to terminate the tenancy in this case was not necessary because it did not whether a written notice was required or not. The essential principles, which are embodied in sections 106 & 111 of Transfer of property Act, are that the happening of any event specified in section111 (g); equity and law, equity, justice, fair play and good sense is the change in the complexes of justice and equity. [821 F] 3:2 In regard thereto, equity has been defined as a principle of justice which equity and public good conscience is the alteration of the legal position by the Legislature and is not based on any principle of equity, equity or good conscience. The basic principles, therefore, are those principles of equity and common conscience. [822 A] 3.(i) In regard also, notice was not required because the tenant 's termination of the lease was under section 112.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Governor on a criminal charge. The appellant challenged his dismissal before the High Court and contended that (1) the Governor had no power to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank; (2) the President had no authority to dismiss a person, and (3) the Government servant was not competent to give such an opportunity. Held, that the satisfaction under the unamended clause (2), of article 311 of the Constitution, was that it was not expedient to hold such inquiry. The satisfaction under section 3(1)(c) of the Act, therefore, that in the interest of the security of the State it was expedient to give the said Shri P. K. K., K.K. K K. Hore and B. K.. K. M. KK. H.ore an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him had to be given to the government servant, and that under the proviso to clause (1)(d) of Article 311 of Constitution it was only desirable to give that person such an opportunities. The Governor was further satisfied under sub clause (c) that in view of the amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, the Governor was not justified in giving him an opportunity to show cause against his action proposed. The condition precedent for making a representation on the penalty proposed to have been imposed is that the Government Servant must be given reasonable opportunity of stating his case and to make any representation on it within such time as may be specified by the Government. The order of the Governor under section 7(1) of Act, 1962 was therefore not justified.

The petitioners, who were the Shias ' community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi, had filed a suit for enforcement of which the instant Writ Petition was filed. The respondents 5 and 6 were the Sunni Board of Waqfs for the purpose of defeating the customary rights of the Shia community to perform their religious ceremonies and functions over the plots and structures in question under the decree of competent Civil Court for the enforcement of their customary rights. The petitioners contended that the notification dated 26th February, 1944 issued under section 5(1) of the 1936 Act by the Sunni board is of no avail to them as they had misled the Court into believing that the Notification issued under Section 5(2) of 1936 Act was the Notification under section5 (1) and published in the U.P. Gazette on 1st December, 1956 under Rule 5411(vii) was the notification under section 6 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioners had misled this Court into thinking that the issue raised by them for the first time in the earlier litigation was not between the same parties who were before us and had been heard through their respective counsel. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the dispute involved in the present case is one where the entitlement of the respondents to customary rights to perform religious ceremonies, practices, observances, ceremonies and function over the other plots and structure thereon which had been listed as Shia Wakfs under the Notification dated 1st of December,1956 under Rule5411(viii) was established and is the subject matter of a judicial pronouncement and decree of Civil Court of competent jurisdiction as also by reason of these properties having been registered as Shias to perform its religious ceremonies or functions over and the other 8 plots and buildings thereon which have been listed in the Notification were being identified as Shib Wakfs under section 4(1)(a) of The 1936 Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners and through them the Shie community of Village Doshipsura, Banaras had established their existing customary rights in favour of the respondent No. 7 on Plot Nos. I to 3, particularly when it was now common ground that the mosque on Plot No. I was founded on considerations of high public policy to achieve two objectives namely (a) that there must be a finality to litigation and (b) that the individuals should not be harassed twice over with the same kind of litigation and in our view neither of these aspects is present here so as to bar the present petition by res judicata or principle analogous to res judicata. [523C] 1.2 The petitioners had approached this Court for relief against the respondents 5, 6 and 6 and the Sunni community of village Dosyura, which were fought right up to this court cannot be regarded as between the two Boards (Shia Central Wakf Board and Sunni Central Wakf board) notices were issued to them and they were also im 1135 pleaded as parties to the petition who have filed their respective affidavits in the matter and have been heard by various counsel. Thirdly, the earlier decision of this Court in Civil Appeal No.941 of 1976 did not record any finding on the rights of parties on merits as a result of the final order passed by this Court on the basis of which these members of the Sunni Community sought to prove their existing and established entitlement to their customary right to perform her religious ceremonies/ functions over them under the pretext of imminent danger to peace and tranquillity of the locality. [623D] 1:3 The petitioners have misled the court into believing their existing practice and as such they are permanently restrained by an injunction from interfering with the exercise of their powers in aid of their rights it is being exercised in suppressing their rights under the guise of imminent threat to peace & tranquillity of locality.

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58 under the 1922 Act. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim of set off on the footing that when in the assessment years 1957 58 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of the assessee 's appeal had stated that it was a notional capital loss. The Appellate Assistant commissioner held that there was no genuine loss, but merely notional in nature and that the claim for set off to be admissible had to be notified by the Income tax Officer under Section 24(3) of the 1922 act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the assessee had filed its return show ing the loss and that there were no genuine losses, and that therefore the claim was not admissible in law. HELD: The assessee had not filed its returns before the assessment period 1957 5858 and that it had filed a return showing the loss as computed by him for the purposes of this section. [1166 D] In the instant case, the assessee has filed its Return show ing that the loss sustained was a loss falling under the head 'capital gains '. Such loss cannot be wholly set off in accordance with the provisions of sub section (1) or sub section(2B) of Section 74A. The High Court was Fight in holding that there had been no genuine Loss, and without reference to anything more, this appeal can be disposed of. [1266 E] Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. K.K. Modi & Co., ; , referred to.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air), briefly called DTD & P. at the relevant time, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Director of Tech nical Development and production (Air) (DTD & F.I.) (DDT & P). The respondent was appointed as a Junior Scientific Officer in the Department of Technical Education on October 13, 1966. He retired from service on attaining the age of 60 years. On his retirement, he filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad Bench, contending that he had been entitled to remain in service upto the superannuation age of 58 years and was not liable to be retired at the alleged superannuation age. The Tribunal held that the respondent was entitled to continue in service till he attains the age Of 60 years and that he was not entitled to any benefit. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Government had power to vary the service conditions from time to time. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has no jurisdiction to decide whether the Government has such power. [723D] 2.2 The Tribunal is not competent to decide in this case. [824E] 3.3 The Tribunal was right in holding that the Respondent was entitled t o the benefit of the enhanced superannuation age to the members of one 24 unit while the same was granted to the member of another unit amounts to discrimination, violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [820B] 4.4 The Tribunal had no jurisdiction in deciding this case and it could not decide the question whether the Respondent belonged to another unit or not. [821C] 5.5 In the circumstances, the denial of the benefit by the enhanced age to a member of one24 unit while his same is granted to him to the Members of one of 24 units while the latter has been granted to members of other unit amounts o discrimination, violation of Article 14 of the constitution. [822D] 6.5 The Tribunal could not have decided the question in favour of the respondent. [823B] 7.6 In the instant case, the Tribunal was wrong in holding the Respondent to be entitled to the benefit. [828C] 8.7 The Tribunal erred in holding so. [829A] 9.8 The Tribunal committed an error in holding him entitled to get the enhanced retirement age from 58 years to 60 years in view of the OM dated 24.12.85 read with OM dated 10.2.86 referred to above.

The appellant was a member of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965. He filed an election petition under article 226 and 227 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the Judge; but the High Court dismissed his writ petition in limine on October 4, 1968. The appellant then moved this Court by special leave. HELD: (1) The trial court was wrong in allowing the two persons as court witnesses and that the first publication having taken place on the 8th June 1967 the High court should have set right by quasbing the order. [975 E] (2) The evidence about distribution of the pamphlet by the appellant as alleged by the petitioner was meagre and not beyond reproach it was not for the High Courts to take a different view in exercising jurisdiction under articles 226 and227 of the constitution. [1075 D] (3) The first publication being made on the 9th June, 1967, the trial Judge could have come to the conclusion that there was enough material for the court to come to its conclusion. He did not consider this aspect of the matter and found the appellant guilty of corrupt practice. [776 E] In the instant case, the evidence about the distribution of pamphlet by him as alleged was meagre, not beyond impressive it was neither for the trial judge nor for the Judge to have come into the conclusion he did. The High Court was therefore right in refusing to quash the order on the ground that there were no sufficient material for his court to take an view that there is enough material to justify interference with the order passed by the High. [76 E F] (4) The High court was not right in allowing them to be called as court witness and this was a serious irregularity which the High Curt should have taken, the view of the trial court.

The petitioner, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, its registered office being at Kanpur in the State of Uttar Pradesh and it is carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. The petitioner was assessed to sales tax in accordance with this notification. The Sales Tax Officer held that there was no power in the Provincial Legislature to enact and it was not a 9 law which the State legislature was competent to enact, but only on April 1, 1956, vide Adarsh Bhandar vs Sales Tax officer (1). In appeal by special leave, the petitioner contended that the Validation Act is ultra vires entry 54 of List II of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The High Court held that the validation Act was not ultra vires Entry 54 of the Seventh Schedule and that it was a nullity. On behalf of the State it was urged on behalf of some of the dealers who had been assessed to tax in terms of the notification dated March 31, 1956 that there is no power to enact or it could not be imposed with retrospective operation. Held: (i) The Validation Act does not in fact validate the impugned notification and that the Validating Act is therefore ultra vires. (ii) The validation Act is not a law which Parliament has power to impose a tax on the supply of materials in a contract for the construction of works simpliciter on the footing of a sale, but merely operates retrospectively. (iii) The validating Act is also not ultra Art entry 54, for the reason that it operates retrospectively and the Validation act is therefore illegal.

The assessee was a limited company dealing in land. It maintains its accounts on the mercantile system. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.7,24,914 as compensation payable to the assessee. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Arbitrator, 24 Parganas, Calcutta. This represented the difference between the sum of compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and the amount of compensation payable was left to be determined in accordance with settled or accepted principles. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the first contention and held that the compensation received from the assessee was not a receipt of a revenue nature liable to tax. In appeal by the State Government it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the sum received by it related to acquisition of property which was stock in trading of the business carried on by the appellant, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the trade of its business carried out by the respondent, and therefore, an income arising or accruing to the appellant during the previous year ended March 31, 1956 relevant to the assessment year 1956 57. The High Court rejected the second contention and upheld the first ground. In this appeal it was urged on behalf for the Revenue: (1) that the amount received by him related to a acquisition of the property which is the stock of trade of business carried by the Respondent; (2) that even if a court was awarded enhanced compensation, there is a right of appeal by an assessee to the High Court, and that the High court was right in the view taken by it and, therefore the question whether income could be said to have accrued or deemed to accrue and till then there was no liability in praesenti in respect of the additional amount of Compensation claimed by the owner of the land. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The High court is right in holding that when land was taken over by the Government for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year of assessment, the right to receive payment is admitted and the quantification only of the amount payable is left to the Civil Judge though an appeal was pending against that award. [723C] (ii) The mere claim by the Income tax Officer after taking of possession at a particular rate or for a certain sum is not compensation. It must be borne in mind that, even if an court was awarding enhanced compensation it would arise or accrue and until then there is no liability In praesti in respect Of the additional quantum of compensation claimed is left, to be determination in accordance With settled or accept principles. [823D] (iii) The right to receiving payment is not a right to a particular amount ofcompensation arises. It is sufficient to point out that there is an express distinction between cases 397 such as the present one where the right of receive payment was in dispute and it is not disputed that the right has accrued or vested to the claimant when he sought 396 a reference under section 18 of the Act or when the award was made by the Civil Court though an Appeal was pending challenging that award, but the quantum only is left is admitted.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction from the suit premises and for certain other reliefs. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the respondent had withdrawn his defence to the application filed by the landlord and submitted to a decree for eviction unconditionally. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree of the trial court and remanded the case back to the trial Court for fresh disposal in accordance with the terms of the compromise. The appellants preferred an appeal to this Court against the order of remand. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The compromise was legal and valid. [519D] 1.2 The compromise is not a lawful agreement. It is merely a device to avoid litigation. It does not create any interest in favour of the landlord. It only creates an interest in the property. [619B] 1:3 The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree under the law. The meaning of paragraph 1 of the agreement is clear and definite especially in the context of the pleadings and other materials. It squarely makes out a case of eviction within the meaning of Section 12(1) (f) of the Act on admission of the appellants. [613B] 2.4 In order to get a decree or order for eviction, it must indicate whether the tenant specifically or impliedly agrees to suffer the decree for ejectment because the landlord is entitled to have such a decree as under the Act. The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 23 Rule 3 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise". The meaning Of paragraph 1 is clear, definite and explicit especially in this background of the pleading and other material in the pleadings. It clearly makes out an case of ejectment within the ambit of the plaint. [421C] 2:5. In order recording the compromise the Court must indicate both on its own face or otherwise that the agreement for the eviction of the tenants is lawful, as in any other suit so in an eviction suit the Court is bound to record the compromise and pass a decree in accordance therewith. The words "Where" are used in the sense of the term 'agreement'. [422D] 2ndly, it is not necessary that the parties must make out a ground for passing such a judgment. It can only be done by an agreement or settlement. If on the other hand, the Court finds that the compromise was lawful and was in accordance With the plaint, it will refuse to record its compromise as it will not be a lawful contract. [413E] 3:6. The order recording compromise is clearly illegal. It cannot be said that the Court was so satisfied and the decree was passed.

The assessee company was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1962-63. The Income Tax Officer took the view that in view of the capital loss of Rs. 12,00,000/ suffered by the assessee on account of depreciation in the value of 83 shares held by the company in Elphinstone Mills Ltd., Bombay, the assessee was entitled to a dividend in respect of those years in view Of the loss incurred by it on account thereof. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner took the same view and rejected the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the loss of depreciation was due to the loss caused to the company on account Of depreciation in its value of 84 shares held in Elpinstone Mill Ltd., of Bombay, and that the assessee had suffered a capital loss. Held: (i) The word used in section 23A(1) is not confined to losses previously incurred by the Company and to the smallness of profit made. It is difficult to arrive at a conclusion as to reasonableness by considering the two matters mentioned isolated from other relevant factors. [696 B] (ii)The statute does not say 'having regard only to losses actually incurred by a company and to that smallness or profit' are never lost sight of require all matters relevant to the question of unreasonableness to be considered capital loss, if established is one of them. The form of the word used no doubt lends itself to, the suggestion than regard should be paid to the two matter mentioned isolatedfrom other relevant considerations. But it appears to their Lordships that it is impossible to arrive reached a conclusion that the Legislature by the words used while making sure that "losses and smallness" are never loses sight of requires all matters necessary to the questions of unreasonableness, to be decided in each case. [796 C] (iii)The word used 'no doubt lends themselves to,the suggestion than to regard should also be paid only to the three matters mentioned separately isolated from others relevant considerations and that too with reference to losses already incurred by them and to smallness. The statute does Not say ' having regard to the losses actually distributed, if any, referred to in clause (a), clause (b) or clause (c) and the dividends actually distributed are not lost sight.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in dispute. The respondent filed an objection against the award on the ground that he had been appointed under section 37 of the Act, and that the Civil Judge was not justified under section 12(4) of the , and that he was not entitled to modify the award. The District Judge held that the appellant was not a tenant in respect of the lands in dispute and that as the respondent had failed to prove that he did not apply under section 15 of the . The High Court dismissed the petition on the grounds that the respondent was not an 'tenant' within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, and held that an order of the Civil judge modifying the award was appealable under section 39 of the (X of 1940). The appellant thereupon filed a petition in the High Court for special leave to appeal against the decision of the District Judge. The High court dismissed the application on the view that the provisions of sections 46 and 47 of the U. P. Consolidation Act, 1953 were applicable to arbitrations referred to in section 12 of the ; , therefore, the appellant had no right to challenge the correctness of the award merely because he disagreed with the finding. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The effect of section 37 is that it makes the applicable to the proceedings before the arbitrator in the matter of procedure only. [935G] 2. Section 12(6) must be read with section 37 and if it is so read it is quite clear that what is made final is the decision 'of the arbitrator as it emerges after appropriate proceedings, if any, have been taken under the provisions Of the . [936H; 937A] 3. The words "any matter" in section 2 (1)(a) of Act must be given their plain meaning and not to their ordinary meaning. [736B] 4. Section 37 is a special provision which provides that where there is a dispute as to title, such question has not already been determined by any competent Court. The object of the section is to provide for appeals against the order of an arbitrator. It is quite obvious that what was made final must be understood in the sense that what it makes final is only the decision after appropriate proceeding, if necessary, have already been taken. [836C] 5. Section 13(6), read with sections 46, 47 and 47, provides for a statutory arbitration and section 37 provides for an appeal does not apply because the appellant has failed to establish that he does not applied under section 10 of the. The Act is quite plain that what can be made final was the decision in the case of Attar Singh 's(1) case. [889A] 6. Section 36 is a general provision which gives a right to an appeal against an award passed by an arbitrator, and it provides for appeals from the order passed by the Civil Court. It does not say that what has been made final shall be final. The section does not provide that the decision under sub section (4) shall be conclusive. [891B] 7. Section 39 of U P. Act provides for appeal against a decree or order passed in an arbitration proceeding. It only makes the provisions relating to arbitrations under section 13(4). It is clear that when there is an objection as to the title and the question of title referred to, i.e., whether section 39 applies to arbitrations, the Consolidation Officer has to refer the question for determination to the Civil court having jurisdiction who will thereupon refer it to the arbitrator. [871C] 8. Section 38 provides for the appointment of an Arbitrator by the State Government.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. The Corporation made regulations by passing a resolution and continued the same practice. In 1988, the corporation issued a resolution, for the first time, making 75 per cent of the posts of superintend Engineers available to the executive Engineers holding degrees and 25 per cent to the Executive Engineers who were diploma holders. This resolution was also challenged by the petitioner by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the classification was discriminatory in nature and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The classification made between members holding the same post on the basis of educational qualification is permissible and does not violate Articles 14 or 16 of Constitution. [723D] 2.1 In the absence of rule or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. The principle that in the absence o a separate quota for promotion on a basis other than that in case before the them the classified for purpose of promotion on an basis other then that they were drawn from different sources, would not violate Article 14 or16 of the constitution is well known and permissible. [823E] 2:2 The rule providing that graduates shall be eligible for such promotion to the exclusion of diploma holders does not offend Articles 14 & 16 of The Constitution and must be upheld. [820G H; 824A] 3.1 There was a common seniority of the Executive Engineer maintained. Hence, the observation made in that case while dealing with the relief claimed, do support the petitioner: " Prayer No. 4 is to declare the petitioner Graduate Engineers as a separate category amongst Junior Engineers and give them equal quota like the Diploma holder Junior Engineer Junior Engineer. Hence the observation are per incuriam as regards the next contention, admittedly neither the practice followed till 1988 nor the resolution passed by the respondent corporation in 1988 nor, the resolution made in accordance with section 64 of the Act. It is well settled that in absence of rules or regulations the authority cannot prescribe service condition by executive instruction and this can be done except by carving out two classes in the same category on the ground that they belong to the same cadre on the date when they belong t o the same posts on the principle of educations. Hence it is what is done tillthe year 1988, and is further sought to been done since1988 by the respondents taking into consideration the nature of work, the requisite qualification for the work and the necessity for making such a classification that quotas could be prescribed on the assumption of educational qualifications. Hence this observation are also per incuriam. [ 824E] 3:2 In the instant case, the petitioner was degree holder Junior Engineers. He got the said resolution and was promoted to the said post on that date. It was also not disputed that respondent No. 2 was a degree holder, he got the same salary as his qualification. Hence there is no discrimination in nature or violative of Article 14 and16 of Constitution and consequently violative of articles 14 and 19 of theConstitution. [824G H] 3 :3 The classification was already made which was challenged before the Court.

The petitioner was appointed as a Judge of the High Court in the year 1971. He was promoted to the post of Additional Chief Justice of India on the basis of an order passed by the President of India under Article 124(1) of the Constitution. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said order before the High court which dismissed the writ petition. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and quashed the orders of the State Government. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the Chief Justice had no jurisdiction to entertain a petition under Article 32 of the constitution as he had no personal or pecuniary interest in the matter of appointment to the Supreme Court and, therefore, the petition should be dismissed. HELD: 1.1 The Constitution has made a clear distinction between the two sources viz., (i) the appointment of Judges of the Supreme court and (ii) the appointments of Judges on the recommendation of the Chief Minister of the Government of India. [1303C] 2.2 The consultation with the Chief Justices of the high courts is not justiciable. It is true that the consultation with them is only a formality and it is not open to the Court to examine the two questions indicated above, namely (i ) whether the appointment is made by the Governor or by the Minister so as to reach the hands of the President; and (iii) whether the recommendation is to emanate di rectly from a source other than that of the Central Government. [1003C D] 3.1 In the instant case, the consultation was not made by any person before the Parliament or outside had stated that it has, as matter of policy, not made any appointments to the superior judici ary without the name being cleared by the ChiefJustice of India through the Ministry of Justice and the Chief Ministers of the States. [1103D] 3:2 The question is whether the consultation is justiciable should be re considered by a larger bench. If the recommendation was to emanated di rectingly from an source other like that of a Chief Justice or the Chief minister of the state, it would be difficult for an appropri ate selection to be made. [1203C E] 3 :3 The question whether consultation is necessary before the Court can examine the question is not whether the proposal is to be considered by the Central Minister or the Minister but whether it is to consult a person who has a consultative role and the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Govern ment. [903C H] 4.2 In the present case, there was no change in the personnel of the appellant State which would require re consideration. The correctness of the opinion of the majority in S.P. Gupta 's case relating to the status and importance of con sultation, the primacy of the position the Chief Judge of India and the view that the fixation of Judge strength is not warranted should be examined in the view of the fact that there has been a change in tact of theChief Justice or Chief Minister justifying the same should not be reopened and if in a given case the Union Government is of the view, that the role of the institution be recognised as of crucial importance in the matters of appointments to such Supreme Court, it will be difficult to be re consider by a smaller bench. [127A B] 4:3 The consultation is merely constitutional functionaries having a consultatory role andthe power of appoint resides solely or exclusively in th Central Government . If the recommendations are to emaned di reamsily from a sources other than those of the executive Government, it may be necessary for an appropriate authority to be appointed.

The respondent was appointed as an Enquiry Officer under the Chief Executive Officer 's Order dated January 9, 1979 authorising him to appoint Enquiry Officers and Appellate Authorities under the provisions of Chapter 19 of the Bi parTrade Settlement Act, 1966. The respondent did not raise any objection against the continuance of the enquiry by the said Enquiry Officer. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of discharge. The High Court quashed the impugned order of punishment and directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the impugned orders of punishment were without jurisdiction or competence, there was nothing for the Appellate Authority to confirm 'all consequen tial benefits ' flowing from the declaration that the impugned action was without jurisdiction and therefore null and void. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was in error in directing payment of all consequential reliefs. [723C] 2.1 In the circumstances, it would be sufficient to state that instead of directing 'all Consequen tents' flowing from a declaration that no formal order of dismissal was passed by the competent Disciplinary Authority, his report upto the stage pre ceding the issuance of a second ,how cause notice could be saved because both sides to the proceedings had not raised any objection to the continuance or otherwise of the said enquiry by him. [823B] 2:2 The respondent succeeded in getting the order passed by Shri U.B. Menon as an official of the bank. He did not raising any objection challenging the continuance o f the enquiry before the Enquiry Officer and therefore the High court ought to have remitted the matter to the competent disciplinary authority to take a fresh decision based on the report of the Enquiry officer. [923C D] 3.1 It is for this reason that the High Curt was right in quashing the impugned ord er dated January 18, 1988 by substituting the words fifty percent ' in place of the word 'all ' in the penultimate paragraph of the learned Single Judge 's order. The appeal will stand allowed to the extent indicated above but, in the facts and circumstances of this case, we think it appropriate that the ends of justice would be met if instead of ordering 'all consequential benefits' the appellant is ordered to pay '50% of the consequential benefits ' to which the respondent would be entitled on superannuation. [1023D] 3:2 In the instant case, the respondent succeeded by getting the orders of penalty quashed on a mere technicality and that too on the conten tion belatedly raised before the Court for the first time in a writ Petition more so because he had submitted to the jurisdiction of Shri U B. Menon, as an officer of the Bank. The fact, however, remains that the said order of penalty has to be quashed not because the merits of the case so demand but because the technical plea of incompetence suc ceeds. In the facts & circumstances, we are of the opinion that the course suggested by Shri Shetye can be safely adopted. [1123E] 3 :3 The respondent succeed in getting his order of punishments quashed on mere technicalities and that therefore the ends o f justice would meet if instead Of directing 'All consequen dents' coming from the charge le velled against the respondent and the reply thereto one may carry the impression that the appellant was duped or not. [1223F] 4.1 There is no reason why the High, Court should not have ordered payment of 'all consequent benefits ' arising from the declarations made by Shri M.B., Singhvi as an Officer of the respondent. The order of the High curt would stand. The matter will stand remitted to the Competent Disciplinary Authority to take appropriate fresh decision in accordance with law.

The appellant, a Municipal Corporation of Delhi, was granted permission to construct a building on the land in question. The plans submitted by them did not contain any proposal regarding the width of the road and that it was proposed to be used for a particular use of any land or building otherwise than in conformity with the Zonal Development Plan. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Commissioner refusing sanction, contending that the order passed by him under section 336 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 (Act LXVI of 1957) (hereinafter referred to as the Development Act) was legal and justified by the provisions of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 of the Corporation Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to entertain a writ of mandamus issued to the appellant to approve the plans submitted for the purpose of erection of a building or the execution of a work unless such a building is prohibited for an indefinite period. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court had erred in holding that since the Master Plan prepared under section 7 of the Act did not contravene any of the provisions, of sub sections (2), (3) and (4) of Section 336 or Section 340 of that Act, the order refusing sanction is legal and valid. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Master Plan has been prepared under Section 7 of Delhi Development Act,1957 (Act LXI of 1957 ) (hereinafter called the Development act). [515E] 2.2 The Master plan provides for a specific use of land adjoining that road. It cannot be put to a different use. If neither of the plans provide for the particular use or any land in that zone, section 14 will have no application whatsoever. [516F] 3.1 Section 14 does not require the Zonal Authority to give sanction for the erection of building or work unless it contains a proposal regarding width that a road should have, all use of lands adjoining that land cannot be permitted. The Master Plans are prepared for the area concerned and after it comes into operation in the Zone, the procedure indicated in section 10 will have to be followed and parties will have opportunity of sending their objections and suggestions. [617C] 3:2 In order to sustain the validity, the appellant has to establish that any part of the land of the respondents will be covered by a road or portion of a road it is not possible to accept the contention of the learned Solicitor General that there will be no violation of section 14 of the DevelopmentAct if the respondents be permitted to use the site for the building, by the Zonal Authorities. [717F] 4.3 The reasonable interpretation to be placed on section 14 would be that if any particular and definite use of property is indicated in a Master Plan, a different user of that land can be permitted, because any part thereof may be permitted for an uncertain period. If either of the plan provide for a certain use, then section 14 shall have no. application whatsoever.] [618G] 4:4 The Master plans prepared by the respondents as per the plans sent for sanction are not in contravention of section 15 of the Municipal Act. [613B] 5.5 In order that the moment a Zonal Development plan provides about a particular user of land is indicated, it cannot be placed to a separate use of a land or any building otherwise except in conformity With the Zonal Plan, the procedures indicated in Section 10 will also have no applicability. [418C D] 6.6 The Master Planning Plan for each of the Zones in which Delhi will have been divided will have also to be prepared and has not come into operation.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No, 2 for the purpose of carrying on business in the manufacture of cement. The appellant No 1 was a member of the judiciary. He was asked 1102 to see the appellant 's house and the respondent No. 2 was also present there. The respondent No 2 was the Secretary of the appellant company. The appellants were directed by the police authorities to make arrangements for the supply of certain documents which were produced before him by Nagindas, but the appellant did not comply with the directions given by the Police authorities. The police authorities made a search and seizure under section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code and on completion of the investigation the Magistrate submitted a charge sheet against the appellants. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and issued summons to the appellants for their appearance before the Magistrate. The accused were then tried by the Additional District Magistrate, who acquitted them. On appeal by the State the High Court set aside the order of acquittal passed by the Magistrate and remanded the case back to the Magistrate for fresh trial. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had erred in holding that the appellant had committed an offence under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Act No. 25 of 1974) because he had brought these moneys from his home and handed over them to Nagindassas when the raid was organised and which numbers were also specified in the memo prepared at that time was enough to establish the falsity of the allegation made by the appellant that he had come to know about the demand of bribe or illegal gratification by the appellants No. I and that the offence under sections 161 and 164 of Criminal procedure Code was never committed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The statement made by a person who is not a member or leader of the party in whose case the statements are recorded under section164 of the Cr. P.C., cannot be used to corroborate his evidence. [25B] 1.2 The statement which was made by an accused person in whose favour the statements were made by him, can be used only for corroboration and not for corroboration. [26G] 1:3 The statement recorded by a police officer under section 162 of the Evidence Act cannot be treated as substantive evidence and it is inadmissible in evidence and could not be proved orally by the prosecution. [27C D] 2.1 In the instant case, the statements made by appellant No., 1 to him were not recorded by him in accordance with the provisions of section 164 Cr.P.C. The statement was thus eliminated from the evidence given by Shanti Lal Ahuja, the Additional Sessions Magistrate and came to our conclusion that the numbers of the currency notes which had been handed over to Nagindaas were also included in the number of the notes which were handed over by him to Naguthas. [28G] 2:2 The statements made on behalf the appellant Nos. 1 to 3 were not admissible in evidence, and could be proved oral by them. [29A B] 3.1 There is no substance in the contention that the statement was not eliminated from evidence as nothing remained so far as the witnesses Nagindias and Pannalal on the one hand and the police witnesses supported a% prosecution case that they had brought this moneys from their home when the search was organised, which numbers are also specified therein. [30C D; 30A] 3:3 In the present case, there is no evidence to show that the number was of the denomination of Nagindus or that of the police officers who were charged with the offence of taking of the bribe or unlawful gratification by them in regard to the handing over of that sum by the accused No.1. [31C D].

The plaintiff was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the plaintiff along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the plaintiff was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. It was alleged that the accused were found guilty under section 325 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and several other sections, and were sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months each. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plain tiff was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in dismissing the second appeal as illegal inasmuch as the judgment assumes that no law of limitation is applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void, and that later he was again dismissed. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question involved in this suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High court while allowing the plaintiff to file a relevant affidavit in regard to the further orders passed against Kahan singh subsequent to the civil court 's decree in his favour. [824D] 2.1 Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 mandatorily directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed and this mandate of law cannot be ignored on the ground that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. [820G H] 2:2 The High Court should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage as the case is an old one. In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the High Curt shall permit the plaintiff ' to file relevant rebutting evidence. The operation of the decree of the first appellate court shall remain stayed till the final disposal of the second appeals by the trial court. [828G] 3.1 Section 34 of Indian Penal code is a special provision and it has been specifically provided that no Court shall take any decision in regard thereto unless it considers necessary to do so. The authority was also permitted to take a decision in respect of the pay and allowances for the period the plaintiff remained out of service because of his being in jail.

The assessee was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. In the course of its business, it was sold by the respondent to the appellant (hereinafter referred to as the assessee) who was a Private limited company. The Income tax officer held that the transactions described above entered into by the assessee were speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to sec. 24(1). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal held that there was no actual delivery of the goods to the transferee and that loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs Bhuwalke Brothers Ltd., (2) and D. (P) Ltd. vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta(1), and held that loss was allowable under section 24( 1). The Tribunal relied on the decision of the Calcutta High Court in D. N. Mukherjee vs Commissioner Of Income tax (supra) and held in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transaction described above was speculative transactions as contemplated in explanation 2 of section 24 of the Act, and that the loss should have been treated as trading loss relying upon two decisions: D. C. Patel vs Commissioner for Income tax(2) , D. K. Mukherjee & Co. vs Commissioners of Income Tax (supra), D. R. Mukherjee and Co. Ltd. v Commissioner of Incometax, Calcutta, ; and Duni Chand Rataria vs Bhuipurke Brothers Limited, (3) that the sales in question were speculative and consequently the losses suffered by the appellant in these transactions could not be set off against the profits made by the Income tax Officer 's non speculative business High Court on reference. Held: (i) The explanation to sec 24(I) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 does not require that the transfer in question should be followed up by actual deli very of the transaction which is otherwise speculative or according to explanation 2 if there was a actual delivery thereof. It merely lays down that where an assessee sustains a loss under any of the heads mentioned in section 6, he shall be entitled to have the loss set off under his head in that year. The explanation does not contemplate that the ultimate purchaser of the P.D.Os has taken actual delivery or the scrips has taken delivery of goods to him. It only lays down a general rule that if any transfer of the p.D.,Os. is not followed up with actual deli gray transaction, the loss, if any, would be a loss in a speculative transaction which could be allowed to be set aside only against a profit in a transaction of the same nature. The object of the explanation is not to invalidate the transaction but only to brand them as speculative transactions so as to put them in a special category for income tax purposes. [184 D] (ii) The Explanation to secs. 24 and 25(1) of Act, 1961 does not permit the set off of a loss which is not completed by actualasti act of delivery of any goods to a transferee but only laid down that if there is no actual or physical delivery, the losses would be an amount of profit in speculative transactions which could have been allowed to set off only against the profit in the transaction of such a nature.

The appellant was a member of the Punjab Legislative Assembly. He had been elected as a member in the Pun jab Legislative Assembly by the Punjab Government on the ground that he was disqualified from contesting the election to the State Legislature. The appellant challenged the validity of his nomination on the grounds (1) that the nomination paper was not signed " by the proposers and seconders in the usual way; (2) that it was not the only method '; (3) that there were no valid signatures of either a proposer or a seconder in any one of the four nomination papers. Held, further, that the word "subscribe" is not defined but it is equally clear when the words " signs " are to be made, we are bound to give effect to the general policy of the Act by drawing the same distinction between signing and the making of a mark as the Act itself does in the definition of "sign" and also because the element of his satisfaction at the proper time, which is of the substance, would be there and the omission formally to record the satisfaction could probably, in a case like that, be regarded as an unsubstantial technicality. The word "sign " means to write under something in accordance with prescribed regulations where any such exist But if it is improper to import the special meaning given to " sign" in the General Clauses Act because the expression " signs" is defined and not " subscribe", it is certainly clear that when the signature cannot be written it must be authorised in the manner prescribed by the Rules. [620 E] The word 'subscribe " does not include signing" so called, but it means "to write under a particular rule". If the Returning Officer had omitted the attestation because of some slip on his part and it could be proved that he had been satisfied at the appropriate time, the matter might be different because the elements of his satisfy satisfaction at that time. [720 E F] The words " signing" in section 36 are mandatory and imperative. They have not been defined but they have not to be construed as " subscribing" or "written upon "(3) 'Subscription is a method of signing; it is also clear that if the proposer or the seconder had omitted to record his satisfaction, he would be entitled to relief under section 33. [820 E H] The expression "sign", wherever used in the context of the Representation of the People Act, and if it was improper to exclude the special category of " signature" and not the word 'sign " it is quite clear that they have omitted the filling of a "signature" for the purposes of the act. [920 E G] The Returning Officer has at the scrutiny stage itself given effect to his general policy by drawing a distinction between signed and the placing of a marked mark as "and it is clear that he has not been authorised in either one way or the other, but he cannot remedy the defect.

The appellants were workmen of the Company. The Company was a registered union called 'the Association of Chemical Workers ' in support of its demand for re instatement of three of the Union leaders who had been dismissed by the Company on September 20, 1972. On September 7, 1972, the Company issued notices to the appellants and 10 others asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the rolls of the company from that date. The appellants filed separate complaints against the respondent Company under section 33(A) of the (Central) Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, alleging that they had abandoned the service of the respondent company during the period between 1972 to September 20 1972 and had abandoned their services. The Labour Court held that the action of the appellant in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls on the presumption that they were no longer interested to continue in service of their Company and had totally abandoned the services of the respondents, was illegal and invalid. On appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants have been employed elsewhere during this period, still we take a total view the whole case and direct that for the entire period from 1972 to the date of reinstatement, 75 per cent of the wages will be paid to all the workmen concerned on the scales and revised scales as the case may be. [636G H] 1.2 The appellants had along with 229 other workmen gone on indefinite strike which ended on October 22, 1972 and were interested in the service. They had neither voluntarily abandoned the employment of the said company nor did they desire to do so, and that they would report for work the moment the strike was called off 616 by their union. [736F] 1:3 The appellants' stand that the letter of the Cooperation dated September 7 1972 was received by them on September 26, 1972 cannot be countenanced. [537G H; 528A C] 1.:4.1 In the circumstances of the case, it could not be said that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned service of 25 workmen (including the appellants) during this intervening period, yet they were interested to continued in service. The action of respondent No. 2 in removing them from their rolls on account of their leave salary gratuity etc., cannot be faulted. [613A B] 1 :4. In the instant case, there was nothing in the surrounding circumstances or the conduct of the parties indicating or suggesting an intention on their part to abandon service which in view of the ratio of Gopal Chandra Misra 's case, can be legitimately said to mean to detach, unfasten, undo or untie the binding knot or link which hold one to the office and the obligations and privileges that go with it Their absence from duty was purely temporary and could by no stretch of imagination be construed to as voluntary relinquishment by them of the service during admitted pendency of the industrial dispute before the Labour Court. [558A B C] 2.4 The appellants were not employed elsewhere in spite of the fact that they did not intend to abandon the services but had also returned the cheques sent to them by the Cooperative Union. They were only interested in their service and could not therefore be countenanced, and could be legitimately held to have voluntarily abandoned their service. [565A B D] 2:5. The workmen concerned have been working elsewhere during these period, and still they did neither voluntarily abandonment nor abandoned the Service of the petitioners in the aforesaid circumstance, the impugned action on the part of the Appellants indicating or implying an intention to abandon services which in fact had never terminated the service would constitute a change in the condition of service of that appellants during the admitted pendency. [567C D] 3:6.

The appellant was the trustee of a public trust, styled "Shri Tricumji". The trustees of a private trust were charged with the execution of a decree for sale of immovable property in execution of which the sale was ordered. The appellant filed an application under section 36 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, for setting aside the sale on the ground that the sale did not comply with the requirements of 0. Raju, J., held that sale of the mortgaged property which belonged to a public Trust was invalid and on that account a sale in execution thereof was void. The District Court dismissed the application holding that sale was without sanction of the Charity Commissioner. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (1) the expression 'sale ' in section 36(a) includes a sale of property of a Public Trust in execution Of a decree, and (2) the sale prohibited without sanction from the Charity commissioner must be deemed invalid. Held, that the expression "sale " in section 37(a), includes a transfer of immovable Property in execution or a decree passed by a civil Court for recovery of a debt due by the trust. The definition of 'sale' in section 2(g) of the Act is wide enough to include a sale which is not intended to be a sale, but it does not mean. It is only when a person sells immovable property that he can sell the same or any part thereof. In order to constitute a larger Bench to examine whether a judgment delivered by a single Judge in a case before a single judge of a High Court without jurisdiction is liable to be regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that Court, it would be impossible to hold that a judgment pronounced by a Single Judge after due consideration of the points before it is liable. The Chief Justice of a Division Bench of the Gujarat High Court was not bound to follow that precedent because by following the precedent the Judge would act contrary to section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act and, would also violate the oath of office taken by him when entering upon his duties as a Judge under the Constitution.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 4, 1935. The Government had the absolute right under Rule 56(j) of Fundamental Rules to prematurely retire a servant at any time after he has completed 30 years qualifying service provided that the appropriate authority shall give, in this behalf a notice in writing to the officer at least three months before the date on which he is required to retire, or three months ' pay and allowances in lieu of such notice, confers unguided powers in the Govern ment and as such is ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The appellant was compulsorily retired by giving him three months notice or pay in lieu thereof. The order of retirement was challenged before this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 Rule 2(2) of Pension Rules provides no guide line provided in the Rule to this effect. The said para 620 of the Railway Pension Manual is a statutory rule and has the effect of amending Rule 2 (2) thereof. [696G H] 1.2 The rule gives unguided discretion to the Government to retire a Government servant at anyone time after attaining the age of 55 years. Any Government servant who has completed thirty years qualifying serv ice can be retired at any stage at the discretion of the Government under Rule 2.(2) Of Pension Rules may also require an officer to retire from service even after he had attained the age o l superannuation which is 58 years. [796G] 1:3 The rule provides no guidance line provided for in the rule to this regard. The memorandum is in the nature of executive instructions but is a statute framed under Article 77(1) of the constitution. Rule 2 does not contain any guide line or gives absolute discretion to t he Government to prematurely retiring a Government employee at any point after he having attained the prescribed age of superannuation. [896F] 1.:4 The rule makes no distinction between Rule 2046 and Rule 2047. The rule is in addition to the provisions already contained in Rule 2. [1097G H; 1098A B] 1 :5 The memorandum has not been issued under Article 309 of the o f India and as Such cannot be statutory. The Memorandum is in nature of administrative instructions but was a compendious rule, the railway employees are only gover 802 ned by the said Rule and para 620 has no parity with Rule 2 of Pension Rule which is inconsistent with it. Para 620 of Railway Pension Rules 1950 to clarify that the power to retire under Rule2(2)(a) of pension Rules on the other hand does not include power already contained therein. The same, having been framed in the name of President of India, is statutory and has effect of amend mentary rule 2(1). [1098G H, 1099A B C] 1.(6) Rule 2 makes no difference with Rule 2045. The proviso to Article 309 provides that such power can only be exer cised in 'Public Interest '. It does not provide any guide lines provided in Rule to the effect. [100C D] 1(7) Rule 2946 of the Pension Rules is a Statutory rule and it has the force of amending the rules. The Rule gives absolute power to the railway authorities to retire an officer who has attained the minimum age of 60 years. If the said rule is read in addition, then there is no reason why the same should be construed as supplementary to Rule 2040. [101C E] 1 (8) Rule 2846 of Pension Manual provides that where a Government Servant who has served 30 years of qualifying service and has not attained the maximum age of 58 years can be picked up for premature retirement under the Rule. The provision is in consonance with the statutory rule.

The assessee firm was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period was 1 4 1943 to 31st March, 1944. On the basis of the assessment under the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940 (hereinafter called the 'Act '), the Income tax Officer did not set off the said deficiency of profits for the chargeable accounting periods ending 31st December, 1942 and 23rd November, 1942 to 29th September, 1943 to 30th September. The assessee was entitled to a set off of the deficiency only for the period 1st April, 1943. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed that there were no profits and losses during the chargeable year ending 31 st March, 1943 and as such there could be no deficiency of income during those periods. In appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that the deficiency in profits pertaining to the chargeable years ending 31St March, 1941 and 23th November, 1944 was not liable to be set off under section 7 of the Act. The High Court also held that since the chargeable account ing periods ending 30th May, 1941 to 29 th September, 1942 were occupied with manufacturing activity alone and there were sales, therefore no part of the profits realised upon the sales could be apportioned to those chargeable accounting years and consequently that it could not be said that there was any deficiency of profit during those period. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The assessee had urged that deficiency in income pertaining to those periods should be computed on that basis and after set off carried forward to be taken into account while computing the excess profits for chargeable accounting year ending 3rd March, 1946. [472G H] 2.2 The method of computation under section 8 of the Excess Profit Tax Act was on the basis that certain part of it had adverted to, the profits earned upon sales effected during those years and after that the deficiencies in profits were worked out on that account in respect of the chargeable period ending 31 March, 1945. [473G H; 473A] 3.3 The method adopted by the Income Tax Officer was on a different context where certain part or the activities occurred at Raichur and the sales took place in Bombay, the question was whether the activity which the assessee carried on at Raichur was part of their business within the meaning of the third proviso to section 5 of the act. [474G H]. 4.4 The method for computation under Section 8 of Excess Profits tax Act, 1948, must be on the principle of apportionment of profits to which it had referred to, and after setting off carriedforward to be laid off during the relevant chargeable accountingperiod ending 31 St March, 1942. [476A] 5.5 In determining whether a deficiency in profit pertaining to any chargeable accounting Period ending 31nd March, 1951 could be attributed to the manufacturing activity between 28th October, 1940 to 31 st march, 1941, must necessarily be on account of 'accounting period ' and after the set off carry forward to become set off during that chargeable accounting date. [477G H, 473A B] 6.5 The method followed by the Appellate Assistant Commission was not correct in law. It was not open to the Income-tax Officer to adopt a different method for computing the deficiency of the profit for the purposes of assessment under section 9 of the Indian Income tax Act. [478C D] 7.6 In determining the deficiency, the method of calculation under section 5 must be On the principle that apportionment of the income should be on basis of 'Accounting period' and after it has been set off in computing the profits for that period should be calculated on that footing and after Set off carried out to be carried forward during the charged accounting period ending 3nd March.

The petitioners who had qualified in Civil Engineering question paper and answered the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had appeared in the written test conducted by it. The respondents, who had already been appointed, filed Writ Petitions before the Kerala High Court challenging the selection and prepare separate rank lists of selected candidates holding Civil and Mechanical Engineering degrees. The Division Bench of the Kerala and the KPSC allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government to prepare two separate rank list for Civil Engineering graduates and other (Mechanical) on the basis of examination already conducted. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the petitioners who were appointed as Assistant Engineers in Civil engineering branch were not entitled to be considered for selection and preparation of separate rank Lists. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the K PSC had advised 239 candidates according to separate lists for Civil and Electrical Engineering. It was also held that the applicants who had been appointed as Junior Engineers in Mechanical Engineering and answered questions in category II on the ground that they had already qualified in Mechanical engineering and answered question paper could not rationally be included in a common rank list after the interview. The State of Kerala filed appeals before this Court against the judgment of the High Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Government and the Public Service Commission of Kerala are directed to prepare separate lists of candidates selected holding Civil or Mechanical Engineering diploma on the strength of directions given by the learned Single Judge in his judgment dated 23rd April 1980 quoted above. [723C] 2.2 The KP SC has stated in its counter affidavit that there were directions to the KPsSC to prepare a common list. But facing difficulties in giving effect to the directions given in his order and he is high enough in the common list for claiming the post. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the position and give necessary directions. [ 723C D] 3.1 In view of the difficulties faced by the KPPSC and the Government of Kerala, it would be necessary to clarified the position that preparation of no common list was directed either by the Single Judge or by the Division Bench. As stated earlier the Kerala Government or the KPC has stated clearly in its affidavit that the expression "the common list prepared by the Public Services Commission should be deleted". Therefore, the petitioner will be entitled to exercise his option and then take his turn according to his rank in the Common List for claiming his post. [ 794D] 3:2 The Kerala Government and KPPC were not directed to preparing separate lists. But because no common List was directed to be prepared or was prepared by them, it cannot be said that there was a common List and since no option was given to the Special Leave Petitioners before us, the KPMSC faced difficulties in give effect to those directions. As such, it will be necessary for clarify the stand and give appropriate directions. Therefore the petitioner would be entitled only to exercise their option and thereafter take his chance according to rank in his common list as Civil Engineering graduate on the date when he was appointed. [ 786D] 4.3 The Kerala Public Service (General Branch) Rules, 1963 are not applicable to the petitioners. They were appointed by the Government and they were appointed in the Civil Engineering branch on the same terms and conditions. Therefore there is no valid ground to reverse the judgments of the Division Benches of the KKPSC and also the order dated 11th November 1980 passed by the High court. [ 823C E] 5.4 The Kerala State Public Service Commissions have stated in their counter affidavit to the S.L.Ps. that there are directions to prepare one separate list for civil Engineering graduates on the base of examination, already conducted and that no option is given to them.

The plaintiff respondent No. 1 was a partner of a partnership business along with his brothers defendant Nos. 2 and 3. The plaintiff respondent filed a suit for dissolution of the partnership firm on the ground that he is a partner in the firm. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the valuation put by the plaintiff on 15.1.1979 to be correct value of the suit was beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and held that the plaint was governed for the purpose of court fees by section 7(iv)(f) of the Act. The High Court also held that it is manifest that relief to the tune of lacs of rupees has been claimed by the appellant in the suit. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiff cannot arbitrarily and unreasonably under value the relief claimed in the plaint. [610B] 2.1 In a suit where the accounts are examined and it is not possible to give an exact valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. It is not only open to the Court but its duty to reject such a valuation. The cases of some of the High Courts which have taken a different view must be held to be wrongly decided. [710C] 2:2 In a case where the plaintiff is required to place the valuation on his claim he must state a valuation which need only be approximately correct but qualified it by saying that, "it must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate. It may also put a tentative valuation upon it. If the court comes to the conclusion that the tentative valuation of the plaint would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure. [810D] 3:3 The courts below have taken into consideration the statement in the written statement that the plaintiff has been ousted from the partnership business. If he is required by saying, "its own right to give a tentative value on the suit", it must be clearly arbitrary and unreasonable. It cannot be accepted. [910E] 4:4 The courts are bound to accept that"it must never be arbitrary and manifestly inadequate or manifestly insufficient. It must not only be open to them but its obligation to reject the valuation made on behalf of the plaintiff before the Allahabad High Court in Aizaz Ahmad vs Nazirul Hasan, AIR 1935 Allahabad 849, was also rightly rejected. [1010G] 5:5 The courts have taken an independent view and that the suit is governed for purposes of court fee by section7(iv) (f) and the plaintiff cannot unilaterally or unreasonably undervalue the relief. [1110E F] 6.1 There is no substance in the contention that the court was powerless to challenge the valuation given by the defendant on the relief sought in the present suit. The courts were not justified in rejecting the plaint as grossly undervalued and arbitrary. [1210G H; 1211A B] 2 :2 In view of the clear language used in section 7 (iv)(b) of Act, the court is bound to reject it and leave the plaintiff to correct the valuation or have the suit rejected. If that be so, it will pass an order under order VII of Code of civil Procedure. The case of some other High Courts who have taken part in the trial of a suit, it is open to such Court but their duty to dismiss such a valued. [1311B C] 3.2 In the instant case, the plaintiff was required to put on the plaint any value he wishes to and the court has no jurisdiction to examine the correctness of the valuation so made on the basis of the assessment made by the Income Tax department.

The respondent in these two matters and the petitioners in the other five Special Leave Petitions were certain concerns in M.P. assess able to sales tax (hereinafter compendiously referred to as the assesses ').
