The State Government issued a notification exempting the class of dealers specified in column (1) of the Schedule below who have set up industry in any of the districts specified in the annexure to this notification and had commenced production after 1st April, 1981 from pay ment of tax under the said Act for the period specified in Column (2), subject to the restrictions and conditions specified in columns (3) and (4) of that Schedule. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification on the ground that the industries run by them are "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption under the notification and that the Director of Industries should have granted them a certificate to this effect. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was entitled to the exemption on the terms and conditions set out in the notification. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the notification did not set out the conditions on which, and the procedure in accordance with which the Director Industries had granted them certificate. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The notification does not refer to the condition on which the Directorate of Industries is to issue eligibility certificate. [620G H] 2.2 The notification merely states that the dealer is entitled to claim the exemption and that he has not opted for the scheme of deferring the payment of tax. It does not say that the exemption granted by the 1981 notification in respect of the industries mentioned by it should be prospective or retrospective, only prospective operation can be given to a notification rescinding an exemption granted earlier. [613G H;613A] 3.1 In view of this interpretation, the 1987 amendment has the effect of rescinding the exemption conferred on the industries listed by it. [520C D] 3 2.3 The Notification does not set specifically the conditions for exemption and the former is not available to traditional industries because of rule 14 above. [558A B] 4.1 There is no scope for the assessee to invoke the doctrine of promissory estoppel. [561G H,613B C] 4 2.4 In view Of this interpretation the 1987 Amendment has the force of rescstructing the exemption given by the Notification in respect o the industries specified by it and not hold it to be ambiguous. The former is only in the nature of an alterna tive to the provision for exemption. [565B C D] 4 3.5 In view, while a notification under it can be prospective, only retrospective operation can also be given. [564C E] 4 4.6 The Notification merely states what the Director has to do is to satisfy himself that those new industrial units are excluded, it is not necessary for the rules of deferment to specifically provide that they will not be available to the industries included in rule 14 particularly when rule 4 has incorporated the requirement of an eligibil ity certificate in accordancewith 623 the previous instructions for the said purpose. [562A B C] 5.7 The notification also does not specify the conditions which, or the procedure for compliance with which, the Director, Industries should grant a certificate (a) that the manufacturer is entitled under the scheme and (b) that he had not opted to the scheme.

The petitioners were appointed to temporary posts in the Delhi Judicial Service on the recommendation of the High Court. The direct recruits were appointed in a temporary capacity to substantive vacancies in the service. They were appointed as direct recruits from amongst the members of the Delhi Higher Judicial Service, who were appointed on merit cum seniority basis. The petitioners were promoted as direct recruit by way of direct recruitment and after completion of ten years judicial service, their names were included in the list of direct recruits. The respondents challenged the validity of the selections made by the Full Court of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in a writ petition filed under Article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that the appointments made by them were illegal and void as they had been appointed regularly in accordance with qualifications laid down under Rule 7(a) and (b). The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the appointment of direct recruit is governed by the rules of continuous officiation in the cadre post i.e. a direct recruit who is appointed after a member of the service, and since the rule of `quota and rota ' is read with rule 16(1) and if such posts have been filled in as it appears to have been done here in consultation with the High court as enjoined by Rule 5(2), the seniority of direct recruited vis a vis the promotees shall be determined according to the dates on which direct recruits are appointed to their respective posts and the dates from which the promotees have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the Service or in substantive vacancies to which were appointed under Rule 16(2) of the Rules. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The rule of 'quota' and rohi ' is a statutory provision and it cannot be said that the rules are not applicable to the direct recruits who are appointed regularly. [810B] 2.1 It is true that under Rule 8(2)(a) the seniority must be governed by rules of uninterrupted officiation in a substantive capacity, but if temporary posts have not been filled up as provided under rule 7(b), the quota rule would break down when such appointments are made. [910C D] 2:2 The rule is not applicable where temporary posts are created as has been done in this case by the Administrator as envisaged by Rule 16 (1) read with Rule 17(2). If temporary posts were created as a result of selection from amongst members of Delhi Judicial service, then the quota rules assuming that there is any, cannot apply to such appointments. [1010E] 3:3 The rule does not provide for a quota of 1/3rd for direct recruits, but it provides for recruitment to the Delhi High Court from amongst persons who are selected on meritcum seniority basis so much so that by legal fiction, he will rank lower in seniority than the latter in the lists of seniority. [1110B C] 4:4 The rule has no application when temporary posts exist as a consequence of selection and after completing ten years of service in the High Service as required under Rule 17 (2) and in the manner contended by the respondents, it might so happen that a candidate 's position may be placed in such a way that by Legal fiction, his will be placed as senior to a person as a District and Sessions Judge by national placement at a time when he did not even reach the age at which he or she would have become eligible for appointment.

The assessee, a firm of persons, was assessed to tax in the status of "an association of persons". The Income tax Officer assessed the income in the assessment year in question. In appeal by Debi Parshad, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the direction for assessing the income should be deleted. The High Court held that the income belonged to Debi Parulshad and he was liable to be assessed personally in respect of the income of the family of Debi Parkash. Held, further, that the Income tax officer had no jurisdiction to direct after setting aside the assessment order that Debi Paranjey Mills be assessed by the Income Tax Officer in respect o the income from the business of Debi parshad represented the Hindu Undivided Family of which he was a member. The Appellate Assistant commissioner had directed that he may be personally assessed by him in respect Of the income, profits or gains of the Ambala Flour Mills. The order of the Appellate Tribunal was not and could not be referred to the High Court because by the order dated December 12, 1966, it was directed that "the Income tax Officers shall make the direction with regard to the assessment of the Income in the hands of DebiParshad". The Appellate Tribunal had also directed that if the assessment had to be made on the assessee or any person 'm consequence of or to give effect to any finding or direction contained in an order under section 31, section 33A, section 66B, section66A". Held, that where as the result of an appeal, any change in, the assessment could be made even after the expiry of four years. "In Commissioner of Income tax U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate(1) this Court held, that when a case has been decided by a court of law and the decision is reversed by the Supreme Court, it would not be open to the Appellate authority to make the order in a reference, the order passed by the appellate Assistant Commissioner must be deemed to have been made on him. The power of the appellate Tribunal to make such an order was not, and could only be referred for the purpose of assessment or re assessment. The powers of the High Courts under section 66(3)(b) were not in doubt. It was not contended before the Appellate Commissioner that Debi parkash was a stranger to the proceedings for assessment.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the plaint did not attract the provisions of section 7(iv)(b) of the Act and that the proper court fee to be paid was determined by article 17 B of Schedule II of the Madras High Court Rules, 1959. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the valuation made by the appellant in respect of his claim for partition should be treated as the value given by the plaintiff for the purposes of jurisdiction and it is on this basis that the court fees payable in suits covered by the several sub sections of section 8 of the Suits Valuation Act, 1955, that the High Court held that the suit did not fall under section 7 (iv)(c) of Act. HELD: The plaint does not strictly attract the provision of article 17B of Schedule I and that it provides for the determination of the value for jurisdiction on the basis of such claim. [50 C] In suits falling under sub section (iv), a departure has been made and liberty has been given to the plaintiff to value his claim on the memorandum of appeal but also on the plaint. The valuation thus made by him for the purpose of court fees is, therefore, mentioned. [51 D E] In view of their prior decision that the present case fell under section 8(iv) (b), they should have allowed the appellant to amend his valuation for the payment of court fee on the valuation as well as the memorandum and appeal.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was formed in the year 1957. The appellant was the owner of certain premises situated at New Delhi. The respondent No. 1 had constructed a building on the said premises. The construction work was completed and the respondent No 1 filed a suit for eviction against the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit holding that the refuge area could be located in each floor separately, provided that it would not be covered in FAR) with a minimum area of 15 sq. m. per person. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the clearance from the Chief Fire Officer envisaged by Bye law 16.4.8 and 16.1.8 were in addition to the requirements of bye laws 16.2.8.1, that the flames contemplated under Bye laws 16, 4.8, the wall abutting such outer vacant space was also an "external wall" for purposes of the said bye laws. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The clearance from Chief Fire Office envisaged by bye law 17.1 is in addition thereto the requirements Of Bye laws 18.4,8.2 and 16.. [612D] 2. The refuge areas could be placed in each of the floors separately provided that they are located on external walls "by cantilever projections or in any other manner" abutting a vacant space from which rescue operations are rendered possible. [613E] 3. The zonal developmental requirements in this behalf and the difficulties and prob lems inherent in the insistence upon construction of such pedestrian walk way in an isolated particular case, could be reconciled with direct the NDMC, in the event of its ap proving the plans otherwise, to keep the requirement of the pedestrianke way and Podium. [713G] 4. The clearances from theChief Fire Officer were considered to provide for adequate fire safety precaution in accordance with its bye laws or in a better measure. The only way in which, perhaps, the zonal development plan could be construed was to direct the respondent 1 and 2 to put up such a pedestrian pathway and Podumium. In this context, the Zonal developmental requirements in the insisted upon construction Of such metroemicrian walkway were considered by the Chief fire Officer as a better and more reliable fire safety measures than those envisaged by the Bye laws. [813E F] 5. The emphasis on the expression "ex Internal" walls is to direct that whenever the policy to implement the Zonal Developmentalal requirements is finally decided upon, the respondent1 and 2 would undertake to put forward such a distance of 15 metres and in the case of an ultimate rejection of plans they would have no claim against the NDMC for any loss occasioned to respondent 1. [913E G] 6. The expression "External" walls means a wall abutting an inner vacant space, which is not an "aable wall". [614G H; 915A B] 7. The word "ex External" walls mean a wall which is constructed by the respondent and which has been constructed by him. It is not necessary that the structure should be located on the external walls of the building or, pro vided further, that in appropriate cases where the plans are otherwise considered to be adequate fire protection measures than what is required under bye laws 15.4 or 16.8 or 16, the NDMC would not have any claim against it for anyloss occasioned to the respondent. [1015E] 8.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in liquor shops 104 carried on by him was expiring on the 1st April, 1946. The agreement between the parties contained an arbitration clause which provided that the disputes arising out of the agreement shall be referred to arbitration and the decision of the arbitrator shall be final. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the motor business from April 1, 1946, in which he alleged that the compromise was made after due deliberation, that accounts of all family businesses should actually have been taken up to March 31, 1946; that the parties agreed by way of compromise that account of all business will be taken up for March 31 and 1946, that the accounts of the various businesses should be takenup to March 14, 1945, the date of disruption of the joint family status, but the parties did not care to ask that accounts for those businesses subsequent to March 1, 1947. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the cause of action in the two suits was identical and not separate and distinct and that the suit was barred by res judicata. On appeal the High Court held that the decree passed by the trial court was not barred under Order II, rule 2(3), of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court reversed the decision and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were in error in holding that a cause of actions in a suit seeking partition is the desire and intention of the family to separate, that though accounts of various businesses were to be taken into consideration only up to April 14, 1946 they did not specifically mention the 31st March, 1946 and that it was not as if there had been an oversight on the part of the parties but the plaintiff knew that the business might go on afterwards; and that in the subsequent suit he had abandoned his claim to account in respect of 108 the motor businesses after the expiry of the licence. Held: (1) The cause of Action in a case for partition is intended to separate from his brothers and to divide the joint property without any reservation and was compromised, the plaintiff having abandoned his claims to account up to February 31, 1947, only implicitly of not explicitly relinquished his claim for the subsequent period. [657 E] (2) The suit was not governed by Order II Rule 2(1)(a) of the Civil Procedure Code. The cause in a partition suit is the need and intention for the family and not merely to give up to the 31 st March, 1947; but it is also necessary that the plaintiff should have obtained the relief he is seeking, in the partition suit as accounts would have been take of all the businesses up to that date. [757 F] (3) The parties did neither care to call upon the compromise decree for accounts of those businesses being taken after the 1 st April, 1947 and there was force, therefore, in this case it was necessary for the plaintiff to separate his brothers or to divide them by metes and bounds and to award monies as found on examination of the accounts right up to December 31, 1948. [857 F H] (4) The compromise closed once for all the controversy about taking any account of the Joint family business including the motor shop after the 31St March, 1945. If the plaintiff really intended that accounts should be made up after the date on which a final decree for payment of the amount found to be due would have obtained his relief in respect thereof, implicitly, relinquished his claims that he was under a misapprehension regarding his legal right inasmuch as he thought that when the accounts were to take up any account, he did not specially care for providing by the compromise decrees for accounts. [957 F G] (5) The plaintiff by confining his claim only to account upto March 31.

The appellant was a partner in the firm of salt merchants. The appellant was employed as a Manager, Sangu Soap Works, Bombay, without obtaining a licence under section 6 of the Act read with r. 3(1) of the Bombay Salt Works (Control of Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1947. On April 9, 1949, the appellant applied to the Deputy Salt Commissioner for permission to convert sea water into salt in connection with the conversion of sea water frommunicipal water into margal Salt Works situate at Wadala, Bombay without obtaining licence under s. 6 of that Act readwith r. 4(1)(a) of that Rules. The application was rejected by the Deputy Commissioner on the ground that the appellant had not made a suitable representation to the Government of India. On appeal, the High Court held that the process of converting sea water in salt did not amount to "manufacture" within the meaning of the word 'factory ' and as there were no buildings except temporary sheds on the Salt Works, the Salt works could not be said to be a " factory " within the definition of the expression " manufacturing process " in cl. (k) of section 2 of the said Act. The State has appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The word 'premises " in the definition is again a general word which is applicable to both open land and to buildings and its use in this section indicates that the word " factory" is also not restricted in scope to buildings alone. [604 E] 1.2 The word " premises " in s. 2 of Act includes buildings " and its adjuncts ". It is not clear from these observations alone why the slate quarries where work was carried on there came within the purview of the definition. [505 B C] 1:3 The process of conversion of air water intomunicipal salt does not amount either to manufacture or processing or otherwise treating or adapting any article or substance with a view to its use, sale, transport, delivery or disposal is carried on in a building. It may also be mentioned that the words " manufacturing" are used in the Act and they indicate that the activity carried out by the process carried out therein comes within the ambit of the term 'factory' and that no human agency is employed in such conversion. [705 C] 2.4 The word ` factory " does not include buildings alone, but only includes something which is intended to be used for manufacturing purposes. It is also clear from the definition that the expression ' premises " means " building or its adjunct or ancillary work". [606 F G] 1 :5. The word '' factory " in section 2(k) indicates that it is meant building and its accessory. It indicates that there comes within this definition, that the Act can be applied to works carried on by a manufacturing process or not and what was stated was in connection With the word I( manufacture). [605 B] 1.:5. In view of the above, the appeal must fail. [0604 C D] 2:6 The appellant 's Salt Works do come within the expression of opinion by the Chief Inspector of Factories in his letter to the Secretary to Government of Maharashtra, Department of Industries & Supply, dated April 9. 1952, that it was just the force of gravity and the solar energy which (1) [1952] S.C.R.

The respondent was appointed as Tailoring Instructor in the Department of Technical Education at Hassan, Devangere and Chintamani. He was transferred to the Polytechnic at Devangaon as Instructor in October 1949. The respondent was sent on deputation to serve in the Polytechnics at Hassan as Instructor. In 1955 56, he was again posted to work in the department of Technical education with effect from November 28, 1949. On his repatriation to service, he joined the new post on November 28. 1949. He continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were similarly situated, they should also be absorbed in the Departments of Technical Affairs with effectfrom November 28 1949, which was the date on which he initially came on deputation. The Public Service Commission recommended his absorption in the grade of Rs. Narayanaswamy Chetty, whose case was identical in all respects, and six other officers who were identically situated, were absorbed permanently in the Government of Mysore by a notification dated December 12, 1949, made these recommendations in favour of the respondent. The State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service commission who examined it and by a communication, dated February 19, 1964, made those recommendations in his favour. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of absorption. The High Court allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption of the respondents in the Ministry of Technical Development with effect effect from December 28, 1950, would adversely affect even Narayanaswamy Chettiar, who was admittedly junior to him in the parent Department. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent ''s work in that Department was found unsatisfactory or that he was not otherwise suitable or qualified to hold the post of Tailoring Operator in that department. That he was suitable and qualified to be absorbed as Tailor from the date of his appointment as such as has been ordered in the case of Sri K. Narayanaswami Chetty, who is admittedly junior than him in that Ministry. [723C] 1.2 The respondent had no legal right to be appointed in the service of the Department. That the absorption in that post was a concession which could not be claimed as of right and consequently, a writ of mandamus, as prayed for by the respondent, should not be issued. [824D E] 2.1 In the special circumstances of this case, the High court was fully justified in granting the relief, it did, to the appellant, to be given effect from the initial date of joining duty on deputation, and consequently a writ Of mandamus, if prayed by the appellant 's, should be issued to issue. [820D E; 824A] 2:2 The High court has rightly held that the respondent had not legal right or claim to be absorption in service of that Department. [828B] 3.3 In the instant case, there was no justification whatever to depart from this principle of policy in the matter of K.N. Krishna Murthy, who were admittedly junior and were absorbed temporarily in the Public Services Commission with effect From November 28; 1949, would prejudicially affect even N. Krishna Swamy Chetty, which is evident from the recommendation of the Public Commission. [829D E F] 3:3 The respondent did not claim any right to being absorbed in that service of a Department of technical Education from a particular anterior date or to be granted the revised pay scales applicable to those borne permanently in that office. That was the case, where the absorption was made in 1951 and there was a break in the respondent's service, this period having been treated as leave.

The appellant was a minor. The respondent, who was the father of the child, filed an application for guardianship of his child in the court of the District Judge, Calcutta, West Bengal and Gujarat. The District Judge rejected the application on the ground that the appellant had not been appointed guardian of the minor. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had not taken any step to get the order of appointment as guardian of a child in his place and that the High Court had erred in holding that the order passed by the District judge was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The foreign parents who have taken a child from adoption would normally have the child study report with them before they select the child for adoption. [847G] 2.1 In case the Indian family wants to see the child through which an application is made by such social or child welfare agency in India, it must send without undue delay the name and particulars of such child to the recognised social or Child Welfare agency processing the application for its taking into account the welfare of the foreigner and will be able to integrate and assimilate itself in the family and community of the foreigners. [820G] 3.1 A foreign parent who has taken a minor child in adoption would ordinarily have the children available with it for adopt on and if the Indian Family wants to find out the child in adopting such child, the same should be supplied to them by the recognised Social or child Welfare agency in country where the foreigner is ordinarily taken in adoption. The social or family welfare agency sponsoring the application of its national for taking an Indian child in Adoption would normally has the child Study report with it before they selected the child. [822G] 4.2 In case there are more than one social or children welfare agencies, but every such social and child welfare Agency must also undertake while forwarding the application to the social or Children welfare agency processing its application for adoption and after examining the home study report, they would be ableto gather information as to who are the biological parents of the person concerned. [828G] 5.3 The Indian Council of Social Welfare of the Indian Council for Social Welfare should also undertake whilst forwarding the applications to the Social or Child welfare agency, that it will ensure adoption of the children by the foreigner according to the law of his country within a period not exceeding two years and as soon as the adoption is effected, it will send one certified copy of the adoption order to the appropriate department of the Government of India where Indian children are ordinarily taken into adoption. If any foreign parent wants to get warmth and affection of family life as also moral and material stability and security and whether it will be in the interest of the juvenile and will also be able To gather information from such child before he select the foreigner for adoption, the court should not make an order for appointment of a foreigner as guardian unless it is satisfied that the application has been sponsored by such Social or Family Welfare agency. [829G] 6.4 The Indian Law Council of Child Welfare to which notice is issued by the court would have to scrutinise the application so that the court may be able lo satisfy itself whether the application should be for the welfare and welfare of a minor, child study reports with them after examining and considering the home Study report as also documents and certificates forwarded by the sponsoring social or school welfare agency processed the application. [827G] 7.5 The Indian Legal Service (Regulation) Act, 1986 is not applicable to the foreign parents in India.

The appellant, Indian Cable Company Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the 'Company') was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The Company had its factory at Calcutta. On April 1, 1966, the Central Government by order dated June 23, 1967 directed the Company to pay bonus for the accounting year 1965 66. The appellant company filed an application before the Tribunal claiming that the amount of Rs. 65,764 was not payable to it under section 6 and 7 of the Act. The Tribunal rejected this claim of the Union on the ground that the payment of compensation to induce the workmen to retire prematurely was an item of expenditure incurred by the Company on the basis of its judgment in Metal Box Co. Ltd. vs Their Workmen.(1) It held that the principle adopted by the Tribunal in respect of direct tax is erroneous and that the principles adopted by it are contrary to the decisions of this Court. The High Court, however, allowed the Union 's appeal and directed the surplus amount of bonus payable for the year 1965 67 on the grounds which had not been accepted by the Income tax Officer, the Company can claim depreciation only in the sum of Rs 65, 764 on the footing that his salary is only Rs. The Union preferred an appeal to this Court against the decision of the Tribunal directing reinstatement of the employee on grounds which have not been taken notice of by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The principle adopted in Metal box Co. of India Ltd. etc. vs Its Workmen(2) is that the method of computation of the gross profits has to be worked out by first working out the gross profit and deducting therefrom the prior charges under section6, but not the bonus payable to the employees. [723C] 1.2 The Tribunal was justified in rejecting this claim. [761D] 2.3 The Tribunal had rejected this contention of the Unions on the view that the sum which is granted can subjected to scrutiny. [758E] 3.4 In the original calculation filed by the company, it calculated tax only in respect the direct tax and therefore the recomputation of the available surplus will have to be made after making a calculation of directtax without deducting bonus payable under section 37(1) of the Income Tax Act. [759D] 4. The claim of Union was that Rs.65,7604 has not been declared for the purpose of computing the available and allocable surplus. It is clear from his evidence that bon us at 20% could not have been declared as for the next year, namely, 1965 66 on the assumption that his wages are only Rs.. The Tribunal did not accept this contention. [763D] 5.1 In the present case, it is clear that bon we at 20%, which implies that the mode of computation adopted by Tribunal in regard to direct tax was found to be erroneous by this Court, can subjected either scrutiny or adjustment.

The appellant was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1954, and thereafter as a Joint Commercial Tax Officer in 1962. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. The Government accepted the report of the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption. The Full Board of Revenue then reported that the charges could be dropped. The appellant filed an application before the High Court challenging the order of the Government retiring him from service on the ground that he had outlived his utility as a Govt. servant in the public interest after he had attained the age of SO years or after he has completed 25 years of qualifying service. The High Court dismissed the petition, but allowed the appeal and directed the appellant to reinstate him in service with all consequential benefits. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the respondent including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80 We do not think that the previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored, once he is promoted as Deputy Director. The question whether the earlier history of an employee should be totally ignored, when he is found to possess 'such high merit and ability, which naturally include integrity, as to entitle him not merely to be promoted to a selection post but to be appointed to a very responsible and much desired post in that cadre, what could have happened between May and September was also not noted in the personal file of the petitioner. The learned Counsel for the State of Tamil Nadu argued that the earlier period of service should be taken into consideration while considering the question whether there was any ambiguity about the effect of the order dated November 29, 1974 of the A Government retiring the appellant from service. It was further contended on his behalf that the promotion of the respondents to a Selection post is bound to perplex any right thinking man and make him wonder whether the right hand knows what the left hand has done. The State of Andhra Pradesh argued that there was no ambiguity about this effect in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, it being indeed odd to retire a Government Servant a few months after promoting him to aselection post. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The previous history shows that an enquiry was pending with the Vigilance and anti Corruption Department in regard to the allegations against the appellant just a few month earlier and nothing even mildly suggestive of ineptitude or inefficiency thereafter, it is indeed odd that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. [80G] 1.2 The previous year of service was blotted out by the promotion from the post of Deputy Commissioner. There was an adverse entry in the confidential file of a Govt servant which naturally includes integrity as to enable him not only to be retired but also to be posted to a higher post. It is indeed difficult to sustain the order passed by the Government dismissing the appellant for absence from duty. [81B] 1:3 The previous period of Service should be entirely ignored, if it was prior before his promotion. [82C] 2.4 The previous service of a government servant should ordinarily include integrity as a Lower Division Clerk in the Public Works Department. If there is nothing in the conduct casting an doubt on his wisdom, the promotion would hark back to similar or like entries in the past, read them all in conjunction and conclude that the period had arrived at for the Govt servant to terminate Government service and he was entitled not merelyto be promoted but also a few days after promoting the appellant as Deputy Superintendent. [83D] 2:5 The previous record of the applicant shows that the enquiry was going on with the vigilance and AntiCorruption Department in respect of certain allegations and this was sufficient to proceed against Thiru D.

The appellants were the owners of a bus bearing No. A.P. 47/63 and they had been plying their buses on the routes in question. The Corporation issued a notification under section 68D of the Act for nationalisation of the buses in Andhra Pradesh. The appellants challenged the validity of the said notification before the High Court which dismissed them. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the scheme framed by the Corporation could not be challenged as not in conformity with the requirements of section 68 C and the Rules made thereunder, and that the schemes framed and approved were fully in conformity therewith. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The scheme framed and sanctioned by the Chief Minister at this Conference did not originate from the Corporation as required by section 68C of the , but only the provisions of that Chapter which are to have effect notwithstanding anything in any other law for the time being in force. [776F] 1.2 The scheme was intended to be implemented by the State Transport Undertaking and the procedure laid down therein were to have force notwithstanding anything contained in section 68A or section 68B of the . [778G H; 782C D] 1:3.1 In view of our conclusion that the Schemes now impugned were fully complied with, the schemes now impugned could not have been challenged as invalid by law. [77D E] 2.2 It is true that in Andhra Nadu there was no Regional Transport Authority at all at all [vide e.g. proviso to section 44(1) merely because the Regional Transport authority of that area cannot grant permits under Ch. In view Of our conclusion, it would be necessary to give a short resume of the history of nationalised transport in Andhra State as well as certain events in Andhra Prades and the routes therein to be nationalised in the first instance. [773G H] 2:3 The scheme now impugned was formulated by the Government not at the dictation of the Chief Ministers expressed there, but as a result of their own independent judgment; and so long as the choice of Kurnool was made by them alone, it could not grant permits to ply their buses in the three schemes which were published by them. [777C D; 785A] 2(a) The scheme then impugned was framed by way of resolution dated April 4, 1962 and in order to give effect to the wishes of the Corporation, that brought about this change in the order of the districts to be taken up for nationalisation and not the independent opinion of the corporation as to what was needed in the public interest as required under section68 C. [779D] 2.(b) The schemes now framed by it were to be adopted in every case where there is no Regional transport Authority at All India, the State will compensate the appellants for the loss incurred by them during the period that the appeals were pending in this Court by reason of the fact that they were not allowed to ply buses on routes under the respective permits granted to them by the Regional transport authority. [780C D].

The appellant was a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Act having its registered place of business at Calcutta. Under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1941, the appellant in order to claim exemption thereunder had to furnish declaration forms duly filled in and ' signed by registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. The assessee made several attempts to get duplicate forms for all the declarations that were lost. On November 21, 1957, the Commercial Tax Officer made an order of assessment disallowing the assessee 's claim for exemption in respect of the said sales made to the purchasing dealer amounting to Rs. 1,20,000. The only question which arises is whether under section 5 (2)(b) of Orissa Sales tax Act, 1947, the furnishing of the declaration forms by the purchasing dealers was a condition for claiming the exemption thereunder. Held, that the proviso to the said sub clause does not give any guide for amending the relevant provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder, but only to be made if a demand is made by the authority concerned. The proviso to section 5 makes it clear that the condition is mandatory and only to being made if an demand is raised by the dealer and r. 27A with those of section 5 of the Rules. That proviso does not provide for any guide or amending the provisions of section 8 of the Central Sales Tax Rules, 1956. It merely provides that the person claiming the benefit shall furnish a declaration form in the manner prescribed under the section. The language of the proviso is clear and unambiguous. If so construed, a dealer is not precluded from producing other relevant evidence to prove that the sales to the registered dealers were for the purposes mentioned therein. That is why it is substantially compiled with.

The petitioners were convicted by the Additional Sessions Judge, Patna Central in connection with a case under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The State filed an application before the Magistrate praying that the under trial prisoners whose names and particulars are given in the list filed by Mrs. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the provisions of the proviso to section 167(2) were complied with, inasmuch as the petitioners had not been arrested within three weeks from the date of their arrest and therefore they could not be released on bail. The Magistrate rejected the application and directed the State Government to furnish particulars to the court by a proper affidavit to be filed within two weeks from today whether the under trail prisoners whose particulars were given in his counter affidavit in response to this direction was periodically produced before the Magistrates or the Sessions Courts, as the case may be, provided that no objection is raised to such lawyer on their behalf and if any application for bail is made, the Magistrate should dispose of the same in accordance with the broad guidelines indicated by us in our judgment dated 12th February, 1979. The petitioners filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the validity of the provisions contained in section 167 (2) and section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the proviso was complied with. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 167(1) is not mandatory and it is only if the accused has been arrested and detained in custody for more than six months, the State can furnish him within three days from today particulars as to the location of the courts of magistrates and courts of sessions in the State of Bihar together with the total number of cases pending in each of these courts as on 31st December, 1978 giving yearwise breakup of such pending cases and also explaining why it has not been possible to dispose of such of those cases as have been pending investigation for morethan six months. [520E] 1.2 The State is under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. It is only when these particulas are furnished to us that we can satisfy ourselves in regard to compliance with the requirement of the Proviso to section167(2), and we woudl request the High Court of Patna to pick out a few names from the lists of under trial prisoner which have been filed before the courts as required by the proviso. [620B] 1:3 The State has not furnished to this court the dates on which these under trial Prisoners were remanded from time to time by the Magistrates, the state Government should provide them a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application for Bail and opposing remand provided that any application made for bail shall be disposed of by the Magistrate in accordancewith the broad principles indicated by this Court in our earlier judgment dated 26th February 1979. [720C] 1.:4. The proviso to Section 167 (1) provides that no objections are raised to the lawyer on behalf o such under trial Prison prisoners and if such applications for bail are made, he shall furnish them within three months from today details as to whether they have been periodically remanded fromtime to time or not. [820D] 1 :5. The provisions of section 167 are mandatory in nature and it has no application in regard thereto. [820C] 2.6 Section 167 is a provision which provides for the punishment to be awarded to an accused. It does not provide that any objection is made to such advocate on their own behalf and, if any such application for release is made the Magistrate shall dispose of his application within three week from today.

The appellant was the landlord and the respondent a protected tenant. The appellant filed an application under article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. In the meantime, an amendment was made to the Act by the insertion of sub section (2 A) to section 34 by the Amending Act. The relevant part of sub s.(2A) is in these terms: "If the landlord bona fide requires the land for any of the purposes specified in sub section(1) then his right to terminate the tenancy shall be subject to the following conditions, namely (i) The land held by the landlord is in area equal to the agricultural holding or less; and (ii) If the land held is more than the agricultural holdings in area, the right of the landlord to terminate tenancy of the protected tenant shall be limited to an area which shall, after such termination, leave with the tenant half the area of the lands leased. The High Court allowed the application of the appellant holding that as the tenancy had (1) 571 terminated and the right to obtain possession of land was perfected, the amendment did not affect notices already given. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the notice under section 34(2A), introduced by the amending Act came into force, and therefore the landlord could not be entitled to possession. HELD: (1)(a) The right to termination a tenancy having arisen when the notice was given, the law existing on the date of notice will have to be taken into consideration in determining the right in the matter of the termination of tenancy for the Amending act put certain fetters on this right of termination. [775 D] (2A)(a). The right of landlord to cancel the tenancy is an absolute right and it cannot be said that the tenant has acquired a vested right to get possession of his land. [761 G] (b) The notice having been given before the Amending, Act came in force, the further limitation put on the right by subs.(2 A), introduced in the present case would not apply to notices already issued. It is only when the period of notice has expired and the tenancy has terminated that the landlord acquires a vested rights to obtain Possession of the property.

The petitioners are the other son and two of his daughters. They were evacuees and their properties, being the two houses in dispute, to be evacuee property. Nusrat Ali was evacueed from Pakistan. He died on or about October 1, 1950 leaving three sons and five daughters, who thereupon became entitled to them in certain shares. Numrat Ali filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of January 10, 1952, declaring two houses to be evacueies and their property being the one house in dispute. The Custodian General dismissed the petition on the sole ground that it bad been filed beyond the time prescribed for it. On appeal by the male petitioner against the order dismissing his appeal, the Custodian General held that Nusarat Ali was not a patty to the proceeding in which the order in dispute had been made. He also took possession of the properties and dismissed them. The petitioners then moved this Court by the present petition under Article 32 of the constitution for quashing of the order dated January 10 1952, and for setting aside the order. HELD: (1) The Custodian was entitled to declare the entirety of the two house evacuee property and deprive the petitioners of their rights in them. [723 C] (2) The provisions of section 12 of this Act are not applicable to a case where the order made under section 7 of the Act is without jurisdiction so far as it affected the rights of an evacuee which the petitioners, on the admitted facts, were not concerned, their interest could not in any way be affected by the order passed under section 8 of the , [724 D] (3) The petitioners had no longer, any claim to them. They had, no longer. any claim for them. It was also contended that so far the female petitioners were concerned, his interest in the two Houses never vested in the Custodian. [761 E F] (4) The order of December 10, 1951, was without jurisdiction inasmuch as it did not decide any question as to the right of Zafar Ali to the houses for, it was dismissed on the ground that the male petitioners had not been given a notice under section7 of the .

The assessee Company had two Departments (1) for spinning of yarn from raw and waste wool and (2) for weaving of yarn tops. ' The assessee Company agreed to a deduction of 50% of the loss incurred by the assessee Company from their remuneration. The assessee company entered into a joint venture for distribution of profit between the assesseeCompany and the selling agents after being ascertained between themselves and that is why there was an express provision in the agreement by which the agents agreed to share losses to the extent of 50%. The assessee contended that the agreement amounted to a joint Venture for the distribution of profits between the appellant Company and the marketing agents after the profits were ascertained. Held, that the agreements did not amount to a Joint venture but it was clearly pointed out in the judgment that there is a very thin line of distinction between a contract for payment of a share of profits simpliciter and a payment of remuneration which is deductible in truth from the profits divisible. The High Court had exceeded its jurisdiction in travelling beyond the agreed statement of the case framed by the Tribunal and had relied on certain materials which were not at all found by the tribunal in its order nor were those materials mentioned in the statement of case. The Tribunal was right in holding that the cumulative effect of the interpretation of the various clauses of the agreement dated October 20, 1955 clearly revealed that in the garb of an agency the parties entered into an agreement for payment Of a share profits simpliciter, after being ascertainment between themselves, and that was why there is no express provision therein indicating that it was not incurred by him in the character of trader or it is not laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business. The conclusion reached by the High Court that the payments in question were not expenses incurred for the purposes of the trade or it was only a mere fact that the agents agree to share the losses would not take the case of the assessee beyond the ambit of section 10(2)(xv) of the Act in order to show that the payment made to the agents was not expenditure incurred for carrying on the business of the appellant and to disallow it. The appeal is allowed, the judgment of the High court is set aside and that of the Tribunal is restored.

The assessee company was a non applicant. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, in second appeal, held that the accumulated profits were not included within the accumulated profit of the company and therefore the second question referred to the High Court was answered in favour of the assessee. In appeal by certificate under section 261 of the Income tax Act, 1961, the High court held that since the accumulated losses had been taken prior to the accounting year of which the income profits were being assessed, while current profit would mean the profits of the accounting years in which the loans were advanced to the assessee, that is to say the current profits, and therefore, the second questions referred to it were not liable to be included within section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Appellate Tribunal was right in holding that the assessee was entitled to apply to the Appellate Court for a reference of those questions of law which arose on its submission negatived in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were not competent to refer the second two questions of fact which arise on its submissions negatived in favour, and that the Appellate Tribunals were not legally correct in holding the accumulated income for the purpose of section 2 (6A) of Income Tax. Held: (i) The expression "accumulated profits" in section 2 means profits which have accumulated prior to accounting year. In every case, it is only the party applying for a refer application who is entitled to specify the questions of question of law arising on its behalf negatived in appeals by the appellate Tribunal. [951 E F G] (ii) The word "accompurability" in that clause must mean profits which has accumulated prior thereto the accounting period of which it can be taken into account when determining the accumulated Profits as on March 31, 1958 is not relate to the question whether accumulated profits can take in current profits. [950 A B] (iii) The words "accorded profits" used in section 3(6)(e), must mean profit which has accrued prior to its accounting year and current profit will mean the income of the business during that period. If the application is rejected by the Income Tax Officer, it becomes open to the non applicant who is not aggrieved by the result of the appeal, to ask for a Reference of those question of Law also which arise in future profits.

The respondents were tenants of the lands in question. The suit lands were originally comprised in Mouza Nala forming part of the permanently settled estate of Burdwan, and were Mal lands assessed to revenue, and that more than 200 years previously there had been a permanent Mokarrari grant of those lands by the Maharaja of Burdwan to the Rajgunj Asthal. The defendants claimed to have dealt with the properties as owners under assertion of an adverse title. The trial court held that the documents on which the defendants claimed were not proved to relate to the suit lands, that the relationship subsisting between the parties was one of landlord and tenant, that they did not form part of their Mal or assessed lands of the estate, that no decree in ejectment could be passed but, that there had never been a determination of tenancy, that as there had already been a temporary Moktarari grant, the claim of the plaintiff was barred by reason of article 131 of the Limitation Act. The High Court held that as the defendants and their predecessors had been in possession of the land for over 200 years under an Lakheraj grant, they were not entitled to fair rent on the holdings in their possession. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the document relied on by the respondents as containing assertions that they held under a Lakheaj grant, and, therefore, they could be said to have been validly recorded as tenants free from any encumbrance or charge on the lands, and the suit properties formed part of Mauza Nala within the zamindari of Burdwan. Held, that in the view that there was no presumption of a lost grant could be made in favour of the predecessors of the defendants, it was sufficient to sustain a presumption of lost grant. The document relied upon by the defendants as containing allegations that they were holding under a SUIT of title without challenge, and there is no discussion of it in the judgments of the Courts below.

The appellant was the owner of land admeasuring 45 acres 5 gunthas bearing Survey No. 25 situated in Sholapur Mouje Dongaon in Maharashtra State for a consideration of Rs. 42,000/ out of which Rs. 5,000/- were paid as earnest money and a further amount of Rs, 5, 000/ were paid by him as earnest price and a sum of Rs 5,500/ was paid as advance. The trial Court held that the plaintiff was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Tenancy Act and therefore ineligible to purchase the land in view of the bar imposed by section 63 of the Bombay Tenancy Act. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the trial Court and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to settle, decide or deal with any question which arises under the Tenancy law would alone be barred under section 85A of the said Tenancy Act because the issue is not required to be decided or dealt with under the Land Revenue Code. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that it being an incidental issue in a properly constituted civil suit cognizable by the Civil Courts, it will have jurisdiction to decide or dispose of the suit in accordance with the decision of the competent authority under the said Act. [520E] 2. Section 85A bars the jurisdiction and power of the civil Court to decide any question arising in a proper proceeding before a civil court having jurisdiction to settle decide or dealt With by the competent authorities under the tenancy Act, even if it arises in an incidental manner in a civil suit, cognizable by a Civil Court, it would be no answer to the provisions to say that if upon assertion and denial and consequent contest an issue arises in the context of the provisions of the Land revenue Code, then notwithstanding the fact that such an issue arose in a duly constituted civil Suit cognizable by that court, it shall have to be referred to the competent Authority under the Mamlatdar Act. If section 85B imposes an obligation on the civil court to refer such issue to the appropriate authority under that Act, it is incumbent upon the Civil court to decide the same and upon the reference being answered back, to dispose of it in accordancewith the decision rendered by the Competent Authority under that jurisdiction. [620G] 3. The words "any issues which are required tobe settled, decided or deal" in section 85 A would only mean that if after assertion and denied and consequent litigation an issue arise in a revenue suit cognizable before a Civil court having Jurisdiction to entertain the same, it should be referred C.A. No. 39/66 filed by the appellant against the order passed by the Mamlatdar under the Revenue Act. The jurisdiction of civil Court is ousted because the issues are not required C. A. No.. 39/ 66 filed by him in a competent court under the Bombay Land Revenue Act, 1948, and he has no jurisdiction to deal with such issues. [720G H] 4. Section 84A bars a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of agricultural land governed by the Tenancy Law Act, but it does not bar the jurisdiction or power of civil court in respect of any question that arises in a matter which is required to have been settled, decide and deal with the same. [820G D] 5. Section85A bars an issue arising under the provisions contained in section 84A, imposing an obligation upon the civil courts to refer any issue to a competent authority for deciding or dealwith such issues under the Act, whether such issue arises within a properly appointed civil suit before a criminal court having competent jurisdiction to entertain it. [820G H; 820F] 6.

The assessee company was a textile mill. The assessee company had been carrying on the business of heavy engineering. It was engaged in the manufacture of certain articles and it was registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The company was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1958 59 (calendar year 1957) and 1959 60 (calender year 1958). The Income tax Officer held that the assessee company is an industrial undertaking to which section 15C of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 applied. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on the above facts held that since the articles produced by the two undertakings were used by the Boiler Division of the assessee 's business already in existence, namely, the business already existing and hence the assessee was not entitled (1) 765 to exemption under section 15 C(2) as rightly so held by the High Court. The Income Tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant commissioner on the other hand held that there is no bar to an assessee carrying on a particular business to set up a new industrial undertaking on account of which exemption of tax under section15C can be claimed. On appeal, the Tribunal held that in view of the provisions contained in section 15B(2), the assessee is not entitled to exemption from income tax under Section 15C. The High Court allowed the appeals and held that as expansion and reconstruction of the business was only ancillary activity to the main business of the appellant, there 770 must be a new emergence of a physically separate industrial unit which may exist on its own as a viable unit. Allowing the appeal by certificate, this Court, HELD : 1.1 The assessee is carrying on an industry to setup a new Industrial undertaking on the basis of which he can claim exemption under Section15C. [776F] 2.2 The fact that an assessee by establishment of a new factory expands his existing business, which he does, would not, on that score, deprive him of the benefit under section 14C if that section is otherwise applicable. [771B] 3. In order that the new industrial undertakings are formed out of the already existing business of building machinery, that undertaking will not be denied the benefit of section 15A. The fact of the case that an employee by establishment thereof expansion or reconstruction of a business already set up cannot lead to the aid of the Income tax Act. [761C] 4. In view of this decision, the High court is right in answering the two questions in the negative and against the assessee. [782D] 5. The facts that an industrial concern expands its existing business will not weigh against holding that these are new and separate undertakings. Use of the articles by the assessee will not prevent him from setting up new industrial unit on account Of which exemption granted under section 17C may be claimed, if that Section is otherwise inapplicable.

The inam lands were granted to the inamdars for performance of services connected with the temple and were within the purview of section 44 B(2)(a)(i). The inamdars claimed title to the lands under a grant from the inamdar on the footing that the inam lands belonged to them. The District Judge held that the inams were personal Inams burdened with service and that, in any event, the claim of adverse possession was not established. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the right to resume an inam could not be extinguished by adverse possession, and that the suit was barred by limitation. HELD: (1) The right of resumption could be so extinguished if it was within the ambit of section44 B(3)(a). [696 H] (2) The rights of resumption were extinguished by a adverse possession of the lands after resuming the melwaram rights. The inamdar cannot acquire prescriptive title to his kudiwaram right against the Government and thereby defeat the latter 's right to resumption. [697 A B] (3) The alienation was within section 44B(2). The right to resumed an inam does not, therefore, arise for decision. [796 C D] (4) The inam lands are resumable under section 44A(2) (a)(ii), though the alienations were made before 1934. [76 E F] (5) The grant was within a purview of Section 44 B (2).

The appellant Corporation was a charitable trust. The Indore Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909 and the rules framed thereunder on the basis of the gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The Municipal tax levied under the old Act and the Rules framed thereunder were in force during the years in question made the entries in the assessment list so authenticated. The Corporation was assessed to the tax at the rate of 7% of the annual letting Value less 10%. The appellant Corporation challenged the validity of the levy on the ground that it was not bound to deduct 10% allowance provided by sec. 2(c) and therefore the rate could be treated as conclusive evidence for the purposes of all municipal taxes of the valuation or annual lettingvalue less 10%, as also for the amount of tax leviable on such buildings or lands. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that under the 1954 Act the Municipality had imposed the tax on houses at the rates of 7%. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Municipal taxes levied under old Act are obviously inconsistent with sec. 73 and that saving coupled with the fact that the assessment lists prepared for 1952 53 were in operation during the year, made the entry in the list so adopted conclusive evidence of theannual letting value and the amount thereof entitled the Corporation to collect the tax assessed on the gross monthly letting value. [76 D] 1.2 The Municipal Tax Officer had imposed a tax on buildings at the maximum rate of 10% of their gross annual rent. [77 E F] 1:3 The Municipal Taxes Act, 1950 was an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and the assessment List on the assumption that the Municipality has been levying tax at a higher rate on the net and not the gross Annual letting value of buildings or land or both in any official year in which such list is in force. [78 E] 1 :4. The Municipality was entitled to adopt the assessmentlist prepared for the years 1952 53 for the two assessment years, 1953 54 and 1954 55. [79 F] 2.1 In the instant case the Municipal tax was levied on houses situated in Indore City. Therefore, it could be deemed to have been so made in so far as it is consistent with secs. 73, that is, if it was assessed on net and no gross annual let value after deducting 10% Statutory allowance in respect of costs for repairs or any other accounts whatsoever. 76 lays down that such assessment list when authenticated becomes conclusive evidence regarding the amount payable to the buildings or properties. [80 E] 2:2 The Municipality has not adopted the said list for 195253 nor has it adopted the same standard for the purpose of all Municipal taxes of Delhi. Therefore the rate at which the tax was assessed was saved and could not be challenged.

The assessee Company was incorporated in 1937 and it had been wound up by the Deputy Commissioner, who held that the business had not 964 completely ceased to exist, since the assessee Company had been winding up. The Income tax Appellate Tribunal held that there was no profit other than what results from the appreciation of capital. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sale was of the entire assets and that the sum obtained by way of realisation sale and was only by way Of realisation sale, and that therefore the excess represented a revenue sale and that there could be said to be a realisation sale after the Company had become wound up. HELD : (1) The assessee Company is carrying on business in manufacturing and selling chemicals and raw materials for match manufacture. [328G H] (2) The transaction was not during the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the business, but was for the purposes of putting an end to the business. It was only for the business of manufacturing and sale of companies, that the amount obtained was by way o realisation sale. [334C] (3) The sales were not part of the realisation of the trading stock and winding up of the company. There was no evidence that the assessee company was carrying on a trading busi ness. That the business was sold as a going concern, and was, in fact, worked by the assessee on behalf o the buyer till the entire consideration was paid, makes no difference because the agreement clearly indicated that the, assessee Company would be keeping the factory going, not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf. [435D] (4) The sale was only of the whole assets, and the balance of a slump price, which, with an under taking to discharge liabilities, formed the consideration, was inferentially attributable to the stock. [413F] (5) The transactions were not in the ordinary course of trade but were part of realisation of trading stock. It could not be said that there is a profit other from what results therefrom. [414G H; 414A] (6) The High Court was right in holding that there can be said, no identifiable price for the chemicals and Raw materials except by comparing the two prices offered to be paid by the buyer, that is to say, the price without the chemicals, raw material and the price with them. [ 414B C] (7) The question whether there is profit other or not was a mixed question of law and fact.
